News.title: Healey faces £35bn hole to fund higher defence spending over Iran war, experts warn
News.content:
Next

JOHN Healey is facing a £35 billion headache to fund higher defence spending and avoid sweeping Whitehall cuts, leading experts warn.

The Chancellor has been dealt a pre-Budget blow of having to hike taxes or cut benefits just to protect public services.

The Middle East conflict has caused an inflation spiral which is eating away at departments’ spending power and pushing up benefits costs.

It comes as Mr Healey last night warned that major economies need a credible plan to get borrowing under control, ahead of his visit to the IMF in Bangkok this week.





But Helen Miller, director at Institute for Fiscal Studies, says that if he opts to squeeze spending the plans must be credible or the Budget faces being a “work of fiction“.

A “steady-as-she-goes Budget” is not an option available to him, she adds.

Miller added that sticking with inherited tax and spending plans would allow “inflation to blow departments’ spending plans off course”.

She warned: “It would be a choice to tolerate chunky cuts to the quantity or quality of some public services – cuts that would be larger if defence spending was increased within existing totals.”



But she adds: “Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the Budget a work of fiction.”

The Treasury could be forced to find £25 billion extra for day-to-day spending to avoid brutal cuts, the IFS pre-Budget study shows.

Ambitions for military spending of 3 per cent of GDP by 2030 would cost a further £11 billion by the start of the next decade, they add.

Ministers have committed to spending 3.5 per cent by 2035 and will use the Spending Review next year to set out a path to the 3 per cent target.



Both PM Andy Burnham and Mr Healey have both said they want to reduce the benefits bill – but have yet to set out any definitive timeline.

The warning shot from the IFS comes just over two weeks before Mr Healey delivers his first Budget on October 28.

Mr Healey has previously said that he wants it to offer “breathing space” to both households and to business.

But the body adds that any significant additional day-to-day spending should be met through tax hikes or spending cuts – rather than increased borrowing.

Figures show the debt interest bill has more than DOUBLED since 2019 – now making up £1 in every £13 that Ministers spend.



Mr Healey, speaking ahead of his IMF visit to Bangkok this week, said G7 nations need credible plans to get borrowing costs under control.

He said that “Britain and our allies can face up to these challenges together”

He added: “My Budget will build on this approach with fiscal discipline helping to deliver economic resilience. This means breathing space for today, and hope for the future.”

The Chancellor’s financial buffer could be around £20 billion due to the higher inflation as it boosts tax revenues.

However, the IFS warn that the Budget watchdog could alter this figure by as much as £10 billion depending on issues such as employment, migration and health-related benefits.



Higher inflation has also contributed to higher bond yields which has led to increased government borrowing.

Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith said: “Higher borrowing costs and Andy Burnham’s unfunded spending commitments have swallowed up his headroom and created upward inflationary pressure.

“Labour raised taxes by £66 billion in its first two Budgets. Families cannot afford to be lumbered with even more tax rises at this Budget.

“Labour should cut welfare instead of dumping on working people as they have already done.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Mr Healey is bound by Labour’s manifesto on tax-raising measures which prevents him from hiking income tax, national insurance and VAT.



A Treasury spokesperson last night said: “The Chancellor is fully focused on his priorities to boost business, help with the cost of living and support people in every postcode, underpinned by fiscal discipline and a commitment to meet the fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty.”

News.title: Woman, 45, burns to death in electric car after vehicle crashes into tree & sets on fire in Germany
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

TRAGIC END Woman, 45, burns to death in electric car after vehicle crashes into tree & sets on fire in Germany







Next

A WOMAN has tragically burnt to death in Germany after her electric vehicle hit a tree and burst into flames.

The 45-year-old driver from Wolfsberg died after becoming trapped in the burning car in Lower Saxony.



It is understood the accident occurred around 8.30am on Sunday morning.

She tragically died at the scene.



A police spokeswoman told BILD: “The driver was in a Volkswagen ID.7 electric car .

“Why she crashed into a tree at around 8:20 a.m. is still the subject of our investigation.”

According to initial police findings, the electric vehicle was the only vehicle involved in the accident.

For reasons still unknown, it veered off the road to the right while traveling northbound, crashed head-on into a tree, and caught fire.

The plume of smoke was reportedly visible from afar.

Tobias Nadjib, head of the district fire department’s press office, said: “This is a tragic incident for us because a person has lost thier life.”



Last year, a driver burnt to death after he failed to escape his burning cart following a high-speed crash in China.

Footage of the terrifying blaze captured the Xiaomi SU7 ablaze on a rain-slicked road in Chengdu, Sichuan.

Rescuers could be seen tugging helplessly at its locked doors, punching, kicking and looking through the windows in vain while flames engulfed the vehicle.

Police said the driver, a 31-year-old man surnamed Deng, was suspected of driving under the influence when he collided with another vehicle.

Despite frantic efforts rescuers couldn’t reach Deng before the fire consumed the car.



Similar tragedies have struck Germany, Canada and the US, where crashes have left victims trapped inside burning electric cars after power failures disabled the doors.

In Germany, a man and two children died when rescuers couldn’t work the Tesla’s retractable handles.

In California, 19-year-old student Krysta Tsukahara died in a Cybertruck inferno after she couldn’t locate the manual override “in the smoke and chaos,” her parents claimed in a lawsuit.

News.title: Student ‘drug dealer’ charged after thieves ‘cut 4 paintings worth £8million out of frames’ from Renoir Museum in France
News.content:
CANVAS OF 'CRIME' Student ‘drug dealer’ charged after thieves ‘cut 4 paintings worth £8million out of frames’ from Renoir Museum in France







Next

A STUDENT “drug dealer” has been charged after paintings worth £8million were stolen from a museum in the south of France.

The artworks were taken in a bungled burglary that allegedly saw thieves crudely cut four precious paintings from their frames then dump two of them in the garden.



Cops have arrested six people in connection with the Cagnes-sur-Mer art heist, charging one man who had previously been banged up on suspicion of selling drugs as a student in 2020.

Investigating sources called the crew thought to be behind the thefts an “organised, professional team”.





Some members of the suspected Renoir art heist gang were already known to cops in connection with other crimes.

Two of the crew allegedly targeted the Musée Renoir. Another suspect placed under arrest is said to have acted as a fence to try and pass the stolen works off on the black market.

Police have yet to reveal the roles of the three other people arrested in connection with the heist.

The only suspect to be named is Loïc, 29, who has been placed under formal investigation – the equivalent to being charged in the French legal system – for his alleged role in the robbery.



He was arrested on suspicion of dealing drugs while studying in Nice six years ago, but was released after two years of pre-trial detention on a technicality.

Loïc’s lawyer Jean-Denis Flori, said: “According to the investigators, he played a central part in the museum burglary.”

Thieves are thought to have fled the scene at pace when police arrived minutes after the burglars broke in.

Pursued by a canine cop, the suspects allegedly made a hasty exit and had to dump two of the paintings – Portrait of Madame Pichon and Coco lisant (Coco reading).

But they managed to make off with Madame Colonna Romano and Jeune femme au puits (Young woman at the well).



Loïc was allegedly identified after his DNA was discovered on wrapping that had been used to cover up the abandoned paintings.

Flori said: “The burglars then allegedly drove into the backcountry in a stolen vehicle which they had used for the robbery, abandoned it and retrieved their own vehicle.”

But police had placed a tracker on the vehicle for separate operation and were able to track the suspects down.

They recovered the works earlier this week.

Rassemblement National Mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer Masson said: “Their recovery is a tremendous relief for the people of Cagnes-sur-Mer and for everyone who cares deeply about our museum.”



He said on the day of the theft: “Spotted thanks to the town’s video surveillance cameras, the two individuals fled, abandoning one of the stolen paintings as they ran.”

The mayor said the thieves “knew exactly what they were doing” and were “equipped with an electric knife and a metal saw” to cut through the fence and a painting.

He said the burglars were wearing helmets, gloves and camouflage.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Masson added: “The museum alarm went off at 5.48 am. At 5.53 am, just five minutes later, our municipal police were on the scene.”

Loïc is set to face trial for drugs charges next year.

News.title: Man in his 30s dies after falling from multi-storey car park in busy city centre – as cops probe tragedy
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

TRAGIC PLUNGE Man in his 30s dies after falling from multi-storey car park in busy city centre – as cops probe tragedy







Next

A MAN has tragically died after falling from a multi-storey car park in a busy city centre.

The victim, aged in his 30s, suffered serious injuries after plunging from the building in Liverpool, Merseyside, yesterday evening.



Officers rushed to the ParkBee car park at around 8.45pm following reports a man had fallen from the property.

North West Ambulance Service paramedics discovered him with serious injuries, Merseyside Police said.



However, despite the best efforts of medical crews, the man was tragically pronounced dead shortly after.

His death is not currently being treated as suspicious.



The victim’s next of kin have been informed, the force added.

A Home Office post-mortem investigation will be carried out to establish his cause of death.

Officers have cordoned off the car park, which remains closed as enquiries are ongoing.

Drivers have reportedly been told they may not be able to access their parked cars until tomorrow.

News.title: Innocent dad arrested for rape more than 20 times in 13 years after fugitive suspect stole his identity
News.content:
ID FAKER Innocent dad arrested for rape more than 20 times in 13 years after fugitive suspect stole his identity







Next

AN innocent dad keeps getting arrested for rape after a fugitive suspect stole his identity.

Piotr Galas, 50, has been nicked more than 20 times by cops at the airport since 2013 — even at gunpoint.



The baker, of Redditch, Worcs, says he is now too scared to leave the country.

We told two years ago how an arrest warrant in his name was making his life a living nightmare.



But he was nabbed again last month at Bristol airport as he returned from a trip to Sardinia.

Piotr said: “They stopped me as I flashed up on their system.

“They said Interpol were looking for me too.

“I explained and they compared a photo of the wanted man to me and let me go.

“People think it’s funny, but it’s not.

“Sometimes I’m stopped at customs, sometimes at check in, and sometimes I’m taken off the plane.



“My wife and kids have to watch me being handcuffed and led away.”

The real crook, wanted for a 2012 rape, absconded from bail.

Piotr, who even won a £20,000 payout in 2022 from British Transport Police over the wrongful arrests, said: “This is driving me insane. The police have even been to my home and business to conduct searches.

“Why should I live like I am a criminal when I have done nothing wrong?”

News.title: Young explorer buried alive after cave collapses as rescue team search 32ft below ground for missing researcher in Italy
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

RACE AGAINST TIME Young explorer buried alive after cave collapses as rescue team search 32ft below ground for missing researcher in Italy







Next

A MAJOR operation is underway to save a man buried alive inside a cave, amid growing fears he may already be dead.

Officials believe the young man is trapped under 32ft of rubble in the famous Urzulei caves on the Italian island of Sardinia.



He became buried following a sudden fall of earth late on Sunday afternoon.

A National Cave and Mountain Rescue Corps (CNSAS) spokesman said the rescue is made “complicated by unstable debris”.



It is understood crews are manually removing the material blocking the cave entrance.

Approximately 30 cave rescue technicians, doctors, and clearing specialists are on site, Bild reports.



Rescue operations have been ongoing since 6pm.

By 10pm on Sunday evening, the CNSAS spokesperson said they “still have no confirmed information about his condition.”

The trapped man is understood to be a speleologist – a scientist who studies caves.

Rescuers are racing against time to reach him before it is too late.



It comes as a fisherman survived for 15-days trapped 300ft down a water-filled sinkhole.

Erasto Crisanto Valdez ,31, vanished while fishing with his father in a cenote in San Francisco La Paz, Mexico, in late July.

After more than two weeks missing, rescuers presumed the man as dead and were “prepared to find his body”.

But by some miracle he was found alive.

Erasto survived in an air pocket more than 328ft below the surface.



Mexican explorer Carlos Jiménez described the discovery as a miracle saying “god had other plans” for the lucky man.

In an interview with NMás, Erasto said: “Thank you god for giving me another opportunity at life and letting me see my kids and family again.

“It was a miracle – an unbelievable miracle”

News.title: Fury as advert urging Brits to save water uses AI – which requires HUGE amounts of the precious resource
News.content:
Next

AN advert urging people to save water has used AI — which requires huge amounts of the precious resource.

Critics said the £75million Government-backed campaign also appears to blame customers for shortages instead of water firms.



The “Let’s Save Water” video opens with kids in a classroom watching TV when a cartoon cloud warns the UK’s supply could fall short by five billion litres.

One child is then seen lecturing an adult for running a tap while washing up.



Some viewers slammed the use of AI, which a Government report said was so water-reliant “it is likely to threaten global and national water security, especially in areas of existing water stress”.

One said instead of blaming us, “why don’t we blame the AI company who animated the cloud?”.



Others hit out at the hypocrisy of water firms, who are subsidising the campaign via regulator Ofwat.

Political commentator Bruce Hamill said: “They have spent years leaking billions of litres of water a day.

“They want you to feel responsible for a shortage they created.”

Let’s Save Water said AI-assisted tools were used for “less than six seconds of footage”.



Water levels at Fernworthy Reservoir in Devon are so low they have revealed the remains of prehistoric villages.

News.title: Instead of helping fill Labour’s £35bn Budget black hole, Burnham is trying to re-run the lost argument over Brexit
News.content:
Remains of past







Next

THE clock is ticking fast towards the Budget with Chancellor John Healey facing a gaping £35billion funding black hole.

He is buffeted by global headwinds — caused by wars in Ukraine and the Middle East — while also being weighed down by two years of Labour’s economic mismanagement.



And what is Andy Burnham doing to help, apart from dreaming about a return to the catastrophic socialism of the Seventies?

He’s trying to re-run the lost argument over Brexit.



The PM who — to get elected — told the Leave-supporting voters of Makerfield he had no intention of re-fighting that battle, is doing just that.

He cynically sees an opportunity to mop up the support of Europhiles who went over to the floundering Lib Dems.

Defeat in the 2016 Referendum, he tells fellow die-hard Remainers, was not because Britons were sick of being controlled by the sclerotic EU.

It was supposedly down to a Vladimir Putin disinformation campaign helping to swing the Leave vote.

Except that Parliament’s own Intelligence and Security Committee — which has access to top-secret files — found it was “difficult, if not impossible” to assess Russian impact.

Burnham should stop living in the past and peddling fantasies — and address the crises of the moment.



Slick trick

SO MUCH for Burnham’s pledge to build a new politics and put country before party.

The damaging delay in deciding whether to grant production licences for the North Sea’s Jackdaw and Rosebank gas and oil fields — which could bring down bills and restore energy security — was blatantly party-political.

Labour did not want to risk pushing eco-sensitive voters to the Greens in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election.

They need not have worried, since the Gaza-obsessed cranks who have taken over the Greens successfully sabotaged their own campaign.

But now that political battle is done, the PM needs to urgently listen to Tory demands to grant those licences.



For all our sakes.

Kop to it, Andy

FOOTBALL fans nationwide took their first opportunity to voice their disgust at the serial cheating by Manchester City, and nowhere more so than at Anfield yesterday as Liverpool fans berated their City rivals.

So the PM’s vocal support for City’s United Arab Emirates owners looks even more unwise.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

That is why he must bow to pressure and publish details of ALL meetings between ministers, officials and the club’s hierarchy, not just his own.

A lack of transparency will only cause a bad stench to linger.

News.title: Two men charged after British pensioner, 85, beaten to death in idyllic French village
News.content:
Two men charged after British pensioner, 85, beaten to death in idyllic French village

Prosecutors have said the main suspect is a 32-year-old man with 21 previous convictions - he has now been charged with robbery preceded by or accompanied with violence resulting in death

View 2 Images Police found John Agner with severe head injuries two weeks ago (Image: Getty Images)

Two men have been charged after an 85-year-old British man was beaten to death in his French village home.

Police found John Agner, a retired wood carver, with severe head injuries two weeks ago in his house an hour north of Pau. This after his stolen vehicle was chased at high speed and crashed in a dead end in Mont-de-Marsan, 25 miles away. The two men were held along with four others in a multi agency operation.

Officers traced the registration plate officers traced to Mr Agner and made the horrific discovery in the early hours of Saturday, September 26.

View 2 Images The victim lived on the outskirts of the picturesque village of Verlus, near Toulouse (Image: Google Maps)

Detectives from the highly specialised Toulouse criminal investigation branch were involved in the operation to arrest the six men as well as local police.

A 60-year-old suspect, who has not been named, was previously arrested in connection with the killing.

Prosecutors have said the main suspect is a 32-year-old man with 21 previous convictions.

The suspect had been charged with robbery preceded by or accompanied with violence resulting in death.

He is also accused of the second attempted murder which took place last week involving a woman in her 70s. She is reported to have been attacked in her home in Mont-de-Marsan, where she was smothered. She survived the attack.

The woman's car was stolen but later found by police with officers highlighting links between the two incidents..

A second man, 26, is held in connection with Mr Agner's death.

Both men are locals and are being held in custody awaiting trial.

Article continues below

No details of the other four held have been shared.

News.title: Police's AI road safety test reveals 19,000 violations in just two weeks
News.content:
Police's AI road safety test reveals 19,000 violations in just two weeks

Examples of life-threatening risks taken by drivers included a front-seat passenger seen with a small child on their lap with no seatbelt, and a driver with two hands on the phone rather than on the steering wheel

View 5 Images PCC Simon Foster, Mayor of the West Midlands Richard Parker and road safety commissioner Mat MacDonald. (Image: West Midands Combined Authority/PA Wire)

Motorists have been urged to belt up and switch off mobile phones after an AI-powered road safety trial captured images of almost 19,000 driving violations in just two weeks.

‌



‌



Mayor of the West Midlands Richard Parker said the “frankly shocking” findings of the trial conducted at two sites in Birmingham and Wolverhampton showed risk-taking among drivers at far higher levels than was anticipated.

‌



Examples of life-threatening risks taken by drivers included a front-seat passenger seen with a small child on their lap with no seatbelt, and a driver with two hands on the phone rather than on the steering wheel. Dozens of other images showed children travelling in vehicles without age-appropriate restraints.

‌



View 5 Images Undated handout photo issued by the West Midands Combined Authority of an unretrained child on the lap of a front seat passenger. Motorists have been urged to belt up and switch off mobile phones after an AI-powered road safety trial captured images of almost 19,000 driving violations in just two weeks. (Image: West Midands Combined Authority/PA Wire)

AI camera technology set up outside Ladywood and Fallings Park fire stations was used to capture the images in March.

At the Ladywood site, 11,045 potential non-use of seatbelt offences and 1,163 potential mobile phone use offences were identified, with 6,030 potential seatbelt offences and 757 potential mobile phone offences recorded at Fallings Park.

‌



Commenting on the scale of the problem, Mr Parker said: “The number of people risking their own lives and the lives of others, including some very young children, is frankly shocking and far higher than we expected when setting up the trial. The law is clear on seatbelts and mobile phones.

View 5 Images Undated handout photo issued by the West Midands Combined Authority of a person driving with non use of a seatbelt. Motorists have been urged to belt up and switch off mobile phones after an AI-powered road safety trial captured images of almost 19,000 driving violations in just two weeks. (Image: West Midands Combined Authority/PA Wire)

“I’ve met families who have lost loved ones to reckless driving. They never recover from these tragedies, the grief is always there. People need to stop doing this, it is simply not worth the risk.

‌



“As we review these results with our road safety partnership and look to next steps, I promise to use every resource available, including new technology like this, to make our streets safer for everyone.”

The trial was funded by the West Midlands Combined Authority (WMCA) in collaboration with the police and the fire service.

Simon Foster, the West Midlands Police and Crime Commissioner and chair of the area’s road safety partnership board, said: “These initial findings are deeply concerning.

‌



View 5 Images Mayor of the West Midlands Richard Parker arriving at No 10 North in Manchester for a meeting of regional mayors from across Englan (Image: Gary Oakley/PA Wire)

“Let me be absolutely clear: reducing the number of people killed and seriously injured on our roads remains our absolute top priority. We are closely evaluating these trial results to consider how this advanced AI technology can be deployed for future police enforcement.

“We cannot tolerate reckless behaviour that puts lives at risk, and we will use every effective tool at our disposal to ensure our roads are safer.”

‌



No follow-up enforcement is planned following the trial, which aimed to establish the potential scale of illegal phone use and lack of child restraints.

Mat MacDonald, West Midlands Road Safety Commissioner, said: “Mobile phone use at the wheel and failing to wear a seatbelt are two of the leading causes of death and serious injury on our road network, and yet you barely have to leave your front door before you see someone taking these potentially lethal risks.

View 5 Images PCC Simon Foster, Mayor of the West Midlands Richard Parker and road safety commissioner Mat MacDonald (Image: West Midands Combined Authority/PA Wire)

Article continues below

"Our work with this cutting-edge technology shows we will stop at nothing to stamp out such behaviours.”

The WMCA said road safety data for 2025 showed mobile phone use was linked to 32 deaths and unbuckled seatbelts to 133 deaths on UK roads, while about 2,000 motorists a year in the West Midlands are fined and given penalty points for driving while using a mobile phone.

News.title: NHS prescription alerts now available on phones and even smartwatches
News.content:
NHS prescription alerts now available on phones and even smartwatches

Patients welcome new NHS development which sees alerts sent out when prescriptions are ready to be picked up

View 5 Images Prescriptions handed out to patients who can now get special alerts on phones and watches (Image: Getty Images)

Millions of NHS app users in England can now get alerts on their phones and smartwatches when their prescriptions are ready.

‌



‌



The update will help tackle unnecessary calls or premature trips to the chemist to pick up medication, NHS England said.Users will need to enable push alerts on the app to receive the notifications.

‌



Health innovation minister James Frith said: "This is a practical example of how digital technology can make a difference to people's everyday experience of the NHS, while also helping to reduce unnecessary calls and free up valuable time for pharmacy staff to focus on supporting patients.

‌



"Anyone that uses the NHS app should switch on notifications so they can benefit from this brilliant new service."

View 5 Images Patients can now get prescription alerts on smartwatches (Image: Getty Images)

Rob Thompson, chief digital, data and technology officer at NHS England, said: "The new prescription ready alerts are the latest step in the NHS giving people more control over how they manage their healthcare, as well as helping to reduce admin for staff.

‌



"Thousands of pharmacies are already live with the service, so I'd encourage all NHS app users to enable notifications in the app so they can get the full benefit.'

View 5 Images Patients can now get prescription alerts on mobile phones (Image: Getty Images)

The latest feature follows the launch of the "Amazon-style" prescription tracker on the NHS app, which officials said has been used by almost 2.9 million people.

‌



Around one in three pharmacies in England is now offering the tracking service.

Mr Thompson added: "The NHS app's prescription tracking feature has been incredibly popular since we launched it last year, and we're now making it even easier to find out when your prescription is ready.

View 5 Images Patients' pills and prescriptions can now be sent via special alerts on phones and watches (Image: Getty Images)

‌



"Millions of app users will be able to get near real-time alerts on their smartwatches or mobiles, avoiding the need to regularly check the app or make unnecessary trips or calls to their pharmacy."

Rachel Power, chief executive of the Patients Association, also welcomed the new feature.

"Making it easier for patients to know when their prescription is ready can save time and reduce unnecessary trips to the pharmacy," she said.

‌



"It's something many people have been asking for, and alongside other non-digital ways of accessing information and support, can help make it easier for patients to get the information they need in a way that works for them."

View 5 Images Prescriptions handed out to patients who can now get special alerts on phones and watches (Image: Getty Images)

Henry Gregg, Chief Executive of the National Pharmacy Association said: "This is an important step forward in making pharmacy services more accessible, making it easier for patients to access the medicines they need. It also frees up staff time from answering phone calls so they can focus on delivering first class care.

Article continues below

"This will also encourage more patients to download and make use of the NHS app.

"Pharmacies want to do all they can to embrace new technology and make the vital services they offer as easy and convenient as possible for patients to access.”

News.title: Donald Trump claims he's plotting to rename the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean as 'Trump Ocean'
News.content:
Donald Trump claims he's plotting to rename the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean as 'Trump Ocean'

Donald Trump has floated renaming one of the world's biggest oceans after himself, suggesting the Atlantic or Pacific could get a new name as he looks to put a stamp on America

View Image Donald Trump made the comments at a rally in Tennessee (Image: Getty Images)

Donald Trump has suggested renaming the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean as "Trump Ocean," as he revealed the one major landmark he would leave untouched.

‌



‌



The US President made the comments during a midterm campaign rally in Clarksville, Tennessee, on Saturday, where he suggested either ocean could also be called "Ocean of the Americans". Trump did not announce any formal plans to push ahead with the idea, but told supporters he wanted the country to have an ocean and a major river named after it.

‌



Addressing the crowd, the president revealed he would not be renaming the Hudson River, praising the explorer Henry Hudson, who the river is named after - despite his suggestion that other major bodies of water could be given new names.

‌



"We've got the Gulf, we've got a beautiful lake, and now someone said 'you need a river'," Trump said during his speech on Saturday.

‌



"I don't want to change the name of the Hudson River. Henry Hudson, he did a good job sailing up that sucker a long time ago. We need a river. We need an ocean," he said. "We'll call it 'Trump Ocean' or 'Ocean of the Americans, something like that. Before I get out, I think we should have an ocean. And we need a great river."

His comments follow previous efforts to change the names of prominent geographical features, including the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario.

In January 2025, Trump signed an executive order to call Lake Ontario "Lake America". However, the lake is shared by the United States and Canada, and the move does not require Canada to adopt the alternative name. Trump's attempts to put his stamp on prominent landmarks have extended beyond bodies of water.

Article continues below

Washington DC's Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts was renamed the Trump-Kennedy Center following action by its board, a move that faced legal challenge.

A federal judge ruled in May 2026 that the move was unlawful and ordered Trump's name to be removed in June.

Other ideas floated by the president include renaming the state of New Mexico as New America and calling the Strait of Hormuz the Trump Strait. These proposals have not been implemented.

News.title: Nigel Farage hits panic button and vows to ban all asylum seekers for five years after Reform poll plunge
News.content:
Nigel Farage hits panic button and vows to ban all asylum seekers for five years after Reform poll plunge

Nigel Farage will vow to scrap all asylum tribunals and close all legal refugee routes if his party is elected as he struggles with falling poll ratings and ongoing donor scandals

View 2 Images Nigel Farage's latest announcement comes as Reform UK continue to struggle with falling poll ratings (Image: Gary Oakley/PA Wire)

Nigel Farage is set to announce a desperate pledge to ban anyone from being granted asylum for five years if Reform wins the next election.

‌



‌



Under the plans, all asylum tribunals, legal refugee routes and resettlement schemes will be scrapped for a full parliamentary term - while any applications in progress would be declared void. All asylum tribunals, legal refugee routes and resettlement schemes will also be closed.

‌



It comes as the Reform UK leader attempts to reverse months of flagging poll ratings, with the party now trailing Labour by several points and even falling behind the Tories in some recent surveys.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 2 Images Any refugees granted asylum in the last five years would have their cases reviewed under the plans (Image: AP Photo/Jean-Francois Badias)

Ongoing controversy over donations has rocked the party since this summer, triggering an internal crisis, high-profile resignations, and a criminal investigation by the Met Police.

‌



On Monday, Mr Farage will say that a Reform UK government would not hear the around 90,000 outstanding asylum and humanitarian protection appeals - and instead deport the claimants. The party would immediately close resettlement schemes that Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood recently said would reopen, with around a quarter of those admitted to the UK expected to be Palestinians and women and girls from Afghanistan.

Reform claims there is "no mandate" for such schemes and that anyone who has arrived under them would be deported. Any refugees granted asylum in the last five years would have their cases reviewed by the Home Office under the plans.

Mr Farage told The Telegraph: "The country is currently facing a national security emergency and the first duty of government is to protect its citizens. We cannot accept more asylum seekers while we still have no idea how many people are in the country illegally and the threat they pose. A Reform government will always put British people first and protect our borders."

Article continues below

The party will also pledge to use tariffs to force countries to take back migrants. It comes after the party unveiled plans earlier this year to impose "visa freezes" on those wanting to visit the UK legally from countries including Pakistan, Afghanistan and Syria if they do not accept deportees.

These would halt any new visas for nationals of those countries - as well as Eritrea, Sudan and Somalia - which the party would target due to having significant levels of visas issued to the UK.

Reform UK also recently proposed Trump-style tariffs on countries who refuse to take back deportees from the UK, and bans on their airlines using British airspace.

News.title: Strictly Come Dancing 2026: Melanie Walters voted out second after splitting the judges
News.content:
Strictly Come Dancing's second results show of the year saw fan favourite Melanie Walters head home after the judges were divided following the dance off

The Strictly Come Dancing leaderboard is more sporadic than ever and sadly someone has to go home - bring on the results show!

Sunday's pre-recorded show has seen Melanie Walters head home in the second elimination. The judges were divided on who to send home, with Motsi picking to save Melanie but Craig and Shirley picked Shaun, meaning deciding judge Anton had to get involved. He picked Shaun.

In a since deleted post, Cach Mercer seemed to leak the results on his Instagram. He posted over an hour before the results show began, leaving many fans confused as to what happened.

There was more drama off-screen with Amy Dowden sneaking a moment in the dressing room to fire back at Brendan Cole for slamming her this week. Brendan said the professional was 'not good enough' to compete. Safe to say, Amy's had her say in the best way at the 'obsessed' former dancer.

News.title: Russia attacks Ukraine power plant just hours after Trump boasts about ceasefire in utter humiliation
News.content:
Russia attacks Ukraine power plant just hours after Trump boasts about ceasefire in utter humiliation

The power plant in Kharkiv was struck at least twice and burst into flames shortly after Donald Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an 'energy ceasefire'

View 3 Images Damage and smoke at the site of a Russian air strike in Kharkiv (Image: SERGEY KOZLOV/EPA/Shutterstock)

Russia has attacked a Ukrainian power plant shortly after Donald Trump said both sides had agreed to an "energy ceasefire".

‌



‌



The thermal power plant CHP-5 was struck at least twice before bursting into flames on Sunday, a local official said.

‌



President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed Russia had attacked the plant, as well as another in Kyiv, reports ABC News.

‌



It came just hours after Trump urged the two countries not to break an "energy ceasefire" which he claimed was "effective immediately" this morning.

Posting to Truth Social shortly after 10am US time, Trump said: "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine.

‌



"Both parties have agreed. Do not break it! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP."

Zelensky was said to have been caught off guard by the announcement, which he only came to learn about through social media, a senior source in Ukraine's presidential office said.

Zelensky said Ukraine would have been ready to accept a ceasefire deal if Russia were to agree. Russia has yet to comment on the announcement by Trump.

‌



View 3 Images Rescuers at the site of a Russian guided bomb strike in Kharkiv (Image: Pavlo Pakhomenko/NurPhoto/Shutterstock)

It came after Zelensky appeared on ABC's 'This Week' and said Ukraine wanted an immediate "energy ceasefire" that would put an end to the attacks on both sides.

He said Ukraine would stop striking Russian oil refineries if the Kremlin agreed to halt attacks on Ukraine's power infrastructure.

‌



Ukraine was "ready not to strike at Russian energy" and was "counting on Russia's similar readiness," Zelensky added.

"Ukraine has proposed many de-escalation steps," he said. "Ukraine wants peace. The question is whether Russia wants it."

The attack on the power plant in Kharkiv came at around 8pm local time.

‌



View 3 Images Zelensky said Russia launched two strikes on a power plant in Kharkiv (Image: Pavlo Pakhomenko/NurPhoto/Shutterstock)

Speaking after the strikes, Zelensky said: "Today, there was a statement from the President of the United States that an energy ceasefire has been secured. This is good news for everyone - and it is important that it become reality.

"Unfortunately, Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian "shaheds" all day today. There have been glide bomb strikes and strikes on our energy infrastructure too. A power plant in Kharkiv was attacked this evening."

Article continues below

Zelensky said Russia had launched more than 200 strikes on Ukraine's electricity generation and transmission facilities this week alone, as well as 17 strikes on gas and oil facilities.

The attacks killed more than 150 people and injured over 700 during that period, he added.

News.title: Saudi Arabia's Riyadh airport attacked for second time in 24 hours as UK issues travel warning
News.content:
Saudi Arabia's Riyadh airport attacked for second time in 24 hours as UK issues travel warning

Passenger terminals at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh came under fire as Iran-backed Houthi militants launched a second missile attack - travel warnings have been issued

View 4 Images Missile strikes on Saudi Arabia's main airport have caused travel disruption further afield (Image: Harun-Or-Rashid/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

Saudi Arabia's biggest airport was attacked for the second time in 24 hours on Sunday - after a devastating missile strike killed 12 and injured more than 300 the day before.

‌



‌



The UK has criticised a "dangerous escalation" by Iranian-backed Houthi militants, who issued a warning against using Saudi airports or airspace. US President Donald Trump has said he is weighing up whether American forces should join Saudi strikes against the rebels.

‌



Passenger terminals at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh were targeted by missiles in Saturday's carnage, which was branded appalling by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband. On Sunday the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said the airport has been struck again.

‌



It follows a string of attacks in recent weeks by the Houthis, who have seized key islands and ports along crucial Red Sea shipping routes and targeted Saudi energy infrastructure, causing chaos on world markets.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 4 Images It is the second time the airport has been struck in 24 hours (Image: AP)

‌



UK not currently considering strikes on Houthis after airport kills 12, says Wes Streeting READ MORE :

Riyadh airport attack kills 12 and injures hundreds more after Houthi missile strike READ MORE :

On Sunday Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the UK would continue to support Saudi Arabia - but said it is not currently considering joining military offences.

Mr Streeting said strikes on civilians "can't possibly be justified in any circumstances". But asked if Britain intends to get involved in offensive operations against the terror group, he said: "That's not what we're looking at at this stage, and we've always been clear that there isn't a military solution to this conflict. We need to see a diplomatic solution, and Saudi needs to do that from a position of strength."

On Sunday the Foreign Office advised against all travel to parts of Saudi Arabia, including anywhere within 10km of the border with Yemen. It also urged people to avoid non-essential travel to Aseer province, Riyadh province, Najran province, Jizan province and Taif city and Taif International Airport.

‌



View 4 Images Iran-backed Houthi rebels have vowed to continue hitting Saudi targets (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said he was appalled by the airport attack. Meanwhile the Houthis issued a warning against using Saudi airports and airspace in a hint of further attacks to come.

Saudi authorities said those killed in Saturday's airport attack included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said the injured were being treated at several hospitals.

‌



Asked if the US would commit forces to support Saudi Arabia following Saturday's attack, Trump told reporters outside the White House: "We may. We’re going to look at it.”

The unpredictable US commander-in-chief went on: “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”

Last month Andy Burnham agreed to give military support to Saudi Arabia in the form of “defensive” air-to-air refuelling for Saudi jets.

‌



Mr Streeting told Sky News of the strikes: "This is completely contemptible action and it’s one of the reasons why the UK is providing support to Saudi Arabia in the form of air defences, but also air-to-air refuelling.

“We want to see an end to this conflict. It cannot be right that the Houthis are attacking civilian targets in this way.”

He said: "Even in the context of Houthi attacks and an escalation, what we saw in terms of the attack on the airport in Riyadh was a shocking escalation. Hundreds of casualties, and an attack on a civilian target that can't be possibly justified in any circumstances."

‌



View 4 Images Foreign secretary Ed Miliband said he was 'appalled' by the latest attack (Image: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing via Getty Images)

Mr Miliband said: "I am appalled by the latest attack on King Khalid International Airport, my thoughts are with those families who have lost loved ones, and those injured in this horrific attack. We stand in solidarity with those affected."

The Houthis are a militant group with around 20,000 fighters forming part of Iran's so-called 'axis of resistance' - a coalition of forces operating across .

‌



They sparked a devastating civil war by launching a coup in 2014 and remain in a brutal conflict with Yemen's Saudi-backed government. The Houthis have been targeting shipping routes in the Red Sea since the October 7 attack in 2023.

Last month militants seized two strategic islands in the region - Greater and Lesser Hanish, having previously taken control of the port of Mokha and Perim Island.

These are on key shipping routes connecting the Red Sea to the open ocean, crucial for transporting oil and gas. They have also been targeted facilities run by Saudi state-run energy firm Aramco.

Article continues below

The heightened tensions have caused oil prices to soar - between June and September this year the global oil price rose from £52 to over £80.

Escalating conflict between the Houthis - who represent the Zaidi branch of Shia Islam - and Yemen's government has led to the displacement of around 100,000 people in recent months.

News.title: PM says it is 'clear' Russia interfered with Brexit vote
News.content:
Andy Burnham has said Russia did interfere with the Brexit referendum and warned that similar activities were taking place in France and Germany.

The prime minister told The Rest is Politics podcast, external that upon arriving in No 10, he had asked about possible Russian interference in the 2016 vote, adding: "I've had the clear answer that, yes, there was."

"I think we've been too much on the back foot on that actually and we haven't informed people sufficiently about the extent to which people are seeking to disrupt the political process from overseas," he added.

Burnham did not provide further details about the type or extent of Moscow's activity during the Brexit referendum.

Britain Unbound, a pro-Brexit campaign group, said Burnham's comments were "another crude attempt to undermine the legitimacy of the decision that the British people made in 2016".

It said that foreign interference in UK elections was "obviously unacceptable" but added: "There is no good reason to believe that Russian intervention influenced the outcome of the referendum in 2016.

"It is also insulting to suggest that voters were so easily duped."

In his interview, due to be released on Monday, Burnham said he had discussed the problem of Russian interference with Chancellor Friedrich Merz during his visit to Germany earlier this week.

"There is certainly misinformation, disinformation that is emanating from Russia into German politics," he said.

He continued: "These things are important now to put clearly on the record and I believe help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia."

It is the first time a UK prime minister has said Russia sought to sway the 2016 Brexit poll but there have long been warnings about efforts by the Kremlin to exert influence on UK politics.

In 2020, Parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee published a report into Russian interventions in UK elections and referendums.

It did not provide a definitive conclusion on whether Russia had attempted to influence the results of the EU referendum but did criticise successive governments for failing to fully assess or counter the threat.

In response, the Russian foreign minister dismissed the report out of hand and called it "Russophobia".

And a Kremlin spokesman said Russia did not meddle in other countries' elections.

In the same year, however, the then-Conservative government said it was "almost certain that Russian actors sought to interfere" in the 2019 general election.

BBC Verify has tracked Russian-linked disinformation campaigns including using AI to create fake videos which impersonate journalists and news organisations reporting on Ukraine.

One fake news website falsely claimed that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had bought a mansion owned by King Charles at a discounted price.

Earlier this year, Vijay Rangarajan, head of the UK Electoral Commission, told MPs that Russian deepfake videos had been "used extensively in elections around the world".

"There is no reason to assume Britain would be an exception," he added.

Last month, during his speech to the United Nations, Burnham accused Russian agencies of using "every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people's fears".

He announced that the UK would set up a new centre to "stem the poisonous tide" of disinformation.

A Downing Street spokesperson said: "We are focused on ensuring our citizens and our institutions are protected from foreign powers and their proxies seeking to threaten lives and undermine our democratic values.

"We are doing this by strengthening our powers through the National Security Act, strengthening the resilience of our institutions and critical national infrastructure, strengthening our borders, and strengthening our police and intelligence agencies."

News.title: Wildlife park remains closed after fatal tiger attack
News.content:
Yorkshire Wildlife Park remains closed after a man climbed into a tiger enclosure and was fatally attacked by the animal.

Emergency services were called to the park near Doncaster, South Yorkshire, at about 13:30 BST on Saturday after reports of a man climbing down into the enclosure from a walkway.

An eyewitness described seeing the man wearing headphones and "pacing around" near the enclosure before he went in and was attacked. Police said the man sadly died at the scene.

A park spokesperson said their "thoughts and heartfelt sympathies" remain with the man's family and confirmed the Amur tiger, called Altai, remained in the enclosure and would not be euthanised.

The spokesperson says many people had contacted them about the tiger and he was safe and well.

Staff who were at the scene who were "deeply affected by events" would receive specialist support, they added.

South Yorkshire Police said the man's family were being supported by officers. "Our thoughts are with them at this distressing time," the force said in a statement.

It added: "We are aware of videos circulating online and we would encourage people not to share this footage."

Earlier on Saturday, in a statement posted on its website, the park said its emergency response procedures had been "immediately activated" and it was "working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened".

News.title: DUP MP says her party could help remove O'Neill as first minister over Drumcree row
News.content:
Sinn FÃ©in assembly member John O'Dowd rejected claims that the move to ban the parade went in favour of his party, saying "the decision went in the way of the residents" who he said have "faced an awful four weeks" since the application to walk was lodged.

O'Dowd, who is also finance minister in the executive, was one of a number of Sinn FÃ©in politicians who joined a protest with residents on the Garvaghy Road.

On Thursday, the police said they had begun issuing letters inviting people "reasonably suspected" of committing offences linked to the protests to interview.

Speaking on BBC News NI's Sunday Politics programme, O'Dowd said: "I own my decision", adding that he thinks it was "the right thing to do".

"I got into politics to stand against the intimidation of communities such as the Garvaghy Road, who went through hell and high water over many, many years.

"I stood with the people of the Garvaghy Road. I will continue to stand with the people of Garvaghy Road because it was the right thing to do."

He added that he believes the community responded in "a peaceful, democratic way" to the decision to approve a march on 27 September.

"I would appeal, not only to Gavin, but maybe hopelessly to Carla and others, to calm their language and to show responsible leadership and calm leadership at this stage," he added.

"I don't think that continued demonisation or an attempt to criminalise the community of the Garvaghy Road is an appropriate way forward.

"What we need in Portadown is reconciliation."

News.title: Iran war threatens Healey's Budget plans, think tank warns
News.content:
The price spike caused by the US-Israel war in Iran poses a major challenge for Chancellor John Healey as he puts together his first Budget, an influential think tank has warned.

Higher-than-expected inflation could eat into what the government hoped to spend on public services, meaning Healey will have to choose between spending cuts, tax rises, or a mixture of both, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said.

It urged the government to ensure its spending plans are credible, as opposed to proposing unrealistic future cuts to make the Budget add up.

The Treasury declined to comment on "rumour and speculation".

However, speaking ahead of the annual International Monetary Fund meeting this week, Healey said: "The consequences of conflict in the Middle East and Europe are hitting countries worldwide, leading to higher prices at the pumps and more expensive mortgages at home.

"But Britain and our alliesâ¯can face up to these challenges together."

He said his Budget "will build on this approach with fiscal discipline helping to deliver economic resilience" and give people "breathing space".

However, the government is under growing pressure to show financial markets that it has a tight grip on finances as the cost of borrowing rises.

The IFS cautioned Healey about making any spending announcements in the 28 October Budget speech he has no intention of honouring.

"A 'steady-as-she-goes' Budget is not an option available to the chancellor," said IFS director Helen Miller said.

"Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments' spending plans off course.

"Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the Budget a work of fiction," she added.

The US-Israel war against Iran and Russia's invasion of Ukraine have together helped drive up energy prices around the world.

These higher costs have been passed to customers via higher prices on shelves and at the pumps.

The wars have also contributed to a rise in the cost of UK government debt interest payments, adding to the pressure on Healey.

Although higher inflation will boost tax revenues, it will also eat into the value of departments' cash budgets, the IFS said.

News.title: Children among 139 dead after boat capsizes off Djibouti, UN says
News.content:
At least 139 migrants including 15 children have died and dozens more are still missing after a boat sank off the coast of Djibouti, the UN's migration office has said.

The boat had been travelling from Djibouti to Yemen with 305 people aboard when it capsized near the port town of Obock on Thursday night. Around 82 people were rescued, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said.

IOM's Djibouti mission chief Alexandre Coissac called the tragedy a "stark reminder" of the dangers migrants face when seeking a new life elsewhere.

Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa make the perilous journey each year hoping to reach Gulf countries for safety and work, the agency says.

The organisation revised its toll from 109 on Sunday after 30 more bodies were recovered.

"This is a devastating loss of life," Coissac said. "Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives."

Local authorities are also arranging burials for those who have died, while the survivors - all Ethiopian nationals - have medical care readily available to them.

Yemen remains engulfed in a devastating civil war that has lasted more than a decade. Despite this conflict - and growing instability across the wider region - migrants still cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen driven by poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change.

Since 10 September, the IOM said its Displacement Tracking Matrix had observed more than 20,000 "movements" from Ethiopia to Djibouti.

News.title: Reform would suspend asylum system for parliamentary term if in government
News.content:
Reform UK has announced plans to close down the UK's asylum system for a full parliamentary term if it were to enter government.

The party said all new asylum applications would be rejected and existing applications voided, with all claimants marked for deportation, which Reform said would effectively suspend the asylum system.

Reform would scrap the asylum tribunal system, which hears asylum appeal cases, and claimants in more than 90,000 outstanding appeals would be deported.

It said no grants of humanitarian protection or refugee status would be made.

Labour chairperson Bridget Phillipson called the proposals a "clear sign of desperation and weakness".

"Running away from basic decency by entirely abandoning those escaping war and persecution might look to Reform like a way of winning a bidding war with other parties on the right, but the vast majority of British people will reject it as an assault on our common values," she said.

Conservative shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the proposals "largely copy" his party's policies, arguing: "Only the Conservatives have a serious and credible plan to fix our borders."

Liberal Democrat home affairs spokesperson Max Wilkinson said: "Reform and the Conservatives were the architects of the failed asylum system and now they will exploit it at every opportunity - including Farage's latest announcement."

Reform said it would pull the UK out of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), repeal the Human Rights Act 1998 and disapply the 1951 Refugee Convention to prevent legal challenges to its plans.

Party leader Nigel Farage said the UK is "facing a national security emergency" and "we cannot accept more asylum seekers while we still have no idea how many people are in the country illegally and the threat they pose."

Home Office staff who currently oversee asylum claims would be "reprioritised to reviewing and overturning previous refugee grants", Reform added.

The party said it would attempt to pressure other countries into accepting those marked for deportation from the UK by using visa bans and tariffs on goods and services.

Pakistan, Somalia, Eritrea, Syria, Afghanistan and Sudan could be hit with visa bans under these measures.

If these policies are unsuccessful, Reform would "apply further sanctions, including banning a country's airlines from British airspace and their citizens from transit", the announcement added.

In "extreme cases" where no country is willing to take custody of a deportee or it is inappropriate to return someone to their home country, Reform said it would negotiate deals with third countries.

In April, Reform pledged an immediate review of all asylum claims from the last five years should the party win the next general election.

Around 400,000 people would be liable for deportation under the plans, which would target anybody granted asylum, overstaying a visa, or from a country deemed safe by a Reform-led government.

The party previously announced it would bar anyone arriving on a small boat, and suggested this could mean 600,000 deportations over five years.

Both Labour and the Conservatives have also pledged to make changes to the asylum system.

Phillipson said Farage is "casting around for more and more extreme policies" as he deals with questions about finances and rival party Restore Britain.

Phillipson said Labour is showing "we can control immigration and get numbers down with serious action, not by abandoning the asylum system altogether", adding the "right approach" is "not giving up or caving to the most extreme voices, but ensuring that the rules we have are properly enforced".

News.title: Buildings swept away as flash floods hit central Nepal
News.content:
A flash flood has washed away houses, bridges and damaged a hydropower project along a river in central Nepal.

The army said on Sunday that it had rescued 49 people from flood affected areas, but five are still missing, the district's top official confirmed.

It is believed that the flood was caused by a landslide upstream of the Budhi Gandaki River in the Gorkha district.

Four bridges and nearly two dozen houses have been swept away, as well as a camp at a hydropower project along the river.

Nepal is still trying to recover from catastrophic floods and landslides that swept through its border towns with Tibet two months ago, wiping out thousands of houses, destroying critical energy infrastructure and leaving thousands dead and missing.

More on this story.

News.title: Sacha Baron Cohen to star in Quentin Tarantino's West End play
News.content:
Borat actor Sacha Baron Cohen will star in a new play in London's West End from Hollywood director Quentin Tarantino.

The Popinjay Cavalier, set in 1830s Europe, was announced earlier this year and is the first play to be written for stage by the US filmmaker, who is also set to direct.

Baron Cohen said he was "beyond delighted" to be working with Tarantino, saying: "When the best director in the world calls, you don't ask questions."

The director, best known for violent film classics Pulp Fiction and Reservoir Dogs, has said he is "keen with anticipation to give the West End a great night out".

The play is set to premiere in March next year, with tickets available from Monday.

The production was announced in March this year as a "rambunctious comedy of deception and disguise inspired by the grand swashbuckling epics of stage and screen".

Baron Cohen, 54, is known for his self-created comic characters including infamous spoof wannabe gangster Ali G, Kazakh reporter Borat Sagdiyev, and Austrian fashionista BrÃ¼no Gehard.

He has won two Baftas and three Golden Globes, as well as being nominated for three Oscars and six Emmys.

The full cast for The Popinjay Cavalier is planned to be announced at a later date.

The play will be co-produced by Sony Pictures Entertainment, which distributed Tarantino's most recent film Once Upon a Time... in Hollywood, and Sonia Friedman Productions, which has overseen hits like Harry Potter and the Cursed Child and Paddington the Musical.

News.title: Roofing scammers con homeowners out of thousands of pounds
News.content:
Scammers pretending to be legitimate workmen are charging homeowners thousands of pounds for roofing work that is not completed, done badly or not necessary, according to Citizens Advice.

The consumer advice charity says one in 10 of all the scams it recorded over the past year were related to roofing, making it the most common type of scam brought to them.

It can leave victims like Crystal, from the Midlands, thousands of pounds out of pocket.

The 68-year-old was frightened and found it hard to sleep after a rogue builder left her roof with dislodged bricks and blocked gutters.

She said she felt pressured into agreeing to having her roof re-done and paid a total of Â£5,500, only for the original contractor to send his son instead, who left work in the eaves incomplete.

"We had heavy rain a couple of weeks after he did the job, and it ended up like a waterfall coming down the wall," she said.

Her neighbour's house was also damaged.

"They took the lead off my neighbour's side of the chimney, which caused bricks to fall into his attic and the rain to go into his house," she told the BBC.

The experience still haunts her: "I can't sleep. I don't eat properly".

In the year to August the Citizens Advice Consumer Service received 9,000 complaints about roofing work, including problems with construction, repairs and weatherproofing.

Of those 2,205, or about one in four complaints, were suspected scams, up from 2,098 the year before.

Dame Clare Moriarty, chief executive of Citizens Advice, urged consumers to carry out thorough checks on traders before agreeing to hire them.

"Scammers exploit the fact that roofs are out of sight and reach, knowing most people can't easily inspect the work themselves," she said.

Victims also reported aggressive and intimidating behaviour, with three quarters of fraudsters using "doorstep" sales tactics.

Citizens Advice cited the case of Charlotte, 65, who lives alone in north eastern England.

Tradesmen she found online initially offered to fix her leaking gutter for Â£250. The two men then said there was further work that needed to be done, that would cost Â£2,500.

"An hour later they said it was sorted, but they'd found another problem," she said.

It was dark and Charlotte felt afraid. "They knew I was alone, I didn't feel like I could deal with anything that might happen after, so I paid Â£3,500," she said.

But the next day she could see no sign of any work having been done, she said.

To avoid falling victim to roofing scams, Citizens Advice suggests:

Be alert: Always ask for references and for everything to be in writing. Be wary of unsolicited doorknockers and callers

Gather evidence: If a trader causes problems, be sure to take photos and gather the necessary paperwork and receipts

Know your rights: Traders must give you the information about your right to cancel in writing. If the job is not done with "reasonable care and skill," the Consumer Rights Act 2015 also entitles you to ask for the problem to be fixed or a refund

Lord Bichard, chair of National Trading Standards, said rogue traders were "criminals deliberately preying on people in their own homes".

He described roofing fraud as "particularly cruel", and said Trading Standards would pursue fraudsters through legal routes.

"Victims can lose life savings in a matter of hours and be left with damaged homes, financial hardship and a profound sense of vulnerability long after the criminals have gone," he said.

News.title: Burnham to release details of Man City meetings
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will release details of his meetings with senior figures at Manchester City following criticism of his comments in the wake of the club being found guilty of all charges related to breaches of the Premier League's financial rules.

An independent commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than Â£830m into their football operations.

Burnham's previous role as mayor of Greater Manchester has led to questions about his relationship with City's Abu Dhabi ownership, with Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch demanding No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club.

"I've been asked by the leader of the opposition to publish details of my meetings, which I'm happy to do and I'm going to," Burnham told the Rest is Politics podcast.

"I will quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as Mayor of Greater Manchester.

"None of it is recent, actually, in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting, actually, and that was in 2021."

The prime minister initially told the BBC he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's owners decide to sell up following the guilty verdict before later denying his reaction had "downplayed the seriousness of the findings".

However, some Premier League clubs were so "astonished" by Burnham's stance that sources told BBC Sport they were "concerned" about political interference in the appeal process.

Sanctions are yet to be announced and City have lodged an appeal against the verdict.

City returned to action for the first time since the guilty verdict when they played at Liverpool on Sunday, winning 3-0.

News.title: Legoland Windsor evacuated over burst water main
News.content:
The Legoland Windsor attraction has closed abruptly due to a burst water main.

Customers were told to leave rides and exit the resort at lunchtime on Sunday.

Thames Water said it had to shut off the damaged main near St Leonards Reservoir to prevent flooding, which affected supplies to the theme park.

It said some local residents had reportedly suffered flooded gardens and it apologised for the disruption.

Merlin Entertainments, the operator behind Legoland, said it is continuing to work with local partners and thanked guests for their "patience and understanding".

One Legoland visitor, who came with her children from Cornwall, said the sudden evacuation felt "surreal".

The woman, who asked not to be named, said: "We were queuing for a ride and had got right to the front when, all of a sudden, everything stopped moving.

"Then they came out and said, 'Right, come on, everybody off.'

"Over the announcement system, they said there had been some sort of Thames Water disruption in the local area and they didn't have any water.

"We'd booked a night in the hotel and stayed there last night, so we're absolutely gutted because we've just had to drive home.

"It's a good five-hour drive to come up for a nice day, only to come back after half a day."

Thames Water said supplies had been restored and repairs were under way. It said it would provide an update on Monday.

A spokesperson for Merlin Entertainments said the resort was closed while Thames Water worked to restore normal service.

"We apologise for the inconvenience and thank our guests for their patience and understanding," the group said.

The BBC understands the resort will reopen on Monday under normal operating hours.

News.title: UK does not support Trump's Russia diesel deal, says Streeting
News.content:
The UK does not support Donald Trump's deal with Vladimir Putin, which would see the US purchase millions of tonnes of diesel from Russia, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has said.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Broadcasting House, he said the agreement had been done in the context of the US president facing elections in November and at a time when politicians across the world were under pressure to ease the cost of living.

He argued that the US and other allies should focus on increasing pressure on Russia to shorten the war "and to secure Ukraine's freedom".

Trump's diesel deal is aimed at lowering fuel prices in America, which have risen following the US and Israel's conflict with Iran.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the agreement would allow Moscow to raise funds to source new military equipment to continue the war.

In response, Trump suggested Ukraine should "get a new leader" who could reach a deal with Russia to end the long-running conflict between the two countries.

Streeting said it was a matter for Ukrainians to choose their leader but added that the country was "fortunate to have someone of his calibre, his courage and his integrity leading their war effort".

He added that responsibility for the war "lies squarely and solely with President Putin and his imperialist ambitions".

The defence secretary said it was not the first time there had been public disagreements between Washington and Kyiv, adding: "In these situations we see it as our role and our responsibility to try and bring our friends back together again."

He also sought to emphasise the US's support for Ukraine, saying there was "often an understatement" of how much help they had provided.

"We're seeing US support for Ukraine in a number of ways from the provision of weapons - and we do a lot of procurement through the Americans - through to intelligence support and through the diplomatic initiative that Washington is leading."

News.title: MPs seek to overturn ruling that stops police being sued for failings
News.content:
Backbench MPs are seeking to roll back a court ruling they say will have "devastating consequences" for victims of crime by preventing them taking legal action against the police, even when there have been grave investigative failings.

The 2025 Court of Appeal judgment, which applies to England and Wales, held that police officers are immune from civil litigation both in their role as witnesses, and for conduct or statements they make when carrying out criminal investigations.

Conservative Andrew Mitchell and Labour's Jess Phillips have submitted an amendment to a bill being debated in Parliament next week seeking to counteract the ruling.

Separately, the judgment could also be overturned at a Supreme Court appeal this month.

The MPs are seeking to stop immunity applying, including in cases where police have fabricated evidence, been dishonest or negligent, and where there has been a reckless disclosure of confidential information relating to victims.

The ruling came in a case brought by a victim of serious domestic violence who fled her abuser for a secret refuge, but Sussex Police included her new address in a file sent to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) without sufficiently flagging its confidentiality.

A CPS lawyer subsequently disclosed her address in court during a bail hearing, thereby revealing it to her abuser. As a result, she had to flee again.

The woman said the disclosure of her address had meant the place she was supposed to be safe "no longer felt safe at all" and she was still living with the impact of what happened and that loss of security.

She brought claims against both the police and CPS, arguing their failure placed her in fear for her life, compelled her to leave her home, caused her to suffer loss of earnings, and resulted in her developing a psychiatric injury. Her claims were initially rejected, reinstated on appeal, then struck out again.

The key issue was who could be held legally responsible for what happened, and who would benefit from legal immunity. Witnesses and lawyers have what is known as "core immunity" for things they say in court, so that they can speak freely there.

The Court of Appeal ruling further expanded such immunity, holding that it extends to an extremely broad range of police activity, including conduct or statements which are part of an investigation leading to a potential prosecution

Most types of legal claim are thus blocked by this immunity, including cases about serious human rights abuses and data breaches, and there are no exemptions for unjustifiable conduct.

Officers can still be prosecuted in the criminal courts and held accountable by police misconduct processes.

News.title: Swinney backs Flynn in ferry gas leak row and says 'nobody's perfect'
News.content:
First Minister John Swinney has backed Stephen Flynn in the row over whether the transport secretary had been briefed about a gas leak on a CalMac ferry.

Speaking to the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg programme in an interview to be broadcast on Sunday, Swinney said emails showed Flynn had not been briefed ahead of a Holyrood committee meeting last month.

The first minister said he had confidence in his transport secretary, who "recognised that he should have been across an issue to be in front of the transport committee and he remedied that right away".

Swinney added: "Nobody's perfect, nobody's infallible".

Flynn was appearing before the transport committee on 9 September when he said he was not aware of a BBC Scotland News story published online more than nine hours earlier.

It revealed how a faulty valve led to 700kg of flammable methane gas being vented from the side of the ferry MV Glen Sannox while it was carrying passengers from Arran to Troon in June 2025.

News.title: Man, 36, arrested six years on from double murder
News.content:
A man has been arrested on suspicion of murder in connection with the fatal shooting of two men more than six years ago.

Junior Ajose, 36, and Cheriff Tall, 21, were shot dead at a lockdown party in the Moss Side area of Manchester in the early hours of 21 June 2020.

A Greater Manchester Police (GMP) spokesperson said a 36-year-old man was detained in Turkey and transported back to England on Saturday, where he was met at Stansted Airport by GMP officers. He remains in custody.

Det Ch Insp Neil Higginson from the force's major incident team said: "This arrest demonstrates our unwavering commitment to securing justice for Junior and Cheriff and their loved ones."

"Over the last six years, myself and my officers have been carrying out multiple warrants, analysing evidence, examining devices that have been seized during the investigation and pursuing every opportunity to identify those responsible," he added.

Ajose and Tall, who did not know each other, were both shot in the head in a car park off Caythorne Street shortly before 01:00 BST and died in hospital.

GMP said it was estimated that between 300 and 400 people were present in the car park that night.

The force issued a further appeal for information on the fifth anniversary of their deaths last year.

Higginson said they were continuing to appeal for information that could help them to establish the full circumstances of what happened that night and to identify any outstanding suspects.

A Â£50,000 reward remains available for key information that leads to the conviction of the killer.

News.title: Russo named England player of the year
News.content:
Forward Alessia Russo has been named England women's player of the year.

The 27-year-old, who also won the award two seasons ago, has been a key player in the 2025-26 campaign, featuring in all 10 games and scoring five goals.

She started nine of those games, including all six of England's 2027 World Cup qualifiers.

Last week, she scored the third goal as England beat Greece 3-1 in their 2027 World Cup play-off semi-final first leg, with the second leg at Leicester's King Power Stadium on Tuesday.

Arsenal's Russo pipped Chelsea pair Lucy Bronze and Hannah Hampton to the award, which is voted for by fans.

"To receive the award is really special, particularly as it comes directly from the fans. I am so grateful for their support," said Russo.

Russo is among 30 players who were nominated in September for the women's Ballon d'Or, with Alex Greenwood the only other English player on the shortlist.
