News.title: Kelly Clarkson fumes over ‘Pretty Woman’ treatment at expensive store: ‘You just lost a huge sale’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Kelly Clarkson has told an upmarket toy store in Brooklyn that they’ve made, in the words of Julia Roberts’ character in Pretty Woman, a “big mistake.”

The 44-year-old singer and former talk show host took to social media to claim that she was treated poorly by staff at Art of Play.

She compared the experience to the famous scene in the 1990 movie where Roberts’ character is looked down on while shopping on Rodeo Drive in Beverly Hills.

Clarkson wrote on X: “Just drove all the way to Brooklyn to check out this store I thought looked really rad and had a few things in mind to buy and literally was looked at as if I couldn’t afford it and was told he could find something comparable for me.”

She continued: “Wow, dude. You’re an idiot and just lost a huge sale. But y’all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts character in Pretty Woman. For sure, check it out.” She concluded her message with a “thumbs down” emoji.

Kelly Clarkson says staff at the New York store looked at her ‘as if I couldn’t afford it’ ( Late Night with Seth Meyers )

The store has since responded to Clarkson’s claim with a statement on Instagram.

Earlier this month, Clarkson surprised fans when she revealed she is “obsessed” with using AI and supports the use of it for creative purposes.

However, she did add that she draws the line at having AI songs on the music charts.

Speaking on the Las Culturistas podcast with Bowen Yang and Matt Rogers, Clarkson said: “It’s controversial, I don’t care – I love AI.

“There’s very amazing things with AI that I’m obsessed with. I’m very into it artistically, too.”

She went on, discussing her argument that there should be separate music charts for AI-generated music.

“But when you see AI artists competing on a chart with humans, I have an issue. I think there should be a separate chart. I think it’s welcome to the table; it’s really cool and creative what we’re going to create with AI musically – people that maybe can’t do certain things will be able to do it now,” she said.

She added that she thinks AI is a “fun field to play in” but she doesn’t believe that robots should be competing with humans in the music industry.

“I’m down with it. It’s a very interesting thing and what we’re gonna do with it is gonna be fun, but I do not think they should be competing,” she said.

News.title: Trump’s new press secretary has a history of pushing bananas conspiracy theories
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The newly appointed White House press secretary Katie Zacharia previously promoted the debunked Pizzagate conspiracy theory and shared posts accusing Democrats and Hollywood elites of being pedophiles and cannibals.

Zacharia, who previously worked as a communications adviser for the president’s Trump Media and Technology Group, shared her deep belief in Pizzagate — as well as other fringe beliefs — on her Truth Social account, according to a report published Sunday by Popular Information.

The fledgling press secretary’s Truth Social posts reveal a deep belief in Pizzagate, the unfounded conspiracy that prominent Democrats, including Hillary Clinton and her 2016 presidential campaign chairman John Podesta, were involved in a child sex trafficking ring.

Pizzagate baselessly claims that Clinton, Podesta and other powerful Democrats ran their sex trafficking business out of a Washington, D.C., pizzeria called Comet Ping Pong.

Zacharia, 41, was so invested in shining a light on the theory that she took to Truth Social on several occasions to try to urge Fox News to report on it.

open image in gallery White House press secretary Katie Zacharia has posted on Truth Social about Pizzagate, QAnon and other fringe conspiracy theories, according to a report ( Getty )

“[W]hy doesn’t Fox News do a ‘feature’ on what a pedophile Podesta is,” she wrote on Truth Social on September 7, 2022, tagging President Donald Trump and Fox News host Sean Hannity.

On September 4, 2022, when it was announced that Podesta had agreed to work in the Biden White House, Zacharia posted “Pedo Podesta. #pedoPodesta.” Later that day, the California native also wrote, “The radical left Hollywood elites are sick pedo cannibals. Change my mind.”

Zacharia continued her petitioning to Hannity a month later, writing on October 17, 2022, “[W]here’s the feature on John Podesta?”

She also shared a post on Truth Social earlier that year that read: “Democrats want to mask and rape your children. That’s their satanic platform,” according to the report.

The new press secretary has also previously publicized her support of QAnon, a conspiracy theory that originated in 2017 as a result of Pizzagate. The theory claims that Trump is secretly fighting a child-abuse group consisting of Democrats, Hollywood and “the deep state.”

open image in gallery Trump said it was his ‘great honor’ to appoint Zacharia to the role of White House press secretary ( PA Wire )

The details of Trump’s apparent fight against pedophiles, according to believers, are revealed through coded messages from the president and online postings from an anonymous account known as Q.

Zacharia responded to a Truth Social user in November 2022 who shared some thoughts on the theory: “Did you notice Trump drinking bottled water last night during his announcement? He drank at least 2-3 times. I have not seen him do that at his speeches or rallies. It reminds me of Q posts 765, 767, and 847. Or was it a signal for something else; by land or by sea.”

Zacharia replied to the post, writing, “I was wondering the same thing…”

When asked about Zacharia’s promotion of conspiracy theories, the White House referred The Independent to Trump’s Truth Social post announcing Zacharia’s appointment on Friday.

Trump wrote that it was his “great honor” to name Zacharia as his latest press secretary. The appointment fills a role that had been left vacant since August, when former press secretary Karoline Leavitt resigned to spend more time with her two young children.

open image in gallery The new press secretary has also shared social media posts promoting QAnon ( Getty )

“She was previously involved in my Campaigns, assisting in key Swing States, where we won 7 out of 7. She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning. She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA,” Trump wrote in the post.

“I am confident that Katie will deliver strong results for our Country as the next White House Press Secretary, as she has the respect of, and will work fantastically with, the Media, the American People, and my Administration.”

In addition to working for the president’s Trump Media and Technology Group, Zacharia, spent roughly a month working at the Department of Homeland Security as a spokesperson earlier this year, according to her LinkedIn.

She has also been a longtime conservative commentator, writing an op-ed declaring Trump “the greatest president in U.S. history,” in The New York Post earlier this year.

News.title: Social care postcode lottery revealed: Study lays bare huge disparity in access in different areas
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

England is facing a social care “postcode lottery” with a huge variation in the number of people who access social care depending on where they live, a new study has found.

A difference of thousands has been found in the number of people who accessed publicly funded long-term social care depending on the council that funds their care, according to a study by think tank The King’s Fund.

Comparing local authorities with similar social and economic makeup, the study found that more than half of councils had variances of 20 per cent more or less people accessing care.

The gap was wider for working-age adults, with variances of up to 101 per cent in the number who access care between comparable councils and up to 60 per cent in care access by those over 65.

In one example given, the King’s Fund found in Thurrock, 7,680 older people per 100,000 accessed long-term care in compared to just 4,810 in Medway. This means that in Thurrock there are 60 per cent more older people accessing care compared to Medway despite being demographically and economically similar.

For working-age adults, however, Thurrock had 10 per cent fewer people accessing care compared to Medway.

The study comes after prime minister Andy Burnham pledged a major overhaul of social care services in the UK, promising to move towards a National Care Service, akin to the National Health Service, from 2028.

The King’s Fund has called for major reforms including “universal access” to publicly funded care, but with co-payments from those using it, a cap on lifetime care costs, a national rather than locally decided funding model for social care and clarity over what individuals are entitled to in terms of support.

Simon Bottery, co-author of the study and senior fellow for social care at The King's Fund, said: “A national care service, which the prime minister has promised, must be genuinely national and ensure that all people, wherever they live, have the same access to social care support.”

“Our new proposals for an ‘equal access’ national assessment would help prevent this issue of unwarranted variation and ensure that access to social care support is not decided by your postcode.”

However, he said that reform of social care must go even further and ensure there is universal access to at least some publicly funded support and a cap on the costs people are expected to pay for care.

He said: “Currently, one in seven people aged 65 will spend at least £100,000 in lifetime care costs. We must also introduce fairer, national funding of social care, with greater choice and control for people and their families over how their care needs are met.”

“The prime minister and Baroness Casey's commitment to reform is clear, but we are still awaiting the concrete policies that will turn this vision into a reality. To achieve that, their proposals will need to focus not just on who pays but on how the wider system operates on the ground.”

The Department for Health and Social Care was approached for comment.

News.title: Burnham warned ‘steady as she goes Budget’ would mean ‘chunky cuts’ to public services as inflation bites
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Leading economists have warned Andy Burnham against a “steady-as-she-goes” Budget later this month, saying it would lead to ‘chunky cuts’ to public services because of inflation.

The problem would be exacerbated if defence spending rises as ministers want, the leading think tank the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) found.

Following former chancellor Rachel Reeves’ battles to create enough fiscal “headroom” in the public finances, the IFS said new chancellor John Healey’s key problem would be tackling high inflation, driven in part by the war in the Middle East.

Inflation will erode the budgets of government departments, creating the need for injections of potentially tens of billions of pounds or large cuts to some public services.

Director of the IFS Helen Miller said: “John Healey likely faces a forecast in which borrowing is still expected to fall in coming years and the fiscal rules are still being met.

open image in gallery ( PA Archive )

“Despite that, a ‘steady-as-she-goes’ Budget is not an option available to the chancellor.

“Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments’ spending plans off course.

“It would be a choice to tolerate chunky cuts to the quantity or quality of some public services – cuts that would be larger if defence spending was increased within existing totals.”

The IFS said Mr Healey must also clarify the spending limits he is “willing to live within”, warning that his plan to meet the fiscal rules, and not spook the markets, would only be plausible if it is based on “credible spending totals”.

open image in gallery Chancellor John Healey will set out his first Budget later this month (PA) ( PA Wire )

Unless ministers implement highly controversial cuts to health spending or to plans to increase defence spending remained unchanged, the figures imply real-terms cuts to other departments.

These pressures mean avoiding cuts to departments’ budgets could require a combined top-up to day-to-day and investment spending of around £25bn in 2030–31, the IFS said.

It added: “A choice to leave spending totals unchanged would implicitly be a choice to cut some budgets and allow the quality and/or quantity of some public services to fall.”

“On the other hand, increasing spending to avoid cuts to budgets and fund higher defence spending could require tax rises or benefit cuts of around £35 billion.

“The chancellor must decide where to land on that spectrum.”

The think tank also said the chancellor’s plan to reduce borrowing in order to meet the fiscal rules will be predicated on the spending totals he sets out.

“If John Healey sets out spending envelopes for public services that he would not be willing to live within, his plan for meeting the fiscal rules will not be credible,” it added.

The IFS also stressed that “now is not a good time to substantially increase borrowing” as debt remains historically high, with interest costs having more than doubled as a share of GDP since 2019.

open image in gallery Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the Government ‘will not take risks with people’s living standards’ in the Budget (Stefan Rousseau/PA) ( PA Wire )

Ms Miller warned the chancellor does not have to set out detailed spending plans at the Budget. She said: “If he chooses the path of squeezing public spending, he should be transparent that there are tough years ahead for some public services.

“Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the Budget a work of fiction.”

Mr Healey is set to visit Bangkok for the IMF annual meetings this week, where he will tell international counterparts that major economies need credible plans to get borrowing under control.

“The consequences of conflict in the Middle East and Europe are hitting countries worldwide, leading to higher prices at the pumps and more expensive mortgages at home, but Britain and our allies can face up to these challenges together.

“I will work with our international partners to keep trade moving, support families and businesses, and make Britain’s economy stronger and more resilient to deliver good growth in every postcode.

“My Budget will build on this approach with fiscal discipline helping to deliver economic resilience. This means breathing space for today, and hope for the future.”

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: “Higher borrowing costs and Andy Burnham’s unfunded spending commitments have swallowed up his headroom and created upward inflationary pressure.

“Labour raised taxes by £66 billion in its first two budgets. Families cannot afford to be lumbered with even more tax rises at this Budget. Labour should cut welfare instead of dumping on working people as they have already done.”

Green Party leader Zack Polanski said: “Economists are telling the Chancellor today that a steady-as-she-goes budget ‘is not an option’.

“With three in five families already cutting back on spending, and many about to see a £300 increase in their bills in January, we’re challenging the government to take bold and immediate action on the cost of living.

“For a start, this means moving more costs off energy bills, properly funding a national home insulation scheme, clamping down on profiteering by energy companies and rapidly scaling up cheaper, cleaner energy.”

News.title: Warning AI-generated complaints are pushing stretched NHS GPs to the limit
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Family doctors are being sent 20-page complaints written by artificial intelligence, according to a healthcare defence organisation.

The Medical Protection Society (MPS), which provides legal and indemnity advice to health workers, warned that overly complicated AI-assisted letters are adding to GP workloads.

A survey of nearly 160 UK practice managers revealed that just 7 per cent have never received an AI-generated complaint.

Meanwhile, 45 per cent stated that patient complaints drafted with AI are compounding workload pressures and damaging staff morale and wellbeing.

Dr Sarah Townley, deputy medical director at MPS, said: “AI can empower and support patients in communicating concerns – particularly if confidence, language barriers or health conditions make written communication difficult.

open image in gallery The study suggests some complaints are as long as 20 pages long ( AFP/Getty )

“Even where these issues do not exist, AI removes much of the time involved in producing written material.

“However, at MPS, we are concerned about the surge in GP practice staff seeking support with AI-generated complaints, and the impact this appears to be having on practice teams’ wellbeing and workload.

“Letters can be 20 pages, sometimes longer. They are often complicated, include detailed but occasionally questionable legal arguments, and many fail to remove the AI tool’s ‘coaching’ and common tells.

“Our members take patient complaints seriously and consider each one carefully, but responding to AI-generated correspondence takes a considerable amount of time and work, as the patient’s concerns are often more difficult to decipher.

“This may be diverting time away from patient care, and leading to a less satisfactory outcome for patients.

“One MPS member, after working with us to reply to such a letter, received a further response from the patient within minutes, raising new issues not included in the original complaint. Understandably they felt bewildered and frustrated.

“The benefit of being able to produce a complaint in a matter of seconds also appears to be having the effect of lowering the thresholds around what patients will complain about, and encouraging more complaints to be made in the heat of the moment rather than using simpler routes to resolve an issue.”

Professor Victoria Tzortziou Brown, president of the Royal College of GPs, said patients have the right to raise concerns or make complaints about the care they receive “and complaints can play an important role in accountability, learning and improving services”.

She added: “GP practices take complaints seriously and will have processes in place to investigate and respond appropriately.

“Technology, including AI, may make it easier for patients to raise concerns and improve accessibility for some people, but it also risks producing complaints that are unnecessarily lengthy, complex or contain inaccurate information.

“AI-generated complaints may also include legal language that is disproportionate to the concerns being raised, making them more difficult and time-consuming for GPs and our teams to interpret and respond to.

“What matters is understanding the patient’s concerns, what has happened and what can be done to address them.

“GPs are also increasingly dealing with complaints that reflect wider frustrations with pressures across the NHS, including delays in hospital or community care that are outside the control of individual practices.

“Dealing with complex or threatening complaints can place considerable additional pressure on already overstretched teams and take an emotional toll.

“It’s vital that complaints processes maintain careful human judgement, and that concerns are considered fairly, proportionately and on an individual basis.”

The Public Service Ombudsman has issued guidance for patients on using AI to write complaints.

It says “simple, clear language that explains what happened is always more helpful than complicated, formal writing.”

It says AI providers may use personal information to train their systems and may process it in other countries.

The guide also says patients should not “ask AI to add legal arguments, use formal legal language or refer to laws to make your complaint sound more ‘official’.”

News.title: Max Verstappen is back and Mercedes are already worried
News.content:
Kimi Antonelli, third: “It was a very tough race out there but really happy with a podium at the end, I managed to take advantage of the fight between Lewis and Lando. To take P3 is a great result from the team, very happy with that.”

He is told that he can clinch the title at the next race:

“Can I, really? Let’s not worry about that. Let’s try to do the best weekend possible and finish the job.”

Charles Leclerc, second: “We were quite strong at the beginning of the race and then we started degrading at the end of the first stint. I pushed a lot at the beginning of the last stint and then degraded a bit more than the others. I gave it all and I don’t regret anything.

“I don’t think there’s anything more we could do but be a bit more aggressive at the start. It’s true that we brought some small new parts to the car which maybe helped us to do a little step forward but it’s enough. Today I think we had a good pace overall.”

Max Verstappen, winner: “It’s taken a while but I think this race was very good. We had pace when we needed to have it on the soft tyre and the medium. Very happy to win here. You always try to do your best and luckily [the start] it was just good enough.

“I think the last few races have been really positive for us. It’s great to see and we have a lot of motivation in the team to try to deliver even more results... hopefully we can have a bit more fun until the end of the year.”

News.title: The cheats prosper: Man City thrash 10-man Liverpool
News.content:
Just when the Premier League and the world outside of east Manchester and Abu Dhabi needed Liverpool to step up, to strike back, to make a point, they faltered. Maybe it was unfair to expect them to do so, given the circumstances. But unfairness, lack of clarity and uncertainty are all prevailing moods in English football at present.

How we had rubbed our hands in anticipation of Manchester City having to play their first league fixture here at Anfield after being found guilty of industrial-scale fraud with 114 of the 115 financial charges being proven against them.

It felt apt that it was at the home of Liverpool, who, along with Arsenal, possess the strongest sense of grievance at having been denied trophies and glory by City’s cheating. As expected, there were banners everywhere at Anfield. “A generation of supporters cheated,” one read and it summed up the depth of the anger.

News.title: Three tasks to get your home ready for autumn, according to a professional cleaner
News.content:
When I was sweating away this summer, I never thought the weather would turn, but it’s almost time to crank up our radiators and crack out the big duvet.

They’re the tasks no one likes doing, but luckily for you, I’ve worked as a cleaner for more than a decade. I’ve discovered some shortcuts to make the hated jobs that bit easier.

Tip one: Keep your summer duvet fresh in storage

If, like me, you want to get your winter duvet out, your summer one needs to be cleaned and packed away to keep it fresh come spring.

Start by spot cleaning any stains. You can just use a standard household fabric stain remover for this. If you want to wash your duvet, most domestic washing machines aren’t big enough to fit a double, let alone a king or a super king. Your best bet is to take them down to the laundrette and follow the care instructions on the label.

News.title: Man Utd make worst start in 40 years after being hauled back by 10-man Spurs
News.content:
The Tottenham boss told Sky Sports: “I think we played very well against a great team. We had many chances to score in the first half. Three or four. The second half is normal to suffer against this quality. I am very happy because I have seen the right spirit and character.

“We suffered in the game but every situation of the game. I like the situation we were in with the red card. We need this situation. We have not accepted the defeat. We have to react in all ways we can. It is a bad way, it is not the right way. I kiss Bentancur in the dressing room. Football is character.

“We win the game if we play as a team. We didn’t win this game playing as a team. Every game like today, we will win many games.”

When asked about Solanke, he replied: “He is a good player for Tottenham. There for not too many strikers better than Solanke. Today he was captain because he deserved it, especially in this moment because he suffer because Tottenham didn’t score or win any games. He is a great guy, great player and we are behind him.

“We have to believe in ourselves and this football way. If we believe, improve and play as a team, we will score many goals and win many games. If we don’t play as a team, it is impossible.”

News.title: Guimaraes looks a £75m bargain as ‘super sub’ makes difference
News.content:
Before the game we talked about two things, the challenge ahead against a team that had not lost in the Premier League. They full deserved to be where they are and it was going to be really tough. The second was to restore our identity and be ourselves again.

We weren’t pleased with our performance against Brighton and we wanted to put it right. But the context is that this was a difficult one [opponent]. But we reacted in a way that was unique and made it so special.

[Leeds] are very well organised, very physical and very committed in everything that they do. They are a threat. They are incredible the way they attack the ball and set-pieces, with belief. They came close to punishing us. They have individual quality and they are in a good moment.

When you play at 12.30 at home and you go one-nil down there’s a lot to do. You have to restore a lot of things. Energy is one of them. We had an incredible response. The crowd changed. You could see it.

We brought a lot of leadership on [with his three subs]. We brought goal threat, to win duels, people who can play forward and penetrate against their high press.

The timing, movement and execution of it [the winning goal], yes, it was a beauty.

News.title: Resurgent Verstappen on fire in the Singapore smog
News.content:
Welcome to our live coverage for the sprint race for the 2026 Singapore Grand Prix from the Marina Bay Circuit. Given the way the championship standings are, it looks like Kimi Antonelli has one hand on the drivers’ title. That means that the most significant thing is the battle for individual race victories. That includes grands prix, but also sprint races, like we have today.

Formula One is very keen on sprint races, increasing their number significantly next year, but we have never had one in Singapore before. We will find out today whether there was good reason for it. I suppose the logic is that even a processional sprint race is better than a free practice session and that having two qualifying sessions on a street circuit such as this is exciting, too.

Still, although he might be strolling towards the championship, he and Mercedes are not the dominant force they were at the start of the season when he won five in a row having finished second in the opening race. In fact, in the last 10 grands prix, Antonelli has won three and Russell two. With Max Verstappen’s win in Malaysia last weekend it meant each of Red Bull, McLaren, Ferrari and Mercedes have won races this season.

It is Verstappen who is in strong form in an upgraded Red Bull, as he snuck pole position from George Russell by just over a tenth of a second. He was followed by Charles Leclerc in the Ferrari and then Oscar Piastri in the McLaren. Antonelli, in the upgraded Mercedes, found things more difficult, finishing down in seventh nearly 0.7sec off the pace.

Anyway, the sprint gets under way in about 30 minutes and we will be here for all the updates from that, as well as qualifying later today.

News.title: Majestic All Blacks copy Springbok playbook to dismantle Australia
News.content:
Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of this Bledisloe Cup Test as New Zealand host Australia at Eden Park in Auckland.

The All Blacks are enduring one of the toughest periods in their history, having suffered three successive Test defeats against South Africa in August and September, which saw the Springboks claim the inaugural Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series tour. Dave Rennie’s men are under immense pressure to avoid a fourth consecutive Test defeat for the first time since 1998.

You could argue there’s never been a better opportunity for Australia to beat New Zealand at Eden Park. The Wallabies are enjoying a six-Test unbeaten run – their longest such streak since 2017, with five games in this rejuvenated period coming under new head coach Les Kiss. In their most recent outing, Australia secured an extraordinary 42-38 victory over a much-changed South Africa side in Perth, despite being reduced to 11 players at one point.

Australia will feel further encouraged due to several key absences for New Zealand, as Ardie Savea, Ruben Love, Richie Mo’unga, Caleb Clarke, Fehi Fineanganofo, Billy Proctor and Anton Lienert-Brown are all out injured. In a reshuffle for the All Blacks, Damian McKenzie will begin at fly-half for the first time in 2026. Other notable inclusions for the home side see all three Barrett brothers, Codie Taylor, Tupou Vaa’i, Cam Roigard and Will Jordan starting.

Meanwhile, the visitors are without the suspended Hunter Paisami, with Isaac Henry taking his place at centre. The likes of Ryan Lonergan, Len Ikitau, Harry Wilson, Ben Donaldson and Max Jorgensen, who were all key to the triumph against the Springboks, retain their starting spots.

All the statistics overwhelmingly favour New Zealand. The All Blacks have not lost any edition of the Bledisloe Cup since 2002, winning 51 series to Australia’s 12, and are unbeaten at Eden Park since 1994, when they lost to France. Australia are winless at Eden Park since 1986, tasting defeat there 30 times in 34 games, and have lost their last 11 Tests against New Zealand.

However, given the landscape heading into this historic rivalry between these two heavyweights, it genuinely feels like anything could happen.

Kick-off is at 7:10am.

News.title: Black British Business Awards 2026 winners revealed
News.content:
The chief executive of Dr. Martens has been named the Black British Business Person of the Year at the 2026 Black British Business Awards (BBBAwards).

Ije Nwokorie, who became chief of Dr. Martens in January last year and is the only black chief executive in the FTSE 250, was awarded in recognition of his role shaping Dr. Martens’ growth strategy.

He is recognised inside Dr. Martens for his strong communication with staff, according to the judges.

Before joining Dr. Martens, Mr Nwokorie spent more than 11 years at Wolff Olins, the marketing giant, before working as a senior director at Apple.

Born in the US but brought up from age six against the backdrop of post-civil-war Nigeria, Mr Nwokorie has described how he and his family went from the lifestyle trappings of 1960s America to a small Nigerian village and a home with no running water.

On winning the award, Mr Nwokorie said: “This recognition means a lot to me. While this award bears my name, it reflects the talent, dedication and generosity of the incredible teammates, mentors and leaders who have shaped me as a person and a professional.

“It is a powerful reminder that there is nothing more important in our leadership journeys than the time we invest to help others thrive.”

Alongside his executive career, he has served as a trustee at Charity: water for nearly a decade and held board roles at cultural and humanitarian organisations including the Institute of International Visual Arts and Malaria No More UK.

He also served as chairman of trustees for the Chineke! Orchestra, a British orchestra championing change and the first in Europe to feature a majority of black and ethnically diverse musicians.

The Black British Business Awards started in 2014 to celebrate the achievements of black people in British business. The Telegraph is the national media partner for the awards.

Mr Nwokorie was presented with the award at an exclusive ceremony sponsored by JPMorgan Chase at London’s Hilton Park Lane hotel.

Speaking at the ceremony, Sophie Chandauka, the executive founder of the awards, said: “You lend the BBBAwards credibility not simply to celebrate excellence, but to ensure the best and brightest from all communities get a fair shot. That commitment has made the BBBAwards the UK’s premium awards programme for black business achievement.”

A spokesman for JPMorgan Chase said: “We couldn’t be prouder to support and celebrate such an outstanding breadth of black British talent.

“Their accomplishments continue to inspire future generations and demonstrate the exceptional value they bring to businesses, communities and the wider UK economy.”

This year’s winners are as follows:

Black British Business Person of the Year: Ije Nwokorie, chief executive of Dr Martens

Arts and Media Rising Star: Sheniece Charway, artist partnership manager [EMEA], YouTube/Google

Arts and Media Senior Leader: Amie Parker-Williams, director, digital commissioning and production, Paramount

Fashion, Beauty and Consumer Senior Leader: Andrea Thompson, journalist, brand consultant and former editor-in-chief, Marie Claire UK

Fashion, Beauty and Consumer Rising Star: Yasmin O’Neal, senior director for global brand and impact, DECIEM

Entrepreneur Rising Star: Dr Elsa Zekeng, founder and chief executive, SökerData

Entrepreneur Senior Leader: Antonia Okonma Shittu, founder and chief executive, A-List Lace Hair

Financial Services Rising Star: Nana Agyemang, proposition delivery manager, Barclays

Professional Services Rising Star: Jack Van Cooten, senior manager – external vendors and data, Oliver Wyman

Professional Services Senior Leader: Laurie-Anne Power KC, barrister, 25 Bedford Row

Sports.title: Hits & Misses: Anderson and Wirtz offering opposite value for money
Sports.content:
Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player FREE TO WATCH: Highlights from Liverpool's match against Manchester City in the Premier League

Manchester City's siege mentality won out at Liverpool. Their quality with a man over telling, if not quite so obvious when both sides had a full complement of players for an hour of the game.

Absolutely everything good about City in their 3-0 win was summed up by the classy performance of Elliot Anderson.

Not for the first time since his mega-money move from Nottingham Forest, the midfielder's mastery on the ball was matched by his maturity off it. A "bargain" at £116m, according to Jamie Carragher, every bit capable, in his own way, of exerting as much control and influence on games as Rodri did in this role.

While the spotlight shines ever brighter on City as a club, and forensics pour over their spending, Anderson remains the picture of calm. Everything a manager would want in a modern-day holding midfielder: a robust runner, aggressive tackler and clever distributor. "He dominates big games," says Gary Neville.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Gary Neville says Elliot Andersen looks a real top performer and has quickly proven he is worth every penny that Manchester City have spent on him

Rarely fazed by the occasion, Anderson has won at Anfield two years running - with two different sides. Of course the way Forest went about success last term shared few similarities with City's more technical display. The only common denominator? Elliot Anderson.

Laura Hunter

Florian Wirtz played his part with the pressing and the constant movement that was a hallmark of Liverpool's up-tempo approach that made life so difficult for Manchester City for an hour at Anfield. But that bit of magic that the supporters wanted was missing.

Rayan Cherki provided that for City's third and final goal, by which point Wirtz was sat on the Liverpool bench having been substituted. Another big game in which the Germany international was unable to provide the spark for his side.

Wirtz's goals for Liverpool December 27th 2025 – Premier League – Wolves (h)

January 4th 2026 – Premier League – Fulham (a)

January 12th 2026 – FA Cup – Barnsley (h)

January 17th 2026 – Premier League – Burnley (h)

January 28th 2026 – Champions League – Qarabag (h)

January 31st 2026 – Premier League – Newcastle (h)

April 25th 2026 – Premier League – Crystal Palace (h)

Too many loose touches and loose passes, one or two tackles shirked. Victor Munoz and Lewis Koumas are easy for supporters to embrace with their bustling styles but Wirtz is a player who glides across the turf and he needs end product to justify his role.

Wirtz lost possession 17 times Florian Wirtz lost possession 17 times in Liverpool's 3-0 home defeat to Manchester City, more than any other player.

There was one shot lashed wide with the game goalless and better options to his left. It is no goals for Wirtz this season and just one in his last 16 Premier League appearances. Another opportunity missed for a classy player still seemingly unable to impose himself.

Adam Bate

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player FREE TO WATCH: Highlights from the Premier League match between Crystal Palace and Nottingham Forest

Crystal Palace have shown signs of rediscovering their attacking spark under Pierre Sage, with their 3-1 comeback win over Nottingham Forest the latest example.

The Eagles have now scored three or more goals in two of their last four league games - as often as they managed across their previous 37 Premier League matches combined.

Goals and entertaining football were a problem during Oliver Glasner's latter days in charge, as Palace struggled to balance their domestic and European commitments.

There is an early sense of a throwback to the more free-scoring side that flourished under the Austrian in his first season, when their pace, movement and attacking combinations made them a threat to anyone.

It is still early in Sage's tenure, and two high-scoring performances do not guarantee a lasting change. But Palace look to be playing with greater freedom and confidence, with Daichi Kamada, Jefferson Lerma and Yeremy Pino all finding the net against Forest.

If Sage can sustain that attacking momentum while tightening up a defence that has been vulnerable this season, there are encouraging signs of a more dangerous Palace taking shape.

William Bitibiri

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the Premier League match between Hull and Everton

Everton are unbeaten after six matches for just the third time in the Premier League era. In 2006/07 and 2013/14 they finished sixth and then fifth from this position.

It is a testament to the hard work of David Moyes, who has returned to challenging circumstances in his second Everton spell, that he has got the club back to looking upwards.

For the last five seasons, Everton have been in the bottom half, often battling relegation. Now, it seems, they have a genuine chance to push up the table and dare to dream bigger.

However, it is hard to see how Moyes can drag them into Europe with Thierno Barry as his only striker. The 23-year-old scored in the end in the 2-2 draw at Hull, but, according to Opta, he needed five big chances to find the back of the net. At least two of those had to go in.

If Everton are to qualify for Europe, they will need a striker who wins them points. At Hull, you could argue they had a striker who cost them points.

Barry, who is Everton's top scorer since the start of last season in the Premier League (11 goals), is improving all the time, but the current situation is unfair on him and his manager. Right now he cannot be depended on consistently.

The Frenchman, who has started all eight of Everton's matches this season, appeared to pull up with cramp towards the end at Hull and Moyes had no choice but to replace him with Charly Alcaraz, who is a midfielder by trade.

There was only four minutes plus stoppage time to go, but it almost felt as if Everton were forced to give up on chasing a late winner. This was a match that was there for the taking.

The plan, of course, was to have Folarin Balogun in the squad. However, his move from Monaco collapsed at the last minute on Deadline Day.

The obvious solution would be to go back in for a striker in January. It remains to be seen how the uncertainty at ownership level will impact their plans. Moyes needs - and deserves - another striker to have a proper chance at a push for Europe.

Zinny Boswell

Mohamed Belloumi is making the difference for Hull City - even when he is tired.

The Algeria winger was benched for the first time this season against Everton after telling head coach Sergej Jakirovic on Friday that he was fatigued after playing three times for his country during the international break.

Belloumi still made a crucial impact on Sunday, netting Hull's equaliser to earn them a point. He has been pivotal in the club's good start, scoring or assisting five of their eight Premier League goals this season.

The 24-year-old was signed from Portuguese side Farense in August 2024 and scored only five goals in 35 Championship appearances over two seasons, but, at a higher level, his pace and fearless dribbling has made a significant contribution already.

Belloumi will return to being the first name on their teamsheet at Fulham next weekend and, if his early-season form is anything to go by, defences will have plenty more to worry about.

David Richardson

Sports.title: How Antonelli could win F1 world title as soon as the next race
Sports.content:
Kimi Antonelli could become Formula 1's youngest world champion as early as the next race - the United States Grand Prix - on October 25.

Mercedes' Antonelli increased his lead at the top of the Drivers' Championship to a season-high 102 points with a third-place finish in the Singapore Grand Prix.

George Russell remains second in the standings but a ninth-place finish after engine penalties had left him starting at the back of the grid dropped him beyond a century of points behind his team-mate for the first time, while Lewis Hamilton's late slide off the podium leaves the Ferrari driver 111 points off the pace in third place.

With such a large lead and with a scheduled six races left in the 2026 season, the world title now looks a formality for the 20-year-old Italian in just his second year of F1 to usurp Sebastian Vettel as the sport's youngest title winner.

A first chance - albeit an outside one - to clinch the crown will arrive as soon as the next race at Austin's Circuit of the Americas, live on Sky Sports F1…

Image: How it stands after the Singapore Grand Prix

How Antonelli could win the title at the United States GP

There will be five scheduled races left - Mexico, Brazil, Las Vegas, Qatar and Abu Dhabi - after the United States Grand Prix takes place on Sunday October 25 and a maximum of 125 points left to play for.

To win the title in Austin, Antonelli needs to increase his championship lead by 23 points. For that to happen he must win the grand prix AND then hope both Russell and Hamilton do not score sufficient points to stay within 124 points of him going to Mexico.

The permutations for Antonelli to become champion in Austin are:

Antonelli wins the race (25 points)

and

Russell finishes ninth or lower (2 points or less)

and

Hamilton finishes fifth or lower (10 points or less)

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Russell takes over from Antonelli's engineer during the Sprint rain delay in Singapore

Were Antonelli to win the race and Russell finish ninth, Antonelli would hold a 125-point lead over his team-mate with exactly 125 points left to play for. But that would still be enough for Antonelli to become champion, provided Hamilton was also still outside the top four in the race.

That is because victory in Austin would be the the Italian's ninth of the year and with Russell on three wins the Briton would only be able to get to a maximum of eight in the five races left. Antonelli would therefore be guaranteed the title on results countback, with race wins the first tiebreaker in event of an end-of-season points tie.

What about the other drivers still in mathematical contention?

Max Verstappen (119 points back), Charles Leclerc (125 points back) and Lando Norris (139 points back) all remain in mathematical title contention too after Singapore but would all be automatically knocked out by an Antonelli win in Austin wherever they finished that race.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Toto Wolff hits back at accusations that Mercedes favour Antonelli over Russell

'If I don't do my job well, then the result won't come' - Antonelli vows to stay focused

Antonelli is now within touching distance of an incredible historic achievement but stressed after Singapore that he cannot afford to let that fact distract him from his performance in Austin.

"I know it's very close, I know it's there, but I just need to make sure that I keep doing the best I can," he said.

"You know, the mindset is always the same, to go out there and win and perform the best way I can. I think this weekend [in Singapore] I haven't particularly driven that well. I felt like I could have done a better job, but I feel confident that, you know, a week to reset and I'm really looking forward to being back in Austin.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the 2026 Singapore Grand Prix

"But, at the end of the day, if I don't do my job well, then the result won't come. So in order to achieve what I want, I need to perform, as simple as that."

Sports.title: Man City defiant and top of the table - but Anfield delivers its own verdict
Sports.content:
The chant from The Kop went up early. "You haven't won a trophy since 1976." It was a reference to Manchester City's League Cup triumph, the last major honour that the club picked up prior to the period of ownership that now finds itself under such scrutiny.

As it is, City remain top of the table having won six games from six. But this victory will not quieten the noise. They departed to boos and the accusations of cheating that were a feature of the day.

Liverpool, three times runners-up to Manchester City in 2014, 2019 and 2022, made for perfect but hostile hosts, with the Anfield crowd perhaps the ideal outlet for the emotions, a proxy for supporters everywhere. It was an atmosphere like no other.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Man City arrive at Anfield ahead of their Premier League match against Liverpool - their first since being found guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of Premier League financial rules by an independent commission

The enterprising flag and scarf sellers in Liverpool were certainly prepared, with an unusual emphasis on the visitors, this being City's first game since an independent commission judged that they broke Premier League rules between 2009 and 2018.

City are appealing that verdict and continue to deny any wrongdoing.

But the court of opinion is making its voice heard too. Anfield has made up its mind. The banners referred to "a generation of supporters cheated" and a playful take on Wonderwall with the amended line that "you really robbed us all".

Even the choice of songs over the public-address system appeared to be pointed. Before kick-off at Anfield, we had Blame by Calvin Harris and a blast of The Joker and the Thief by Wolfmother. Upon the final whistle, it was Little Lies by Fleetwood Mac.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Roy Keane shares his thoughts on Manchester City following the club being found guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of Premier League financial rules by an independent commission

As expected, City's supporters opted for defiance in the face of the criticism. The boos for the Premier League anthem are nothing new but carried extra resonance. The banner declaring that 'In Khaldoon we trust' an eye-opening indication of the devotion of some.

Others preferred to shift the focus from their current predicament. There was more than a hint of nostalgia in a nod to the fact that there is far more to their club than how their rivals perceive them. Poznan dances and inflatable bananas served as a symbol of that.

The latter custom, one that dates back to Imre Varadi - 'Imre Banana' to the fans in the late '80s - is a reminder that City were always really here. This remains a proud club. The message being sent is that the downs are part of their story just as much as the ups.

Image: Man City fans wave inflatable bananas during their win over Liverpool at Anfield

But the overriding emotions inside the stadium belonged to the majority, those wearing Liverpool red, and the reality is that City and these charges are part of their story too. Anyone allowing the mind to wander at Anfield on Sunday could not escape that history.

Glance down to the spot on the turf where Steven Gerrard slipped to let in Demba Ba in 2014. Liverpool lost that game to Chelsea but lost that title to City. How can this ruling not change the tone and temperature of that regret? Sadness is now tinged with anger.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Micah Richards says he is devastated and confused by Manchester City's guilty ruling and claims that, as a player during the period in question, his integrity is being questioned

And so, for Liverpool, this is not only about City's trophies not being 'real' but those phantom triumphs of their own. "Until you've repaid the dreams you bought for your lies you'll be castaway alone under stormy skies." A banner in the Sir Kenny Dalglish Stand.

This game itself was a reminder that these matters are ongoing. The charges are historic but the consequences are part of the present.

A strange afternoon had a strange ending too - The Kop chanted 'going down' while the league table shows that City are top.

"That is the backdrop to not knowing where these points and this season is going," rued Gary Neville on commentary. "There is going to be a 'but' all the way."

Resolution cannot come soon enough.

Sports.title: 'Barely a foul' - Carra criticises 'shocking' Gravenberch red card decision
Sports.content:
Ryan Gravenberch's sending off in Liverpool's 3-0 home defeat to Manchester City was a "shocking decision" by referee Chris Kavanagh, according to Sky Sports pundit Jamie Carragher.

Gravenberch, the standout player for an hour, was shown red after receiving a second yellow for a challenge on Jeremy Doku with the game tied at 0-0 in a flashpoint that turned the game, which had been finely poised, in City's favour.

Erling Haaland's opener came just two minutes and 37 seconds after Gravenberch was dismissed, and within six minutes Doku had doubled City's advantage before Rayan Cherki added a third with 12 minutes to play.

Gravenberch had picked up his first caution shortly after the restart for a foul on City midfielder Elliot Anderson, which Sky Sports pundit Carragher described as a "nothing challenge".

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player FREE TO WATCH: Highlights from Liverpool’s match against Manchester City in the Premier League.

"It's such a poor decision by the referee," Carragher said after the game. "The thing that frustrates me is that he wasn't going to give a yellow card. He only gives it when he thinks Anderson is hurt.

"That has nothing to do with whether a foul should or should not be a yellow card."

He added: "It's barely a foul. It's a shocking decision."

"It feels really harsh when you think of the two challenges," Carragher said of Gravenberch's sending off on co-commentary.

"The first one was not a yellow card. It was so harsh for a nothing challenge on Anderson, and the referee was far too quick to get the yellow card out."

Sky Sports' Gary Neville, also on co-commentary, said Gravenberch's second yellow was "very soft", before adding: "The only thing I would say is, knowing you're on a yellow and wrong side of Doku, does he need to make the challenge?

"He's given the referee a dilemma."

'Liverpool looked like they had four sent off'

Manchester City had an xG of 0.16 before Gravenberch's sending off but dominated once Liverpool were down to 10 men.

Sky Sports pundit Roy Keane felt Gravenberch's dissmissal turned the match in City's favour but criticised Liverpool's response to the red card.

"I don't see how he can get a yellow card for that," Keane said of Gravenberch's first booking. "The whole game then changes.

"Liverpool struggled with the physicality. There were spaces everywhere. Liverpool looked like they had four men sent off. City were controlling it. For the first hour it was a tight game."

Daniel Sturridge was in full agreement and said the decision to award Gravenberch's first yellow card was "a joke".

"The game changed on the red card. We have to be truthful about that," Sturridge said on Sky Sports. "City delivered after the red card changed the game. Prior to that, it was very even."

Sky Sports' Micah Richards was equally puzzled about the first booking the Liverpool midfielder received. "That is soft. How is that a yellow card? I don't understand," said Richards.

Sports.title: Greaves ends Women's Series season with record-breaking win
Sports.content:
Beau Greaves ended her 2026 PDC Women's Series season with a record-breaking streak of victories on the way to two tournament wins at Event 23 and 24 in Wigan.

Greaves - who had already claimed back-to-back titles in Event 21 and 22 on Saturday - averaged 98.75 on the way to her third successive competition title at Event 23, marking the highest event-winning average in the history of the Women's Series.

The Yorkshire native - who has won 17 out of a possible 24 Women's Series events this year - won all of her first four matches by a 4-0 scoreline, posting a stunning 103.66 average in her victory against Steph Clark.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Chris Murphy suggests Beau Greaves should be given more opportunities to play against the men after she once again won the Women's World Matchplay.

She lost her first legs of the day in her 5-2 victory against Gemma Hayter in the quarter-finals, before beating Fallon Sherrock - who confirmed her own return to the World Darts Championship on Saturday - in the semi-final.

Her 5-3 victory against Jade Gofford in the final confirmed her first title of the day, before beating Laura van den Berg, Sara Walton, Vicky Martin and Lauren Bloomfield to reach the quarter-finals of event 24.

Image: Sherrock and Greaves will both compete at Alexandra Palace

Wins against Kirsty Hutchinson and 20-year-old Italian Aurora Fochesato confirmed her second title of the day and her fourth of the weekend to cap off a successful 2026 season.

"I felt good," Greaves said. "I was chuffed with the first competition. I had some good averages and then I played steady enough in the second event.

"I knew I hadn't been playing at my best recently, but I've had some good moments today and I'm ready to build on it and take this into the back end of the year."

The Wigan double-header also saw Vicky Pruim claim the final spot on offer to compete in the World Darts Championship through the Women's Series rankings, joining Greaves, Sherrock, Hayter and Lisa Ashton.

Sports.title: Cherki cracker caps Manchester City win at Liverpool in face of Anfield taunts
Sports.content:
It is a soundtrack that Manchester City have heard before but never for such sustained spells during a match. It came from the Liverpool support, first ringing out around Anfield before kick-off and coming at regular intervals thereafter.

It was always going to be like this as City felt their way into a new reality, one conditioned by the guilty verdicts handed to them by an independent commission on virtually all of the 115 charges they have faced for breaking the Premier League’s financial rules. City maintain their innocence and have appealed.

The Kop wanted to tell City what they are. And where they were going. They wanted to tell them again and again. According to them, they are cheats, who are set to be relegated. It was not exactly a bear pit of an atmosphere; not truly intimidating. It was just an outpouring of anger and it was impossible to ignore.

City did not care. They rolled with the invective. And after a slow-burn contest turned on a second yellow card for the Liverpool midfielder, Ryan Gravenberch, in the 62nd minute, City cut loose. All that their players can do is try to blot out the noise. They did so here, running all over Liverpool’s 10 men to maintain their 100% start to the Premier League season. The key theme from them – and their fans – was defiance. City intend to keep doing what they do.

It was Erling Haaland, inevitably, who lashed them in front and Jérémy Doku, on as a game-changing substitute in the 56th minute, who curled them further ahead with a beauty. The best was still to come. Again, Doku was involved. And after Rayan Cherki dummied a pass from Elliot Anderson, he ran on to a backheel from another substitute, Josko Gvardiol. Cherki had work to do. He did it when he cut away from Jeremie Frimpong, on as a substitute, and rolled home. It was a team goal marked by individual brilliance.

Liverpool were broken and en route to a first defeat under Andoni Iraola. The manager was undermined by the absence of arguably his three best players so far this season; Dominik Szoboszlai, Cody Gakpo and Alexander Isak all picked up injuries during the international window. Liverpool lacked punch.

City had reason to curse the timing of this fixture. Apart from Manchester United at Old Trafford, it could hardly have been worse than a visit here. And not only because Liverpool were one of the clubs most seriously undermined by their accountancy practices. City sneaked their team buses around the back of the stadium on the way in, avoiding the jibes from the streets, but it only postponed the inevitable. It was always going to be lively.

When the Premier League published the document that provided the first raft of detail about the decisions against City on the Tuesday before last, it hit hard. It was the weight of the language – how it dripped with contempt – as well as the sheer extent of the transgressions. Proven misconduct. Sham arrangements. Concerted attempts to frustrate the investigation. How some of the club’s witnesses gave evidence that they knew to be untrue. It served to frame this game. It will continue to frame each one that City play for the foreseeable.

View image in fullscreen Jérémy Doku doubles Manchester City’s lead with a stunning curling shot. Photograph: Michael Regan/Getty Images

The City fans came armed with scores of inflatable bananas. Some of them wore old-school replica shirts. There was a message in there somewhere. Maybe to say that their club predates the Abu Dhabi takeover. It was also possible to spot banners in support of Khaldoon al-Mubarak, the club chair.

You want banners? The Kop had that boxed off. There were some that riffed off Oasis lyrics, including one with the line that “after all, you really robbed us all”. The most eye-catching was unfurled before kick-off, featuring the word ‘cheats’ and a very long sequence of pound signs.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

There was very little to report in terms of first-half action. Even the melee that broke out in the 12th minute after Alexis Mac Allister tussled with Anderson was the definition of handbags. There were no big chances; the precision on the final ball was frequently absent.

Iraola gave Lewis Koumas a full league debut up front and it was the 21-year-old who had the first decent effort straight after the restart. Gianluigi Donnarumma stood tall to save. Liverpool upped the intensity and they had a spell where they pushed and the Kop felt the breakthrough was coming. Gravenberch worked Donnarumma. Mac Allister volleyed wide.

View image in fullscreen Ryan Gravenberch (right) walks off after receiving a red card from the referee Chris Kavanagh. Photograph: Michael Regan/Getty Images

Haaland blew a glorious chance from an Antoine Semenyo pass on the hour, dinking past the far post but City had otherwise created little. Then everything changed. Gravenberch caught the eye with his surging runs but he was on the wrong side when he challenged Doku, who was ready to spark a counterattack. It was clumsy from the Dutchman, the contact on Doku not exactly strong. But having been booked at the start of the second half for a foul on Anderson, Gravenberch was running an almighty risk. He did not get away with it.

City had their opening and how they piled through it. The way that they overwhelmed Liverpool was really something; a demonstration of their strength. It was not a game for the neutral. Are there any such viewers where City are concerned any more? Doku almost teed up Nico O’Reilly and City were on their way when Haaland swept home from a deflected Doku cross. A new reality? It was the same old City on the pitch.

Sports.title: Premier League returns in shadow of Manchester City’s judgment day | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
The Cimbri are heading menacingly south, but in Rome life goes on. The asteroid is definitely coming this way, but people go to work, eat, drink, plan as usual. The White Walkers are approaching the Wall, but the squabbles between the great houses go on. Everyone in the Premier League knows the crisis is approaching, thinks – hopes, fears? – it may be apocalyptic, but until it arrives, what can you do but carry on?

After any break, there’s always an awkward moment while everybody resets. What was the cliffhanger we left the soap opera on? What new plotline had just been seeded? This is one of the reasons international weeks are so disruptive. It’s not just that the Premier League story slows for a while, it’s that we are reminded that these entities are not eternal but alliances of convenience between paid employees who have a life outside the soap opera.

But there has never before been an international break so disruptive as this, never such a sense of unreality about a weekend of Premier League football. It’s not that, the 2022 World Cup aside, this has been the longest international break in history. Nor can anyone, surely, be unaware of the dominant narrative of this window: between 2009 and 2018, Manchester City cheated. Perhaps an away game at Anfield for City is not quite the event it was when Pep Guardiola and Jürgen Klopp were at their peak, but it should still be a great footballing occasion. Yet this was an afternoon when the football felt secondary.

City continue to protest their innocence, clinging to the now-familiar formula that they have a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence that will somehow clear their name, if only people wouldn’t keep refuting it. They have launched an appeal, but if that fails the sanction is likely to be unprecedentedly severe. Do their games matter? Will they be annulled before the season’s end? Was this victory just the difference between finishing the season on -100 points and -97? Could they be expelled from the league? Until sentence is announced, there will an air of provisionality about everything they do. It’s the seconds after an incident that everybody knows VAR will check, the ghost football that might be cancelled, but extended for weeks.

This, though, is not only an issue of the present; it’s an issue of the past. The sanction may or may not strip City of their titles. Many City fans will ignore such a punishment, continue to claim those honours, will point out that memories cannot be so easily extinguished. But even if City’s appeal is successful, or even if the sanction does not relitigate the past, there will be asterisks there in the minds of those who are not City fans, and perhaps also in the minds of some of those who are. Add in Chelsea’s offences, and the Premier League is coming to the end of an 18-year period in which very little was quite as it seemed.

View image in fullscreen Manchester City fans remain defiant despite the guilty verdict against the club they support. Photograph: Michael Regan/Getty Images

The inflatable bananas brandished by City’s support at Anfield on Sunday may have harked back to an earlier, more innocent era, but there is no going back. City are not the club of Imre Varadi any more; as it stands they are the club guilty of the greatest act of cheating in English football history. Their fans can do the Poznan in a spirit of resistance, but they cannot turn their back on the shame their leaders have brought upon them.

What that means for the longer-term credibility of the league can only be guessed at. The basis of sport is faith. Incredible finishes mean little if nothing can be believed. Why go through the emotional agonies if a result might be struck off a decade later for offences committed in the air-conditioned offices of a distant state? Will the City decision undermine faith, or reaffirm it, come as proof that cheats do not prosper, that they will – eventually – be exposed, that the Premier League, almost alone in this grubby world of compromise with and abasement before the mega-rich, is prepared to do what is right?

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

City were booed, there were some chants of “going down” and there were a handful of banners, but Anfield was not the seething pit of disgust many had anticipated. Nor was there much City-related fury at other grounds, although Manchester United fans, erasing all the silverware of the past 15 years, reinstituted their counter on the Stretford End recording the length of time since City last won a trophy. The general sense is of bafflement and bewilderment; what does this mean? What might happen?

It is as though the scale of City’s offences have not yet been fully grasped, that no one quite knows what might happen next. City fans, similarly, seem set on a policy of defiance, as though the scandal is something that has been done to them, rather than the result of the actions of their own directors. To an extent, that is understandable. Until the sanctions are announced, until the result of the appeal is known, the sense of unreality, the phoney war, will go on. The crisis is coming, but its impact has not yet been felt.

Sports.title: ‘We make our own noise’: Maresca hails Manchester City after Liverpool triumph
Sports.content:
Enzo Maresca praised Manchester City for “making their own noise” at Liverpool as they brushed aside the controversy and threats surrounding the club with a comprehensive 3-0 win at Anfield.

City, in their first outing since the club were found guilty on 114 charges relating to Premier League financial rules, maintained their 100% start to the season courtesy of goals from Erling Haaland, the excellent Jérémy Doku and Rayan Cherki. A sixth successive league win ensured Maresca equalled the best start to a managerial reign in Premier League history and kept City at the top of the table.

The City head coach said: “My message to the players since we were together three days ago, when they all came back from their national teams, has been quite clear: guys, the noise will always be there so it’s about how we learn to deal with the noise and it’s our duty to make our noise. Our noise is to win games in the way we did today and to be happy. It was our fans making the noise at the end of the game today.”

Maresca smiled when asked whether he needed City’s appeal to be heard as quickly as possible in order to celebrate such an impressive win. “You cannot imagine how happy I am,” he replied. “I don’t care. I’m here to try and prepare games and to win games. Hopefully I can speak about this situation when we win the appeal.”

City’s chief executive Ferran Soriano was present at Anfield as the fallout from the club’s guilty verdict continues. Maresca reflected: “We were all together. For the importance of the game, Liverpool away, Anfield away, it was a good idea from the club to be all together. That togetherness is what we need.”

The game turned on the 62nd-minute dismissal of Liverpool midfielder Ryan Gravenberch for a second bookable offence. Haaland opened the scoring one minute later and City then ran riot.

Andoni Iraola, the Liverpool head coach, said: “We played two different games: one until the red card, and one from the red card until the end. I think we were the better team until the red card and they were better than us, obviously, after the red card. But I think the players deserve credit today because they’ve given everything.”

Iraola insisted Gravenberch’s red card was harsh. “I think the first foul of Ryan is never a yellow card, never,” he added. “The referee doesn’t even call the foul straight away. He lets it go, Elliot Anderson does a couple of steps and then decides to go down. I don’t know why he shows the yellow card after that because it’s not a situation where it leaves an advantage.”

Sports.title: Impervious City shrug off chaos and controversy to silence Anfield | Andy Hunter
Sports.content:
Anfield welcomed Manchester City to their new reality, a sullied place where every touch is accompanied by cries of “cheat”, any favourable decision is considered proof of further conspiracy and every victory hollow. But Welcome to Hell this was not. The only body of irrefutable evidence in City’s favour since the guilty verdicts landed is that Enzo Maresca’s league leaders appear immune to prosecution and persecution.

That may well change depending on the outcome of City’s appeal and any punishment that eventually arises, likewise the merits and value of a commanding 3-0 win on Liverpool soil. The sight of Erling Haaland savouring a statement victory in front of City’s supporters after the final whistle, while chants of “going down” echoed around the rest of the stadium, captured the schism at the heart of this Premier League season.

City were transformed by the introduction of Jérémy Doku and the dismissal of the Liverpool midfielder Ryan Gravenberch. They were never intimidated, always composed and look a genuine threat to Arsenal’s defence of the title. And yet this could prove their last Premier League appearance at Anfield for the foreseeable future.

It may be difficult, nigh on impossible, to sustain this level of motivation and desire knowing that relegation beckons. Knowing that no one outside City will give them credit for another title triumph did not affect them here, however.

In the 17 days since news of City’s guilt first emerged, and the gestation period of a prolonged international break, their return to action in a Premier League undermined and distorted by their 114 breaches had been built up as a chastening day of reckoning for Maresca’s side. It proved nothing of the sort.

Anfield can still make its voice heard to seismic effect and in the frantic start when Liverpool flew at City, with a fired-up Ronald Araújo whipping up the crowd after winning a challenge against Antoine Semenyo, the collective sense of injustice at a club pipped three times to the title by those in sky blue inspired Andoni Iraola’s players. But bear pits rarely feature in the corporate packaged world of Premier League entertainment 2026.

The “reception committee” for the City team coach before the game was populated by fans carrying selfie-sticks and club shop carrier bags, not an incensed brooding mob. At half-time the Kop was asked to cheer on corporate guests of the club sponsor Standard Chartered as they took part in a penalty shootout, many clearly kicking a ball for the first time in their lives.

There were incessant chants of “you cheating bastards” and various banners of damning judgement, many with an Oasis twist that may have been appreciated by Noel Gallagher in the away end. “And after all you really robbed us all” read one. “All of your stars are fading away,” read another. “A generation of supporters cheated,” cut to the heart of the issue confronting not only Liverpool but the Premier League itself.

View image in fullscreen Liverpool supporters point out that their side finished second to Manchester City three times in the space of eight years. Photograph: Peter Byrne/PA

The City support responded in kind. “In Khaldoon we trust – we’ve won it all!” proclaimed the away flags. The visitors, while performing the Poznan before kick-off, also reclaimed one of the “Cheat” flags that had been doing a healthy trade outside the ground before the game. The inflatable bananas that were once part of the City fanscape also made a comeback, a throwback to more innocent days when their club was not in the dock for inflating sponsorship deals. There was more bickering than tangible animosity. The four men who walked on to the pitch carrying the Premier League hoardings before kick-off received a more hostile reception than City’s players when they appeared for the warm-up.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The decision for City’s team coach to arrive by a different route ensured a tame reception for the visitors. All eyes were on the usual entrance on Anfield Road as City were ushered in from the opposite side of the stadium. It meant even the referees’ chief Howard Webb could walk in almost unnoticed. The hostility cranked up as soon as the contest started and City, using their vast experience to telling effect, gradually drained the venom from the atmosphere and the threat from a depleted Liverpool team. But it was the 62nd-minute dismissal of Gravenberch that had the greater bearing on the outcome.

Doku proved a devastating substitute for Iliman Ndiaye and tormented Liverpool from the left, being involved not only in the red card but all three City goals. The hosts, minus their two most potent attacking players this season in Cody Gakpo and Alexander Isak, plus a hamstrung Dominik Szoboszlai, had no answer with Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola largely anonymous.

The Kop made no calls to be handed the trophies lost to City – and what would that really mean now anyway? – but took solace in demanding that punishment be served in the form of relegation this season. “No trophies for 50 years, que será, será,” the home crowd chanted. But there was no immediate retribution for Liverpool here. City dealt with the chaos and the controversy serenely.

Sports.title: Pino finishes off Nottingham Forest on Glasner’s unhappy Crystal Palace return
Sports.content:
It is fair to say Oliver Glasner has had more enjoyable afternoons. The Nottingham Forest head coach arrived in south London dressed like a bouncer from All Bar One in a black bomber jacket, as if he was anticipating trouble, but was instead given a rapturous reception by the home fans who used to worship him.

The generosity towards their former manager seemed to have extended to Palace’s players as Dan Ndoye was handed a goal in the third minute. Pierre Sage’s side were awful in the opening 40 minutes. Yet Forest could not find a way to beat Walter Benítez again as Liam Delap missed a golden chance to extend their lead and the Argentina goalkeeper’s heroics inspired a thrilling comeback that secured Sage’s first home victory in the Premier League since taking over from Glasner in the summer.

The irony that Daichi Kamada, who won the Europa League under Glasner while they were at Eintracht Frankfurt before he brought him to Selhurst Park on a free transfer, should score his first Premier League goal to equalise in his 68th appearance was surely not lost on the Austrian.

But he and the notoriously trigger-happy Evangelos Marinakis – the Forest owner who was conspicuous by his absence from the directors’ box after his public spats with his Palace counterpart, Steve Parish – will have serious concerns about how his team capitulated after conceding the equaliser. Jefferson Lerma bundled home the second from a corner just before half-time and Yéremy Pino wrapped up the points with a goal that was greeted with a chorus of: “You’re getting sacked in the morning”, directed towards Glasner.

“Call it karma or whatever but it was like I didn’t deserve to win at Selhurst Park because the players did everything,” said Glasner, who claimed not to have heard the taunts from the Palace fans. “I think this was the most dominant Nottingham Forest performance. But not the right result. So, this gives me confidence. My job is not to be influenced negatively by the result.”

There has been plenty of water under the bridge since these two sides met here 14 months ago. Marinakis is suing Palace and “persons unknown” after a banner featuring an incendiary cartoon of him was unfurled during the first half of that game, with the supporters’ group that is thought to have been behind it having since disbanded. Glasner’s decision to join Forest in the summer only added to the ill-feeling that was created by the dispute over Palace’s demotion from the Europa League last season, even if the Austrian was given a warm welcome before and after the game.

The home fans made it clear where their grievances remain as they immediately launched into the anti-Uefa and Marinakis song that was the soundtrack to their Conference League triumph under Glasner, while the Forest supporters responded with taunts of: “We’ve got Ollie Glasner”. They had more reason to celebrate after only two minutes when Anan Khalaili’s weak header presented Ndoye with the chance to run through and score. Forest could barely believe their luck.

View image in fullscreen The Nottingham Forest head coach, Oliver Glasner, responds to a generous reception from the Crystal Palace supporters. Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/Action Images/Reuters

They piled on the pressure, with makeshift defender Lerma – only playing in the absence of the suspended Axel Disasi – looking particularly vulnerable.
