A pregnant Pennsylvania woman who was reportedly just four days away from giving birth and her two young children were among eight victims killed in a mass shooting at an Erie home Friday.

Angelina Stone, who was eight months pregnant, was killed along with her children and several other relatives, according to local reports.

CBS Pittsburgh reported that Stone was four days away from giving birth, while a family friend told Erie News Now she was expected to deliver "in a couple of days."

A GoFundMe organized to help with funeral expenses identified Stone's children as Isiah and Amari’anna and her unborn baby as Kyrie.

MONTANA MAN WHO KILLED 4 CHILDREN, 4 OTHER FAMILY MEMBERS AT SUNDAY DINNER WAS ASKED TO MOVE OUT: RELATIVE

"This situation is horrific and unimaginable," neighbor Jennifer Macko told CBS Pittsburgh.

Lisa Simmers, a family friend, remembered Stone's children as "beautiful, beautiful children" who "definitely did not deserve what happened to them."

"She had a daughter that was almost two, and her son Isiah, who I believe was like four or five," Simmers told Erie News Now.

Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said Saturday that eight victims were killed in the Friday evening shooting before the suspected gunman, a 45-year-old man, died from what investigators believe was a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

8 FAMILY MEMBERS, INCLUDING 6 CHILDREN, FOUND DEAD IN MICHIGAN FIRE; AT LEAST ONE VICTIM SHOT: POLICE

The suspected gunman was related to seven of the eight victims and was the family's patriarch and a grandfather, according to police and a relative who spoke to The Associated Press. The eighth victim was a family friend, Lorah said.

Police Chief Rick Lorah said mental health may have played a role in the shooting but cautioned that it was too early to determine a motive..

Investigators believe all eight victims and the suspected gunman died before officers arrived.

The GoFundMe organizer said the family was seeking help covering funeral expenses for Stone and her children.

"I'm raising funds for Angelina, Isiah, baby girl Amari’anna, and unborn Kyrie after an unthinkable tragedy," the fundraiser states.

TWO TEEN SUSPECTS HELD AFTER 5 FAMILY MEMBERS KILLED IN 'TARGETED MASS SHOOTING'

The organizer added, "This is more than our family can carry alone right now, and we truly need the community to rally around us. Any donation, no matter the amount, will help ease the financial burden and help us give Angelina, Isiah, Amari’anna, and Kyrie the farewell they deserve."

The Erie Police Department continues to investigate.

The Erie Police Department could not immediately be reached by Fox News Digital for comment.

Fox News Digital's Michael Sinkewicz, Robert McGreevy and Brittany Miller contributed to this report.

World.title: Minnesota homecoming shooting suspect out on bond after gunfire sends football fans fleeing
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A Minnesota homecoming celebration shattered by gunfire has become the latest flashpoint over crime and bail after the accused shooter was released from jail just two days after his arrest.

Adam Abdihakeem Adam, 18, posted bond and was released Saturday evening, according to Hennepin County jail records reviewed by Fox News Digital.

Police say he shot two teenagers outside Eden Prairie High School during its Oct. 2 homecoming football game, prompting the evacuation of the stadium.

His release drew criticism from President Donald Trump’s Rapid Response 47 account, which highlighted police statements linking the shooting to rival Somali gangs.

POLICE MAKE ARREST AFTER GUNFIRE DURING CALIFORNIA HIGH SCHOOL FOOTBALL GAME LEAVES 1 DEAD

"A Radical Left judge immediately granted him a no-condition bail," the account wrote on X.

Jail records list a $100,000 bail or bond option without conditions and show Adam was released at 7:04 p.m. Oct. 10. He faces two felony counts of second-degree assault with a dangerous weapon and one count of second-degree riot while armed with a dangerous weapon. His next court appearance is scheduled for Monday afternoon.

MARYLAND MAN ACCUSED OF GIRL'S FATAL SHOOTING RELEASED FROM PRISON DAYS BEFORE

The shooting injured an 18-year-old and a 17-year-old and launched a multi-agency hunt for those involved, according to Eden Prairie police.

Investigators allege the violence began after two cars entered a parking lot and a fight involving about 10 people broke out. The driver of one car got out, opened fire on the victims and fled, according to charging documents cited by affiliate FOX 9 Minneapolis.

Authorities identified that driver as Adam, who allegedly was driving his brother’s car. Investigators tracked his phone with the vehicle before, during and after the shooting, the outlet reported. He then allegedly abandoned the phone and changed his number.

SHOOTING NEAR BALTIMORE YOUTH FOOTBALL EVENT LEAVES 12-YEAR-OLD GIRL DEAD, 3 ADULTS WOUNDED

A search of his St. Louis Park home turned up clothing matching what the shooter wore in surveillance video, according to the charges cited by FOX 9.

Police caught up with Adam Oct. 8 near Highway 55 and Penn Avenue in Minneapolis, taking him into custody without incident.

The Hennepin County Sheriff’s Office credited detectives with its Auto Theft Task Force and West Metro Drug Task Force, along with St. Louis Park and Hopkins officers, with safely boxing in the vehicle.

"I’m incredibly proud of our officers and investigators who have worked nonstop alongside our law enforcement partners to identify those responsible and hold them accountable," Eden Prairie Police Chief Matt Sackett said after the arrest.

AMY KLOBUCHAR CALLS FOR MAJOR ANTI-TERRORISM INVESTMENTS AFTER ALLEGED MALL OF AMERICA PLOT

The case has intensified concerns about Somali gang-related violence across the metro area, prompting regional public safety agencies to meet under the coordination of the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension. Police leaders said they are sharing intelligence and coordinating investigations to prevent further shootings.

Republican U.S. Senate candidate Michele Tafoya pointed to the homecoming shooting and other recent violence while warning last week that Minnesotans increasingly feel under threat.

TRUMP’S LAW-AND-ORDER BLITZ MARKS ONE YEAR WITH EYE-POPPING HAUL OF SUSPECTS, GUNS IN BLUE CITY

"Our law enforcement here are calling it out as the product of Somali gang violence, and we’ve got to identify it, and we have to find a way to deal with it," Tafoya told Fox News Digital.

Eden Prairie police also are investigating an Oct. 5 shots-fired incident at a Speedway gas station, where no injuries were reported. Investigators said they have not identified a connection between that incident and the homecoming shooting.

Sackett said the homecoming investigation remains active, with additional arrests or charges possible.

World.title: Trump and Rubio weigh firing Kimberly Guilfoyle as misconduct and donor bailout allegations mount
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle may soon be fired amid reports she sought a six-figure credit card bailout from a Trump donor while offering access to administration officials, adding to mounting allegations over her conduct in Athens.

President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are "extremely pissed off" by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and are weighing her removal, The Associated Press reported Sunday, citing a senior U.S. official.

The official told the AP that a decision on what action to take would likely come this week after Monday’s Columbus Day holiday. No departure has been confirmed.

Guilfoyle, onetime fiancée of Donald Trump Jr., came under scrutiny this week after The Wall Street Journal reported that she asked Trump donor Eric Deters to pay off a $100,000 American Express bill shortly before her Senate confirmation hearing.

MARCO RUBIO ANNOUNCES SWEEPING FINANCIAL SANCTIONS AGAINST THE INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL COURT

According to messages reviewed by the Journal, Guilfoyle urged Deters to wire the money directly to American Express, saying the transaction would not leave a paper trail, while offering to help him gain access to senior Trump administration officials. Deters said he never made the payment.

Guilfoyle's attorney, Jesse Binnall, disputed the authenticity of the messages.

The allegations followed an earlier Journal investigation into Guilfoyle's conduct in Greece, including claims that she promoted the interests of Greek construction and energy company Aktor Group and allowed its registered lobbyist, Christos Marafatsos, to accompany her to private diplomatic meetings with senior officials.

FORMER TRUMP CABINET OFFICIAL HAD 'INAPPROPRIATELY CLOSE' RELATIONSHIP WITH BODYGUARD, IG FINDS

The Journal also reported that Guilfoyle suggested at a dinner with Greek officials that the U.S. would undermine their government, citing political developments in Romania. Greece's foreign minister has since said there was no need to summon Guilfoyle for an explanation because the country's energy minister denied that any threat had been made.

Separately, the State Department's Office of Inspector General opened an investigation into allegations involving Guilfoyle's treatment of embassy employees, private travel, acceptance of gifts and relationships with business interests, according to a report from the Daily Mail.

3 SECRET SERVICE OFFICIALS UNDER INTERNAL INVESTIGATION FOR POTENTIAL MISCONDUCT

Sources described a hostile workplace in which Guilfoyle allegedly threatened to fire employees. They also claim that she demoted members of her security detail over minor incidents, including an officer who reportedly failed to answer a 4 a.m. request for ice while she was vacationing in Mykonos.

The inspector general's office declined to confirm or deny the existence of an investigation. Binnall told the Daily Mail that "any implication of wrongdoing by the Ambassador is unsupported."

The allegations have drawn scrutiny from congressional Democrats, including Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., and Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., who have called for a review of Guilfoyle's conduct. Meeks urged her removal if the allegations were substantiated.

Vice President JD Vance addressed the controversy Friday, cautioning against rushing to judgment while acknowledging that misconduct should carry consequences.

OHIO BAKERY WORKERS RECOUNT SURPRISE JD VANCE ENCOUNTER THAT TOOK AN UNEXPECTED TURN

"Let's actually see what the facts are. Let's see what the truth is," Vance told reporters in Ohio. "And obviously, if there was something bad that happened, then people have to suffer consequences for it."

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who visited Greece this week and delivered remarks with the backdrop of Acropolis, declined to address the allegations directly.

SEC MARCO RUBIO: THE WEST FORGOT WHAT MADE IT GREAT. WE MUST REDISCOVER OUR ROOTS BEFORE WE LOSE THEM

"You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it's the gospel. It's not the gospel," Rubio told reporters Thursday.

Rubio had defended Guilfoyle's performance a day earlier, saying, "Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here."

FOUR AMERICAN TOURISTS AMONG 6 KILLED AFTER EXPLOSION LEVELS BUILDING NEAR ATHENS’ ACROPOLIS

Trump nominated Guilfoyle to the diplomatic post in December 2024. A former California prosecutor and Fox News Channel personality, she previously served as a prominent surrogate and fundraiser for the president.

DONALD TRUMP JR AND BETTINA ANDERSON CELEBRATE PRIVATE WEDDING IN BAHAMAS, SHARE SWEET PERSONAL PHOTO

Guilfoyle was almost Trump’s daughter-in-law. She was engaged to Don Jr. for four years, but the two publicly split in Dec. 2024 — the same month the president nominated her to be the ambassador to Greece.

The president’s eldest son married Palm Beach socialite Bettina Anderson in May of this year.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

She was also previously married to California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, from 2001 to 2006, when he was serving as mayor of San Francisco.

World.title: Federal judge orders pro-Trump TV ads funded by taxpayers off air immediately
World.content:
A federal judge ordered the Trump administration on Sunday to stop airing ads funded by the U.S. government that portray President Donald Trump in a favorable light, effective immediately.

The lawsuit was brought by the watchdog group Common Cause; Robert Hunter, a Democratic candidate for a seat in the Alabama state House; and a labor union in New York and its political action committee. The suit was one of several similar complaints — including one by the Democratic National Committee — that were filed to get the ads off the air.

“Plaintiffs have demonstrated that they are likely to succeed on the merits, will suffer irreparable harm in the absence of an injunction, the balance of the equities tips in their favor, and an injunction serves the public interest,” U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon of the Southern District of New York wrote.

The administration had said in a court filing Saturday that the Department of Homeland Security, via a vendor, had placed ad buys through Sunday and had told the vendor to not purchase ads beyond that day.

Rochon said the plaintiffs’ argument was not moot, however, and ordered the Trump administration to “cancel or cause to be cancelled” any ads from airing or being disseminated, including those set to air Sunday night.

Rochon also wrote that the administration was barred from using funds appropriated to DHS to “develop, create, disseminate, place, distribute, publish, or air the challenged s.”

The White House, DHS and the Office of Management and Budget, which are all named as defendants in the suit, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the ruling. MAGA Inc., which Trump had said last week would help him fund the ads moving forward, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

“We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda,” the plaintiffs said in a statement. “There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda.”

Common Cause President and CEO Virginia Kase Solomón said that despite the ruling, “our fight continues.”

“We won’t stop until this administration is held fully accountable, and no president from any party can waste and abuse taxpayer funds for propaganda ever again,” Solomón said.

The ads — one of which was nearly identical to a 2024 Trump campaign ad — came under scrutiny by critics who argued that using taxpayer money could be illegal and called the spots propaganda.

World.title: South Carolina Senate rivals spar over Iran, AI and Trump in debate
World.content:
Republican Sen. Darline Graham of South Carolina and Democratic challenger Annie Andrews clashed Sunday night in their first and perhaps only debate of the general election, tangling over President Donald Trump’s “one big, beautiful bill,” the high costs of gas and goods, the Iran war and AI data centers.

South Carolina is a ruby-red state where Trump remains popular among Republican voters. But the race has tightened in the closing stretch of the campaign, and Democrats believe they have a shot at knocking off Graham, who was appointed to fill her brother Lindsey Graham’s Senate seat after his sudden death in July. The top Senate Republican super PAC has pledged to spend $5 million to shore up Graham’s campaign.

At the start of the debate, hosted in Columbia by South Carolina ETV, Darline Graham noted that Sunday night marked exactly three months since her brother unexpectedly died at age 71.

Andrews, a pediatrician, sought to portray Graham, who previously led a state agency, as an inexperienced empty suit who refuses to stand up to Trump or his unpopular policies. She mocked Graham as “the White House’s ambassador to South Carolina.”

Graham attacked Andrews as the “most radical liberal” to run in South Carolina and as sympathetic to the Democratic Socialist Party. “Annie Andrews will not stand up to the Socialist Democratic Party; she’s only going to join them,” Graham said — a characterization Andrews rejected.

Graham has “been told to come out here and call me Bernie, Ocasio, Mamdani — that’s what’s in her script. But the truth is my name is Annie Andrews, and there shouldn’t be any confusion about that,” Andrews said. “The truth is I support the Second Amendment, I believe we need a secure border, and we need to deport illegal immigrants who break the law. ... The real difference between me and Sen. Graham is that I will stand up to my own party, and I will always put South Carolina first.”

Graham and Andrews are running for a full six-year Senate term; the winner will make history as the first female senator elected from South Carolina. The debate also featured Libertarian Kasie Whitener.

Graham and Andrews tussled over issue after issue. As the country faces Social Security insolvency, Andrews said she would raise caps to make wealthier people pay more but would not hike the retirement age. She added that Republicans like Graham want to privatize Social Security so “Washington insiders” can profit. “Unfortunately, my opponent is in the race to do what Washington insiders tell her,” she said.

Graham shot back that she understands what people in her state are facing. When her parents died at a young age, Social Security benefits helped her and her brother survive. Graham said Andrews’ criticism of Trump’s “one big, beautiful bill” is misplaced because it lowered taxes on tips and Social Security. “You called it the one big, ugly bill, so here you are deceiving the people of South Carolina,” Graham said.

On affordability, Graham said she has “lived paycheck to paycheck” before and acknowledged that “gas prices are high right now. ... I feel the pain, too.” She said that she supports suspending the gas tax and that easing regulations on drilling would permanently bring prices down.

Andrews pinned blame for high gas prices on Graham, who she said voted several times against a war powers resolution to restrict Trump’s war with Iran.

“The war is the exact reason we now have record-high gas and diesel prices. Farmers are getting crushed, and everything costs more,” Andrews said. “My opponent is the only one who had the opportunity to vote to end the war, but three times in a row she voted to continue it.”

Andrews also dinged Graham for admitting during a previous debate that “national security is not my thing.” “South Carolina, if your surgeon said that appendectomies aren’t really his thing, would you still hand him a scalpel? No,” Andrews said. “So why would we hand Darline Graham a full term in the U.S. Senate? She is unserious and unqualified.”

Graham retorted that she wants the war to end, like everyone does, but said she believes in “peace through strength.” Then, she went after Andrews over the national security quip.

“But talking about not my thing, let’s talk about what’s not your thing. Your thing apparently is not being honest with the people of South Carolina. At least I’m honest. If I don’t know something, I am glad to say it, and I’ll say it again tonight,” Graham said without getting specific. “But you have, you are deceiving the people of South Carolina. You have flip-flopped on everything. There’s so many social media posts out there to prove it. Shame on you!”

The proliferation of data centers, which power artificial intelligence companies, has become a major flash point in the midterm elections.

Andrews went right after Graham on the issue, nicknaming her “Data Center Darline.” Andrews said her data-center plan calls for a “two-year moratorium, protections to ensure your rates don’t go up and a return to real local control.”

Graham fired back that stopping construction of all data centers would allow China to win the race for AI dominance. She said she voted for the Ratepayer Protection Act, which aims to shift higher energy costs from building data centers from consumers onto AI companies.

“Under her Bernie Sanders plan, a two-year moratorium, that is dangerous to the national security of our country, because in two years China is going to be so far ahead [that] we are going to be in so much trouble,” Graham said, adding that local communities should decide whether data centers get built in their backyards.

“I want communities to decide. She wants the federal government to decide.”

World.title: Here’s the biggest news you missed this weekend
World.content:
An unidentified projectile struck Saudi Arabia’s main international airport Sunday, injuring people a day after a deadly missile attack at the same site raised questions about whether the United States would join another conflict in the region.

Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation confirmed injuries in the new attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh but did not provide a count. It said authorities were assessing damage and checking the safety of airport facilities.

Saturday’s strike killed at least 13 people and injured more than 300, according to Saudi civil aviation authorities. The attack was the deadliest to hit the kingdom in a decade and marked a sharp escalation in the Yemen-based Houthis’ campaign against the world’s leading oil exporter.

President Donald Trump said afterward that the U.S. was considering joining Saudi military operations against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

“We may. We’re gonna look at it,” Trump told reporters. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”

Nearly 400,000 in Florida and Alabama still without power as Isaias moves north

Isaias left at least four people dead after it made landfall in Florida late Friday. Getty; Reuters

Hurricane Isaias made landfall Friday near Destin, Florida, as a Category 2 storm before weakening to a post-tropical cyclone.

At least four deaths were linked to the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, including two people killed when trees fell onto homes in Florida and Alabama.

The storm then roared into Alabama with tropical-force winds before heading farther north.

In western North Carolina, rivers overflowed as heavy rainfall raised the risk of flash and urban flooding, according to the National Weather Service.

Tornadoes were possible in parts of Virginia and North Carolina, and life-threatening surf and rip current conditions were expected to continue along the Gulf and southeastern Atlantic coasts.

‘Meet the Press’

Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed said his fellow Democrats need to “win by massive numbers” in the upcoming midterm elections so the result “is unquestionable.”

“Donald Trump has already threatened to do what he did in 2020, which is deny the outcomes of an election,” El-Sayed told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” in an interview that aired Sunday.

Asked by NBC News on Saturday whether he would accept the results of the midterm elections, Trump said, “Of course I will. But we don’t want cheating.”

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that Trump’s decision to ease sanctions on Russia to allow it to release diesel fuel to the global market may be breaking the law.

“I do believe there’s a legitimate case for saying the president’s not following the law,” Tillis said.

Politics in brief

Pool fight: The Justice Department said it is investigating CNN, NBC, ABC, CBS and Fox News after the networks temporarily declined to provide pool coverage of Trump, a department spokesperson said.

The Justice Department said it is investigating CNN, NBC, ABC, CBS and Fox News after the networks temporarily of Trump, a department spokesperson said. Midterm woes: Even as he makes a case that Republicans should win the midterm congressional elections, Trump is bracing for the fallout should they lose.

Even as he makes a case that Republicans should win the midterm congressional elections, Trump is should they lose. Public spectacle: Trump said that he hasn’t yet made a final decision on whether to livestream the execution of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan, who in 2009 killed 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas.

Trump said that he hasn’t yet made a final decision on whether to of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan, who in 2009 killed 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas. Energy deal?: Trump claims Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an energy ceasefire , but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reportedly said this “was news for me.”

Trump claims Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an , but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reportedly said this “was news for me.” Congress whisperer: Trump named Katie Bailey to lead the White House’s Office of Legislative Affairs, appointing her to be the liaison between the administration and Congress.

Pope Leo XIV to undergo surgery to remove a nodule on his lung

Pope Leo XIV in St. Peter's Square at the Vatican on Oct. 7. Maria Grazia Picciarella / LightRocket via Getty

Pope Leo XIV announced that he will undergo surgery to remove an early-stage nodule on his lung.

“Recently, during some medical tests, doctors discovered a localized nodule in my lung,” the American-born pontiff, 71, said during his noon prayer at St. Peter’s Square in the Vatican.

“It was detected at a very early stage and is well localized,” Leo said from the window of the Apostolic Palace. “The doctors believe it is best to intervene, so, following their advice, I have decided to undergo surgery to have it removed.”

He said that surgery had already been scheduled “for the coming days,” and thanked onlookers for their support.

How the Philadelphia Eagles pulled off the wildest loss of the NFL season

Jalyx Hunt of the Philadelphia Eagles and Trevor Lawrence of the Jacksonville Jaguars battle for the ball. Vince Mignott / DeFodi via Getty Images

If you didn’t set your alarm clock this morning, you may have missed the most exciting finish of the NFL season so far.

The Philadelphia Eagles lost 19-17 to the Jacksonville Jaguars in London after a fourth quarter filled with twists worthy of an M. Night Shyamalan movie.

It was an absolutely shocking loss for Philadelphia, which had a 99.9% win probability after the go-ahead field goal, according to ESPN Analytics. The Eagles — already dealing with injuries and the sudden retirement of star tackle Lane Johnson — have now lost back-to-back games in which they led during the final two minutes.

Notable quote

If it makes me smile and I have a little money, I’ll pay for it because everything is so grim right now. A pair of socks with dachshunds on it, I’m like, ‘You know what? I can do that. I could swing it today.’ Ari Monahan, a nanny who describes herself as “like a Disney adult, but for Halloween”

This Halloween, the fright isn’t just at the haunted house. Average prices for chewing gum and candy have soared 8.1% over the last year, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Despite the higher prices, Americans are still buying treats, including Halloween candy.

World.title: The Commanders had seconds left to secure a win — and blew it
World.content:
When the snap that left the entire NFL in disbelief began Sunday, Washington quarterback Jayden Daniels was supposed to do one of two things, Commanders coach Dan Quinn said — throw the ball out of bounds or spike it into the turf.

Both would have stopped the clock and given Washington the chance to earn a season-reviving win in the final seconds of overtime over their division-leading rival, the New York Giants.

When Daniels did neither, however, and instead ran the ball, it set off a chain of events that produced a 27-27 tie that was the result of the most inexplicable ending of the young NFL season so far.

“Leaving tonight with a tie feels like a loss,” Quinn said.

It was a far cry from the optimism the day had started with for Washington.

Playing for the first time since he injured an elbow three weeks earlier, Daniels had at times resembled the player who took the NFL by storm as a rookie in 2024. His 38-yard touchdown run in the third quarter gave Washington a 19-6 lead. In the fourth quarter, another Daniels touchdown run of 26 yards kept his team in front, 27-13, with 11 minutes to play in regulation.

The Commanders had just seven more offensive plays the rest of the fourth quarter, while the Giants roared back for two touchdowns to force overtime, with the teams lodged in a 27-all tie.

And still, the Commanders had the opportunity to win.

With 13 seconds left in overtime, the Commanders were in range of a game-winning field goal, just 26 yards from the end zone. Daniels, feeling some defensive pressure, improvised a run and barely got back to the line of scrimmage with 8 seconds left on the clock. He lay on the turf nonchalantly for 2 more seconds, until the Commanders seemed to remember they did not have a timeout left and that the clock was running out on their opportunity to win the game.

“They don’t have a timeout,” Fox broadcaster Chris Myers said. “What are they doing?”

Rasul Douglas of the Commanders reacts to a play against the Giants on Sunday. Scott Taetsch / Getty Images

Players from both teams scrambled into position, blocking the official from spotting the ball until no time was left on the clock. Myers, on the Fox broadcast, recalled the chaotic final sequence as a “comedy of errors.” Quinn threw his headset to the ground in frustration.

“I was surprised,” Giants coach John Harbaugh said.

The 27-27 tie was officially over. But the explanations had just begun.

Daniels called out the need to play better “situational football” and blamed himself.

“We got to stop the clock,” Daniels said afterward. “It starts from everybody top down, but ultimately, you know, it’s on me.”

Quinn said to blame him, the coach.

“The sequencing of that does not fall on him,” Quinn said. “It’s an outside throw or a clock [spike],” Quinn said. “Those are the two: out-of-bounds throw or a clock, and it has to come from me. I don’t have to put him into that spot. I can do that earlier, and we can finish the kick earlier. We don’t need to gain more yards, so that’s on me.”

Why not just spike the ball with 13 seconds left instead of have Daniels drop back at all?

“I’m saying we don’t need to gain any more” yards to make the field goal shorter, Quinn said. “We’re just trying to gain more. We don’t need to.”

Commanders minority owner Magic Johnson posted on X that he was “in total disbelief my Commanders had such poor clock management in today’s overtime game against the Giants. All we had to do was kick the field goal and we would have won the game! 🤦🏾‍♂️”

Quinn’s desire to run a play and either gain a few more yards or drain a few more seconds of clock was perhaps rooted in what had taken place during a pair of wild finishes earlier this season that had shown the perils of leaving too much time on the clock.

Only hours earlier Sunday, the Philadelphia Eagles kicked a go-ahead field goal to take the lead on Jacksonville with just 8 seconds left in regulation. But that was enough time for the Jaguars to run the ensuing kickoff back into range for what became a game-winning field goal to stun the Eagles. Two weeks ago, Baltimore trailed when it got the ball back with only 7 seconds left in regulation but was able to move into field-goal range for a game-winning kick to beat Dallas.

Both of the wild endings produced by the Jaguars and the Ravens required huge, yard-gaining plays. All the Commanders needed to secure their own win was a spike, one of the simplest plays in football.

“I’m gutted for our team,” Quinn said. “And that’s the hardest part.”

World.title: The 49ers look like the NFL’s best team after surviving a heavyweight fight
World.content:
The last time San Francisco 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy played in Seattle, he could lead an injury-laden 49ers team to only two field goals in a 35-point playoff loss to the Super Bowl-bound Seahawks.

On Sunday, Purdy led San Francisco to a game-winning drive in the fourth quarter of a 32-29 win, handing Seattle its first home loss in 371 days.

Is San Francisco headed to the Super Bowl next? There’s a long way to go, but the 49ers are 5-0 for the third time under coach Kyle Shanahan — and the last two times they were still playing in February.

Sunday’s game was an instant classic, a matchup filled with wild moments and playoff intensity. The teams combined for a whopping seven turnovers and multiple personal fouls, and one player — San Francisco linebacker Dre Greenlaw — was even ejected.

The defenses largely dominated until the fourth quarter. That was when Purdy, perhaps the MVP favorite through the first four weeks and change of the NFL season, stepped up.

Trailing 26-21, Purdy led the 49ers on a 12-play, 74-yard touchdown drive that culminated in a 7-yard touchdown pass to Mike Evans. Purdy then threw to Evans again to convert a 2-point attempt to put San Francisco ahead 29-26.

San Francisco receiver Mike Evans scores a 2-point conversion against the Seahawks on Sunday. Steph Chambers / Getty Images

After a Seattle field goal, the 49ers traveled 43 yards in eight plays for a 44-yard field goal that proved to be the game winner.

“I thought Brock did an unbelievable job finding a way there to win at the end,” Shanahan said. “There were some ups and downs. By no means was everything perfect. He was really good in the fourth quarter.”

On the Seahawks’ final possession, the offense couldn’t convert a fourth-and-10 — though whether receiver Cooper Kupp was able to stretch the ball for a first down on the play seemed up for debate.

While neither quarterback was great Sunday, Purdy had some impressive moments considering the circumstances. Facing the NFL’s second-best defense in expected points added per play, Purdy capitalized on early turnovers before he managed the two scoring drives in the fourth.

And he did so with a depleted receiving corps. The 49ers entered Sunday with four receivers on injured reserve. Then Deebo Samuel and Jacob Cowing were injured during the game.

“We got a bunch of warriors,” Shanahan said of the backups who stepped up. “Everyone knows the talent and the stars of some of the guys on our team. What makes our guys special is how much they love football, how much they give it up every week.”

Among those who played key roles Sunday was Evans, who caught a season-high seven passes for 113 yards and a score, plus the 2-pointer for good measure.

“He’s a game-changer,” Purdy said. “As a quarterback, any time I have to go to him it always feels good.”

Evans told Fox after the game: “We knew it was going to be a dogfight. They’re a great team, and we came out here and showed we’re a great team, as well.”

Purdy finished with a so-so stat line by his standards: 19 of 29 passing for 189 yards, two touchdowns and one interception. More important, though, he outplayed his counterpart, Sam Darnold, and found a way to shepherd two go-ahead drives in the game’s biggest moments.

The 49ers now have the league’s most impressive résumé through five weeks. San Francisco has the best point differential in the NFL, and three of its five wins have come against teams with winning records. And two of those wins came against teams that are both legitimate championship contenders and divisional rivals: Seattle and the Los Angeles Rams.

Purdy has been spectacular this season. After the Week 5 win, he has now thrown for 13 touchdowns and only two interceptions. Sunday’s game was the only one this season in which he has posted a passer rating under 100, and he still posted a mark of 92.5.

The 49ers have done all of that despite being beset with injuries. While the Seahawks were down some of their own key players Sunday, San Francisco ultimately pulled out an ugly win on the road against a team that hadn’t lost at home in over a year — a sign of how much stronger the 49ers look compared with a season ago.

World.title: To counteract a spooky economy, America prepares to spend on Halloween candy
World.content:
This Halloween, the fright isn’t just at the haunted house. Rising prices for everything from groceries to gas are driving many consumers to cut back.

“I’m walking to save a little bit of money,” said Lakisha Reardon, a legal assistant. “I’m bringing in my own lunch.”

Reardon said she has especially seen her electric bill spike this year. She said she is paying an extra $150 every month.

“I’m ready to invest in candles,” she said.

But one thing she won’t give up? Halloween candy.

Average prices for chewing gum and candy have soared 8.1% over the last year, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Despite the higher prices, Americans are still buying treats.

“I remember being a little kid and being super excited when I would get Reese’s Cups,” said Abby Mynatt, a college student who lives in Knoxville, Tennessee. “I want to give that to some other children.”

Mynatt, 21, said she usually spends around $50 for Halloween candy. She is expecting to shell out a bit more money this year despite financial pressures.

“I certainly think there are a little more tense things with my budget right now,” she said. “But I still think that certain things, even just little pleasures, are still worth it.”

The price of nonchocolate candy items has averaged $3.31 this year, up 1.8% from last year, according to PwC. But Halloween chocolate prices have jumped 15.5%, to an average of $5.67 per package.

Industry experts attribute the rise in chocolate prices partly to a cocoa shock over the last couple of years.

Extreme weather in key cocoa-producing countries like Ivory Coast and Ghana sent global cocoa prices soaring — they quadrupled from January 2023 to January 2025, according to data from the International Monetary Fund.

“Because chocolate makers buy cocoa months, sometimes up to two years ahead, shoppers are paying for that spike now,” said Ali Furman, PwC’s consumer markets industry leader. “Cocoa prices have since fallen by about half, but lower costs take time to reach the shelf and won’t show up on shelves this Halloween season.”

The market research firm NIQ has seen a more muted increase in prices, with chocolate overall up 9.4% from a year ago but Halloween-specific chocolate just up 1.7%.

Analysts say tariffs this year aren’t helping, either. In July, the U.S. imposed tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on 60 trade partners.

“Chocolate comes from elsewhere, so tariffs being added onto it have certainly increased costs that manufacturers are feeling as well,” said Chris Costagli, the leader of food and nonalcoholic beverage insights at NIQ.

Still, the National Retail Federation projects that Halloween spending will soar to $13.5 billion this season, with 96% of Halloween shoppers expecting to buy sweets.

It’s part of a broader trend this year of consumers leaning into little luxuries like makeup and movie tickets as an antidote for economic gloom.

A lot of that gloom stems from concerns about inflation and the rising cost of living. Consumer prices have jumped 3.4% over the last year in large part due to rising energy costs, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

With wages up just 3% over the same period, paychecks aren’t keeping up with prices.

It has led many people to forgo bigger purchases and cut back in small ways every day.

Leonard Smith is planning to buy Halloween candy this year, but says he may cut back.

“I don’t want to spend that much money because I need money for other things besides candy,” said Smith, 36, who lives in Delaware.

But he has a strategy to save: Smith buys candy after Halloween when many stores slash prices.

Ari Monahan, a nanny who describes herself as “like a Disney adult, but for Halloween,” said she may get candy that’s a little less expensive, but she still wants to treat the kids in her New York City neighborhood.

“I want to be the good house,” she said. “There’s not that many kids in my area, so I want to give them a little prize for coming.”

Monahan, 30, also buys little treats for herself. “Dark chocolate, a lot of coffees, anything pumpkin spice,” she said.

“If it makes me smile and I have a little money, I’ll pay for it because everything is so grim right now,” she added. “A pair of socks with dachshunds on it, I’m like, ‘You know what? I can do that. I could swing it today.’”

Monahan says rising prices are taking a big bite out of her paycheck, and she worries she might never be able to buy a house.

Home prices are near record highs, and mortgage rates have spiked over the course of the war with Iran — with the 30-year fixed rate topping 7.6% earlier this month, a nearly three-year high. It’s a double whammy that is putting a key pillar of the American Dream further out of reach for many people.

And yet in an economy where the big things might seem far away, there are always little treats to get by.

“I’ve been in a real ‘buy yourself little treats’ mentality,” said Monahan. “I keep buying too much stuff for my dog. I guess I didn’t buy another dog. That’s saving, right?”

World.title: Hurricane Simon lashes Mexico's Pacific coast as a powerful Category 3 storm
World.content:
Hurricane Simon's eye remains just off Mexico's Pacific coast, but the Category 3 storm's most powerful winds and rain slammed people living between the Sierra Madre and the ocean.

The hurricane's center swirled parallel to the coast, closing in on the Puerto Vallarta area, where its most damaging winds and rain were expected to hit around midnight and continue through Monday morning. The storm has weakened throughout the day, with its maximum sustained wind speed decreasing by about 25 mph and being downgraded after spending much of the day as a Category 4 storm. And while the National Hurricane Center said additional weakening was expected throughout the day, it noted Simon was still expected to be a strong hurricane as it passes Mexico's west-central coast on Sunday.

That's not good news for people in the Puerto Vallarta area, a popular destination for U.S. tourists. Just inland and uphill from the resort areas, many Mexicans live in communities where housing might not stand up to the storm.

A person uses their phone while waves hit the shore, as Hurricane Simon approaches Mexico's Pacific coast, bringing heavy rain and strong winds to Manzanillo, Mexico, on Oct. 11, 2026. Daniel Becerril / REUTERS

As of Sunday evening, Simon was centered about 50 miles south of Cabo Corrientes, and moving north-northwest at a relatively slow 5 mph.

A senior hurricane center specialist, Phillippe Pappin, said this westernmost tip of mainland Mexico is the area most likely to get a direct hit from the system. Cabo Corrientes is at the southern tip of Bahia de Banderas, the wide bay where Puerto Vallarta looks out to the Pacific.

Hurricane-force winds extend outward up to 25 miles, and tropical-storm-force winds reach up to 60 miles from Simon's center, meaning the entire area between Mexico's western coast and the Sierra Madre mountains could be affected.

"We're expecting catastrophic wind and life-threatening storm surge impacts along that west central coast of Mexico where the hurricane warning is currently in effect," Pappin said. "They're also getting very heavy rainfall associated with the storm that's likely going to produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides in areas of higher terrain along the Mexican coastline, and there will be significant swells."

As the storm approached Puerto Vallarta, National Guard vehicles patrolled the streets while police used a megaphone to call out the few people who were jogging, walking their dogs or biking by the waterfront. Officers reminded people that the area was closed and urged them to take shelter. Not everyone followed the orders.

A man rides a bicycle as Hurricane Simon approaches Mexico's Pacific coast, bringing heavy rain and strong winds to Manzanillo, Mexico, on Oct. 11, 2026. Daniel Becerril / REUTERS

Meanwhile, the hurricane was dumping rain over parts of southwestern Mexico. It could bring 10 to 20 inches of rain in many places, with some areas in the states of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco receiving up to 30 inches.

Jalisco state suspended classes on Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating dozens of people from at-risk areas.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum took to the social platform X on Sunday to urge people in Jalisco, Colima, Nayarit and Michoacan to stay sheltered until the government issues a notification that the danger has passed. She also asked people to follow recommendations from civil protection officials and to avoid traveling on public roads.

"Precautionary evacuation efforts to safe zones are ongoing; the priority is our safety," she wrote.

Hotel worker Víctor Martínez went shopping for nonperishable food Sunday afternoon. He said he could not go to work because public transportation service was suspended and most of the hotel had been evacuated.

Martínez said he found people's concerns about the hurricane comforting.

"It happened to us before. It hit us years ago," Martínez said, referring to a Category 5 hurricane that hit the area in 2002. "People didn't expect it. We were very skeptical that it would ever hit us. Now, though, we're different. Precautions are being taken. It happened to us once, and we won't let it happen again."

On Saturday, ahead of the storm's arrival, convenience stores, hotels and other businesses in Puerto Vallarta were boarding up their windows. Few were walking the streets under overcast skies.

A man boards up a shop as Hurricane Simon approaches Puerto Vallarta, Mexico, on Oct. 10, 2026. AP Photo/Fernando Llano

"Let's hope it doesn't hit us, right? That it doesn't affect us," Jesús Gómez said as he stood outside a shop and handed out free samples of candied peanuts to passersby. "We'll be working as usual throughout the day, but when Civil Protection officials come and tell us we need to close, then we'll close and take shelter until the storm passes."

The hurricane center expected a dangerous storm surge "along the immediate coast near and to the east of where the center makes landfall." The agency warned that near the coast, large and destructive waves will accompany the surge.

Despite the risks posed by Simon, tourists were still arriving in Puerto Vallarta.

Visitors Ricardo Ramírez and Brenda Villarreal, who have never lived through a hurricane, went looking for food by the city's boardwalk and came across police urging people to take shelter. Ramírez said they were completely unprepared for the situation.

"The boardwalk is closed. Be responsible. Understand!" police told passersby using a megaphone.

Ramírez said he and Villarreal had planned their four-day vacation since last year and traveled from Guadalajara, Jalisco's capital.

"We don't know the extent of the danger yet," Villarreal said. "We're just starting to see what's going on."

Canadian tourist Ed Currie, who, along with his wife, still has five more days to enjoy Puerto Vallarta, said the hurricane had not yet affected his plans.

"Just stay in the hotel and look out the window hopefully," he said of what the couple would do Saturday. "I just don't know what to expect."

Unlike the Atlantic, which saw just its first named hurricane of the season this week with Isaias, the Pacific season has been very active. Simon's arrival comes on the heels of Polo, which slammed Mexico last week as a Category 2 hurricane before reaching the southwestern U.S. and bringing heavy flooding to the region.

World.title: Terminal in Riyadh airport hit again, a day after deadly strike killed 12
World.content:
A passenger terminal at the international airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, was attacked again on Sunday, one day after a deadly strike on the Riyadh airport killed at least 12 people, including a U.S. citizen, and wounded hundreds of others.

The second attack comes as Yemen's Houthi group said they carried out at least four operations targeting King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh since Saturday.

Saudi authorities said there were injuries in the latest attack on the King Khalid International Airport complex for terminals 3 and 4, serving domestic flights. The airport — struck four times in the past five days — has been closed since Saturday's missile attack, which was the deadliest in a Gulf Arab nation since the Iran war began. Over 300 other people were wounded, some critically.

Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said on Telegram that the attacks are in response to "brutal Saudi aggression against our country and our people," CBS News partner BBC News reported. He claimed Saudi Arabia launched more than 120 airstrikes in the past 24 hours in Houthi-controlled territory in Yemen.

The Houthis said their other targets included the Shugadam gas facility, which belongs to Saudi's national petroleum and natural gas company Aramco, the Tanajib oil refinery, and King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, the BBC reported.

Saudi's civil aviation authority confirmed the strike on King Fahd Airport.

Saturday's strike at the airport, the deadliest on Saudi soil in more than a decade, marked a major escalation in the war between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and the kingdom and further complicated sputtering efforts to halt the U.S.-Iran war.

Saudi Arabia has moved Riyadh schools online amid the Houthis' latest threat. Flights were diverted elsewhere, the Flightradar24 tracker said. Countries including the U.S., Britain, Germany, Australia and Canada warned citizens to avoid the airport.

Earlier on Saturday, the Houthies threatened new attacks on the kingdom's airports, except for the holy sites of Mecca and Medina, warning passengers not to travel.

"The airports and airspace are exposed to targeting and constitute a theatre of operations for our forces," Saree wrote on X.

He urged "everyone to take our warnings seriously."

On Sunday, the Houthis said the airport under their control in the Yemeni capital of Sanaa had been struck again. They blamed the Saudis but provided no details.

The attack on Riyadh's airport on Saturday drew condemnation from the United Nations and world leaders, including President Trump, who said he was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis.

"The United States strongly condemns the recent attacks on the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia by the terrorist Houthis, including today's strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh that took numerous innocent lives, including an American citizen," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a social media post.

A State Department spokesperson told CBS News the Trump administration is in close contact with its "Saudi partners."

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the attacks by Iran's proxies are "pushing the region into a spiral of violence."

"They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes," she wrote on X.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday condemned "in the strongest possible terms" the attack on King Khalid Airport and extended his condolences.

"Terrorism targets innocent people and seeks to spread fear and instability. It must be confronted with resolve," he said in a statement shared on X. "Israel looks forward to a strong Middle East—one that stands united against threats, protects its people, and builds a future of security, cooperation, and prosperity for all the peoples of our region.

The Saudi statement about Saturday's attack said the dead included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said several hospitals were treating the 309 people injured, some in serious condition.

The Egyptian woman was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flynas, according to the Egyptian state-run Al-Qahera News television.

The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said Sunday that one of its citizens died after being wounded in the attack on the Riyadh airport a day earlier.

"It is learnt that one Indian national injured in the Riyadh attack has unfortunately lost his life today. We convey our heartfelt condolences to the family of the deceased," the embassy wrote in a statement posted on X.

The Houthis claimed attacks earlier in the week on King Khalid International Airport that killed three Saudis, including a pilot. The airport has no military facilities.

The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis.

World.title: Trump announces Russia-Ukraine "energy ceasefire" after criticizing Zelenskyy
World.content:
President Trump said Sunday that Ukraine and Russia have agreed to an "energy ceasefire," shortly after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy vowed to continue striking Russian oil refineries in response to criticism from Mr. Trump.

"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it! Thank you for your attention to this matter," Mr. Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.

It's unclear exactly what the ceasefire entails, and Zelenskyy told Axios after Mr. Trump's announcement that the ceasefire "was news for me." The Ukrainian president later said in a statement posted to social media that he spoke with U.S. members of Congress and thanked allies for their support. But he said that despite the ceasefire announcement, Russia has struck energy infrastructure in Ukraine, including a power plant in Kharkiv.

"Ukraine wants peace. The question is whether Russia does," Zelenskyy said Sunday. "The Armed Forces of Ukraine have received all the appropriate orders. We are awaiting clear details of the dialogue between America and Russia - and we expect Putin to follow through on what President Trump said."

Burnham says backs Trump's 'call' for Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire

CBS News has reached out to the White House for clarity on the agreement.

U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney both said in separate statements Sunday that they supported the energy ceasefire.

"Ukraine is ready if Russia stops its attacks," Burnham wrote on X, confirming he spoke with Zelenskyy on Saturday. "This is the best route to get energy and fuel back into world markets."

Carney expressed his "strong support" for an energy ceasefire when he spoke to Zelenskyy earlier Sunday. However, he denounced the U.S.-Russian deal on diesel supplies, saying it undermines efforts for stability in Europe and ending the war in Ukraine.

Trump criticizes Zelenskyy's leadership

Mr. Trump previously took aim at the Ukrainian president's leadership, suggesting Zelenskyy should be replaced and blaming him for high diesel prices. The Ukrainian president clapped back, saying Russia alone was responsible for the war in Ukraine.

The exchange came as Kyiv pressed its campaign against infrastructure deep inside Russia, with a drone attack on Sunday shutting down a data center run by Russian technology giant Yandex, the third strike on the company's facilities in four days. Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4 1/2 years since Moscow's full-scale invasion.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has also pushed back on Mr. Trump's comments, writing on X late Saturday that Zelenskyy was leading the country through a war for its independence.

"He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide. Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well," Sybiha wrote.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks to the media after a German-Ukrainian business forum in Kyiv, Ukraine, Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026. AP Photo/Dan Bashakov

Mr. Trump said Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S.

"I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does," Mr. Trump said.

U.S. Senators: "Immediately reverse course" on Russian diesel plan

A bipartisan group of six U.S. Senators on Sunday called for the Trump administration to "immediately reverse course" on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices.

Four Republican senators — Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah — and Democrat Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut signed onto the statement released Sunday in protest of the deal. They said the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute.

"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course," they wrote.

According to an announcement from Mr. Trump on Friday, the U.S. has made a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy more than 300,000 tons of diesel from Russia right away, followed by 500,000 tons in November, and 1 million tons after that. Amid the deal, which attempts to address high fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections, Mr. Trump has also urged Zelenskyy for weeks to stop strikes on Russian energy infrastructure. Zelenskyy criticized the deal and said it would help fund Russia's war in Ukraine.



Mr. Trump has sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia's war effort.

Ukraine strikes Russian data centers

The Ukrainian drone attack on the Yandex data center in the city of Vladimir, east of Moscow, caused outages across the company's services, leaving users in dozens of Russian cities and in Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia unable to order taxis or access banking services, according to Russian independent news outlet Astra.

"As a result of the drone attack, the infrastructure of Yandex's data center in Vladimir was damaged. Operations at the data center have been completely halted. There were no injuries," said the Yandex Cloud Telegram channel, which provides operational updates on service availability.

A Yandex food delivery courier rides his scooter in Moscow, Russia, Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026. AP Photo/Alexander Zemlianichenko

In Moscow, residents described disruption to everyday tasks. Pavel Belyavskiy, a driver for Yandex Taxi, said it was unclear whether orders were coming through at all, and that on several rides he had to cancel after waiting a long time because he could not reach the passenger.

"I'd press the 'call' button to contact them, but nothing happens," he said. "There's nothing I can do, so I'm just forced to cancel."

Igor Mann said he went to check the status of an order on the Yandex Market shopping platform but the page was unavailable, and connecting through a VPN did not help. "Nothing worked," he said.

Another Moscow resident, Eduard Malyavko, said the outages had "direct impact" and weren't just about "convenience."

"It's also about work," he said, adding that they also affected "healthcare, and everything else."

On Thursday, a drone attack took a Yandex data center offline in the Ryazan region, southeast of Moscow. A day later, Ukrainian drones hit the company's major data center in the Kaluga region, southwest of Moscow, partly putting it out of action, Yandex said.

Yandex, often described as Russia's Google, runs the country's most popular search engine and a wide range of digital services, and is heavily involved in Russia's artificial intelligence development.

Elsewhere, Zelenskyy said search and rescue operations ended in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia after a Russian bombing on Saturday.

Zelenskyy said 23 people were killed in the attack, including four children. More than 30 people were wounded, Fedorov said, eight of whom remain hospitalized.

A man was killed and two women wounded in a Ukrainian drone strike on Russia's Bryansk border region, local officials said Sunday.

World.title: Pope Leo to undergo surgery after nodular lesion found in lung, Vatican says
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV will undergo surgery this week after a nodular lesion was found in his lung, the Vatican said. Recovery is expected to take a week.

Leo, 71, said Sunday that doctors recently discovered the nodular lesion during medical checks. He said it was found in an early stage and was "circumscribed."

"The doctors believe it's best to take action, so, following their advice, I've decided to have surgery to remove it," Leo said in remarks during his Sunday noon blessing. "Thank you for your spiritual support, and I entrust myself to your prayers."

A statement by Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni didn't say when the pope would be hospitalized but that it would be in the "first days" of the week. He was expected to be treated at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, which has a special apartment for the pope.

A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 1 inch that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen, according to the American Cancer Society. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening.

"Lung nodules are fairly common and are often benign, but benign and cancerous nodules can have a similar appearance on imaging," said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown's Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center.

"When there is sufficient concern, and when it is safe to do so based on the location of the nodule and the overall health of the patient, surgical removal can provide a definitive diagnosis," he said in an email.

The pope has a major trip planned Nov. 6-17 to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It's unclear whether the planned surgery and recovery would affect the itinerary, but Leo said earlier in his remarks Sunday that he planned to go.

The American pope has no previously known health problems and is known to be physically active, with weekly tennis games and swimming at the papal summer retreat in Castel Gandolfo. This, Dr. Massimo Di Maio, president of the Italian Association of Medical Oncology, said, is "an important starting point for coping as well as possible with treatment, including surgery."

Di Maio said it will be important to determine if the nodule is benign or malignant, and if it is malignant, whether it has spread. When the disease is detected at an early stage, "the aim … is curative," he added.

Depending on what is found, possible treatments can include chemotherapy and radiation therapy, Di Maio told Italy's private Sky TG24.

"When we talk about something being localized, that can also refer to the need to establish whether the disease is confined to that one site or whether scans show signs of disease elsewhere," he said, adding that he has not treated the pope and was speaking about the disease in general.

Leo's predecessor, Pope Francis, died April 21, 2025, of a stroke following a long hospitalization brought on by a respiratory crisis that developed into double pneumonia. Francis suffered from chronic lung disease and had part of one lung removed as a young man.

World.title: Tropical Storm Rachel downgraded as high winds and rain turn inward
World.content:
Tropical Storm Rachel downgraded as high winds and rain turn inward

toggle caption i Jill Connelly/AP Photo

The National Weather Service said on Sunday that Rachel has been downgraded to a post-tropical storm after causing flooding and damage in southern California over the weekend before moving inland across the desert southwest.

The region is still at risk of flash floods as the storm's remnants were expected to continue dumping rain and bringing wind gusts through the weekend, the weather service said , adding that high surf would continue battering coastal communities.

Oceanfront homes in coastal California cities, such as Long Beach and Newport Beach, were partially submerged as heavy surf breached sand berms that had been erected to keep the water away.

Sponsor Message

Flood warnings remained in effect for much of the California coastline through the weekend, from San Diego up to the San Francisco Bay area.

As the storm moved inland and northeast, some areas saw rockslides that temporarily blocked roads. Rain pounded Las Vegas, which broke a daily rainfall record Sunday. And the National Weather Service issued a flood watch for much of Utah, including Salt Lake City, which it said would get heavy rain beginning Sunday evening.

toggle caption i Jill Connelly/AP Photo

Forecasters warned that Rachel could be just a preview of what's to come for California over the next several months. They expect this winter to usher in the strongest El Niño weather pattern on record — which brings hotter-than-average ocean temperatures — and with it likely record rainfall, explosive surf and mudslides well into next year.

Last month, California Gov. Gavin Newsom issued an emergency proclamation, releasing money and other resources so the state could start preparing to protect critical infrastructure and educate the state's residents on how to prepare for severe weather.

"That means getting flood-fighting supplies into position, bolstering our water infrastructure, and helping communities across the Golden State prepare," Newsom said in a statement following the proclamation.

The state is pre-positioning more than 4 million sandbags, more than 50,000 feet of portable flood barriers and 400,000 tons of rock to repair levees. It's also inspecting dams across the state and taking other precautions, such as strengthening the pillars that hold up beach piers.

Sponsor Message

The strong El Niño is also expected to bring severe weather to Mexico. Over the weekend, Hurricane Simon lashed at the country's Pacific Coast as a Category 4 hurricane. The eye of the storm was moving parallel to the coastline about 60 miles offshore, near the city of Manzanillo. It's unclear if the storm will make landfall, but Mexican officials said they expected heavy damage from its pounding rains and winds nonetheless.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum urged residents to stay indoors.

World.title: Pope Leo XIV to undergo lung surgery this week
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV to undergo lung surgery this week

toggle caption i Gregorio Borgia/AP

Pope Leo XIV announced Sunday that he would have surgery this week to remove a "localized nodule" in his lung.

Leo said the nodule was found at a "very early stage" with doctors recommending surgery.

"Following their advice, I have therefore decided to undergo an operation to remove it," Leo said during his weekly Sunday noon blessing in St. Peter's Square.

The surgery will take place at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, which is the primary location for popes to receive medical attention.

"I thank you for your spiritual closeness and entrust myself to your prayers," Leo said to the crowds on Sunday. He later posted the message about his surgery on social media.

According to the American Cancer Society, a lung nodule is a small abnormal area , less than or equal to 3 cm, found during a CT scan of the chest or abdomen. These tests are often conducted as routine screenings for "trauma, heart disease, non-cancer related lung disease, or lung infection."

Sponsor Message

Dr. Panagis Galiatsatos, a pulmonary physician at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, said lung nodules are common in older adults.

"The majority of lung nodules are benign," Galiatsatos said. "I usually call them the lungs' wrinkles"

When they're discovered, doctors will test them to determine whether there is cause for concern.

"If they're now discussing that they need to remove the lung nodule, one of his tests must have crossed their threshold … and the suspicion and concern for cancer became a little bit higher," Galiatsatos said. "So that's why he's undergoing this surgery."

Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni said in a statement that "the operation is scheduled for the first days of this week and the estimated post-operative recovery time will be about one week."

Leo's next major international trip is scheduled for early November to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It's unclear if the surgery would affect his itinerary.

During his papacy, Leo has been outspoken about peace throughout the world. He spent part of his Sunday address renewing calls for peace in Ukraine.

"I make a heartfelt appeal to the parties to the conflict to allow the safe transport of grain across the Black Sea," Leo said. "The daily bread of millions of people cannot be held hostage by war."

Sponsor Message

On Saturday, the Pope also called for the death penalty to be abolished, saying on X that it is "inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person."

"The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment: effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption," Leo said.

World.title: Hurricane Simon nears Mexico with 155 mph winds and flooding fears
World.content:
Hurricane Simon nears Mexico with 155 mph winds and flooding fears

toggle caption i Fernando Llano/AP

PUERTO VALLARTA, Mexico — The eye of Hurricane Simon was just off the Pacific coast of Mexico early Sunday and was expected to move inland later in the day as an extremely powerful storm.

Simon has strengthened to 155 mph (250 kph), only just below the threshold for becoming a Category 5 storm, the highest on the Saffir Simpson scale. It was about 60 miles (100 kilometers) west-southwest of Manzanilla and moving north-northwest at 6 mph (9 kph).

The hurricane could bring 10 to 20 inches (25-50 cm) of rain over parts of southwestern Mexico, with some areas in the states of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco receiving up to 30 inches (76 centimeters).

Sponsor Message

"This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," the center warned.

Jalisco state suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating dozens of people from at-risk areas. It also asked the tourism sector in Puerto Vallarta, a popular destination for U.S. tourists, to ensure that both workers and visitors were fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones.

Convenience stores, hotels and other businesses in Puerto Vallarta were boarding up their windows Saturday, and few were walking the streets under overcast skies.

"Let's hope it doesn't hit us, right? That it doesn't affect us," Jesús Gómez said as he stood outside a shop and handed out free samples of candied peanuts to passersby. "We'll be working as usual throughout the day, but when Civil Protection officials come and tell us we need to close, then we'll close and take shelter until the storm passes."

The hurricane center expected a dangerous storm surge along the immediate coast near and to the east of where the center makes landfall. The agency warned that near the coast, large and destructive waves will accompany the surge.

Canadian tourist Ed Currie, who along with his wife still has five more days to enjoy Puerto Vallarta, said the hurricane had not yet affected his plans.

Sponsor Message

"Just stay in the hotel and look out the window hopefully," he said of what the couple would do. "I just don't know what to expect."

World.title: Justice Department investigates TV networks, citing possible anti-trust violations
World.content:
Justice Department investigates TV networks, citing possible anti-trust violations

toggle caption i Alex Brandon/AP

The Justice Department has launched a formal anti-trust investigation into five major U.S. television networks for their actions during a court battle over whether several news outlets should have access to the White House despite angering President Trump.

While the five networks — ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News — did not comment, press rights advocacy groups denounced the move.

"[S]ummoning antitrust authority, on top of the retaliatory actions the White House has already taken to bar certain outlets, is another and even more brazen attempt to try to intimidate journalists," said Bruce Brown, the president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press.

Sponsor Message

Last month, Trump had aides bar CNN, MSNOW and Politico from the White House after blasting them for what he characterized as unfairly negative coverage. The administration stripped White House press passes from more than 70 journalists. The three news organizations sued in federal court to have their access restored. In court, the Justice Department is citing national security grounds for the decision.

The federal judge overseeing the case issued a temporary stay requiring their passes to be restored and says he will make a more enduring decision by Tuesday evening.

However, the White House also blocked CNN from fulfilling its planned shifts as part of the White House television press pool, which includes the other television networks now under investigation. While the news outlets' decision-making is day-to-day, The five have agreed not to substitute for CNN on the days that the administration blocks the network, though they are handling decisions day-to-day.

As part of a longstanding practice, the members of the pool share the logistical burden and the costs of covering Trump's actions in public appearances that take place in smaller places, such as Air Force One. As a result of the ban on CNN, the networks did not cover an event Trump had with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Sponsor Message

The Justice Department says it is reviewing whether the coordination of that decision constitutes anti-trust behavior, which is to say, anti-competitive.

"Members of the television press pool have proudly boycotted covering White House events. Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act," the Justice Department said in a statement Saturday. "The Antitrust Division is investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws."

Four people with direct knowledge of events affirmed the outlines of the investigation. They spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly on the matter. The development was first reported by the New York Times.

Michael Dorfman, a professor of Constitutional law at Cornell University's law school, says that political motivation on the part of the president or the Justice Department in investigating the networks does not shield them from legal repercussions in court.

But Dorfman says it would be subject to a review of whether the networks' actions were reasonable. These were, he says. And he highlights what he calls another "oddity."

"If the networks agreeing not to cover the White House is illegal, why isn't the press pool itself illegal? Presumably the answer is that the kind of cooperation involved in the press pool is necessitated by the limited space in particular venues," Dorfman writes in an email. "But if that's a sufficient justification for the cooperation in coverage, why isn't standing up to protect the free press at least as an important a justification?

Part of an ongoing conflict

The incident highlights the increased tensions between the president and the news media. ABC and its parent company Disney are suing Trump's chief broadcast regulator for mandating an immediate review of whether it should hold all eight of its local TV station licenses — threatening a hit to its bottom line. A judge is weighing whether to intervene in the process.

Sponsor Message

Trump has frequently called for ABC (and NBC) to lose their broadcast licenses.

Disney calls the review of the ABC station licenses retaliation over content Trump doesn't like on The View and Jimmy Kimmel Live.

Federal Communications Commission chief Brendan Carr says it's all a question of upholding "the public interest." Under Carr, the FCC has also launched investigations of all other major broadcast networks, including NPR, with the exception of Fox broadcast network, owned by Trump's political ally Rupert Murdoch.

Trump is also suing many major news organizations as an individual. Those outlets include the New York Times, BBC News, and the Wall Street Journal (which is also owned by Murdoch but sometimes draws Trump's ire). ABC and CBS settled earlier lawsuits Trump brought against them.

"The investigation is nonsense," said Seth Stern, Freedom of the Press Foundation's chief of advocacy. "Trump may view the presidency as a business venture, but news outlets' standing up for their constitutional rights has nothing to do with antitrust law."

World.title: Don't be scared: Being afraid is outright fun, and maybe useful
World.content:
Don't be scared: Being afraid is outright fun, and maybe useful

toggle caption i Ryan Benk/NPR News

It's October and that can only mean one thing – the spooky season is in full swing.

Americans are expected to spend more than $13 billion dollars on celebrating this season, whether that's on horror films, costumes, candy or attractions, according to the National Retail Federation.

As much as $300 - $500 million of that spending comes from attending a haunt, where people willingly give up their hard-earned cash to be frightened. And tens of millions of people take part in this kind of activity every year.

But why do people like getting scared? The search for that answer starts with one of the largest haunted attractions in the country, Markoff's Haunted Forest in Dickerson, Maryland. Markoff's has more than a mile of haunted trails and dozens of themed haunted houses. It employs hundreds of engineers, retail attendants, makeup artists and actors.

Sponsor Message

Open since 1992, the attraction starts with towering skull-emblazoned wooden gates reminiscent of folk horror movies like "The Wicker Man."

Just inside, director of operations Paul Brubacher stands in between two huge bonfires.

"Some of our designers, including myself, have done some music festivals before. So yeah, that's the inspiration… from kind-of [a] Van Helsing vampire village aspect of things," Brubacher says.

There is hardly a thing that happens in this haunt without him knowing.

"This is an emergency radio that we have in each one of our scenes. In case an actor has a problem or somebody falls down and needs to be evacuated," Brubacher says. Before hitting the trail, he takes us behind the scenes to a barn where scare-actors are getting finishing touches of makeup.

Art director and makeup manager Chris Knowles and his team are using a bevy of pressurized airbrushes to quickly creep-ify all kinds of ghouls, vampires and aliens.
