"It's great because you can get color on really finely or cover areas. [It] swaps colors really quickly as well, which is essential because we've only got like about seven minutes to do the makeup because we got like 100 odd people and two hours to do it," Knowles says.

toggle caption i Ryan Benk/NPR News

Robert Doyle, 38, is in Knowles' chair at the moment.

Sponsor Message

"I love Halloween. I love going out and interacting with people, entertaining them, making them laugh. Giving them a good scare, you know, giving them a good dopamine rush," Doyle says.

Doyle has played all kinds of frightening characters in his five years at Markoff's. He's been a killer clown, a demon and tonight he's a Nosferatu-style vampire with sharp fangs, a bloody mouth and pupils as dark as coal.

toggle caption i Ryan Benk/NPR News

Doyle thinks people keep coming back to places like Markoff's to face down their fears safely.

"People want to challenge themselves and they can say they accomplished something," Doyle says.

Another scare-actor, wearing a black top hat and looking like a cross between a straw and hair covered zombie, and hoodoo shaman is ready for his opening night.

His day-walker name is Jermaine Hoes.

"I am something that you see when you wake up at 3 o'clock in the morning," Hoes says.

toggle caption i Ryan Benk/NPR News.

Hoes has been a scare actor at different haunts around Maryland for years, and he says his reason for moonlighting as a horrific beast is pretty simple.

"I like scaring people. I like to make you run and scream and holler everywhere," Hoes says.

Leaving the actors so they can get into character, it's time to take to the trail, which begins with an ominous, steady heartbeat pumping through hidden speakers.

The trail is dark, foggy and winding. It's constructed in such a way that you can't escape the scares. Even trying to escape signals to the actors that you're ripe for a fright.

There are snakes, zombified pumpkin heads, ghosts, vampires, ghouls, aliens and even cannibals.

The trail is barely a mile, but between the terrain and its twists, it can take more than an hour to get through.

Voices cry out in pain and shriek in fear. Many seem menacing.

Sponsor Message

"You can join us," one voice in the shadows snickers.

"Don't you want your face on one of these pumpkins?," another cackles. "It just takes a little bit of a beating!"

Anything that could scare you is here, and it didn't take much in this secluded, murky environment.

The science of screams

"Fear is extremely fast," says Harvard Medical School associate professor of radiology Nouchine Hadjikhani.

For much of her career, Hadjikhani has studied what happens in the brain when someone is afraid. She uses computer screens and brain monitoring equipment to show subjects frightening images and measure their brain's reaction.

"If I show you very briefly, so for, you know, 30 milliseconds or something, snakes and spiders, I will see that your amygdala gets activated," Hadjikhani says.

She says it's this activation that makes a jump scare so effective.

"Your heart goes faster. You go a little further back and you start sweating. Your pupils get high for a stupid image on the screen," she says.

According to Hadjikhani, we get scared when something – usually visual – sets off the fear center of the brain. And she says she can elicit that same brain reaction in people just by showing them pictures of other folks who are scared. But she says it's difficult to know why some people derive pleasure from fear.

You have to talk to them.

Fear is fun

For that we need the scientists at the Recreational Fear Lab at Aarhaus University in Denmark.

YouTube

Co-directors Matthias Clausen and Marc Andersen have created all kinds of studies into what keeps people coming back for frights.

Over the years, what they've found is that there is more than one type of recreational fear.

"We did an early study where we tried to see if we could identify the personality profile of the horror fan and what we found was a god-forsaken mess," Clausen says.

A rollercoaster enthusiast, for example, may detest horror films. And a scary movie scream queen might lose her lunch at a theme park.

Sponsor Message

But Clausen says survey after survey at the Fear Lab shows fear-for-fun is surprisingly universal.

"When you engage in recreational activities, you're essentially administering a fear vaccine," Clausen says. Seeking out fear is our way of preparing our bodies for the sometimes scary real world.

And this vaccine is actually fun for most people. "It doesn't hurt," Clausen says.

The duo has called this a "fear inoculation."

Co-director Marc Anderssen has also interviewed subjects who say they treat their own psychological disorders using fear.

"We have a ton of anecdotal stories about horror fans that we meet that tell us that they deal with their clinical anxiety by popping in a horror movie," Andersen says.

"The first time we heard it, we almost fell off of our chairs because it sounds so counterintuitive."

Playing with fear is also incredibly social , says Matthias Clausen. After going through a haunt for example, groups have told him they've experienced a sense of bonding.

"That's something that characterizes in fact most kinds of recreational experiences," Clausen says.

Back at Markoff's Haunted Forest, scare-actor Jermaine Hoes says his coworkers and the people he's scaring are like a family.

"The people, man. The vibes are great. You know, you meet a lot of people here. They have a ball. You get to mix and mingle with them," Hoes says.

Nothing brings people together like a good scare. Next week, find out how monsters, ghouls and slashers can also mean big bucks.

World.title: She was a global star: Teen bikes 700 miles carrying injured dad. Where is she now?
World.content:
She was a global star: Teen bikes 700 miles carrying injured dad. Where is she now?

toggle caption i Deepak Paswan

Fame is a strange beast. It brings applause, attention and promises of a better life. But when the spotlight moves on, those promises are often forgotten. No one knows this better than 22-year-old Jyoti Kumari.

When she was 15 years old, during the peak of India's COVID shutdown , she shot to international fame for cycling over 700 miles, from northern India to her village in the eastern state of Bihar, with her injured father riding on the back of the hot pink bike she'd bought for $20.

Her dad, Mohan Paswan, drove an autorickshaw for 20 years in Gurugram, a city near Delhi, sending money to his wife and five children in the village of Sirhulli. After he suffered a debilitating road accident in January 2020, Kumari and her mom took the train to Gurugram to care for him.

Sponsor Message

Five months later, he still hadn't made a full recovery and his family was running out of money for food and rent. The family decided they would all be better off at home. But at the time, authorities had shut down public transportation for the pandemic lockdown. No one knew how Mohan Paswan could make the journey. That's when Kumari insisted she would bring him back home, riding on a pad attached to the main seat of her bicycle.

She cycled for seven consecutive days on a relatively empty stomach at the height of the lockdown to get him to safety. Even though it was a test of sheer endurance, Kumari discovered that she loved cycling — it came naturally to her.

Her epic ride grabbed headlines around the world. NPR's previous reporting noted promises of cash rewards, training for a career as a cyclist, even a movie deal.

Six years later

That was in 2020. "Now — life is hard," Kumari told NPR in a phone call from her home in Bihar.

What happened to all the promises made — for financial support, especially to support cycling as a competitive sport?

Many promises were not kept, she says.

"The politicians who made promises, saying they would give money for my sports or education — nobody actually gave anything," she says. "Whatever reward money we collected back then [from individuals who extended help and a government award that came with a cash prize], we put it all into our house, rebuilding it. We had a brick house before, but it only had bare walls. Now we have completed it, added a toilet, a bathroom, and a running water connection. By doing all that, the house has finally become livable," she says.

Sponsor Message

This is no small achievement. An estimated 300,000 people are homeless in the state of Bihar in spite of government programs . For a family living in poverty, having a home can make a huge difference in the fight for survival.

For Kumari's family, making their house livable meant securing something that burst of fame had failed to deliver on — a more stable place from which to build their lives.

But they are doing so without her dad.

Mohan Paswan passed away of a heart attack in May 2021, just months after his daughter brought him home. Kumari says she felt heartbroken. After his passing, financial security has been precarious for the family.

At the moment, her mother works as a cook. Her meager income supports Kumari and her three siblings at home (an older sister has married and moved out).

"There are days when we go to sleep hungry," she says. "Our brother-in-law used to help us earlier, but now he also has a child, a wife and his father to take care of. He works a small job in the city — how much can he really do? So now he isn't able to help us much."

Still she holds out hope for a better future.

"Once my education is fully complete, only then will I be able to do something else. Only then can I prepare for things and look for a job," Kumari says.

But she has yet to pass the final exam required to complete Class 12, her final year of secondary school. That's an important credential to apply to university or qualify for certain jobs. It's a stepping stone to a better life, especially for disadvantaged students.

A typical day

Finding time for her studies has been a challenge. Kumari's day begins at 7 a.m. She cooks and cares for her younger siblings after her mother rushes off to work. "I give my brothers breakfast for school and get things ready for my sister. Then, I clean the house, mop the floors, do the dishes, wash clothes by hand, take a bath," she says.

Sponsor Message

By the time she can turn her attention to her studies, she says it feels as if she has already done a gazillion chores. "There are days when I sleep because of the sheer exhaustion of it all."

What she hopes for

Whatever the future holds, she is determined to stay in their native village rather than seeking employment in the big city, as her father did. His experience showed her how precarious day labor can be — he had no savings and no medical support after his injury.

Kumari is firm about living in their native village. "Whatever I do, I want to do from here," she says.

She says she still loves cycling as much as ever. She loves the wind in her hair, the feeling of going somewhere, of feeling free. That's what the bike represents to her. But she doesn't have the time to do it as much these days as she's bogged down by household chores and small but persistent everyday worries. She can't just cycle for the joy of it or train as a competitive sport. She only cycles to do errands for the family.

With her own progress on hold, the family has quietly set their hopes on her younger sister who will take her 12th grade exams in mid-2027. If she manages to pass and get into a good college, their prospects will improve once she graduates and starts working.

But Kumari hasn't given up. "When you're poor, fame doesn't help. Only education can help you out of your difficulties. Otherwise, life becomes a never-ending obstacle course," Kumari says.

Kamala Thiagarajan is a freelance journalist based in Madurai, South India. She reports on global health, science and development and has been published in The New York Times, The British Medical Journal, the BBC, The Guardian and other outlets. You can find her on X: @Kamal_t.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

World.title: Sweating the details: Sauna's potential health benefits draw scientists' interest
World.content:
Sweating the details: Sauna's potential health benefits draw scientists' interest

toggle caption i Siv Dolmen for NPR

For more on the science of healthy living, try NPR's Health newsletter.

Scientists have long marveled at how the human body tolerates extreme heat — and what that means for our health.

In the late 1700s, British scientists ran bold experiments on thermoregulation, subjecting themselves (and a dog) to a piping hot room and observing that — unlike the steak and eggs accompanying them — their own bodies did not cook.

The acute physiological response to heat is now well understood.

Faced with extreme temperatures, our blood vessels dilate, heart rate speeds up and blood is pushed to the skin where it's cooled down as we sweat. Our body releases hormones and activates heat shock proteins that protect our cells.

This understanding of our physiology has shaped medical care, for example, with heat-related illness. However, the other side of the equation — the potential therapeutic benefits of heat exposure — have received considerably less attention from modern medical science.

Sponsor Message

Meanwhile, age-old practices, such as sauna, built around stressing the body with heat are enjoying newfound popularity.

From social sauna meetups to the broader wellness and optimization movement, the level of public interest has surprised even long-time devotees like Dr. Hans Hägglund , a hematologist and stem-cell researcher at the Karolinska University Hospital in Stockholm.

toggle caption i Siv Dolmen for NPR

"It's really booming," says Hägglund, dubbed the "sauna doctor" in his home country thanks to a popular book he authored on the subject. "Unfortunately, there is still not very much evidence out there."

At least, not the caliber of studies that Hägglund and other scientists can point to if they want medical societies and government agencies to view sauna and other forms of heat therapy as a bonafide intervention — a lifestyle approach that can be recommended for preventing and treating chronic health conditions.

But Hägglund and a small group of international scientists are pushing to make this happen — and organize what's been a niche and disparate area of research.

Bringing science to the sauna

In late September, about 15 of them convened for the first time at the International Heat Therapy Research Symposium to hash out how to rigorously study heat therapy — a bucket that includes Finnish sauna, infrared, hot water immersion and more — and to form an organizing scientific body that will help steer the field forward.

toggle caption i Siv Dolmen for NPR

The two-day gathering was held at a trendy resort outside Oslo, Norway, called The Well, where nude bathing is the norm and essential-oil-infused rituals, based on traditions like the German Aufguss , are held throughout the day. It took place on the eve of the International Sauna Congress , an event that attracts hundreds of sauna lovers and experts every four years.

Sponsor Message

Some of the symposium's organizers, like Ashley Mason , a clinical psychologist at the University of California, San Francisco, acknowledge their goal is partly to dispel the whiff of wellness hype.

"We want to introduce this as an actual field of research, not something fringy, or woo-woo," says Mason, an associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral science who is currently running trials on heat therapy for depression, sleep and other aspects of mental health.

While sauna has been studied on and off for decades, very little of that research comes from well-controlled human trials. And it's often hard to draw firm conclusions from what evidence does exist; the studies are small, the methods vary significantly and key measurements are sometimes missing.

"We're all over the place," Mason says. "If we want to be taken seriously, we need to have consistent terms, so that people understand how to refer to and talk about our work."

The nuances of measuring environmental humidity and body temperature, or how to best define heat therapy, may be afterthoughts to the average sauna-goer, but all of this matters enormously when pulling together data from different countries and institutions.

Earric Lee, a postdoctoral researcher at the Montreal Heart Institute who's spearheading the initiative, says scientists first need to agree on standards. That's a painstaking process involving dozens of other experts that will ultimately set the stage for the kind of larger, multisite trials that can get at some fundamental questions for scientists and the public.

What are the actual benefits? How often do you need to go? What are the risks? Just how hot does it need to be?

"People want information. I know 'listen to your body' doesn't cut it,'" says Lee, "but I really can't give you recommendations, and that's the honest truth of it."

Sponsor Message

Early evidence suggests benefits from sauna exposure

There are certainly reasons to believe heat – delivered as a strong stimulus in a time-limited manner — holds promise for health.

"Passive heat therapy," as it's known in the scientific literature, works the cardiovascular system in ways that are similar to light physical activity and delivers some of the same benefits, such as improvements in blood pressure, arterial stiffness and vascular health.

Some experiments also indicate improvement in markers of inflammation, though, here, as with many areas, the findings are not conclusive, says Lee.

There's particular interest in how heat can help people with cardiovascular and metabolic conditions, as well as the elderly, says Ant Shepherd , a professor of clinical environmental physiology at the University of Portsmouth in the U.K.

For example, his lab has shown spending time in a hot tub improved resting metabolic rate and some measures of insulin sensitivity for people with Type 2 diabetes.

"Exercise is king, exercise is medicine, but for those who can't do that easily, can we get some of the same effects?" he asks. "It looks like we can."

In one of the only randomized controlled trials on sauna bathing, Lee has found that adding it to an exercise regime conferred added benefits for people at risk of cardiovascular disease. He's now running a trial on patients undergoing cardiac rehabilitation.

Separately, several research groups are exploring whether heat can help treat depression , building on a landmark study that showed meaningful decreases in symptoms after one session in a special infrared machine.

"We've got lots and lots of lovely little studies," says Shepherd, "The governments aren't going to listen until we put the hardcore, randomized-control trials in front of them."

Sauna research gathers steam

The uptick in recent scientific interest largely stems from a series of observational studies done in Finland.

Sponsor Message

The first — published just over a decade ago — showed using the sauna four to seven times per week was associated with a 40% to 60% lower risk of cardiovascular disease and death, compared to those who only went once a week.

"It was a strong signal and the impetus for a lot of labs to stand up and say, 'Hey, there might be something here,'" says Lee, who earned his Ph.D. working with the research leader of the group at the University of Eastern Finland, Dr. Jari Laukkanen .

toggle caption i Siv Dolmen for NPR

Subsequent studies suggested other benefits , like lower rates of Alzheimer's, respiratory disease and lower markers of chronic inflammation. Long-running studies from Japan have also linked regular hot tub use with lower risk of cardiovascular disease.

While promising, experts stress you can only extrapolate so much from this kind of observational data because it relies on self-reports and the results can be skewed by other factors.

"The effects are quite large, so we're fairly optimistic, but that's about as far we can go as scientists," says Shepherd.

In countries where heat practices are deeply interwoven into society — such as Finland and Japan — public funding has supported some of this research. In the U.S., the National Institutes of Health is funding Mason's work related to mental health.

The Montreal Heart Institute's Lee says this newly formed research group hopes to secure funding from public agencies in Europe, but the kind of expensive, large-scale trials that scientists dream of doing may largely rely on foundations and private funders, too.

The Oslo symposium was funded by the Norwegian Sauna Society, the wellness resort where it took place and the Sauna Research Foundation , a nonprofit backed by a Minnesota-based longevity entrepreneur and several other private funders.

While not at the gathering, Laukkanen, who has led much of the influential research on sauna in Finland, said he welcomes the effort to organize the field and look for ways to replicate their findings in other parts of the world.

Sponsor Message

The challenge with conducting the necessary studies, he notes, are the same as with other lifestyle habits like exercise or diet.

"They are really demanding," said Laukkanen, a professor of internal medicine at the University of Eastern Finland, "Pharmaceutical companies are doing this kind of study, but they have the resources. We don't have those yet."

World.title: It's taking longer to find a new job after losing one
World.content:
It's taking longer to find a new job after losing one

toggle caption i Joe Raedle/Getty Images North America

Evan Smith lost his job at a Colorado RV dealership this past spring after the company was sold. He's applied for numerous jobs since then, but hasn't found much traction.

"You find something that you're excited about or something that you think fits your profile and you go in and over 100 people have already clicked 'applied for it' in the last two weeks," Smith says. "So you just feel like you're a number."

In today's stagnant hiring environment, the numbers are not encouraging. U.S. employers added just 29,000 jobs last month. That's one job for every 244 unemployed workers. The average worker is taking longer to find a new job, and that means more people are exhausting their unemployment benefits before any new paychecks begin.

Sponsor Message

To be sure, the unemployment rate has remained very low: just 4.2% in September. But that's little consolation for those who are stuck on the outskirts of the job market, knocking on doors that rarely open.

"When you're one of the people that doesn't have a job, it doesn't really matter what the percentage is," says Cheryl Huff. "It's impacting your life in a big, big way."

toggle caption i Cheryl Huff

Huff was laid off from a state government job in Colorado four months ago. Since then, she's applied for dozens of positions, spending hours on each one, tailoring her resume to the specific job requirements. She's gotten only a handful of interviews —all by telephone — and a lot of what seem like automated emails.

Huff once got two messages at once from the same employer, one saying her application was under review and the other saying the job had already been filled.

"That's one of the frustrations that people are having," Huff says. "Did you even look at my stuff?"

In the meantime, Huff is paying $1,300 a month to maintain her old employer-provided health insurance. Her husband is retired, so their family budget is tight.

"It's Social Security for him and unemployment for me," Huff says. "It's amazing how little money that is when you go to the store and you see a bag of granola is $8.50."

Sponsor Message

Workers are bumping up against state limits for unemployment benefits

The clock is ticking. Colorado offers six months of unemployment benefits, and Huff's are set to run out in early December. In many states, benefits expire even faster.

North Carolina offers less than three months of unemployment. Keke Moore in Raleigh has been out of work for almost a year.

toggle caption i Keke Moore

"With so many people being out of work, we're all out here, it feels like to me, fighting for scraps," says Moore, who lost her job as a meeting planner last December.

Even when she was receiving unemployment, North Carolina benefits are capped at $350 a week. Now that even that limited aid has expired, Moore's 21-year-old son has been helping out with the household bills.

"Bless his heart, he does have a part-time job, so he's been doing what he can to help his mama out," Moore says. "But I mean, I feel like a failure as a parent, because it's like I don't want him worrying about bills."

Of the more than 7 million unemployed people in the country, nearly 2 million have been out of work for six months or more.

Aside from the financial stress, there's an emotional toll to being out of work so long.

Evan Smith, the laid-off RV worker, says job-hunting itself is an exhausting full-time gig. Sometimes he goes for a hike just to give himself a break.

"My wife, usually on a Friday when we're sitting on the back porch after work — after she gets done with work — she's like, 'How are you feeling?'" Smith says. "Keeping a good attitude, I think, is huge. Getting discouraged is really freaking easy."

World.title: Cleveland-Cliffs CEO says he's prepared to fight Canada in court over Stelco layoffs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The CEO of the American company that owns Hamilton-based steelmaker Stelco says he's prepared to fight the Canadian government in court to preserve Stelco's plan to lay off hundreds of workers.

Speaking Sunday on CBC's Rosemary Barton Live, Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves disputed the government's characterization that the company is violating binding employment commitments under the Investment Canada Act.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said last week that Cleveland-Cliffs' 2024 purchase of Stelco included "undertakings to continue to employ at least the same number of unionized employees and the vast majority of non-unionized employees as were employed when the transaction was announced" through 2029.

"There is no provision in the contract that I have to keep employment at a certain level every single day of the five years," Goncalves said on Sunday. "If that was an imposition of the Canadian government, I would not have accepted."

Goncalves reiterated Stelco's position that the layoffs are a temporary measure until Canada and the U.S. reach a trade agreement, and that the jobs will be restored.

He also said he's open to selling the company and voiced support for U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel, despite Stelco citing tariffs as a key reason for its economic struggles.

WATCH | Goncalves says he's open to selling Stelco: Stelco owner open to selling company amid fight with Ottawa over layoffs | Duration closed caption 10:00 Lourenco Goncalves, CEO of Stelco parent company Cleveland-Cliffs, speaks with CBC's Rosemary Barton following his company's official response to the federal government's threat of legal action amid layoffs at the company’s Hamilton, Ont.-based steel plant. In a letter obtained by CBC News, Stelco says it is not violating employment commitments.

Ultimatum from Canadian government

Joly issued an ultimatum to the company last week: share a plan to save the up to 500 jobs that could be impacted at the Hamilton plant or face potential legal action.

Prime Minister Mark Carney also said last week that Ottawa will "use all powers that we have" against Cleveland-Cliffs as it pursues the Ohio-based company to the "fullest extent of the law."

Stelco Inc. said in a letter responding to Joly that the company will proceed with the layoffs and the government's characterization of the move as a breach of undertakings is "false."

T he company emphasized "Stelco's situation is a result of factors beyond its control," citing the impact of U.S. President Donald Trump's 50 per cent tariffs.

But Goncalves said Sunday he supports steel tariffs against Canada.

"I am in favour of tariffs against all the countries in the entire world that dump steel into the United States," he said, adding that the Section 232 tariffs have brought "the American steel industry back."

A drone photograph shows the Stelco Hamilton Works steel mill, owned by Cleveland-Cliffs, in Hamilton last month. (Carlos Osorio/Reuters)

"I'm in favour of Section 232. There's no doubt about it."

Asked whether he would consider selling the company, Goncalves said, "For a good offer, yes," but added that he still believes the company can "continue to be a good citizen in Canada."

He told CBC News in a previous interview that he "would not have acquired the Stelco if I knew that Canada and the United States would become what they became — enemies in trade."

Layoffs underway

Jordan Williams, a Stelco employee who received a layoff notice last week, is calling on Goncalves to provide a written response to workers' concerns, including a "credible" plan for Hamilton's cold-rolled and coated steel operations in the future.

"What steps will you take to protect jobs, support our families and provide a path back to work?" he said in a statement sent to CBC News Sunday. "These layoffs reach beyond the plant gates and into the businesses and neighbourhoods that depend on Hamilton industry."

Ron Wells, president of the United Steelworkers Local 1005, which covers Stelco workers in Hamilton, told CBC News last week that layoffs are underway and expected to roll out over three weeks.

He said he expects 300 to 350 layoffs in Hamilton, with more at Stelco's Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke, Ont.

Wells told CBC News at the time that Goncalves, who has previously expressed support for Trump and his tariffs, is eager to make it appear as though Trump's tariffs are working ahead of midterm elections in the U.S.

"I hope, basically, the federal government makes an example out of them," Wells said. "We just want to make sure they … follow through with it."

World.title: Trump announces Russia-Ukraine 'energy ceasefire,' which Zelenskyy says he hasn't seen but supports
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he has discussed the possibility of an energy ceasefire with Russia with Prime Minister Mark Carney, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte but is waiting for more information from the United States.

U.S. President Donald Trump had said in a social media post on Sunday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to what he described as an "energy ceasefire" without offering specifics on terms.

In an interview with Axios, Zelenskyy said Trump's post was the first he had heard of the deal, though a senior Ukrainian official told Reuters that Ukraine was ready to agree to such a ceasefire if Russia was.

In a social media post of his own, the Ukrainian president said he had just spoken with Carney, Stubb and Rutte to discuss the alleged ceasefire announced by Trump.

"Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well. We are awaiting details from the American side," Zelenskyy wrote on X on Sunday afternoon. "For our part, Ukraine always FULLY supports steps toward de-escalation, the protection of lives, and the decisions needed to end the war and guarantee lasting peace."

Speaking in his nightly video address, Zelenskyy said Russian forces were still launching air attacks on energy infrastructure, including a strike on a joint heating and power plant in Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city. A Ukrainian official confirmed the attack had taken place after Trump's announcement of the ceasefire.

The Prime Minister's Office said Carney spoke with Trump on Sunday and that he told the U.S. president that Ottawa has "strong support" for the energy ceasefire.

"The new energy ceasefire being brokered by President Trump between Russia and Ukraine has the potential to significantly de-escalate the war and protect thousands of civilians from harm and hardship," Carney later said on social media.

"Canada calls on Russia to uphold this agreement as we keep working with our Allies to secure a just and lasting peace for Ukraine and Europe."

The announcement comes a day after Trump blamed Zelenskyy for attacking diesel facilities in Russia and contributing to a global shortage. Russia and Ukraine have repeatedly attacked each other's energy infrastructure during the war.

Trump's brief post said only that the ceasefire takes effect immediately and that both sides had agreed to it. "Do not break it!" he said in his social media post.

The White House did not immediately clarify the president's post or add detail. The Kremlin did not provide comment.

Zelenskyy meets with U.S. President Donald Trump during the United Nations General Assembly, in New York on Sept. 22. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/The Associated Press)

Trump, whose war in Iran has been blamed for high diesel prices that are weighing on Republicans' prospects in next month's midterm elections, had previously announced an energy ceasefire in Ukraine in mid-September, though neither side ever confirmed such an agreement was reached.

"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Earlier on Sunday, Zelenskyy had repeated Ukraine's long-standing position that it was willing to halt attacks on Russian refineries but only if Moscow ceased its own strikes on Ukrainian power infrastructure.

Any such deal would need to come with "real guarantees," Zelenskyy said.

"The real cause of the war in Europe is Russia and Russia alone," Zelenskyy said. "It's possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so."

Promise of elections

In a dramatic deterioration in their relations, Trump on Saturday had warned Zelenskyy that he had "better damn well stop" attacking Russian refineries, and he urged Ukrainians to replace Zelenskyy as their leader via new elections because he had missed several opportunities to strike a deal with Moscow.

Appearing on ABC's This Week on Sunday, Zelenskyy responded that he would organize elections in Ukraine if Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to a 60-day ceasefire.

Zelenskyy said it was "up to Ukrainians" to choose their leader but noted that there needed to be an end to the fighting first. Ukrainian law prohibits elections under martial law for security reasons.

"Please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections," Zelenskyy said.

The Ukrainian leader rejected being blamed for energy price rises, adding that "everybody in the world" knew that the war in the Middle East was a bigger factor.

The steep rise in global diesel prices, which followed the outbreak of the Iran war in February, has become a political liability for Trump's Republican Party ahead of the midterms, when opposition Democrats could gain control of one or both houses of Congress.

On Saturday, Zelenskyy had responded angrily to Trump's announcement of a diesel supply deal with Russia, saying it would embolden Moscow's attacks on Ukraine and lead to a greater loss of civilian lives.

WATCH | Trump brokers deal to buy Russian diesel: Trump reverses course on Russian oil sanctions | Duration closed caption 2:08 U.S. President Donald Trump has announced a deal to import Russian diesel as fuel prices soar, reversing course on sanctions against Moscow. Ukraine is condemning the move, warning it will directly benefit Russian President Vladimir Putin.

In a readout from the PMO on Sunday, Carney told Zelenskyy that Canada believes the Trump-proposed diesel deal with Russia is "in direct opposition" to the goal of supporting Ukraine and that such a move would enrich the Kremlin and help finance its war effort.

Analysts said Trump's diesel supply agreement with Moscow was unlikely to lead to sustained lower fuel prices as the volumes involved were too small.

The diesel deal was also criticized by U.S. lawmakers, including one of Trump's fellow Republicans, Rep. Don Bacon, who said it was time to apply more sanctions, not lift them.

Kyiv residents angry

On the streets of Kyiv, several residents expressed anger at Trump's suggestion that Ukraine should find a new leader willing to make a deal with Putin.

"No one has the right to tell us what to do, especially since elections cannot be held during wartime," said Sabina, a 40-year-old primary school teacher. "In my view, it is a betrayal by our partners," she said, describing Trump's remarks.

Zelenskyy said he would continue discussions with European leaders on Sunday, and there were daily conversations around additional air defence packages, including ammunition for combat aircraft that are used to down Russia's jet-powered drones.

On Monday, Ukrainian Foreign Affairs Minister Andrii Sybiha is due to participate in a European Union foreign affairs council meeting that is expected to discuss increasing sanctions pressure on Russia and advancing negotiations on Ukraine’s EU accession.

World.title: Turkey gravy brand sold in Canada recalled due to undeclared mustard
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A brand of turkey gravy sold in Canada has been recalled because it contains undeclared mustard.

Kevin's Natural Foods turkey gravy is sold in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba.

The Canadian Food Inspection Agency says the product contains mustard, which is not included on its label.

The agency says the recall was triggered by the company and there have been no reported reactions associated with the product.

It says the turkey gravy should not be consumed by anyone who is allergic or sensitive to mustard and is advising customers not to distribute or sell it.

The agency is investigating and says it is verifying that the product is being removed from the marketplace.

Health Canada recognizes mustard as a common food allergen.

World.title: Banff is in Treaty 7 territory and leases its land from the feds. So what happens to it if Alberta separates?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In the thousands of pages of negotiations that would surely result if Alberta were to secede from Canada, at least one chapter would likely be dedicated to the Town of Banff.

This tourist mecca is already a jurisdictional anomaly: situated on federal parkland that the town has leased for $550,000 a year since it incorporated in 1990. Residents own their homes but not their land; that's also leased from Ottawa.

The province operates the local hospital and schools, but the federal government has veto power over most bylaw changes.

In short, governance is complicated. And with Oct. 19 approaching — when Alberta will vote on, among other questions, whether to hold a referendum on separating from Canada — many of those who live in this mountain resort town are worried about the future.

The Town of Jasper, roughly 300 kilometres northwest of Banff, faces similar issues, given it's also based in a federal park in Alberta.

But it's the questions raised particularly in Banff, which has almost twice the population of Jasper, that indicate the scale of the seismic shift should a province secede.

WATCH | How locals feel about the referendum: What the Alberta separation debate means for Banff | Duration 1:57 What could an independent Alberta mean for Canada's oldest and most-visited national park? CBC Radio's The Sunday Magazine was in Banff to hear how locals feel about the upcoming referendum.

Even if Albertans eventually voted to leave federation, they cannot legally do so without Canada's agreement, according to a 1998 Supreme Court decision that provides a framework on separation.

Negotiations over how to divide assets and debts could take years, according to political science professor Tom Urbaniak, based on the few comparables, such as the dissolution of Czechoslovakia or signing of the Nisga'a Agreement — which took a decade of negotiations between British Columbia and the involved First Nations.

"Separation means that everything is an open question," said Urbaniak, director of Cape Breton University's Tompkins Institute, adding that he hopes the concept remains hypothetical.

In Banff, the core questions are about belonging. Would Alberta — as Quebec separatists have asserted through the indivisibility principle — claim all land within its current borders, regardless of whether it is federal or provincial? What would it have to trade for Ottawa to agree?

Or would the town of roughly 8,000 people become a tiny piece of Canada isolated within a new country?

"This is what makes separation so perilous and, just from an objective perspective, so irresponsible [because it's not] a simplistic option," Urbaniak said. "The give and take of resources, payment of money, assumption of debt, renegotiation of treaties, compensation to the rest of Canada — all of this is on the table."

A plea from Banff's mayor

Banff's mayor has urged Albertans to vote against a referendum.

Ottawa has been a partner for decades, Corrie DiManno said, collaborating on major portfolios, including conservation management, wildfire prevention and housing.

The questions sparked by separation have created anxiety for her constituents, she said in a recent interview with CBC's The Sunday Magazine.

LISTEN | Banffites worry what might happen in a separate Alberta: The Sunday Magazine 24:34 What would an independent Alberta mean for Canada's original national park?

DiManno keeps hearing from businesses worried about potential secession deterring visitors — last year, 4.5 million tourists went through Banff National Park — or what it might mean for those who live in Banff but work elsewhere in the Bow Valley.

"People have talked about, you know, am I going to need a passport to go to Canmore," she said, referring to another mountain hub a 20-minute drive southeast on Highway 1, but outside of the federal park.

"We really haven't had any formal conversations and, frankly, I really hope that we don't need to. I'm hoping that Albertans come out and finish this conversation once and for all to say that we will stay in Canada."

Banff Mayor Corrie DiManno is officially sworn in as a member of council during a swearing-in process on Oct. 28, 2025. DiManno is urging Albertans to keep the province in the federation. (Greg Colgan/CBC)

Her comments echo her May 25 Instagram post, which received widespread support — with hundreds of commenters thanking her for standing up for their community, for Alberta and for Canada.

In it, DiManno emphasized the law of the land runs deeper than municipal or provincial governance.

"Banff is on Treaty 7 territory and this treaty predates both Banff National Park and the province of Alberta," she said. "We all share a responsibility to respect the spirit and obligations of the treaties that created Canada."

A sacred place

For centuries, the Stoney Nakoda Nations have referred to Tunnel Mountain, which overlooks Banff on the town's eastern edge, as the Sacred Guardian Buffalo Mountain. The mountain and the area's hot springs are sacred to the surrounding Indigenous communities and are both included in the 149-year-old Treaty 7 agreement.

What that means is "not only would Indigenous nations have to have a seat at the table [in negotiations], if a treaty is being cancelled or significantly altered — but the consent of the affected Indigenous nations would be required for this all to be legal and constitutional," Urbaniak said.

A coalition of First Nations has already launched a legal challenge against the question of separation being put to a referendum.

The calls for separation to be put to a vote were initiated by the citizen group Stay Free Alberta, which claimed in the spring to have more than 177,800 signatures backing its push.

A judge annulled the petition in May, saying the province had failed in its duty to consult with First Nations. But Premier Danielle Smith then announced Alberta would appeal that decision and went ahead with the referendum on whether to hold a vote on separation.

Though Smith's office has since maintained it wants Alberta to remain in Canada, pundits have noted the decision to hold the referendum was made to appease hardline separatist factions in her voting base.

When asked about the premier's vision for Banff should Alberta separate, Smith's press secretary responded in an email that the United Conservative Party and caucus are committed to unity.

"We remain focused on our work to restore Albertans' hope in our country by building a stronger Alberta within a united Canada," Sam Blackett wrote in the statement.

Parks Canada did not directly answer questions about what would happen in the case of a separation, saying the federal government "respects the democratic process taking place in Alberta" and that it works "in collaboration with provinces, territories, Indigenous groups and communities" to protect "national historic sites and national parks."

'We are home'

Stoney Nakoda elder Alice Kaquitts scoffs at the idea of land ownership, noting that the area's First Nations have been part of Banff's stewards "since time immemorial" and have a deep and sacred connection to the area.

Kaquitts recalls how, as a girl, she and her parents would drive to Banff to sell crafts, with family pointing out landmarks and their connection to her culture along the route; how, as they drove into the park and the mountain rose up, her parents would pull over and get out of their vehicle to pray.

Stoney Nakoda Nations elder Alice Kaquitts says her people have been stewards of the Banff area since time immemorial. (Andrea Hoang/CBC)

"They would tell that sacred guardian, ‘We're home, we are home,'" she told The Sunday Magazine.

"That sacred connection to this area is something that I've never lost.… I can drown the town out, I can drown out urbanization in my mind, and I can hear my ancestors."

She notes the idea of land as a possession is a colonial concept and does not align with her traditional beliefs; instead, she believes in preserving a relationship with her natural surroundings.

It's why she is thankful, she said, that Indigenous leaders advanced the legal challenge against the question of separation.

"From a First Nations perspective, we viewed the treaties as a peace treaty — and what that entailed was 'We'll share the land with you,'" she said.

"That agreement was made with the Queen, not the province. We didn't sign a treaty with Alberta to give up this land."

World.title: Judge orders Trump administration to end taxpayer-funded TV ads
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump must cancel any remaining television commercials paid for with millions of dollars in taxpayer money to promote his political message, a federal judge ordered Sunday night, even as the administration said the ad campaign was coming to an end.

U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon in New York sided with a coalition, including the non-partisan watchdog Common Cause, that challenged the ads and called them an illegal misuse of funds.

In granting a temporary restraining order, she told the administration to cancel any remaining ads, including any set to air Sunday night.

"Defendants shall not enter into, renew, or expand any agreement authorizing the development, creation, dissemination, placement, or airing of the challenged s" during the two-week duration of her order, Rochon said.

The White House did not immediately respond to an email requesting comment on Sunday night. In a court filing late Saturday, the Justice Department argued that the temporary restraining order was unnecessary because "the alleged offending conduct will end tomorrow."

The Department of Homeland Security tapped $20 million US in taxpayer money for the ads. Legal experts have suggested they ran afoul of a federal statute against congressionally appropriated money being used for "publicity or propaganda" and potentially other federal laws.

The Homeland Security money tapped for the ads comes from a $175-million package Congress gave to the department as part of Trump's immigration enforcement agenda.

The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have done to promote various policies.

But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they aren't aimed at helping members of the public benefit from specific government programs. One of the ads is a near replica of a 2024 ad that Trump ran during his presidential re-election campaign.

World.title: How good is this year's flu shot? Here's what to know about flu season
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Walking down the street this week, it may seem like everyone is sneezing and hacking up a lung. But as health officials announce the start of an earlier than usual flu season, how worried should Canadians be? And as we head into Thanksgiving weekend, should we be scrambling to update flu and COVID-19 shots?

Some experts say that while this year's flu season may have arrived on our doorstep sooner than usual, it's not necessarily a cause for alarm — but other experts are stressing the importance of prevention in heavy-hit regions such as Toronto and Calgary, where one of this season's two influenza deaths so far has occurred, according to authorities.

The strain making up roughly 98 per cent of cases in Canada so far tends to be a milder one, according to Brian Ward, professor emeritus at the Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre in Montreal.

"So far at least, this looks like an H1N1 dominated year, and the years where H1N1 dominates, you can have very large outbreaks, but the number or the proportion of people … who get very sick, is relatively small compared to years that are dominated by H3N2," he told CBC News.

"I'm not convinced yet that we're actually seeing the beginning of a real outbreak. What we're seeing is sort of isolated, small outbreaks."

But where the flu is striking, doctors say it's striking hard. There are currently more than 400 confirmed flu cases in Alberta, where vaccines aren't yet widely available.

Some regions have started rolling out flu and COVID-19 shots to high-risk populations, with most regions set to offer shots to the general public by mid-October.

Here's what we know.

Is everyone getting sick right now?

According to the latest national numbers, which include data on influenza trends up to Oct. 3, there have been 3,315 detections of influenza across the country since the end of August. More than 1,140 of those cases were detected in the most recent week of available data, showing that cases are picking up.

Influenza has been associated with two deaths so far this flu season, national figures state. The person who died in Alberta lived in the Calgary area and was in the 70-79 age range, authorities say. Authorities haven't yet shared where the second death occurred.

It's an early start to the season. Between Sept. 27 and Oct. 3, 4.7 per cent of influenza tests came back positive, much higher than the average 0.6 per cent rate seen this time of year in 2023-2025.

But much of this national increase is driven by an uptick of cases in B.C. and in large cities such as Toronto and Calgary. Other areas seeing cases creep up include Yukon, the Northwest Territories and Alberta.

"The rest of the country is really very quiet," Ward said.

WATCH | B.C. launches fall immunization campaign: B.C. warns of early start to flu season, launches fall immunization campaign | Duration closed caption 7:05 Flu season has started early this year and the province has launched its fall immunization campaign to prevent the spread. Dr. Jennifer Vines with the B.C. Centre for Disease Control shares what the vaccine rollout will look like and what precautions people can take to stay healthy.

He noted that in B.C., outbreaks in long-term care homes are driving the increase in cases, warning that families getting together this holiday weekend could result in further spread.

"That may be the seed that moves the virus … into the schools and universities and marketplaces and so on."

Official figures don't catch every case of flu, as not everyone seeks out a test when they fall ill.

In hard-hit Toronto, family doctor Joseph Param told CBC News the increase of flu patients he's seeing at his practice is mainly among young adults who are more likely to travel on public transit and may still go to work when feeling under the weather, perhaps because they're used to flu season starting later.

WATCH | Ontario deals with earlier-than-usual flu season: You're not imagining it — flu season has started early this year | Duration closed caption 2:10 Some Ontario doctors say they're noticing an early start to this year's flu season in their waiting rooms, as influenza cases tick up across the province ahead of schedule.

"Over the last couple of weeks, patients who are very healthy who see me rarely have been coming in with severe symptoms," he said.

"So it is important that the general population is aware that we are seeing … early cases now and so that we start taking precautions earlier than expected."

Doctors advise Canadians to stay home if they feel ill and to get vaccinated as soon as shots become available in their area, particularly with the long weekend coming up.

How effective is the flu shot this year?

The protection of flu shots varies from year to year depending on the most dominant strain of influenza in your area.

This year, it's a "good" match, Ward said. Although H3N2 viruses dominated for much of 2025, that subtype hasn't cropped up much in 2026, and this year's vaccine is well-positioned to protect against H1N1.

He said "influenza viruses march to their own drummers" and can mutate even within one flu season.

It's not just flu season in Canada — historically, we see more respiratory illnesses in general cropping up during the fall and going into winter, including colds and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), the latter of which is most dangerous in young children.

About 98 per cent of lab-confirmed cases of influenza in Canada since the end of August have been of the H1N1 strain, according to government data. (New Africa/Shutterstock)

Rates of COVID-19 are currently trending lower right now than last year, with 4.1 per cent of tests coming back positive in the last week of September compared with 10.5 per cent at the same time in 2025.

The National Advisory Committee on Immunizations (NACI) said in September that it continues to "strongly recommend" the latest COVID-19 booster shots for those at a higher risk of developing severe COVID-19, including health-care workers, adults over the age of 65, those with immunocompromised systems and people in long-term care homes.

When can I get my flu and COVID-19 shots?

Several provinces such as Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia are already advising residents that appointments for flu vaccines and COVID-19 booster shots are available now for residents over the age of six months.

New Brunswick , Saskatchewan and Manitoba are currently allowing residents to book their flu and COVID-19 vaccines, with immunization efforts officially kicking off on Oct. 13.

Those living in Newfoundland and Labrador can receive flu and COVID-19 shots starting Oct. 19.

In Ontario, flu and COVID-19 immunizations have been available since last week for high-risk groups, including seniors aged 65 and up, hospitalized patients, long-term care residents and health-care workers, according to the provincial government. They don't open to the general public until Oct. 26 .

In Quebec, you can start making appointments as of Oct. 13, but the flu and COVID-19 vaccination campaign itself doesn't begin until Oct. 20 . It is only free to eligible residents deemed high-risk, meaning non-eligible residents must pay for the shots.

Flu and COVID-19 shots can be booked now in Alberta , with the first appointments starting Oct. 19. While flu shots are free to everyone, Albertans who aren't considered high-risk for COVID-19 will have to pay.

In B.C., those registered in their Get Vaccinated system will receive a notification reminding them to get their flu shots. Flu and COVID-19 shots are available starting Oct. 13.

COVID-19 and flu shots will be available at specific clinics in the Northwest Territories this fall, but a timeline hasn't been released yet. Those in Yukon have been able to book appointments for flu and COVID-19 shots since the end of September. No details have been released for Nunavut's rollout as of Oct. 8.

Before heading out to the pharmacy or clinic, it's important to check the requirements in your area to be sure you're eligible and that providers near you have received the necessary supplies to offer shots and aren't experiencing delays.

Most regions offer RSV vaccines to eligible patients as well.

In the future, we could see more variety in our flu vaccines: an mRNA influenza vaccine made by Moderna was approved by the FDA in the U.S. in the summer, making this the first flu season it'll face. It's still under review by Health Canada.

World.title: Hurricane Simon hits Mexico's Pacific coast, slamming towns and resorts
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hurricane Simon was pounding Mexico's Pacific coast as a Category 4 storm on Sunday, its eye remaining just offshore as its most powerful winds and rain slammed people living between the Sierra Madre and the ocean.

Simon's eye was moving northward just off the coast, and forecasters at the U.S. National Hurricane Center said it's not clear if it will make landfall. This could mean Simon maintains its extremely dangerous strength, sustaining winds of 240 km/h.

That's not good news for people in the Puerto Vallarta area, a popular destination for Canadian tourists. Just inland and uphill from the resort areas, many Mexicans live in communities where housing might not stand up to the storm.

At daybreak, Simon was centered about 175 kilometres south-southeast of Cabo Corrientes, and moving north-northwest at a relatively slow eight km/h. A senior Hurricane Center specialist, Phillippe Pappin, said this westernmost tip of mainland Mexico was the most likely place for landfall.

"Simon is very close to the coast of Mexico this morning," Pappin told The Associated Press on Sunday.

"We're expecting catastrophic wind and life-threatening storm surge impacts along that west central coast of Mexico where the hurricane warning is currently in effect," Pappin said.

"They're also getting very heavy rainfall associated with the storm that's likely going to produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides in areas of higher terrain along the Mexican coastline, and there will be significant swells."

As for predicting whether or not Simon will make landfall, "it's a little tricky right now" to forecast, since the eye "is basically moving very close or parallel to the coast currently," Pappin said. But he predicted that Cabo Corrientes is the area most likely to get a direct hit from the system on Sunday.

Waves hit the shore in Manzanillo on Sunday. (Daniel Becerril/Reuters)

Heavy rainfall elsewhere

Meanwhile, the hurricane was dumping rain over parts of southwestern Mexico. It could bring 25 to 50 centimetres of rain in many places, with some areas in the states of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco receiving up to 76 centimetres. "This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," the centre warned.

Jalisco state suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating people from at-risk areas while asking the tourism sector to make sure workers as well as visitors are fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones.

On Saturday, just ahead of the worst weather, convenience stores, hotels and other businesses in Puerto Vallarta were boarding up their windows.

A man removes water from a building in Manzanillo on Sunday. (Daniel Becerril/Reuters)

The hurricane centre expected a dangerous storm surge along the immediate coast near and to the east of where the centre makes landfall. The agency warned that near the coast, large and destructive waves will accompany the surge.

Canadian tourist Ed Currie, who, along with his wife, still has five more days to enjoy Puerto Vallarta, said the hurricane had not yet affected his plans.

"Just stay in the hotel and look out the window hopefully," he said of what the couple would do. "I just don't know what to expect."

World.title: Saudis say Riyadh airport struck for 2nd day in a row, separate airport also attacked
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said a projectile struck a passenger terminal at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Sunday, less than a day after a missile attack on the same airport killed 12 people and wounded more than 300. This marks a major escalation in the war between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and the kingdom and further complicated sputtering efforts to halt the U.S.-Iran war. CLARIFICATION (Oct. 11, 2026): A previous version of this video showed the aftermath of an earlier attack on the airport on Oct. 8. The video has been updated to show only the aftermath of Saturday's attack.

A projectile struck a passenger terminal at the international airport in Riyadh on Sunday, a day after a missile hit the same terminal and killed 12 people, the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said.

The Houthis claimed responsibility for those attacks and others.

The Saudi Civil Aviation ‌Authority said one person was killed in Sunday's attack on the King Khalid International Airport — a Pakistani resident — and 11 others were injured.

Saturday's missile attack was the deadliest in a Gulf Arab nation since the Iran war began in February, with another 300 people wounded, some critically.

The sharp escalation in the new front in the Iran war threatens to draw in greater U.S. military involvement as U.S. President Donald Trump has said he is weighing joining the fight against the rebels.

This screengrab from surveillance footage released by the Saudi Ministry of Media shows people reacting to an attack at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday. (Saudi Ministry of Media/Reuters)

The Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died Sunday of injuries sustained in Saturday's attack, which would bring the death toll to 13.

Saudi authorities later said King Fahd International Airport in Dammam had also been attacked, with few details. The city is on the Persian Gulf near Bahrain and Qatar.

The strikes came shortly after the Houthis said the airport under their control in the Yemeni capital of Sanaa had been struck again. They blamed the Saudis but provided no details.

At stake, again, are global supplies and prices of oil, as well as commercial shipping through a crucial alternative waterway to the Iran-threatened Strait of Hormuz — along with civilians and aviation throughout the region.

Trump on Saturday also said he planned to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who has been seeking assistance.

A U.S. intervention could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen and further restrict the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf. The rebels seized key areas along the strait last month, and the Saudi-led coalition has been trying to seize them back.

Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defence support to the region, regional officials told The Associated Press last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran.

Sunday's attack occurred as the Saudis hosted a major international energy conference in Riyadh, with other high-profile events, including an investment gathering, on the horizon. Saudi Arabia under bin Salman has sought to open more to the world as a business and tourism destination, but the Houthi attacks threaten those efforts.

"There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix, we come out of the ashes all the time," the Saudi energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud, told the conference.

He added that the kingdom is also working on pipelines, in addition to the East-West one that was attacked and closed for days last month, with no details.

Airports a 'theatre of operations': Houthis

Earlier Sunday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry reported that a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa.

The ministry says 91 Yemenis have been killed and 168 injured by the Saudi-led coalition in five weeks. It said that 60 per cent of those killed were women and children.

There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities.

WATCH | A look from 2024 on how the Houthis gained prominence: How the Houthis became major Middle East disruptors | Duration 6:51 Once a rag-tag group in Yemen — one of the world’s poorest countries — Iran has helped the Houthis become major players capable of disrupting global shipping traffic in the Red Sea. CBC’s Paul Hunter breaks down the rise of the Houthis and what the world needs to watch for. [Correction: In a previous version of this video, we reported that Hamas is considered a terrorist organization by several countries and entities, including the United Nations. In fact, the UN does not consider Hamas a terrorist organization.]

On Sunday, the Houthis claimed the attack on the airport in Dammam as well as attacks on oil and gas facilities in the kingdom's east. They have targeted the Riyadh airport, which has no military facilities, every day since Wednesday.

The rebels again warned "all airlines, experts, employees, workers and ​travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theatre of operations for our ​forces." Several international airlines have suspended flights for varying periods.

Saudi authorities said the dead in Saturday's attack included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese.

Relatives display a portrait of Syrian citizen Buthaina Ahmad Oweida, who they say was killed in Saturday's attack on the international airport in Riyadh. (Omar Albam/The Associated Press)

The Egyptian woman was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flynas, according to Egyptian state-run TV.

The Syrian woman was a widowed mother of four who had been living in Saudi Arabia for five years, a relative told The Associated Press. The Syrian Embassy in Riyadh identified her as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida.

Impact on Iran war

Until recently, the Houthis had been largely on the sidelines of the Iran war. Now, the rebels are helping Iran to pressure a key U.S. ally.

The Saudis and the Houthis began fighting in 2015, when the kingdom entered Yemen's civil war on behalf of the internationally recognized government.

Relative calm after a 2022 ceasefire ended in July, when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land. That revived anger over the Saudi-led blockade that has largely isolated Houthi-run areas.

Now fighting has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea.

Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb, a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.

Ahmed Nagi, the International Crisis Group's senior analyst for Yemen, said the Houthi pressure tactics could backfire: "Rather than pushing Riyadh to step back, attacks on critical Saudi infrastructure could make the Saudis more determined to continue the campaign."
