World.title: Panama Earthquake Aftershocks Continue as Residents Survey Widespread Damage
World.content:
Residents near the epicenter of a major earthquake in southern Panama began cleaning up on Saturday, traumatized by the previous day’s heavy shaking that left widespread damage but so far no reported deaths. “This is something we’ve never seen before. We weren’t prepared for this kind of event,” said Aldulfo Quintero as he cleared debris from a store in Chitre, about 250 kilometers (155 miles) southwest of Panama City.

The 41-year-old said he has a “great fear” that a new earthquake could strike any moment. After the initial 7.7-magnitude quake around midday Friday, over 100 aftershocks have been recorded, some as strong as magnitude 6.0. Like many others in Chitre, the capital of hard-hit Herrera province, 28-year-old Yakshuri Castillo chose to sleep outdoors due to fears of another quake.

She said she “went into shock” when the first quake struck. Dozens of homes were damaged in the city, whose 66,000 residents were still without electricity on Saturday. The epicenter of the initial quake was registered by the US Geological Survey (USGS) about 60 kilometers away, near the border of Herrera, Los Santos, Veraguas provinces.

Earthquakes are rare in Panama and usually occur in western Chiriqui province, bordering Costa Rica. Strong shaking in Panama City, over 200 kilometers from the epicenter, sent panicked people pouring into the streets from the capital’s numerous high-rise buildings. While no deaths have been reported from the quake, about 30 people have been treated for minor injuries.

Authorities are still assessing the damage in remote areas. Several communities have been cut off due to roadways damaged by the quake. “The disaster we are facing is massive,” President Jose Raul Mulino said upon arriving in one of the affected areas. The United States, which counts Panama among the members of President Donald Trump’s new “Shield of the Americas” initiative, has pledged rapid support.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that he was “closely monitoring” the situation, with his office “rapidly mobilizing resources and personnel to assist.” The top US military commander in the region, Francis Donovan, has “directed immediate support to help the people of Panama, including on-the-ground support from rotary-wing aircraft… and the airlift of key personnel and supplies into the country,” US Southern Command said in a statement on Saturday.

The Panamanian quake is at least the fourth quake this year in Latin America surpassing 7.0 in magnitude, after devastating back-to-back earthquakes in Venezuela’s Guaira in June and a powerful earthquake in western Colombia in August.

World.title: Home movers raise safety concerns after crash that killed Sgt. Ponce
World.content:
Home movers raise safety concerns after crash that killed Sgt. Ponce

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Belize Home Movers Group says it has serious concerns about the circumstances of Saturday night’s crash on the George Price Highway that claimed the life of Police Sergeant Jovanni Ponce.

Sgt. Ponce, 50, died after his SUV collided with a house being transported on a flatbed truck between Miles 42 and 43 in Cotton Tree Village.

In a statement on Sunday, the group said it was devastated by the tragedy and extended condolences to the family and loved ones of the deceased.

The group said its members recognize the added risks of moving houses on weekend nights and have consistently tried to avoid moves on Saturdays and Sundays. It said it is deeply disappointed that a house was being moved on a Saturday night.

It also pointed to what it called apparent shortcomings in the safety lighting on the house involved.

“Public safety must always take precedence,” the group said. “These precautions exist for one reason: to protect human life.”

World.title: Social media influencer Benjamin Garcia, Mexican businessman formally charged following shooting incident in Belize City
World.content:
Social media influencer Benjamin Garcia, Mexican businessman formally charged following shooting incident in Belize City

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Social media influencer Benjamin Eduardo Garcia, 27, and Mexican businessman Sergio Martinez Ramirez, 36, have now been formally arrested and charged with discharging a firearm in public following an incident on the Philip Goldson Highway early Saturday morning.

The Belize Police Department confirmed the development in an update issued at 11:35 a.m. Sunday, putting to rest earlier uncertainty surrounding the status of the two men.

The charges follow earlier media reports that Garcia, who has been publicly associated with newly appointed Minister of National Security Michel Chebat, had been released without charges after police detained both men in connection with gunshots heard near Social Lounge at approximately 1:45 a.m. on October 10. The Belize Police Department subsequently disputed those reports.

According to the initial police report, officers conducting business checks heard several gunshots and observed a grey Ford F-250 pickup truck leaving the area. A pursuit ended near the Pallotti roundabout, where police intercepted the vehicle and detained both occupants.

During a search, Garcia informed officers that he had a licensed 9mm firearm in the glove compartment. Police recovered the weapon with one round in the chamber and 11 rounds in the magazine.

Earlier Sunday, police issued a clarification disputing media reports that Garcia had been released, maintaining that the individual concerned remained in custody while investigators prepared charges.

The department has now confirmed that both Garcia and Ramirez have been formally charged with discharging a firearm in public.

The incident has attracted public attention because of Garcia’s previously documented association with Chebat, who assumed responsibility for the Belize Police Department less than a week ago. There is no verified evidence or suggestion by BBN that Minister Chebat intervened in the investigation or influenced the handling of the case.

The two men are now facing criminal proceedings in connection with the incident. The charges remain allegations, and neither man has been convicted.

The police statement does not indicate whether either man has appeared before a magistrate or whether bail has been considered.

World.title: Belize Police mourn Sergeant Jovanni Ponce
World.content:
Belize Police mourn Sergeant Jovanni Ponce

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A Saturday night drive ended in tragedy for Sergeant Jovanni Ponce and his family.

The 50 year old police officer was travelling along the George Price Highway near Cotton Tree Village when his SUV collided with a house being moved on a flatbed truck heading the other way.

The impact left his Chevrolet Equinox trapped under the structure. First responders found Sgt. Ponce unresponsive at the wheel. He was rushed to the Western Regional Hospital but did not survive.

His wife and a child travelling with him escaped without serious injury.

The 58 year old driver of the flatbed truck was served with a Notice of Intended Prosecution, and a urine sample was taken as part of the investigation.

Sgt. Ponce’s death is a heavy loss for his family, his colleagues and the Belize Police Department.

BBN extends condolences to his loved ones and fellow officers.

World.title: Police dispute reports that Benjamin Garcia was released following shooting incident; Say he is still detained pending charges
World.content:
Police dispute reports that Benjamin Garcia was released following shooting incident; Say he is still detained pending charges

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The Belize Police Department has issued a clarification disputing media reports that a social media influencer was released without charges following a shooting incident on the Philip Goldson Highway early Saturday morning.

In a statement issued Sunday morning, police said that, contrary to reports circulating in the media, particularly those published by Channel 7 News Belize, the individual at the centre of the investigation remains in police custody.

“The individual in question remains in police custody and is presently being processed as investigators prepare to lay the appropriate charges,” the department stated.

The clarification follows reports concerning the detention of 27-year-old social media influencer Benjamin Eduardo Garcia and 36-year-old Mexican businessman Sergio Martinez Ramirez, who were intercepted near the Pallotti roundabout after police heard several gunshots in the vicinity of Social Lounge at approximately 1:45 a.m. on October 10.

According to the initial police report, officers pursued a grey Ford F-250 pickup truck after hearing the gunfire. During a subsequent search, Garcia reportedly disclosed that he had a licensed 9mm firearm in the glove compartment. Police recovered the weapon with one round in the chamber and 11 rounds in the magazine.

The initial report indicated that both men would be jointly charged with discharging a firearm in public. Subsequent media reports, however, suggested that no charges had been laid and that Garcia had been released.

In its clarification, the department urged media houses to ensure their reporting reflects the current status of the investigation and that accurate, verified information is disseminated to the public.

Police also reaffirmed their commitment to transparency and professionalism, adding that further updates would be provided as appropriate.

The department did not identify the individual by name in its clarification, specify which charges investigators intend to pursue, or explain the circumstances that led to the earlier reports of a release.

The incident has drawn attention because of Garcia’s publicly documented association with a known Minister of Government, and comes amid growing concern over a recent spate of deadly shootings in Belize City.

As of Sunday morning, police have not announced any formally laid charges in connection with the incident.

The police clarification follows the department’s initial report, which expressly stated that both men would be charged with discharging a firearm in public.

While police now maintain that the individual remains detained and charges are being prepared, they have not explained the discrepancy between that account and the earlier reports of his release.

World.title: Social media influencer reportedly released without charges after shooting incident
World.content:
Social media influencer reportedly released without charges after shooting incident

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Less than a week after a reshuffle of Cabinet, questions are emerging over the reported alleged release without charges of a social media influencer, following a shooting incident in Belize City early Saturday morning.

Benjamin Eduardo Garcia, 27, and Mexican businessman Sergio Martinez Ramirez, 36, were detained after police responding to gunshots along the Philip Goldson Highway pursued and intercepted a grey Ford F-250 pickup truck. Although an initial police report indicated that both men would be jointly charged with discharging a firearm in public, a Channel 7 report indicated that Garcia was subsequently released without charges.

According to the police report, officers assigned to the P4 Support Team were conducting business checks at Social Lounge at approximately 1:45 a.m. on October 10 when they heard several gunshots. Officers observed the pickup truck leaving the area and initiated a pursuit that ended near the Pallotti roundabout, where additional police units intercepted the vehicle.

Garcia, who was travelling as a passenger, and Ramirez, the driver, were detained. During a search, Garcia informed officers that he had a licensed 9mm firearm inside the glove compartment. Police recovered the weapon and found one live round in the chamber and 11 rounds in the magazine.

Both men were cautioned in connection with the alleged offence of discharging a firearm in public. Scenes of Crime personnel were called to process the relevant locations, and the report expressly stated that both men would be taken to the Belama Police Station to be jointly charged.

Garcia’s reported release without charges raises questions about what transpired between the initial police investigation and his release, including whether ballistic evidence was examined, whether either detainee was found to have discharged a weapon, and who may have authorized the alleged decision not to proceed with charges.

The incident comes at an especially troubling time for Belize City, where a fresh wave of deadly gun violence has claimed several young lives in recent days. On Thursday, October 8, 17-year-old Kaylon David was fatally shot on Iguana Street Extension, while 20-year-old Shamar Smith was murdered on Pelican Street later that evening. Another victim, 27-year-old Jory Bowden, was killed on Central American Boulevard on Friday night. The three killings have heightened public concerns about escalating firearm violence and the police department’s ability to contain it.

The Garcia incident also places renewed attention on how the police department handles high profile cases and that this matter will not be shrugged under the rug. The police department underwent leadership changes on October 6, when Michel Chebat was appointed Minister of National Security, replacing Julius Espat, who had served as interim Minister of Home Affairs since June. The Cabinet reshuffle placed both the Belize Police Department and Belize Defence Force under Chebat’s leadership.

In July, during Espat’s short stint as Police Minister, he had handled a politically sensitive police matter. Following allegations that Stoney Ferguson, the son of Agriculture Minister Rodwell Ferguson, assaulted a police officer and damaged a police vehicle in Placencia, Espat reportedly directed police to pursue his arrest despite his family connections. Ferguson had initially been released without charges, reportedly following telephone calls made on his behalf. Espat subsequently made clear that police officers were expected to act according to the law rather than political considerations.

The question now is whether that same standard of accountability will be upheld under the police department’s new leadership. The fact that Garcia possesses a licensed firearm does not, by itself, establish that he discharged it unlawfully. Equally, the initial police report’s stated intention to charge both men does not establish their guilt. However, the apparent reported reversal warrants an explanation, particularly given the seriousness with which firearm offences are ordinarily treated in Belize.

As of publication, BBN has not independently established who fired the shots, whether ballistic testing linked Garcia’s firearm to the incident, or the official grounds for his reported release. There is also no verified evidence that Minister Chebat intervened in the police investigation or influenced the decision not to charge him.

With Belize City confronting another deadly surge in gun violence, the circumstances surrounding the incident raise broader questions about consistency, transparency and equal treatment under the law.

World.title: Greed does not run the world, envy does, the old man’s verdict and the Belizean books
World.content:
Greed does not run the world, envy does, the old man’s verdict and the Belizean books

By Horace Palacio:

A quote has been moving across Belizean timelines this week, and readers know the house ritual. Before we discuss any famous line, we check the signature.

This one, for once, is genuine. Charlie Munger, the late vice chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, said it plainly at his shareholder meeting in 2022, at ninety eight years of age. The world is not driven by greed. It is driven by envy. His partner Warren Buffett spent decades quoting the line on his behalf. So this is not an internet orphan. It is the considered verdict of a man who spent a full century watching money move through human hands, delivered a year before he died, still worth billions, still unimpressed.

When a witness that qualified files a report that strange, a Sunday is well spent examining it. So let us make the old man’s case, and then bring the books home to Belize.

Start at the kitchen table with the distinction, because the two sins are commonly confused and they are entirely different machines.

Greed is wanting more. Envy is wanting what he has. Greed is absolute, a bigger number on your own page. Envy is relative, a smaller gap between your page and your neighbor’s. And that difference changes everything, because an absolute hunger can be fed. A relative one cannot, ever, because the reference point walks. Researchers once famously found that people would accept a smaller salary, provided it exceeded their neighbor’s, over a doubled salary that fell short of the man next door. Read that twice. Human beings will pay real money, out of their own pockets, purely to win a comparison. That is not greed. Greed would take the bigger check. That is envy, and it is the stronger force.

Now the case for Munger’s verdict, and it stands on three legs.

First, universality. Greed, in its grand form, is a specialist’s sin, the engine of the tycoon, the hoarder, the few. Envy is issued to everyone at birth. The man with nothing feels no greed for a yacht he has never imagined, but he feels envy for his cousin’s pickup truck by Tuesday. Greed drives the top of the pyramid. Envy drives every floor of it. A force that operates in every heart will always move more of the world than one operating in a handful.

Second, the oldest evidence on record. Open the Book our grandmothers kept by the bed. The first crime scene in human history had no money in it. Cain did not rob Abel. He envied him, and a brother died over a comparison. And study the Ten Commandments with an economist’s eye. Nine of them ban actions, stealing, killing, lying. The tenth bans a feeling. Thou shalt not covet. The ancients legislated against envy itself, the only commandment aimed directly at the heart’s bookkeeping, because they understood what Munger confirmed three thousand years later. The other sins are envy’s employees.

Third, the modern proof, and this one Belize carries in its pocket. The entire advertising industry is an envy refinery, selling not products but comparisons. And the feed, the algorithm this column has dissected all year, is envy at industrial scale. Your grandmother compared her life with one village. You compare yours, hourly, against the curated highlight reel of the entire planet, and the machine profits precisely from the width of the gap it manufactures. The richest companies in history run on harvested attention, yes, but ask what holds the attention. Munger answered. The scroll is a mirror rigged to lose.

Now bring the books home, because Belize runs some of the most envy-leveraged accounts on earth.

Count the household entries. The loan taken not for the land but for the show, the rims before the roof, the September splurge calibrated to the neighbor’s September, the funeral and wedding spending that bankrupts families in the name of appearances. This column begged you months ago, land before car. Understand today who writes the opposite purchase order. Envy does. Envy is the silent co-signer on half the bad debt in this country.

Count the political entries. The ham economy works because the gift is relative, visible, comparative. The deepest cry in our politics is rarely build it for all of us. It is why did he get it. And both parties farm that crop expertly, aiming each tribe’s resentment sideways at neighbors, never upward at ledgers, exactly as the unpaid bodyguards column described. Envy is the cheapest fuel in Belizean politics, and the tank is always full.

And count the oldest entry of all, the one this column named long ago. The crab bucket needs no lid, and now you know the engine underneath it. The crab does not dream of climbing. He dreams of the climber falling. That is envy’s signature move, it prefers leveling down to building up, because leveling down closes the gap without requiring a single day’s work. Every mocked student, every slandered success, every whispered must be connections is the bucket doing envy’s accounting.

Very well. The diagnosis is Munger’s. The medicine, mercifully, is also his, and he left three doses.

Dose one, see the sin’s absurd economics. Envy, the old man loved to say, is the one sin with no fun in it whatsoever. Gluttony at least offers the meal. Envy is all pain, zero pleasure, a trolley ride consisting entirely of the fare. Why, he asked, would anyone board that trolley?

Dose two, retire the race you cannot win. Someone, Munger taught, will always be getting richer faster than you, and this is not a tragedy. The only comparison that compounds is you against your own yesterday. The farmer measuring his field against last season grows. The farmer measuring it against his neighbor’s seethes, and seething has never fertilized an acre.

Dose three, and this is the conversion that turns the poison into fuel. The safest way to get what you want, Munger told a graduating class, is to deserve what you want. So when the burn rises in your chest at another Belizean’s success, run the test this column gave you once, and then go further. Do not merely refuse to stone the climber. Enroll with him. Envy, interrogated honestly, is just unprocessed information about what you actually want. Convert every pang into one question, what did he do that I have not done yet, and envy becomes a curriculum. The bad mind becomes a reading list.

Close the books, then, with the national arithmetic. Belize runs a chronic envy surplus and a building deficit, and the two lines are connected, because every hour spent minding the neighbor’s progress is an hour unavailable to your own. Imagine this country converting its envy budget, the whispering, the clawing, the comparison scrolling, into the builder’s question this column planted weeks ago. What are you building. That single currency exchange, performed in enough Belizean hearts, is worth more than any foreign loan.

The old man watched money for a hundred years and left us the finding free of charge. The world runs on envy, and envy runs on us.

It is Sunday, Belize. The trolley is at the stop, doors open, fare ready, no fun aboard, same as every day.

Let it leave without you.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: Belize officially off the EU tax grey list
World.content:
Belize officially off the EU tax grey list

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): It’s done. Belize is off the EU’s grey list.

The European Union’s Economic and Financial Affairs Council announced on Friday, October 9, that Belize has been removed from Annex II, the “grey list” of non cooperative tax jurisdictions.

That means Belize is now completely out of EU tax governance monitoring.

The decision follows a positive rating from the OECD Global Forum on Transparency and Exchange of Information for Tax Purposes on Belize’s system for exchanging tax information on request.

Belize was taken off the EU’s main blacklist, Annex I, in February 2024 after major legal and procedural reforms. But it stayed on the grey list while waiting for the Global Forum’s supplementary review.

Now that review is complete, and the verdict is clear. The EU says Belize has met all its international tax transparency commitments.

No more routine monitoring. No more grey list.

World.title: Police officer reportedly killed after SUV collides with house being transported near Cotton Tree
World.content:
Police officer reportedly killed after SUV collides with house being transported near Cotton Tree

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Jovanni Ponce, a police officer has reportedly lost his life in a tragic road traffic accident near Cotton Tree Village, Belize District, on Saturday night.

Preliminary reports indicate that Officer Ponce was travelling in a white SUV with his family after attending a church concert when the vehicle collided with a house being transported on the roadway as a wide load.

The accident reportedly occurred near a gas station in the Cotton Tree area.

Information received indicates that the officer died at the scene. His family members reportedly survived the collision.

Images circulating from the scene show a house being transported on the roadway, with emergency personnel and equipment visible nearby.

The circumstances surrounding the collision remain unclear, including whether adequate warning signs and escort vehicles were in place for the wide load.

This is a developing story.

World.title: Dunbeholden grab first win of JPL season
World.content:
Coach Alex Thomas (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

Dunbeholden FC earned their first win of the Jamaica Premier League season on Sunday, edging Molynes United 1-0 at the Dunbeholden Sports Complex to move off the foot of the points table.

After four straight losses, the Alex Thomas-coached team got their first points after Tuwain Merrick’s 66th minute goal eased the pressure on the St Catherine based club.

Meanwhile, despite conceding a goal for the first time this season,

Montego Bay United (MBU) reclaimed the lead in the standings after beating Cavalier SC 3-1 at Turners Oval.

MBU improved to 13 points, three more than Waterhouse FC who play on Monday, while Cavalier FC stayed in sixth place on seven points after their first loss this season.

In the other game played on Sunday, Humble Lion earned back-to-back points after holding Chapelton Maroons 0-0 at Wembley Centre of Excellence.

Dunbeholden jumped four places to 11th place on the points table after Merrick finished off a superb team move by curling the ball past the Molynes goalkeeper into the far left corner in the 66th minute, his first goal of the season and his team’s second.

At Turners Oval, Deonjay Brown and Dwight Merrick both scored their second goal of the season and Richardo Ramsey scored his first with Christopher Ainsworth scoring for Cavalier, ending MBU’s run of not conceding a goal at 412 minutes.

Brown was well placed at the far right post to volley home a cross in the 17th minute to give MBU the lead and Merrick doubled the lead 20 minutes later with a spectacular left footer from about 27 yards away, beating Cavalier’s goalkeeper Taywaine Lynch at his left post.

Ainsworth was well placed to tap home a cross in the 52nd minute to halve the deficit but Ramsey, who had replaced the injured Jourdain Fletcher, and who had missed an easy scoring chance just minutes earlier, made the points sure when he dribbled his way past two defenders and fired past Lynch in the 80th minute.

-Paul A Reid

World.title: Heroy Clarke nominated as JLP Area Council 4 Deputy Leader
World.content:
The newly nominated deputy leader of the Jamaica Labour Party (JLP), Heroy Clarke who was nominated during an Area Council 4 constituency meeting held at the Montego Bay Convention Centre in St James on Sunday, October 11, 2026.

ST JAMES, Jamaica — The Member of Parliament for St James Central, Heroy Clarke has been nominated as deputy leader for the Jamaica Labour Party’s (JLP) Area Council 4.

Clarke, who was the lone nominee after nominating himself, accepted the position during an Area Council 4 constituency meeting hosted by St James East Central at the Montego Bay Convention Centre in Rose Hall, St James, on Sunday.

While his nomination is set to go to the JLP’s National Conference for official ratification in November, Clarke noted that additional nominations remain open up to the 14th of this month.

Expected to succeed JC Hutchinson in the role, Clarke expressed confidence and readiness to begin his duties immediately.

“I do understand that the work is cut out for me because, as the saying goes, anywhere the West goes, the rest goes. Therefore, I cannot afford to allow the West to fall out of the winning column,” said Clarke in an interview following his nomination.

He emphasised that strong family support will be crucial as he balances his political obligations.

“I know the work is there for me to do, and I will continue in light of what is happening. One thing I am grateful for is that my immediate family is very political — they understand what it means when I say I am going into the trenches, into every nook and cranny, to get the job done. Most of the time, they will be accompanying me to those areas,” stated Clarke.

Clarke added that his immediate focus will align with the strategy of the party’s senior leadership.

“I know what the work requires, and we have to deliver because elder statesmen like Dr Horace Chang, Edmund Bartlett, and JC Hutchinson have vowed that the West must return to where it was,” noted Clarke.

With local government elections scheduled for 2028, Clarke identified leading the party through that campaign as his first major task in his new post.

— Anthony Lewis.

World.title: CAFFE in crisis
World.content:
Voters queue outside a polling station during the 2025 General Election. CAFFE had initially intended to recruit 1,000 volunteers on a budget of approximately $15 million for the 2025 poll, but a funding freeze forced the observer group to cut that number in half. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

AFTER almost 30 years of monitoring elections in Jamaica, the internationally acclaimed agency Citizens Action for Free and Fair Elections (CAFFE) is now cash-strapped and desperately in need of assistance from the private sector to continue observing the country’s democratic process.

CAFFE is still navigating the financial fallout from the Donald Trump Administration’s 2025 withdrawal of United States Agency for International Development (USAID) funding from non-governmental organisations globally.

Speaking at a Jamaica Observer Press Club at the agency’s New Kingston office last Thursday, CAFFE Chair Grace Baston said its financial position has deteriorated further since the September 2025 General Election.

For that poll, CAFFE had initially aimed to recruit 1,000 volunteers on a budget of approximately $15 million.

Frozen funding, however, forced the organisation to halve its target to about 500.

The shortfall has heightened concerns about its capacity to monitor future local government elections, by-elections, and the country’s next general election.

Baston warned that such a setback could erode the democratic gains the country has made.

“There is no doubting the work of the ECJ (Electoral Commission of Jamaica) and the EOJ (Electoral Office of Jamaica).

There has been remarkable progress in those electoral processes; we are the first to give credit.

That being said, we believe strongly [that a] democracy not monitored is democracy threatened.

“CAFFE’s presence has made a huge difference.

The respect people have for the CAFFE observer entering a polling station; the confidence they have in what we are going to say, or what we pronounce about the quality of the conduct of the poll — it is extremely important.

[If] you ease up on that you are inviting a return to what was before,” she insisted.

The election watchdog was established in 1997 amid lingering political strife and fears that Jamaica’s democratic process could be undermined, based on the experiences in the 1980s and early 1990s.

Although the country has moved beyond those dangers, Baston said new threats have emerged, demanding continued vigilance.

“Once, the big threat was overvoting in a polling station — [you have] 100 people on the list and 150 people voting — or the stuffing of a box.

There are other threats now, and we are working hard to make sure we can monitor those.

They are difficult.

One of the new things coming on that we have to think about is going to be precisely this AI (artificial intelligence) that you hear talked about so much,” Baston said.

“How are elections going to be free and fair if campaigning is going to involve the use of deepfake videos? How are we going to hold politicians accountable to make sure that is not happening? The public is being duped because of the power of artificial intelligence in political campaigning.

I am saying not only do we need to be there to prevent the recurrence of the old things that used to threaten our democracy, but there are new threats that we must be prepared for,” charged Baston.

CAFFE Deputy Chairman Anton Thompson also named voter apathy as a major threat to democracy, noting that the agency had established clubs in schools on a $5-million annual budget to foster political awareness and engagement among young people.

However, he told the Sunday Observer that budget cuts have since forced approximately 85 per cent of more than 40 clubs to close.

“We have about half a dozen active clubs, which is far less than we had when we launched this.

And when we launched this with some funding we were able to hire somebody to energise the schools, talk to them, arrange for them to meet.

I met with several schools online — because it was still COVID time — encouraged them, and told them what we were trying to do,” he said.

Thompson added that turnover among school and student leaders had also contributed to the closure of some clubs.

Additionally, many of CAFFE’s volunteers are sixthform students who are trained by the agency at their respective schools and receive a stipend for their civic service.

Baston added that the enthusiasm and dedication that she had seen from engaged students emphasised the need to keep the programme going.

“This is 2026.

The average young person can’t take himself or herself away from their phone for five minutes,” she said.

“When you see these young people making their way to polling locations at six o’clock in the morning because they take so seriously their duty to be there to observe the set-up of the poll.

Once you engage them; once you begin raising their awareness and their consciousness of how precious, how hard-won our democracy was, how fragile it is; once you begin engaging them, their energy and their interest levels are so impressive.

That is why the lack of the resources to have the clubs active is so painful, so difficult,” lamented Baston.

For his part, former Chairman Dr Lloyd Barnett warned that the volunteer count, having been reduced for the September 2025 General Election, could shrink further unless the organisation secures additional funding.

“We are not going to get it from the European Union or USAID anymore.

It’s clear that just like the election monitoring, it has to be Jamaicans.

And as we have said, we have been grateful to Jamaicans…

the commercial interests have been helpful [but] we need more help because of the absence of a major part of our funding from the international sources,” he explained.

“That is why we have been appealing to them.

We have a strong programme in which we are trying to convince them that it’s in their interest, and in the interest of all Jamaica, that they should participate,” added Barnett.

He maintained that the right to choose the country’s leadership is a cornerstone of democracy, and urged the private sector to help ensure that CAFFE’s election-monitoring work does not disappear.

“The electoral system is at the foundation of democracy, and democracy means the Government is of the people, by the people, for the people…

It is in everybody’s interest that democracy should be preserved, and the preservation of elections is the first step in preserving democracy.

You can’t have a democracy without free and fair elections, and that’s why we can’t afford to have CAFFE die,” charged Barnett.

World.title: ‘Effectively, it’s a drizzle’
World.content:
A drone photo of the Mona Reservoir taken on Saturday, October 10, 2026. National Water Commission data show the water level at Mona Reservoir is now 35.6 per cent.

FRIDAY, October 9, 2026, just before midday, dark clouds, pregnant with rain, hovered ominously over Kingston and St Andrew.

By early afternoon the sun had disappeared and the heavens burst open, drenching a city that had endured months of punishing drought.

“Finally, the drought done now!” one woman declared, her face lighting up as the long-awaited rain came in heavy torrents for about halfhour, flooding streets in the process.

“I hope this falling in Mona and Hermitage,” said another woman, referencing the Mona Reservoir and Hermitage Dam — the two major water storage facilities that supply the capital city.

However, Water and Climate Change Minister Matthew Samuda says Friday’s rain was not enough to ease the drought.

“Effectively, it’s a drizzle when you compare it to what we really need,” he told the Jamaica Observer Saturday afternoon.

“This is our rainy period where we’re supposed to have sustained rainfall from the last week in August, but six weeks later we’re celebrating an afternoon shower.

Nobody should be of the opinion that we’re out of the woods,” Samuda added.

He said while the volume of rain has improved water levels at the Mona Reservoir and Hermitage Dam, “There is no [rain] storm that has the ability, in a single day, to fill those two storage facilities.

What we have experienced is six weeks of sustained reduction in rainfall in our rainy period, on the back of our six-month reduction, so we can’t romanticise this thing.

An afternoon shower is not going to correct this problem,” Samuda told the Sunday Observer.

On Saturday, National Water Commission (NWC) data showed the water level at Hermitage dam had increased by 5.7 million gallons to now stand at 45 per cent, while Mona Reservoir saw an increase by 10 million gallons, pushing the storage to 35.6 per cent.

Against that reality, Samuda and the NWC are urging Jamaicans to continue conserving water, and the restrictions on use are still in force.

At the September 30, 2026 post-Cabinet press briefing, Samuda said the drought has impacted 106 water systems islandwide, the majority of which are in the east.

“Forty-five of our systems in Kingston and St Andrew…10 in St Catherine and Clarendon, and 42 in the north-east, are indeed experiencing the impacts of severe drought conditions,” Samuda said.

“In the western division, one is in Manchester and St Elizabeth, four in Westmoreland and Hanover, and four in St James and Trelawny,” he added.

Last week the NWC had signalled that if the drought worsens it may be forced to ration piped water on alternate days.

Asked about that on Saturday, Samuda said the inflows from Friday’s rain could result in a delay in that strategy.

“We’re evaluating and should make an announcement next week,” he said, adding that the Meteorological Service has forecast “some rainfall” for Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday this week.

“So that would ease the pressure,” Samuda said.

On Saturday the Met Service said there is a trough across Jamaica and a tropical wave across the western Caribbean.

The Met Office said that while the trough is expected to remain over the next few days, the tropical wave is forecast to continue moving westward and away from the island.

The office also forecast windy conditions across Jamaica on Sunday as “a low-level jet stream is projected to strengthen across the central Caribbean”.

It also said that Sunday and Monday will be mostly cloudy across northern parishes, with isolated showers across north-eastern parishes.

Otherwise, there will be mainly sunny mornings.

Additionally, the island will experience afternoon showers and isolated thunderstorms across sections of southern parishes and hilly areas elsewhere.

Tuesday will become cloudy in the afternoon, with showers and thunderstorms across sections of central and western parishes.

World.title: CAFFE clubs crumbling
World.content:
Voters at a polling station at Seaward Primary and Junior High School during the September 2025 General Election. According to election watchdog Citizens Action for Free and Fair Elections, the majority of its election observers are sixth-form students. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

AN initiative by election watchdog Citizens Action for Free and Fair Elections (CAFFE) to expose youngsters to the democratic process through school clubs is now struggling to sustain itself, following a severing of financial support from international donors.

Democracy clubs in schools, which began in 2021, serves as a platform for fostering discussions among high school students on various aspects of Jamaican democracy, building on the involvement of scores of students in CAFFE’s election monitoring exercises since 2011.

Launched with the assistance of the National Democratic Institute (NDI) and the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), the initiative aims to encourage students who are 18 years old to enrol on the national voters’ list while also preparing those who are over 17 years old to serve as CAFFE observers.

However, while providing an update on the state of the clubs during a Jamaica Observer Press Club last Thursday at CAFFE’s New Kingston office, the watchdog’s Deputy Chairman Anton Thompson shared that the initiative has seen a significant fall-off in participants, with only six of the initial 40 schools still active.

“We launched this with some funding, so we were able to hire somebody to energise the schools, talk to them [the students], and arrange for them to meet,” said Thompson.

He explained that the initiative’s struggle is further compounded by the lack of replacement leaders.

“These activities in school require teacher leadership as well as student leadership…

Once a teacher’s leadership is absent — and they’re often absent because they go to another job or they retire — then the project will not continue until somebody else is found,” he said, adding that in those instances a central coordinator is needed to ensure that the gaps are filled.

“Not only do teachers move on from schools, but students move on, too.

And so, obviously, if the club goes dormant for two years it’s pretty much extinct until you get replacements, then you have to start again.

“But the schools that are active now tend to be very involved.

We have an event planned for next week for them — an online event because they are all over the country.

And so, essentially, we want to continue, and we are trying our best, too, if we can energise more schools to be involved,” he said.

According to CAFFE, the annual budget for the clubs’ operation is $5 million.

“The running of a club in a school is not necessarily a major financial burden for the school because you usually have provisions in your school budget for clubs, and it usually is not very expensive, depending on the type of club.

However we want to provide support to ensure that the clubs are running at a level where the students are really benefiting — particularly in support in the way of material, research ideas, and things like that — so that the students can really benefit.

That’s what we would want to do,” Thompson said.

Underscoring that the majority of the organisation’s election observers are sixthform students, past Chairman Lloyd Barnett pressed that there is an urgency to restore the operation of the democracy clubs.

“The school term start[ed] in September, and then [there were] exam preparations, and so the focus shifts; and next year we[‘ll] have a completely new set of people.

It is very difficult to keep it sustained.

You have to do all that you have done last year, the next year.

Obviously we need more help because of the absence of a major part of our funding from international sources,” he said.

Additionally, CAFFE Chair Grace Baston noted that the clubs are open to students of all grade levels, with the aim of preparing them to volunteer by the time they reach sixth form.

Despite the drop in numbers, she remains optimistic about the future of the clubs.

“It is the lack of funding that accounts for the fall-off in the number of active clubs.

It’s as clear as that..

We hope to be able to attract the funding — and we don’t envision that it will be difficult to get those clubs up and running once we have the financial support,” said Baston.

World.title: High marks for Malie Donn’s The Golden Child
World.content:
Malie Donn

DANCEHALL artiste Malie Donn continues to make significant strides on the international music scene with his debut studio album, The Golden Child, securing multiple positions on Apple Music charts across several territories.

Released on September 4 through VP Records, the 21-track project has climbed to the #1 spot on Apple Music’s Reggae Albums chart in Bermuda, St Lucia, and the Turks and Caicos Islands.

The album has also secured the #2 position in Jamaica, Antigua and Barbuda, the Bahamas, Grenada, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Guyana, and Anguilla.

Its success extends beyond the reggae category, having peaked at #3 on the overall Apple Music Albums chart in Jamaica, St Lucia, and Antigua and Barbuda.

Internationally, The Golden Child has also made its presence felt, reaching #4 on the Apple Music Reggae Albums chart in the United Kingdom and Canada, and #5 in the United States. The project has additionally charted in France, Denmark, Singapore, and Portugal, underscoring the artiste’s growing appeal beyond traditional dancehall markets.

For Malie Donn, the album represents a defining chapter in his musical journey, reflecting both his personal experiences and artistic evolution.

“ The Golden Child represents everything that brought me to this point — the pressure, the growth, the wins, and the lessons,” Malie Donn shared in a previous interview with the Jamaica Observer. “This album gives people a chance to hear more of who I am as an artiste, where I want to take the music next, and the versatility I bring.”

The project, led by the title track Golden Child, featuring Squash, also boasts collaborations with Byron Messia, DJ Frass, Antuwang, and Javo Donn.

Adding to the momentum, the entertainer has released official music videos for two tracks from the album, Live Life and SWFT, offering fans fresh visuals to complement the project.

The album’s strong chart showing follows a successful outing in London, England, where Malie Donn delivered a sold-out headline performance at indigo at The O2 on September 5, one day after its release. His international visibility received another boost during the album’s release week when he was featured on the cover of Apple Music’s Reggae playlist.

With The Golden Child continuing to resonate with audiences across the Caribbean, North America, Europe, and other territories, Malie Donn is looking to build on the project’s success while further establishing himself as one of dancehall’s emerging international talents.

World.title: Balford Henry’s final byline
World.content:
Balford Henry, born on January 24, 1952 and died on September 14, 2026, was laid to rest on Saturday. He was 74.

WRITTEN not by the hand nor the wit of the illustrious veteran journalist Balford Henry but by the enduring ink of a remarkable legacy, his final story finds its authors in the colleagues and family whose tributes attest to the mark he left on their lives.

Gathered on Saturday at Kencot Christian Fellowship in St Andrew for the thanksgiving service for his life, mourners reflected on a career spanning more than five decades during which Henry meticulously documented Jamaica’s political, entertainment, and industrial affairs, and cemented his reputation as a respected pillar of the media fraternity.

Delivering her tribute, Minister of Culture, Gender, Entertainment, and Sport Olivia Grange remembered Henry as the consummate journalist — a man who was dedicated to his career, building a life around expertly sharing facts.

“Jamaica has long been regarded as a liberal democracy within which resides a diverse and active corps of journalists.

Within that corps, however, is a much smaller number of these professionals whose work has truly helped to elevate public awareness and understanding about the role and the actual workings of our Parliament, the decisions made by our elected and appointed representatives, and the electoral process itself.

“Balford Henry was such a man, a man who, through meticulous thoroughness, sheer hard work, ceaseless enquiry, and a longevity that reflected his lifelong dedication to his calling, developed into a towering figure in the field of journalism,” noted Grange.

Henry’s career took root at The Gleaner in 1971 and included work with the Jamaica Observer and the Jamaica Information Service (JIS).

He was also editor of Reggae Times in the 1990s and reporter for the Overseas Gleaner (North America Edition) in New York during the 90s.

His trailblazing work in media earned him several Press Association of Jamaica awards, including recognition for his coverage of reggae icon Bob Marley’s funeral in 1981.

In 2011 he was nationally recognised for his contribution to journalism with the Order of Distinction in the rank of Officer.

Seeking to ensure that Henry’s words would endure not only in memory but also through the body of work he produced over his many years as a journalist, Grange told the congregation that she would pursue the preservation of his writings through national cultural institutions.

“I am going to speak to the National Library [of Jamaica] and the Jamaica Music Museum about working towards collecting Balford’s writings on the entertainment industry over the years, because he did his research, and his work [is] something that is worth establishing,” she said.

Garfield Angus, a senior journalist at JIS and a colleague and friend of ‘Bally’s — as he was affectionately called — also shared anecdotes from their time together throughout the years. His tribute highlighted not only Henry’s many achievements, but also the man behind them.

“As we gather to say goodbyes and to give thanks, not only to the journalist Bally but to the human being he remained, we give thanks for his wit, for his wisdom, for his integrity, for the debates, for his laughter, for the stories, for the friendship,” he said.

“Bally, you served your profession and your country and your friends exceptionally well. You wrote your final column and the copy is clean. The story is complete, the byline remains, and the legacy endures,” said Angus.

In a tearful tribute to her ex-husband, Claudia Stockhausen-Henry told those who gathered about their love story that legally ended in 2006 but lasted until Henry’s last breath.

Emotionally recounting his last days, Stockhausen-Henry shared how she stuck by his side and cared for him.

“I heard when he took his last breath and made a rattling sound. It was a good Samaritan who offered to drive the car to KPH [Kingston Public Hospital], where he was pronounced dead. To Bally, I am always his wife. He hates to hear me say ‘ex-wife’. Here endeth our love story,” she said.

Other tributes were heard from Clarence Brodie, former president of the Press Association of Jamaica, and friend of the deceased, Ainsley Edwards. Also in attendance was Delano Seiveright, minister of state in the Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce.

Henry was born on January 24, 1952 and died on September 14, 2026. He was 74.

World.title: A mother’s tears, a son’s dream
World.content:
Junior Clarke, 20, and his mother Taschel Fisher pause for a photo last Sunday.

ONE young man’s dream of becoming a doctor took shape when he was just four years old. Now, at 20, after securing the academic achievements necessary to pursue a career in medicine, Junior Clarke faces another hurdle — financial hardship.

But, he’s steadfast in his pursuit of the childhood dream.

“I always wanted to not only help people but to also change how the health system works. I want to become a general surgeon,” Clarke told the Jamaica Observer in an interview last Sunday.

Born and raised in the community of Rivoli in Spanish Town, St Catherine, Clarke graduated from Jonathan Grant High School in 2024, securing 11 subjects in the Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate (CSEC) exams. He then moved on to the sixth-form programme at St Jago High School, where he secured an additional eight units at the Caribbean Advanced Proficiency Examination (CAPE) level.

Clarke told the Jamaica Observer that his mother, Taschel Fisher, shouldered raising him alone as his father passed away when he was four months old.

“Growing up was challenging because we didn’t have the resources to make ends meet. I had to help my mother sell at the school gate where I graduated from,” he said, adding that Fisher has been a vendor at the institution for more than 30 years.

Earlier this year, Clarke applied to study medicine at The University of the West Indies (The UWI) and was offered a place in the programme, but the cost of the tuition was beyond his financial means.

“We couldn’t manage it because it’s like $4 million a year, so I decided to take a gap year and do voluntary services, especially at the hospitals, so I can get a scholarship because for a single mother, $4 million is a lot,” Clarke lamented, adding that he’s been unsuccessful in trying to secure a scholarship.

“The scholarships I applied for required me to have six or more grade ones in CAPE, but I only got one grade one. I also started an application for a scholarship but then I realised it wouldn’t be sufficient to cover the cost [of the programme],” he said.

Clarke shared that he is currently in the process of attempting, for a second time, the CAPE subjects for which he did not achieve grade ones, to put himself in a more competitive position to secure a scholarship.

“A setback doesn’t determine your future; it’s just for you to come back and try again. Even though you may face some delays, it doesn’t determine your final outcome. I am going to apply for scholarships again,” he told the Sunday Observer.

Underscoring that there are many others whose aspirations, too, are hampered by financial difficulties, Clarke said helping others will be a priority for him in the future.

“I also want to give back to my community, St Jago High and especially Jonathan Grant High. They did not only build me but they showed me that I was created for excellence. It is not where you are from, it is where you want to go. I know if I get the assistance to achieve my goal, I will later be able to assist others to reach their goals,” said Clarke.

His mother, Fisher, told the Sunday Observer that when she learned of Clarke’s acceptance to The UWI, she could not contain her emotions.

“We were coming home in a taxi, and I held down my head and I started to cry and I said, ‘God, you are in control.’ I asked

God to let him get the help that he needs because even though I am willing to go above and beyond, I know I wouldn’t be able to come up with that kind of money,” Fisher recounted.

She explained that raising Clarke by herself was no easy feat, but with “God as her guide, she was able to pull through,”

“It was very challenging to balance the bills plus attend to his daily needs. Tears after tears, I would go to bed nightly crying asking God to help me,” she said, adding that she often got help from her mother and sister.

“Junior is very driven, well-mannered and very ambitious. Even though he is from the ghetto, his mindset is different. Anyone out there who can help my son please help him,” an emotional Fisher expressed.

World.title: EU lacks influence(rs): No content creators at leaders’ summit
World.content:
Why? Seems they just haven’t got around to it. “Mainly logistical problems and budget constraints,” said one of the diplomats, who was granted anonymity to speak freely, as were others quoted in this piece. Another said they’d not had a chance to discuss it with their capital, but hadn’t ruled out the idea for future summits.

“There is no appetite for this,” said a third diplomat. “If my leader wants an influencer [they] would take one” with them, the diplomat said, adding that countries “don’t need the Council for that.”

Council spokesperson Romain Sadet confirmed that “we won’t be having content creators at the upcoming European Council.”

When the plan was unveiled, a Council official said the influencers would be granted access to areas of the Council’s Brussels HQ that are currently open only to journalists accredited by the EU institutions — though they would be banned from asking ministers and leaders questions.

“Content creators will be accompanied at all times and will not be treated as media,” the Council official continued. “We are working on the basis of about 10 content creators per event max, accompanied by Council staff.”

In June, the Council sent guidance for choosing influencers to national governments, seen by POLITICO.

World.title: Independent wins Kraków mayoral race in setback for PM Tusk
World.content:
“The people of Kraków have just regained their city! Now let’s put aside our differences and show that we can work together,” Gibała said, appearing to acknowledge that he will have to cooperate with Civic Coalition and its national coalition partner, the Left party, which together control 23 of the city council’s 43 seats.

This was Gibała’s fourth shot at the mayoralty. A local councilor and former national lawmaker, Gibała narrowly lost to Miszalski in 2024 in his previous attempt.

This time around, he campaigned on breaking with the political establishment, riding a wave of public discontent over Kraków’s huge debt and attempts to establish a low-emissions zone.

Gibała won the Sept. 27 first round with 36.4% ahead of Piątkowska on 29.9%. The candidate of the main opposition Law and Justice party finished third with 17.5%.

Piątkowska, backed by Civic Coalition, tried to distance herself from Miszalski while arguing that close ties with the national government would benefit Kraków, pop. 800,000.

Nationally, Civic Coalition remains ahead in opinion polls, but current voting intentions suggest that Tusk’s coalition will fall short of a majority in scheduled fall parliamentary elections.

Two October surveys listed by polling aggregator ewybory.eu put Civic Coalition at 31.9%, Law and Order at 17.7%, the far-right Confederation at 14% and another far-right grouping, the Confederation of the Polish Crown, at 8.3%.

Of Civic Coalition’s three government allies, only the Left, at 7%, would exceed the 5% threshold for parliamentary representation, dimming the administration’s prospects of retaining power.

World.title: Ireland’s budget cuts weaken EU, Commission warns
World.content:
The Commission is “very concerned about cuts to flexibility,” said one of the EU diplomats.

As a result of the changes, “we will have no ways left to help farmers and regions when crises hit, because of climate change or geopolitical tensions,” they added.

EU ambassadors gathered to discuss the Irish plan, which envisages cuts of €159 billion in current prices from the Commission’s nearly €2 trillion proposal. Of that amount, €38 billion was cut from foreign aid, €75 billion was axed from competitiveness, and at least €22 billion was slashed from rainy-day funds.

But even those reductions were criticized as insufficient by a German-led group of states pushing for cuts of several hundred billion. During the closed-door meeting, a rival bloc of 17 countries, known as the Friends of Cohesion, welcomed the fact that the Irish presidency had spared agriculture and regional payments from cuts.

EU governments are racing to finalize a deal on the budget among themselves by the end of the year — before elections in France, Italy and Poland that threaten to disrupt the negotiations.

A leaders’ summit on Thursday and Friday will give early signals as to whether the end-of-year deadline is achievable — or whether leaders should start preparing contingency plans.

World.title: MEP Glucksmann wins French center-left primary, becoming candidate for presidency
World.content:
“This result expresses something strong: that a left that is faithful to its values can unite, govern and win,” the MEP wrote online.

“We are here to win the presidential election: Turn the page on Macronism, stop the far right and change our lives,” he added.

But Glucksmann, a staunch supporter of Ukraine and a critic of China, now faces a much greater challenge: how to beat the far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon. The head of the France Unbowed party is surging in the polls, with the latest Ifop survey giving him 14% to 17% support, compared to 11% for Glucksmann.

In recent weeks, Glucksmann campaigned against forming an alliance with the far-left leader.

Three other candidates ran in the primary, including former minister Ségolène Royal and lawmakers Jérôme Guedj and Emmanuel Maurel.

Some 140,000 people were registered to vote in the primary — including, 80,000 who paid €15 to take part but weren’t members of any of the parties whose candidates were running — raising uncertainty over the outcome.

The online voting platform was also targeted by a cyberattack shortly after opening, organizers said in a statement on Friday, but “was never disrupted” and “the integrity of the recorded votes has not been compromised.”

World.title: Parliament split on EU climate rules opens way for conservative deal with far right
World.content:
For years, those four groups have worked together in Parliament to pass legislation that strikes a political middle ground, shunning collaboration with the far right. The sometimes uneasy alliance has ensured consistent, bipartisan support for the ETS, Europe’s most powerful tool for reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

But now, a reform of the landmark cap-and-trade scheme, unveiled by the EU executive in July, looks set to become a bellwether in an era when, increasingly, the center no longer holds.

The EPP is steering Parliament’s work on the proposed ETS revision through veteran German lawmaker Peter Liese, who wants to find a deal that satisfies everyone.

“I don’t want the Venezuelan majority. It’s against my convictions, but it is also not possible because nobody would see [Marine] Le Pen, the Austrian far-right FPÖ or the German extreme-far-right AfD voting for any ETS proposal,” he told POLITICO in September, using the informal term for a controversial alliance of center-right and far-right groups.

Instead, Liese, who maintains close ties with Dutch S&D lawmaker Mohammed Chahim, said he wanted “the broadest possible coalition,” including the right-wing European Conservatives and Reformists as well as “the Greens, The Left, if they want.”

But new amendments filed last week by the S&D, the second-largest group in Parliament, as well as the Greens and Renew, point to major schisms over key aspects of the ETS reform. The biggest divide concerns the so-called linear reduction factor, the mechanism that determines how quickly the supply of pollution permits shrinks each year.

World.title: Europeans back Zelenskyy after Trump calls for new Ukrainian leader
World.content:
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul also reaffirmed his country’s support for Zelenskyy Sunday, while calling for greater pressure on Moscow to return to peace talks.

“We need continued consistency and clarity on the side of Ukraine,” he told Reuters at a meeting of the governing Christian Democrats.

The show of support comes after Zelenskyy and Trump traded barbs Saturday following Washington’s decision to ease diesel sanctions on Russia. “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” Trump told reporters at the White House as he criticized Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil facilities.

On Sunday, the Ukrainian president stated on social media that his country would be prepared to stop attacking Russian oil refineries “if Russia stops striking our energy infrastructure.”

The U.K. also reiterated its support for Kyiv following Trump’s remarks. “We stand with Ukraine. We stand with President Zelenskyy,” British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting told the BBC Sunday morning, adding that Ukrainians alone should decide who leads their country.

Streeting said Russian President Vladimir Putin started the war and could end it, and added that Britain’s priority would be to seek reconciliation between Kyiv and Washington.

On Saturday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham spoke with Zelenskyy and reiterated Britain’s “complete solidarity,” Downing Street said. Burnham acknowledged that “the last 24 hours had been difficult for Ukraine” and pledged to strengthen sanctions, according to the statement.

World.title: Fix airport queues by Christmas, migration commissioner tells Brussels Airport
World.content:
EU countries began rolling out the Entry/Exit System, which records the fingerprints and facial images of non-EU visitors to the Schengen area, a year ago. It has been fully operational at all external Schengen border crossings since April.

But it has led to long waits at many airports — particularly over the summer, when some countries switched it off during peak periods. Delays persist at some airports, including at Brussels Zaventem, where travelers were forced to wait in lines for up to five hours last month.

“Some member states are a bit behind,” Brunner acknowledged. “We have some challenges, like Zaventem for instance, in Belgium, but also in other member states. And they have to do their job. They agreed on the new system, and now it's up to the member states to do their job.”

Brunner also said the Commission had offered support from border agency Frontex and funding to help countries implement the system, adding that he was “very confident” the problems would be ironed out before the next holiday rush.

Belgian Interior Minister Bernard Quintin pushed back at Brunner’s criticism, with a spokesperson saying his responsibility was to ensure there were enough police officers to staff the infrastructure provided by Brussels Airport Company.

The police have “been fully staffing the 12 positions at arrivals,” the spokesperson said, but the airport can process only 500 to 600 non-Schengen passengers an hour, compared with nearly 3,500 who may arrive between 6 a.m. and 10 a.m. on busy days. The airport's infrastructure “cannot cope” with that demand, the spokesperson said, and the company must “make significant changes.”

World.title: Man arrested in connection with alleged assassination plot against Donald Tusk
World.content:
Officials from the police service, the government’s protection service and the Internal Security Agency held an emergency meeting Sunday at the agency’s counterterrorism center to discuss the situation.

Following the meeting, Jacek Dobrzynski, Siemoniak’s spokesperson, told reporters that authorities are “treating this matter very seriously.”

“Month after month, year after year, more and more threats and worrying messages are reaching the police ,” he said. “In this case, we are talking about a strong probability that these threats could have been acted upon.”

No further details on the alleged plot were released and it remains unclear who might be behind it.

Poland has been on the frontline of Russia’s hybrid war against Ukraine’s backers in Europe, and has suffered cyberattacks which have been attributed to Moscow.

In recent weeks, Poland has also seen a wave of violent incidents in schools, including the death of a school caretaker in a knife attack.

This story has been updated.

World.title: Judo: Japan reclaim mixed team world title with eighth gold in Baku
World.content:
Today in Baku at the World Judo Championships, the Mixed Team competition is about more than medals. It’s about team spirit, unity and athletes fighting not just for themselves, but for each other.

 

In the semi-final, Japan went up against the People's Republic of China and UCHIMURA earned Japan an early lead.

Double World Champion MURAO continued their momentum with another ippon.

ARAI executed a lovely turn over and held Japan into the final. After last year’s team bronze, could Japan reclaim their title?

The other semi-final was between Uzbekistan and the Russian Federation.

An early ippon from AHADOV put Uzbekistan in the lead. LISHCHENKO evened the score with a yuko. MURTOZOEV took the score 2 - 1. But RECHKALOVA forced a submission. 2 - 2.

TASOEV scored big, sending his team into the lead. AMINOVA equalised to 3 - 3, forcing a Golden Score contest. +90kg was drawn!

TASOEV didn’t disappoint, throwing for ippon a second time to put his team into their first ever mixed team final.

In the final, tensions were high with the mixed team gold medal on the line.

In the first contest, a yuko was enough for TANAKA Shiho to push Japan into an early lead. MURAO Sanshiro was up next and continued the momentum. 2 - 0 to Japan. Mao ARAI continued the trend to take Japan to 3 - 0.

Tamerlan BASHAEV flipped the script to earn a win for his team. But OMORI Akari clinched the title with her win, claiming an eighth Team gold for Japan.

International Judo Federation President Mr Marius VIZER awarded the gold trophy.

CEO of Harvest Group Mr Almaz Alsenov awarded the silver trophy.

The two bronze trophies were awarded by International Judo Federation Vice President Dr. Laszlo Toth and International Judo Federation Vice President Obaid Al Anzi.

Last year we lost, so I’m super happy that we won this year. MURAO Sanshiro (JPN)

What an incredible celebration of judo it’s been at the World Judo Championships, thank you for watching.

World.title: Shakira sets Amazon Music record in Madrid with most-watched live stream by a female artist
World.content:
The global broadcast of Shakira's concert in Madrid has become the most-watched live performance by a female artist on Amazon Music, according to Claire Imoucha, head of Amazon Music in Spain, speaking in an interview with 'RTVE'.

 

The broadcast allowed viewers to follow the show for free from different countries via Amazon Music, Prime Video and Twitch. The performance, held on 3 October, marked a milestone in the Colombian singer's career, as it was the first time one of her full concerts was streamed live worldwide.

The production, coordinated over several months between the artist's team, the promoter and Amazon Music, deployed some twenty cameras, drones and even a helicopter to bring the show to millions of viewers.

"Madrid has become the epicentre of Latin music, the bridge between Latin America and Europe," Imoucha said, defending the choice of the Spanish capital because of Shakira's prominence in the country and the scale of her music residency. The Amazon Music executive added that Latin and Spanish-language music already accounts for 65% of digital consumption in Spain, a share which, she said, continues to grow.

Shakira and music residencies in Madrid

The performance is part of the Madrid residency of the "Las Mujeres Ya No Lloran World Tour", linked to ES Latina, which has seen the singer give several concerts in the capital since September. The initiative adds to the presence of other major Latin artists in Madrid and strengthens the city's drive to host international-scale shows.

Amazon Music also has extensive experience with major music broadcasts: it has spent more than five years streaming the Primavera Sound festival in Barcelona live to audiences around the world.

World.title: Antarctic penguins emit up to 7 million tonnes of methane a year, study finds
World.content:
Large colonies of chinstrap penguins in Antarctica are a significant natural source of methane, a greenhouse gas whose impact on global warming is greater than that of carbon dioxide (CO₂).

 

This has been demonstrated for the first time by a study carried out by the Institute of Marine Sciences of Andalusia (ICMAN), a research centre of the Spanish National Research Council (CSIC), in collaboration with the University of Granada.

The research, published (source in Spanish) in the journal 'Climate and Atmospheric Science', estimates that the guano produced by these birds generates around 490,000 tonnes of methane a year. This amount is comparable to emissions from other recognised natural sources, such as all the world's coastal ocean areas.

Until now, most studies on methane emissions have focused on human activities such as the use of fossil fuels, agriculture and waste management, as well as on domesticated animals. However, large concentrations of wildlife can also generate emissions through the accumulation and decomposition of organic matter.

"The guano that builds up in these bird colonies, which can bring together tens of thousands of individuals, creates extraordinarily intense methane emission hotspots that until now had never been measured or quantified in situ," explains Alejandro Román, a researcher at ICMAN-CSIC and lead author of the study, quoted in a press release (source in Spanish).

To obtain these results, the team carried out direct gas measurements in two large penguin colonies on Deception Island, in the South Shetland Islands archipelago. It also used drones equipped with optical sensors to map the surfaces covered in guano and to estimate the size of the populations.

If the calculation is extended to all Antarctic land areas influenced by these birds, emissions could reach millions of tonnes. "They could amount to around 7 million tonnes of methane per year, a figure of the same order of magnitude as global estimates for other major methane sources associated with animal activity, such as termites," says Emma Huertas, principal investigator of the DICHOSO project, together with Antonio Tovar.

The authors believe that this phenomenon should be included in global emissions inventories and underline the need to study how climate change could alter it by affecting both penguin populations and the soil microorganisms that produce methane as the guano breaks down.

World.title: French Social democratic primary: Raphaël Glucksmann wins big in first round
World.content:
One round was enough. French MEP Raphaël Glucksmann has won the primary of the French social-democratic camp, taking 66.17% of the vote in the first round of a contest that drew 120,787 voters, the organisers announced.

 

The leader of the Place publique party is far ahead of Socialist Party chief Olivier Faure, who secured 14% of the vote. Ségolène Royal, a prominent Socialist figure and former presidential candidate in 2007, who had hoped to spring a surprise, finished third with less than 8% of the vote.

The two other candidates, Jérôme Guedj and Emmanuel Maurel, each took close to 6%.

A result that "says something powerful", according to the winner, who hailed, on X (source in French), "a left faithful to its values can unite, govern and win".

"We are not here to win a squabble on the left. We are here to win the presidential election: turn the page on Macronism, stop the far right and change lives", Raphaël Glucksmann added.

Turnout was a crucial issue in this primary, and with 86%, this strand of the left now hopes to build momentum.

Disrupted by a cyberattack that slowed down voting, the primary, which began on Friday morning, was extended until 6 p.m. on Sunday.

Speaking to Euronews on the second day of the primary, political journalist and left-wing specialist Rachel Garrat-Valcarcel, author of the "Blocs & Partis" newsletter, said a turnout of "at least 80%" would be needed for the primary to be considered a success.

Other political forces are already firmly in the race, notably the far right with Marine Le Pen and the radical left with Jean-Luc Mélenchon.

Although not invited to take part in the primary, the latter nevertheless remained at the heart of the televised debates that preceded this weekend's vote, amid discussions over an alliance with La France insoumise in the legislative elections and disagreements about possible support for the LFI candidate in the second round, should the centre-left fail to reach it.
