World.title: Eerik-Niiles Kross: The true impact of Trump and Putin's diesel deal
World.content:
The agreement's economic impact will likely be minimal, while its moral and political consequences could be far more lasting and extremely damaging to the U.S. in the long run, writes Eerik-Niiles Kross.

Under an alleged diesel deal reached by phone between U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian leader Vladimir Putin, Russia is expected to supply the global market with an initial 300,000 metric tons of diesel fuel, followed by another 500,000 metric tons in November, then 1 million metric tons and, later, another 3 million metric tons "if possible." A total of 4.8 million metric tons of diesel has been promised.

At first glance, this seems like a large quantity. However, the actual impact depends on how quickly the fuel can be delivered and how much of it represents genuinely additional supply to the global market.

The U.S. consumes approximately 16 million metric tons of diesel per month, most of it domestically produced. The first promised shipment of 300,000 metric tons therefore represents less than 2 percent of one month's U.S. consumption. The 500,000 metric tons promised for November amounts to about 3 percent.

The entire promised 4.8 million metric tons would equal roughly 30 percent of one month's U.S. consumption, but no deadline has been set for its delivery and much of it may never reach the U.S. at all. If those 4.8 million metric tons were indeed delivered to the U.S. over the course of a year, for example, that would amount to 400,000 metric tons per month or 2.5 percent of U.S. consumption. It is ridiculous to assume that this could actually affect fuel prices in the U.S.

Still less is this a quantity that could fundamentally reshape the global fuel market over the longer term.

Another important consideration is that the diesel promised by Russia may not be — and most likely is not — newly produced fuel. At least some of it has already been produced and is sitting in storage facilities or export pipelines. Bringing this fuel to market could temporarily increase supply. However, if Russia simply sells fuel originally intended for existing customers to new buyers instead, total global supply will not increase at all.

Meanwhile, Trump's main objective in reaching the agreement, at least according to his own statements, is to lower fuel prices. The conclusion must be that Trump either hopes releasing Russian diesel onto the market will have a psychological effect and influence markets, intends to further ease sanctions on Russian oil exports or has simply allowed the Russians to pull the wool over his eyes. All three possibilities are rather depressing.

Agreement far more significant for Putin

Russia produced approximately 85 million metric tons of diesel in 2025, of which around 61 million metric tons was summer-grade diesel. Successful Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have significantly reduced production in 2026. At the same time, the Russians are facing a familiar seasonal problem: Winter always catches Russia by surprise. In winter, northern regions need cold-resistant diesel, but refineries that have been damaged and require repairs are unable to switch production quickly enough, if at all.

As a result, Russia may simultaneously face a surplus of summer-grade diesel and a shortage of winter-grade diesel. The summer-grade fuel must either be exported or stored. Once storage tanks are full, refineries have to cut production, further worsening Russia's fuel supply situation.

Putin therefore stands to gain considerably more from this deal than the relatively insignificant increase in export volumes might suggest. The temporary easing of U.S. sanctions allows Russia to sell fuel that would otherwise occupy storage capacity, leaving nowhere to put newly produced fuel. Refineries can now continue operating, generating additional export revenue.

Whether the Russians can actually deliver the promised quantities is another matter. According to various estimates, Russia exported approximately 27 million to 40 million metric tons of diesel in 2025. In the third quarter of 2026, seaborne exports had fallen to around 190,000 barrels (this may be an optimistic estimate from our perspective and does not appear to be based on complete statistics, but no better figures are currently available) or 26,000 metric tons, per day. That represents an 80 percent decline from the beginning of the year.

Thus, delivering the first 300,000 metric tons should not pose an insurmountable problem, provided sufficient stocks are available. The 500,000 metric tons promised for November is also feasible in principle.

However, exporting the entire promised 4.8 million metric tons at the current rate would take approximately six months. Even that assumes Russia diverts all its existing export volumes to the U.S. to fulfill the agreement. If Russia wanted to deliver those quantities in two months, for example, exports would have to roughly triple from their current level. That should be impossible, at least without restoring refinery capacity, particularly assuming Ukrainian attacks continue.

Trump can, of course, announce that he has brought millions of metric tons of additional fuel onto the global market and taken steps to lower prices. As we saw, his post to that effect on Friday drove oil prices down by more than 4 percent.

An actual, sustained decline in prices, however, requires that the promised fuel actually reach the market and that the shipments represent additional global supply rather than simply a redirection of existing exports — for example, diesel going to the U.S. instead of Brazil. A one-off shipment could affect prices for days, perhaps weeks, but it certainly would not resolve a longer-term shortage. Ultimately, I do not see the price decline Trump is hoping for materializing either in the U.S. or on the global market.

The most important effect of the agreement is political and psychological

The biggest weakness of the diesel deal is its striking asymmetry. As usual, the Russians have already gotten what they wanted, while the U.S. has received promises that are unlikely to be fulfilled. So far, Russia has had to do essentially nothing that was not already in its own interests. On the contrary, Russia has effectively received U.S. approval to continue destroying Ukraine's infrastructure.

The U.S. Treasury Department has already issued a sanctions exemption allowing transactions involving Russian diesel fuel until April 7, 2027. The exemption is not conditional on the promised deliveries actually taking place and contains no quantitative limit. This means Russia is already benefiting from sanctions relief, regardless of whether Putin can or even intends to deliver the 4.8 million metric tons of diesel promised to Trump.

Russia's contribution to the deal consists of a promise to sell its diesel fuel. Not to give it away, not to provide it as humanitarian aid, but to sell fuel on the global market that Russia itself has a vital interest in exporting. Putin has gained an opportunity to earn additional revenue and mitigate the impact of Ukrainian attacks on Russia's oil industry.

Russia has made no known reciprocal commitment to stop attacking Ukraine's energy infrastructure, scale back military operations or make concessions in peace negotiations. Instead, Trump has pressured, if not outright threatened, Ukraine to stop attacking Russian oil infrastructure.

The moral problem with the agreement is colossal. For years, Western countries have sought to restrict Russia's energy revenues in order to reduce its ability to wage its war of aggression against Ukraine — yes, sometimes hypocritically, but they have made the effort nonetheless.

Europe and the U.S. have largely been united on this issue. Now the U.S. president is opening up a new opportunity for the Russians to sell fuel and presenting it as a step that serves the interests of the global economy and American consumers. At the same time, he has previously threatened third countries that buy Russian petroleum products with sanctions — India, for example, as recently as a short while ago — and Congress has just passed the so-called Lindsey Graham bill, which would make it possible to impose effective sanctions on Russia.

Trump's deal stands in stark contradiction to all of this. The Russians are being rewarded for destroying Ukraine's infrastructure with an opportunity to earn additional revenue and portray themselves as the saviors of the global energy market.

For Putin, this is an important political and psychological victory in any case. He can demonstrate both to his domestic audience and internationally that the policy of isolating Russia is unsustainable and that even the U.S. needs Russia's help. What is more, Russia has achieved this outcome without making a single concession in Ukraine. I would call that a 4-0 victory for Putin...

For Ukraine, the message is particularly damaging. Ukraine has taken enormous risks to damage Russia's refining industry and thereby weaken the aggressor's economic and military capabilities. It is depressing to recall the damage Ukraine itself suffers every day in this context. And now our principal ally is helping to alleviate, at least in part, the economic consequences of precisely those attacks that have so far been one of Ukraine's main tools for putting pressure on the Russians. Meanwhile, the Russians continue attacking Ukraine's power plants, heating systems and energy infrastructure and murdering civilians.

You can bet that Russia will use the promised diesel deliveries as a tool of political pressure. If Trump starts linking lower American fuel prices to the operational capacity of Russian refineries, Putin will say Ukraine is to blame and that Trump should make the Ukrainians stop attacking them. Trump already seems to be following this logic — or, more accurately, this absurdity. The result is a situation in which the aggressor continues destroying Ukraine's energy infrastructure while Ukraine is pressured to abandon attacks on the aggressor's energy infrastructure.

The agreement also creates problems for relations between Europe and the U.S. The European Union has sought to reduce its dependence on Russian energy and restrict the revenues flowing into Russia's war economy. The U.S., and Trump in particular, has spent years lecturing Europe for continuing to buy Russian petroleum products. Now he is blatantly disregarding all of that.

The U.S. sanctions exemption does not, of course, invalidate European sanctions, but it makes maintaining a common sanctions policy more difficult. Operating Russia's shadow fleet will become cheaper, insurance companies may begin insuring tankers carrying Russian cargo again and so on. All of this has implications extending well beyond diesel.

European companies must continue complying with EU restrictions while the Americans allow the Russians back into the market. It is reasonable to expect European oil companies to start pressuring their governments to make similar concessions.

U.S. credibility has taken a serious blow in both Europe and Ukraine. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has already criticized the deal, understandably and as the only possible response. The only people in Europe who might be celebrating are Putinist right-wing forces such as the AfD.

Against this backdrop, the economic benefits of the agreement for the U.S. are uncertain, to put it mildly. Its impact on U.S. gasoline prices is even more indirect than its impact on diesel prices and is likely nonexistent. Russia, meanwhile, gains an opportunity to expand its customer base, reduce the discounts it offers, earn export revenue and ease storage problems at its refineries. Fortunately, this deal will not resolve Russia's own shortage of winter-grade diesel or restore production capacity damaged by Ukrainian attacks.

So there we have it. Trump gets to promise cheaper fuel, which will not actually help him, while Putin has already secured tangible sanctions relief.

There is probably a longer backstory to all of this. According to an October 10 report in the Financial Times, U.S. representatives Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner warned Ukrainian negotiators in Miami that Washington could restrict intelligence sharing if Ukraine did not stop attacking Russian oil infrastructure. The Ukrainian delegation cut its visit short. In other words, the U.S. is threatening to end the last significant form of assistance it still provides Ukraine while simultaneously providing direct assistance to the aggressor.

The agreement's economic impact will be modest at best and probably minimal. Its moral and political consequences could be far more lasting and extremely damaging to the U.S. in the long run. It undermines the credibility of sanctions, puts Ukraine under pressure and deepens divisions between Europe and the U.S.

Ultimately, this is another Sputnik-style spin operation. During the coronavirus pandemic, Putin marketed a vaccine around the world that did not work and that Russia was unable to produce in sufficient quantities, creating the impression that Russia was coming to the rescue of those in need. Now, in a single stroke, he has eased his export difficulties, demonstrated that Western sanctions do not hold up and dealt a blow to America's reputation.

World.title: Foreign online studies not enough to meet Estonia's compulsory education requirement
World.content:
Children under 18 living in Estonia must attend an Estonian school to fulfill compulsory education requirements, even if they are enrolled in a foreign online school, the Ministry of Education has said.

At an information seminar for local governments and schools, the Ministry of Education announced that all children under the age of 18 who have moved to Estonia, with certain exceptions, must fulfill their compulsory education requirement at an Estonian school. Attending online classes at a foreign school does not exempt them from this obligation.

The Tartu city government's education department asked the ministry which legal provision the requirement was based on as the Education Act does not explicitly establish such a rule.

Marika Peekmann, a senior expert at the Ministry of Education, said the requirement stems from the combined provisions of the Education Act and the Basic Schools and Upper Secondary Schools Act.

"The law does not provide for the possibility of considering the compulsory education requirement fulfilled for a person residing in Estonia solely on the basis of enrollment in a foreign educational institution. This is also supported by the objectives of the compulsory education reform, the obligation of local governments to monitor compliance with compulsory education requirements under the law and so on," Peekmann said.

She added that accepting enrollment in a foreign school as fulfilling the compulsory education requirement for children living in Estonia would raise the question of why the law links compulsory education to residence in Estonia in the first place.

"The central idea of the compulsory education reform is that local governments monitor and ensure the education of young people living in Estonia. If enrollment in a foreign school or participation in an online school were sufficient, local governments would have no real way of verifying whether a student is actually studying, how much they are studying, whether the instruction meets the required educational standards or whether their studies are continuing without interruption," the senior expert said.

According to Peekmann, this would create a gray area in which compulsory education requirements would formally be met, but the state would have no real overview of a young person's educational progress.

"The Estonian state cannot automatically assess the legal status of a foreign school, the standard of its curriculum, how instruction is actually organized or whether learning outcomes are being achieved," she explained.

Peekmann said the problem is particularly acute in the case of foreign online or alternative educational institutions, as the state would have no clear basis for determining which forms of foreign education meet the objectives of compulsory education and which do not.

The ministry's senior expert said the aim of the compulsory education reform was not merely to ensure that young people receive some form of education, but also to reduce school dropout rates and the number of young people who are neither studying nor working.

"Achieving this objective requires students to be monitored within the Estonian education system, their educational progress to be recorded in the Estonian Education Information System (EHIS) and support measures to be made available when necessary. In most cases, this is not possible with foreign educational institutions," Peekmann noted.

Starting this academic year, the Ministry of Education extended compulsory education to the age of 18, meaning that students who complete basic school must continue their education at an upper secondary school, vocational school or in preparatory studies. The compulsory education requirement does not apply to the children of foreign diplomats.

World.title: President Alar Karis: Difficult to convey others' messages when you're sidelined
World.content:
Reflecting on his five years in office, President Alar Karis defends his decisions to veto legislation and his approach to foreign policy, arguing that the president should have a greater role in shaping Estonia's foreign policy.

Which decision do you consider the most important and influential for Estonian society during your presidency?

I believe that if you make decisions, they should all be important. A president doesn't deal with minor decisions, although some decisions may seem small and insignificant.

But the decisions that invariably cause controversy are those involving vetoes of legislation. Those are important decisions, sending a law back for reconsideration.

Looking back today, is there any decision or action where you feel you could have acted differently as president?

There may be several, but again, time comes into play here. Right now, it's difficult to say what I should have done differently. I've always believed that what you should regret isn't what you could have done differently, but what you've left undone. Those are the things that weigh more heavily on your conscience. If you ask me what those things are, I can't say.

What do you consider the greatest achievement of your presidency?

Again, we come back to the same point. We need a little time. We can see from previous presidents that it's only now that people are beginning to assess Lennart Meri's presidency more or less objectively.

And I expect that time will come for me as well. I believe in history and the value of history. I hope there will be journalists and historians capable of critically evaluating sources who won't judge a president solely on the headlines of the day, but will also be able to delve into the substance of the work.

I'd now like to explore some of the more significant issues or those that have attracted the most attention. To begin with, you've said yourself that you've declined to promulgate more laws than your predecessors. How do you assess your record in this area? Does that mean you've been particularly vocal in defending the Constitution?

I think all presidents defend the Constitution. The question is always what kinds of laws come before them. Laws differ from one period to another and ultimately it all comes down to the Constitution or, in fact, to the Riigikogu and the quality of its work.

Sometimes laws are drafted in great haste and certain things are simply overlooked. Sometimes the political desire to achieve something is so strong that the Constitution is forgotten. And that's what has led to all the decisions I've had to make.

But I don't consider it something to boast about, saying, look how many laws I've rejected. Rather, it's a cause for concern. And I've always emphasized that parliament, the Riigikogu, could do its job better and examine things more thoroughly. When a law is returned to the Riigikogu, it shouldn't look only at the specific provision I've drawn attention to as president, but at the law as a whole, to see whether it's really the best it can be. It's a second opportunity to review the legislation.

But very often that hasn't happened. The mistake is corrected and the law still turns out to be less than ideal. Because a president cannot reject a law simply because he doesn't like it or because it's very poorly drafted. There are limits and those limits are set by the Constitution.

With that in mind, let's look at the motor vehicle tax. How do you assess it in hindsight? You sent the law back, emphasizing its impact on a particularly vulnerable group in society. Ultimately, the law was adopted anyway. How do you view it today? Is it now a complete and satisfactory law or were the interests of some groups in society ultimately left unrepresented?

It's exactly as you say. People don't like laws that impose financial or other restrictions on them. But it's necessary to explain why a law is needed and that explanation probably wasn't as good as it could have been. Although the finance minister at the time even said to me, "Let the president come to me and I'll explain it to him."

But I convey what the people are saying and if people don't understand something, I say so. What was particularly interesting about this law was that I ultimately signed it, but it later emerged that the implementing regulations were unconstitutional, so the chancellor of justice had to draw attention to that.

So there are two aspects here: the law itself and how it's implemented. Both need to be thought through.

Another issue is the Churches and Congregations Act. You repeatedly declined to promulgate it and it eventually reached the Supreme Court. Was this the most fundamental confrontation with the Riigikogu during your presidency?

With very complicated laws like these, which stir up strong emotions, it's extremely difficult for a president to make a decision. The easy thing would be to let the law through and think politically, well, what are they up to here? But we already have laws today that allow us to arrest criminal elements and expel them from the country, as has been done. In principle, I wasn't opposed to preventing these people from operating here. Quite the opposite: they must not be allowed to operate here.

And the second element, which people probably don't fully understand, is that the legal and secular world is one thing, but the canonical world is another. Churches don't have borders in that world. Whether we're talking about Orthodox, Lutheran or Catholic churches, the ecclesiastical world operates in a different sphere. We can amend the law on churches and change their statutes, but those ties will remain. That has to be taken into account. They won't disappear.

That's why I repeatedly asked for the law to be reconsidered. And as you saw, when it reached the Supreme Court, quite a few judges there also expressed dissenting opinions. Now we've reached the European Court of Human Rights, which is actually something I warned about from the outset. I said, think through what the next steps will be and how this law is going to be implemented. I don't know how long the proceedings at the European Court of Human Rights will take, but they'll probably take quite some time.

So these are the things I've constantly tried to emphasize: think a couple of steps ahead. Don't rush to adopt legislation based on emotion!

Turning to your foreign policy during the final year of your presidency, it seems to me that this is perhaps the area that has attracted the most criticism. Looking back, how do you assess the claims that some of your messages were unclear to both the government and ordinary citizens? Would you do anything differently today?

I don't think so. Perhaps I should actually have spoken out a little more on the subject. I recently read that President Karis wasn't interested in foreign policy, which is an outright lie. I've visited more than 100 countries. Foreign policy can be conducted in very different ways and today, in a sense, if I can use that expression, people are barking up the wrong tree.

That's because the main responsibility, particularly in the context of the war in Ukraine, lies with the prime minister and the foreign minister. They're the ones who carry that responsibility because they attend NATO meetings and European Council meetings. The president only attends the UN and that's once a year. That's where he delivers his national address and gives interviews. I've also given interviews that have gone completely unnoticed in Estonia. One year, I gave six interviews, including to CNN and the BBC, and none of them received any coverage here.

To understand what the president does in foreign policy, it would be worthwhile for politicians and journalists alike to accompany him on visits. Very few have done so. As I said, I've made more than 100 visits. You could count on the fingers of one hand the occasions when a journalist or a member of the Riigikogu has accompanied me. Those who have done so understand that foreign policy can be conducted in very different ways.

And then there's soft diplomacy, which I've considered very important. It doesn't generate headlines, but its impact lasts considerably longer.

Or take the so-called Kazakhstan incident. When I ask what actually happened there, I don't get an answer because nothing happened. Quite the opposite. I went there with a specific objective: to help curb sanctions circumvention by securing a cooperation agreement for our Tax and Customs Board. They thanked me for that, as they did several other companies.

The fact that the president chooses where to say one thing or another is the president's choice. And there have been many instances where I've decided for myself what to say, whom to speak to and for how long. But the foreign policy framework has remained the same.

If some people have problems with reading comprehension or literacy, I can't help them. I can only recommend that they educate themselves a little and I hope they do. Even starting with something as simple as understanding that a sentence continues after a comma. That makes it easier to understand the meaning.

In light of that, have you developed any proposals or ideas about how this area should be changed or what should be done differently to prevent similar misunderstandings in the future?

Yes, certainly, and we've tried to address this and talk about it. Estonia's president doesn't participate in shaping foreign policy. To put it rather bluntly, the president is given instructions and told to carry them out! That's unlike other countries in our region where presidents participate in the process. And as a former scientist, I find it very difficult to convey other people's messages when I haven't been involved in the process myself or don't believe in what I'm saying.

The simplest example is Rail Baltica. Everywhere I go, I'm told that I have to say it will be completed by 2030. I said I couldn't say that because I know it won't be completed by 2030! And today we're in a situation where it won't be completed. But there's this pressure to demonstrate internationally how important it is! Why do we have to lie? Or convince ourselves that things are working?!

That's a simple example people might understand. Perhaps there's no point going into the finer nuances of foreign policy.

The other issue is that the president doesn't participate in NATO summits or European Council meetings. He could attend one of them and perhaps NATO would be the right choice. That would also create an opportunity for discussion. If the president attended NATO meetings, it would be possible to communicate better with the government and pass on the information he receives there. That's how it works in Finland, Latvia, Lithuania and elsewhere.

That's why it's very difficult to compare the Estonian president with other presidents, because their functions are completely different.

If we were to compare the Estonian president with someone, it could be German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier. He's served as foreign minister twice, but he doesn't exactly stand out in foreign policy today. You can't say he doesn't understand foreign policy, because his role is different. Germany has a chancellor.

Or take Italy. I doubt anyone on the street here even knows who the Italian president is. But he's a very important and well-loved president in Italy. It's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni who handles these matters there.

So people need to learn what the roles of the president, prime minister and foreign minister are in Estonia. And once that's clear, I think perceptions will change considerably.

But it's certainly worth discussing whether attending NATO summits could be one of the president's responsibilities. Then it would also make sense to give the National Defense Council a more substantial role, so there would be something to discuss and talk about.

Because at the moment, we exchange information and often it's information we both already know. We simply get together to issue a press release saying that discussions were held. Well, of course I'm exaggerating, that's understandable.

Finally, I heard an interesting statistic: over these five years, you've spent a month on airplanes...

...and another month in airports.

Is there anything else from your time in office that stands out in your memory, perhaps something enjoyable or another statistic you'd like to highlight from this period that's now coming to an end?

Well, I only heard that statistic myself yesterday. I'm not familiar enough with the data to pick out any other statistics. But just the fact that I've spent two months of my life on airplanes and in airports...

I've never been particularly good at using those moments to get work done. I need longer stretches of time and an environment where I can concentrate. I don't want to say those two months were wasted, but they certainly weren't used as effectively as they could have been.

But I'm sure there are more statistics to be found if someone wants to look for them.

What I tend to remember most, though, are the happy moments. The occasions when I've presented state decorations have always been moving, seeing the emotions people experience. It's so wonderful to watch, all that surprise. It's genuine.

I received my first state decoration in 2007, I think. And that was a very special occasion, knowing that your work had been recognized.

And I think every president would like to award even more decorations. At one point, one president awarded nearly a thousand. But we don't want to devalue the decorations either, so it's better to keep the number limited.

Then again, every president decides how many to award. Those are the kinds of positive moments I remember. And you can find statistics there too, on how many decorations have been awarded.

World.title: Prime minister slams US-Russia diesel pact: Deals with dictators 'road to hell'
World.content:
Prime Minister Kristen Michal has sharply criticized the US decision to strike a diesel deal with Russia, saying agreements with dictators lead to hell.

Trump said Friday that Russia had agreed to bring 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the world market immediately, with more to follow, under a temporary US licence.

Ahead of next month's midterm elections, US President Donald Trump has struck a deal with Vladimir Putin for Russia to supply millions of tonnes of diesel to the world market, a move Trump said was essential to bring down fuel prices.

The US issued a temporary license for Russian diesel supplies to the world market, valid until April 7 next year.

"This is a major miscalculation, because deals with dictators are the road to hell. Innocent people are being killed for gas and fuel money. And what is very likely is that the hoped-for fuel will not come," the prime minister noted on social media.

"Such an agreement runs counter to the Western world's long-standing efforts to limit the flow of money from energy carriers to [Vladimir] Putin. The US has until now persuaded its allies to abandon Russian fuel — we have too," Michal said.

According to him, the long-term line of cutting Russia off from money is correct and must continue.

"It is worth discussing in Estonia and at the European Council next week whether we can quickly contribute more to Ukraine so they can blast Russia's oil refineries to smithereens," Michal added.

Reform MP: Trump is thinking about the midterms

MP Marko Mihkelson (Reform), chair of the Riigikogu Foreign Affairs Committee, earlier said he believes the upcoming midterm elections prompted Trump's diesel agreement with Russia, but at the same time, Russia will draw encouragement from the deal to continue its war in Ukraine.

Marko Mihkelson. Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

"The Trump administration is on its back domestically over its moves and is trying to do everything to avoid a major Republican defeat in the midterm elections less than a month away," Mihkelson wrote on his social media account.

He said the hope of reducing diesel prices at US pumps with Russia's help is short-sighted and carries a much higher strategic cost for the United States.

"At the same time as the Graham sanctions bill approved in Congress would give the president the opportunity to increase economic pressure on Russia, the White House is instead lowering pressure on Russia and demanding that Ukraine stop attacking refineries," the MP went on.

"If it is true that this was accompanied by a Washington threat to Kyiv to stop sharing intelligence if the attacks continue, then this gives Moscow only one unambiguous signal — kill and destroy Ukraine, the US will not stand in the way," he added.

Mihkelson said Trump's efforts to end the war through negotiations have produced not the slightest result.

"The fighting is bloodier than at any previous moment in the entire full-scale invasion," he said. "If you give an aggressor oxygen, the war will not stop."

He stressed that Europe's allies have only one path — to ensure Russia's strategic attack goals fail and the Kremlin's imperial wars end in defeat.

"This clear strategic goal should also be in the US interest, because Russia's long-standing desire, together with China and Iran, to weaken the United States' leadership role is reaching a decisive phase," Mihkelson continued.

Ahead of next month's midterm elections, U.S. President Donald Trump has struck a deal with Vladimir Putin for Russia to supply millions of tonnes of diesel to the world market, reversing years of Western pressure on the Kremlin. Trump said the move was essential to bring down fuel prices, which have soared since Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and warned of a diesel export ban on any EU states that do not release reserves to counter the spike. The G7 agreed earlier this week to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from reserves.

MEP: The important thing is to keep that fuel from reaching Europe

Member of the European Parliament Riho Terras (Isamaa) said Trump's deal with Russia looks like a betrayal, sending a negative message to both Ukraine and Europe.

"I would hope this will lead European allies to realize even more clearly the need to support Ukraine and try to close the loopholes in their own sanctions, so that even if this fuel reaches America, it won't find its way into Europe through the back door. I think this could mobilize Europeans to provide even more support for Ukraine because that's the only option," he said.

Terras added that Trump's actions are unpredictable and may not benefit him.

"The deal struck with Putin is a win-win for Putin. He came out ahead both economically and politically. He demonstrated to the world that Putin is needed to save the global economy. That's actually absurd," Terras said.

Kallas: US-Russia diesel agreement helping to fund Kremlin's war of aggression

An agreement between the United States and Russia to lift sanctions on Russian diesel fuel provides Moscow with "more revenue to wage the war," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Saturday. Kallas added that Russian attacks have caused the death of more than 80 Ukrainian civilians in two days and that Moscow has "intensified its hybrid attacks against Europe, both against EU member states and NATO allies."

Russian strikes killed over 80 Ukrainian civilians in two days. Moreover, it has stepped up its hybrid attacks against Europe, both EU Member States and NATO Allies. Suspending sanctions on Russian diesel provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war. This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't. On Monday, EU Foreign Ministers intend to approve the biggest set of sanctions listings targeting Russia's war machine since the start of the war. — Kaja Kallas (@kajakallas) October 10, 2026

"Suspending sanctions on Russian diesel provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war. This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't. ," she wrote.

World.title: Estonian Artists' Association's charity auction brings in record-breaking €2.3 million
World.content:
The Estonian Artists' Association (EKL) charity auction concluded with total sales of €2.3 million, the highest amount ever recorded for a single art auction in Estonia.

A total of 159 works were sold, representing 98 percent of the 162 works put up for auction.

Thanks to the auction, the association will be able to repay the losses incurred through a fraud scheme ahead of schedule, while all remaining proceeds will go toward supporting Estonian artists and the country's art scene, EKL said.

According to EKL President Maarin Ektermann, the auction's results exceeded all expectations.

"When planning the auction, we didn't dare hope it would cover the entire €700,000 loss, as art auctions are unpredictable. That's why we cut the association's expenses and looked for other ways to free ourselves from the debt burden. But thanks to the people who decided to purchase treasures from the art collection and donated works, showing such strong support for the artists and the association, we can now repay our obligations ahead of schedule and develop plans for how best to support our members and Estonia's art scene," Ektermann said.

The partial sale of the art collection was an exceptional step that could only be taken once in this form.

"We knew from the outset that this was a one-time decision. That's why it was important to us to organize a public auction where everyone would have an opportunity to acquire works from the collection, with starting prices as low as €100," Ektermann said. "Together with experts, we selected the works very carefully to preserve the integrity of the collection. Far fewer works went to auction than we had originally planned, which made the result all the more surprising."

Jaanus Samma, who coordinated the artists' donations, said the artists who donated their works to the auction deserve special thanks.

"Not all the works could even be included in the auction and those remaining will be offered for sale at a separate exhibition in EKL's galleries at the end of the year," Samma said.

Historic records

The auction raised €23,500 on the first day and €786,400 on the second, while 80 works from the third day's selection of paintings, sculptures and applied art sold for a total of €1.5 million.

On Saturday, Tiit Pääsuke's "Lapi kakk" fetched the highest price of the day at €185,000.

The highest hammer price of the entire auction went to Jaan Elken's painting "Juhikabiin," which sold for €205,000. This is the highest price ever paid at auction for a work by a living Estonian artist.

Ludmilla Siim's "Rõdu" set a new auction record for a work by an Estonian female artist, selling for €150,000. Olev Subbi's "Keskpäev" sold for the same amount, setting a new auction record for the artist.

Art market expert Tiina Määrmann said she was particularly pleased that the works' art historical significance was positively correlated with their market value.

Where will the proceeds go?

The auction proceeds will primarily go toward covering losses incurred as a result of the fraud scheme in the spring, including repaying a loan. A portion of the proceeds will also be paid to artists: the creators of works sold from the association's art collection or their heirs will receive 5 percent of the hammer price, while artists who recently donated works will receive 15 percent.

"Although the resale royalty rate under the Copyright Act drops to 3 percent for more expensive works, we will pay the creators of works sold from our art collection 5 percent regardless of the hammer price," Ektermann said.

The association will use the remaining proceeds in accordance with its statutes, which stipulate that EKL's mission is to support Estonian artists and the country's art scene. The management board will submit proposals on how to use the funds to the association's council and some of the money will be allocated to developing the art collection and making it more accessible to the public.

"We want decisions to be made openly and together with our members. We hope to present more detailed plans at the extraordinary general assembly on November 16," Ektermann said.

The Estonian Artists' Association, in cooperation with Eesti Kunstioksjonid OÜ, held an extraordinary art auction from October 8 to 10, offering 162 works from the association's collection and recent donations by artists. The selection ranged from paintings and graphic art to photographs, sculptural objects and textile art. The association selected the works together with an expert committee comprising art historians, critics and art market specialists.

The association organized the auction to cover losses caused by financial fraud. On May 15, 2026, the association discovered that nearly €700,000 had been transferred out of its bank accounts as part of a criminal scheme.

World.title: Vegan powerlifter says diet change solved his health problems
World.content:
Koovit, who grew up with six brothers and a sister, all fed on good countryside fare, said his wife suggested make the change. He now eats 180–240 grams of protein a day, but plant-derived, something which is viable nowadays without getting boared.

"There were six boys and one girl of us. We usually went through eight liters of milk a day, and everything else that goes with it," he said.

"I'm fully vegan, but that doesn't mean I only eat onions and potatoes. AS I'm a powerlifter, I need to be heavy. There's a very wide choice of vegan food. My daily protein intake is between 180 and 240 grams. On top of that comes about three times as much in carbohydrates — oatmeal, rice, potato and the rest. For me it's very important to get a lot of energy from food and for my weight number to be high," Koovit said.

His wife had been vegan for longer. "I reached a point in my sport where my joints started hurting and I felt I'd taken my body so far that if I pushed a little more, health problems would start. That was nine years ago. My wife then very cleverly suggested I try vegan products. When I get stuck with something, my dear wife comes up with a solution — without her I probably wouldn't be here," Koovit explained.

Pretty much every foodstuff has a vegan alternative, he noted. "In my case, it was that after four days of eating vegan food, I realized there was no way back, as I felt so good. For an athlete, the best thing is that the recovery becomes faster."

Koovit recalled that at the time he was living in London, and in the club where he trained he was one of the smallest men. "I was a little squirt there. As things started going so well for me, and I started setting Estonian records and winning medals, burly men who I'd been afraid even to talk to at first started asking me what I was doing to do so well. One after another they started trying vegan food too."

Meat dishes tend to be highly acidic and can cause inflammation in the body, he says. "When heavy training is added to that, more and more inflammation builds up in the body. Eventually the body can't cope with it anymore — that's why more and more athletes in the sports world have been finding vegan food," went on.

"Eating vegan food is very contagious, because you feel good and get the feeling that you'd like to try more. After eating, you don't get a heavy feeling. In sporting terms, that's the charm of it — since I can eat more often, I feed my muscles and cells more often. There are more nutrients, and through that recovery is faster too," Koovit said. "Protein can be obtained from vegan food in concentrated form."

The annual Veganmess food festival takes place in Tallinn this weekend.

World.title: Iraq’s non-oil revenues hit 8.7 trillion Iraqi dinars by July 2026
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s General Commission for Federal Revenues Allocation revealed on Sunday that non-oil revenues reached approximately 8.7 trillion Iraqi dinars (approximately $5.74 billion) by July 2026, compared to about seven trillion Iraqi dinars (around $4.62 billion) during the same period in 2025.

Iraq’s non-oil revenues rose by 1.7 trillion Iraqi dinars (about $1.12 billion) and at a growth rate of 23.5 percent, according to the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA).

These revenues accounted for approximately 22 percent of total federal revenues for the same period.

The Iraqi Ministry of Finance said last week that the country’s total revenues reached approximately 39.09 trillion Iraqi dinars (nearly $30 billion) until the end of July 2026, with oil revenues accounting for about 78 percent of total state resources.

During the first seven months of 2026, Iraq’s total government spending reached 65.42 trillion Iraqi dinars (approximately $43.21 billion).

This massive expenditure, combined with a sharp decline in oil revenues due to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, left a major budget deficit of 26.3 trillion ($17.37 billion) to 29.2 trillion Iraqi dinars ($19.28 billion) for the January–July period.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank project a severe economic contraction for Iraq in 2026, largely due to prolonged disruptions to oil production and export logistics caused by regional conflicts and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

However, the two international institutions expect a robust economic rebound in 2027 as energy markets stabilize and trade flows normalize.

World.title: Iraqis submit over 10,000 weapon registration requests within week
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi Ministry of Interior revealed on Sunday that it received over 10,000 applications from Iraqis requesting to register their firearms during the first week of October.

The step is part of a statewide push to put all armaments under state control.

According to Mohammed Ali al-Hassoun, the ministry’s spokesperson, residents in Baghdad and other provinces submitted 10,222 applications between October 2 and 9.

According to officials, the move demonstrates rising public awareness of the need to limit gun ownership.

Unlicensed guns are often used in tribal confrontations and personal revenge attacks throughout Iraq, weakening the state’s authority over the use of force.

The Iraqi government has initiated a mission to seize all firearms held by tribes and armed organizations. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has set June 2027 as a deadline for militias to submit their weapons.

Al-Hassoun said that the ministry maintains its efforts to regulate weapons possession and improve security across Iraqi provinces. He added that the ministry is expediting weapon registration procedures.

The Undersecretary of the Ministry of Interior, Hussein al-Awadi, said in September that the government is proceeding with the decision to restrict the possession of weapons exclusively to security forces.

Al-Awadi noted that Iraqi authorities intend to collect up to six million weapons in the coming months.

World.title: Iraq attends Riyadh energy summit as Saudi minister declares city ‘capital of energy security’
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq attended the 17th International Energy Forum Ministerial Meeting (IEF17) in Riyadh on Sunday, despite fatal strikes on the Saudi capital’s airport, where top energy officials discussed global energy security, oil market stability, and investment.

Iraq’s Oil Minister, Basim Mohammed Khudair, attended the event, which brought together ministers, business executives, and officials from international organizations under the topic “Energy Security and Shared Goals in a New Era.”

The conference went forward despite bombings on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, which Saudi officials blamed on Yemen’s Houthi militia.

The violence heightened security fears in the monarchy, which was hosting key foreign energy executives.

Opening the conference, Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman presented a message of resilience, stating that the country would continue to meet its energy promises despite the problems it confronts.

“No one can break our resolve, for we are like the phoenix, always rising from the ashes,” Prince Abdulaziz declared, according to an English translation of his Arabic comments.

“We value our commitments and strive to honor them no matter the circumstances,” he continued, referring to Saudi Arabia and its capital as the “capital of energy security.”

The Minister also cited Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, which distributes crude oil to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, as an example of infrastructure built to ensure energy supplies when regular shipping routes are disrupted.

The problem is especially important to Iraq, one of OPEC’s biggest oil producers, which depends significantly on exports via the Arabian Gulf and has been looking into alternate pipeline routes via Turkey and even Syria.

Iraq’s involvement comes as the country strives to enhance ties with Saudi Arabia and other regional partners in energy investment, infrastructure, and economic growth.

Saudi Arabia, Italy, and Nigeria convened the ministerial conference, which focused on ensuring stable energy supplies, robust infrastructure, diversifying supply chains, and strengthening communication between producing and consuming nations.

Participants expressed solidarity and support with Saudi Arabia after assaults on civilian infrastructure, and the conference welcomed news that the United States will rejoin the International Energy Forum.

The gathering also discussed investments in oil and gas production, refining, transportation networks, and future energy technologies, as well as initiatives to promote market transparency and international collaboration.

World.title: Iraq discusses oil and gas projects with TotalEnergies, ConocoPhillips
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi highlighted on Sunday the importance of recovering associated gas, given Iraq’s significant potential in this sector.

Al-Zaidi’s remarks took place during his meeting in Baghdad with Chairman and CEO of TotalEnergies, Patrick Pouyanne, and President of ConocoPhilips, Andy O’Brien, according to a statement released by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO).

The meeting addressed strategies for developing oil and associated gas resources at the Bin Umar field in the southern province of Basra. Additionally, they discussed establishing a timeline for increasing oil and gas production from this field and enhancing output at other fields.

Al-Zaidi outlined the government’s plans to fully utilize the country’s gas resources and permanently stop gas imports within the next few years.

Pouyanne and O’Brien expressed their willingness to increase efforts to meet the established timelines for increasing production rates.

The Bin Umar field stands as one of southern Iraq’s most promising oil and gas reservoirs. The Iraqi government seeks to develop the field in partnership with a French-American consortium, an important step to stop gas flaring and achieve energy self-sufficiency.

TotalEnergies is already spearheading the massive “Integrated Gas Growth Project” in southern Iraq, an initiative focused on gas investment and solar power generation.

As a prominent US investment entity, ConocoPhillips is set to develop strategic fields and modernize them with cutting-edge technology.

Former Prime Minister Mohammed Shia al-Sudani said in June 2024 that associated gas recovery in Iraq had risen to over 60 percent, with the ultimate goal of completely ending gas flaring by 2028.

World.title: Iraq PM plans Saudi Arabia and Kuwait visits
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Falih Al-Zaidi is predicted to visit Saudi Arabia and Kuwait this week for talks on regional security, oil export routes, and long-standing bilateral disputes, according to Iraqi government sources, as escalating attacks on Saudi Arabia raise regional tensions.

The scheduled visit follows a horrific strike on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Saturday, which killed at least 12 people and wounded over 300.

The international airport was attacked again on Sunday, with Yemen’s Houthi movement claiming responsibility.

Iraq condemned the Houthi strikes on Sunday, expressing support for Saudi Arabia and warning that attacks on civilians and infrastructure endanger regional security and stability.

According to Sabah al-Numan, spokesman for the Commander-in-Chief of the Iraqi Armed Forces, Baghdad rejects further military escalation and instead advocates for an end to hostilities, civilian protection, and a stronger emphasis on discourse to address regional issues.

The worsening security situation has created concerns regarding travel plans, however no official notification has been made that al-Zaidi’s visit has been postponed.

Security cooperation is anticipated to be a major focus in Riyadh, where the Iraqi prime minister will likely address regional de-escalation, particularly the situation in Yemen, as well as attempts to avoid attacks on neighboring nations.

According to a government source reported by Shafaq News, Al-Zaidi is anticipated to underline Iraq’s condemnation of strikes conducted from its territory against Gulf nations, as well as its determination to hold those guilty accountable.

Relations between Baghdad and Riyadh have strained recently, with Saudis claiming that drones fired from Iraqi territory attacked its East-West oil pipeline in September.

The visit will also discuss the possibility of reactivating the long-idle Iraqi-Saudi oil pipeline, which would provide Baghdad with an alternate export route to the Red Sea.

The roughly 1,568-kilometer pipeline was constructed in the 1980s to transport Iraqi oil from the Al-Zubair district of Basra through Saudi Arabia to the Red Sea export terminals at Yanbu.

It discontinued operations in 1990 when Iraq invaded Kuwait, and Saudi Arabia subsequently reused parts of the infrastructure on their territory.

Reviving the route has become more important as the prolonged regional conflict delays shipping across the Strait of Hormuz, exposing Iraq’s dependency on southern oil export ports in the Arabian Gulf.

Al-Zaidi is next slated to go to Kuwait, where discussions would center on maritime boundary delineation, transportation via the Khor Abdullah waterway, and Iraq’s water rights.

The planned Gulf travel follows the cancelation of a previous Saudi visit in July due to increased military tensions between Iraq and Saudi Arabia.

World.title: TotalEnergies CEO visits Baghdad to meet Iraq PM for oil and gas investment talks
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – TotalEnergies CEO Patrick Pouyanné met with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi in Baghdad on Sunday to discuss growing oil and gas output, as Iraq attempts to improve its energy economy despite impediments to shipments via the Strait of Hormuz caused by the continuing regional conflict.

Pouyanné was joined by ConocoPhillips CEO Andy O’Brien and accompanying delegations for negotiations about investment in Basra’s Bin Umar oilfield, which includes plans to expand crude output and collect associated gas.

According to the Prime Minister’s Office, the conference discussed investment methods and deadlines for increasing production at Bin Umar, as well as prospects to boost output at other Iraqi oilfields.

Al-Zaidi emphasized the necessity of growing Iraq’s associated gas resources, stating the government’s goal of eliminating gas imports in the future years by increasing local production and making better use of gas that is now wasted via flaring.

Despite the lack of fresh investment estimates or strict deadlines, firm leaders stated a desire to speed work and reach production objectives.

The high-level conference comes at a crucial moment for Iraq’s energy industry, as the continued regional violence and disruptions to shipping via the Strait of Hormuz highlight the country’s reliance on southern oil export ports.

Iraq is also looking for other export routes to minimize its dependency on the strait, such as a massive oil pipeline that would link southern Iraq to Syria’s Mediterranean coast via Baniyas.

The planned route might let Iraqi petroleum reach foreign markets without traveling through Hormuz, thus improving export security during times of regional unrest.

TotalEnergies has previously indicated interest in developing alternate energy export routes, including via Syria, but Sunday’s official statement did not say if the planned pipeline was mentioned during the Baghdad conference.

The French energy company is already a big investment in Iraq, with projects aimed at expanding oil output, collecting associated gas, and boosting power generation.

Iraq continues to depend on imported gas for power generation, despite having huge gas reserves generated alongside crude oil.

The meeting with TotalEnergies and ConocoPhillips shows Iraq’s attempts to recruit foreign knowledge and investment while tackling two significant weaknesses in its energy sector: reliance on imported gas and reliance on export routes threatened by regional violence.

Progress in oilfield expansion, gas capture, and alternate export facilities might help Iraq enhance its energy security and preserve its position as a major oil producer in the face of increasing geopolitical challenges.

World.title: Iraq’s oil exports to South Korea hit 38.3 million barrels in eight months
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – South Korea’s state-owned Korea National Oil Corporation (KNOC) announced that it imported 38.34 million barrels of crude oil from Iraq during the first eight months of 2026.

The volume represents a decrease of 45.6 percent compared to the same period in 2025.

Saudi Arabia was the largest oil supplier to South Korea, with 196.21 million barrels between January and August 2026, a 15.65 percent decline compared to the same period in 2025.

The United States was the second-largest oil supplier to South Korea, with 131.09 million barrels, and the UAE followed with 101.55 million barrels.

Iraq’s oil exports to South Korea fell from 70.55 million barrels during the first eight months in 2025 to 38.34 million barrels in the same period in 2026.

Iraq was the fourth largest crude oil supplier to South Korea in the first half of 2026, accounting for 7.4 percent of the country’s total oil imports.

Iraq’s average oil shipments to South Korea totaled 113.7 million barrels in 2025, which is an average of 311,500 barrels per day. This represents a 12 percent increase compared to 2024.

World.title: Iraq, Turkey discuss oil-for-financing deal to fund Development Road project
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq is discussing an oil-for-financing agreement with Turkey to establish a fund for the Development Road project, where Turkish companies will execute construction in exchange for crude oil, while the project’s first phase will be backed by a World Bank loan.

Director of Projects at the General Company for Iraqi Railways, Fadel Abbas, confirmed that a joint financial framework is being shaped to let Turkish firms carry out infrastructure works paid for through oil exports.

The initiative aims to upgrade Iraq’s railway network, connect several provinces, and provide passenger and freight transport services, according to Abbas.

The Development Road’s primary objective is to transport goods from al-Faw Grans Port to Turkey—and onward to Europe—and vice versa.

Work is currently underway to finalize an agreement with Turkey to establish a fund that would finance the project’s implementation by Turkish companies through an oil-for-financing arrangement, according to the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA).

The $17 billion project, which will connect the al-Faw Grand Port in southern Iraq to the Turkish border by constructing a railway and road network, is anticipated to transform Iraq into a transit center by cutting the time it takes to travel from Asia to Europe.

In addition to pipelines for energy transportation, the project’s railway will significantly assist in the transportation of commodities, with a first-phase capacity of 3.5 million tons and a second-phase capacity of 7.5 million tons.

By connecting the port city of Basra to Turkey via an overland route, the logistics project will compete with Egypt’s Suez Canal and establish Basra as a gateway to Europe.

World.title: HC questions Assam government on woman sent to Bangladesh
World.content:
Gauhati high court has intensified scrutiny of circumstances in which Nagaon's Mumtaz Begum was sent to Bangladesh, warning Assam govt that it would presume a Foreigners' Tribunal's May 30 opinion declaring her a foreigner would be considered "not ready" if the state fails to establish when it was finalised.

In its latest order on Oct 7, the high court recorded MEA's submission that an inquiry into Mumtaz's whereabouts was ongoing and that it needed more time.

TOI had reported that Bangladesh's home ministry began searching for Mumtaz after this newspaper contacted authorities in Dhaka in the last week of Sept.

Not only Mumtaz, another woman also 'missing' after B'desh expulsion

The Gauhati high court, in its Oct 7 order, said, "The court shall presume that the opinion...was

not made ready within the appropriate time, i.e., prior to the taking into custody" of Mumtaz.

The court had ordered an inquiry on Sept 3 and directed MEA to trace Mumtaz and facilitate her return, observing that she was sent to Bangladesh without a "reasonable opportunity" to challenge the tribunal's opinion.

The court had previously set aside an earlier opinion declaring her a foreigner and ordered fresh consideration of her case.





Her son, Momruz Ali, had on Oct 7 disputed Assam CM Himanta Biswa Sarma's claim that she was safe and in regular contact with him and had told TOI that the family had no idea where she was and that the family was "breaking" under the strain of the search.

The case dates back to April, when Gauhati HC set aside an earlier Foreigners' Tribunal opinion declaring Mumtaz a foreigner and remanded the matter for fresh consideration.

She appeared before the tribunal again on May 30, the date borne by the fresh opinion, and was taken into custody.

The central question now before the court is whether that opinion had actually been made ready before officials acted on it.

According to the chronology recorded in court proceedings, Mumtaz was subsequently moved through holding facilities in Assam and handed over to BSF on June 13.

World.title: Don't detain peaceful protesters, says SC; hundreds still taken away on Day 2
World.content:
NEW DELHI:

Sunday sought responses of Union home secretary Govind Mohan,

commissioner Anurag Kumar and Delhi metro rail chief D Thara to a contempt petition for prima facie violating the court's Oct 9 order against complete shutdown of metro and train services in Delhi on Saturday to thwart CJP's protest seeking CEC Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.

The court also said lawyers, journalists, and other professionals should not be hindered in performing their duties "in any manner whatsoever".

On the ground, nearly 700 people were detained (police claimed 400), many far away from protest zones, while barricading and traffic curbs remained on the roads much like Saturday. Protesters changed strategy, staging flash protests in small numbers at short notice. Most of the action was in and around CP as small groups of protesters kept trickling in.

They were detained.

Around 2.30pm, All India Student Association members, including president Neha Bora, started a protest near RK Ashram Marg metro station. As detentions began, Bora and a few others broke away and ran towards CP, where they continued to protest before being detained. Around 7pm, Students Federation of India members gathered at CP to hold a women's tiranga march against alleged police excesses, especially against women protesters.





They were detained and taken away in buses. "How can they detain women at 7pm in the evening?" SFI general secretary Srijan Bhattacharya said.

The widespread detentions - 7,000 estimated Saturday - figured prominently in arguments by the lawyers at SC's unusual holiday hearing on Sunday. Following the submissions, a bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said, "...we are of the opinion that the petitioners have made out a prima facie case.

Accordingly, we issue notice upon the alleged contemnors". It asked them to file their responses by Oct 13.

Normalise internet connectivity, ensure free movement in city: SC

We understand the gargantuan magnitude of detentions. We will have to seek a response from govt," the bench said after hearing the petitioners, who included advocate Shailendra Mani Tripathi, CPM MP M A Baby, RJD MP Manoj Jha and lawyer intervenors like Shadan Farasat, who was detained along with other advocates outside SC on Saturday.

The bench asked for normalisation of internet connectivity and prohibition of "illegal" detentions, especially of those who gather for peaceful protest away from areas where prohibitory orders are in force. "There shall be no illegal detentions, particularly in cases of peaceful unarmed assemblage of people beyond the area where prohibitory orders under Sec 163 of BNS are in force," it said.

On Oct 9, SC had restrained authorities from resorting to blanket closure of metro stations, though it said operations could be regulated depending on the situation.

The order came after DMRC said 57 stations would be shut; that number was later revised to 45.

Solicitor general Tushar Mehta disputed allegations of violation of the Oct 9 order and said Delhi Metro was functioning normally, though 45 out of 303 stations were closed to maintain law and order. He refuted the allegation that metro stations were closed, saying that "all metro stations are open since 10pm Saturday, trains are operating normally and internet connection has been restored".

SC also issued directions to ensure free movement in the city subject to law and order situation/traffic regulations and that installing barricades shall be reviewed forthwith to ensure free movement subject to law and order and traffic requirements. "Lawyers, journalists and other professionals shall not be hindered in discharge of their professional duties in any manner whatsoever," SC said, and also directed withdrawal of prohibitory orders around SC and courts to facilitate free access to litigants and lawyers.

Over 100 lawyers led by senior advocate and MP Kapil Sibal slammed the police brutalities on protesters, and accused authorities of continuing with the shutdown of metro and train services in complete disregard of the SC order and of illegal detention of protesters even in areas where the prohibitory orders were not in force.

Sibal argued that internet shutdown was a blow to fundamental right to free speech and flagged detention of lawyers who participated in the protest.

Senior advocate Farasat, who was detained, informed SC he was manhandled and bundled into a police vehicle. Senior advocate and TMC MP Menaka Guruswamy termed the entire episode as "undeclared emergency" worse than what Indira Gandhi had imposed (in 1975).

When Sibal thanked the bench for holding court on Sunday because of the extraordinary turn of events, Justice Bagchi said, "We are always at the service of the nation."

Later, Justice Bagchi said, "We know things have deeply affected you (the lawyers) and we do not want to trivialise anything."

The bench issued notice to Centre and Delhi Police on a habeas corpus petition questioning detention of TMC politicians Mamata Banerjee, Derek O'Brien and Dola Sen. Solicitor general Mehta said the petition has become infructuous as the detained leaders were released last evening.

As the pro-protest petitioners backed by a team of senior advocates - K K Venugopal, N Hariharan, Shoeb Alam, Arundhati Katju, G Sankaranarayanan, Sanjay Hegde - made a concerted attempt to corner police and Centre by flagging police action, senior advocate Kirti Uppal struck a discordant note by arguing that lawyers should not be stepping into shoes of their political affiliation.

"I was told that a lawyer's job is inside the courts and not on the streets," he said. The pro-protester lawyers inside the courtroom shouted 'shame, shame' to silence him. The bench asked the lawyers to maintain decorum of the courtroom and maintain silence.

World.title: BJP: Rahul Gandhi pushing India towards anarchy, creating north-south divide
World.content:
NEW DELHI: BJP Sunday accused Rahul Gandhi of seeking to stoke division in the country on linguistic grounds after the LoP alleged that PM Modi has launched a "full-scale attack" on the Tamil language and culture.

BJP spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi said the reality is that the Tamil language has received "immense respect" during Modi's tenure, with the PM praising it as the world's oldest language and applauding its rich culture even abroad.

He said, "Efforts have been made to establish the Tamil language across its various dimensions, not only at the national level but also on the international stage."

The BJP MP said Rahul has been trying hard to push India towards anarchy and create a divide between the north and south on a linguistic basis.

"When the sacred Sengol was placed in the new Parliament building as a revered symbol of eternal Tamil culture in 2023, Congress opposed it," Trivedi said.

Modi recently presented a copy of the Russian translation of 'Thirukkural' to Vladimir Putin, he pointed out. Trivedi also slammed Rahul for his "undeclared Emergency" jibe at Modi. "Today, you can say whatever comes to mind about the prime minister, making baseless and reckless comments.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines





There was a time when if you merely said at a public place that the Indira Gandhi govt must be removed, you were jailed."

BJP MP Bansuri Swaraj slammed Rahul for Congress not taking any action against JNU professor Angomcha Akoijam, a party MP who was recently dismissed from JNU over charges of sexual harassment. Indian high commissioner to Canada, Dinesh Patnaik, has said India doesn't mind advocacy and protests for Khalistan, as long as these are peaceful. Modi said urbanisation was an opportunity, not a challenge, and highlighted the expansion of India's Metro network from 250km in 2014 to more than 1,100km, with services operating in 25 cities, up from five. Vijay set a target of making Tamil Nadu a $1.5 trillion economy by 2036, promising a transparent, corruption-free govt and inclusive growth. "Strong states make a strong India," he said, calling for greater Centre-state coordination.

He sought approval for Godavari-Cauvery river-linking project, Tamil as official language of Madras HC, and release of Rs 5,110 crore in pending Samagra Shiksha funds. He thanked Modi for announcing high-speed networks connecting Chennai with Hyderabad and Bengaluru in the Budget.

World.title: Passenger's device starts smoking, flight diverted
World.content:
NEW DELHI: An IndiGo flight from Delhi to Chennai Sunday was diverted to Hyderabad after a passenger's personal electronic device caught fire. The crew put the device in water before the aircraft safely diverted to Hyderabad.

"6E 6115 was diverted to Hyderabad after smoke was detected from a customer's PED. Cabin crew responded promptly and the situation was brought under control. In line with established protocols, the pilots diverted the flight and landed safely at Hyderabad," an IndiGo spokesperson said.

The personal electronic device (PED), containing a Li-ion battery, or power bank that caught fire was kept in overhead baggage.

Many countries, including India, mandate that such devices be kept in front of passengers so they can quickly spot if they start emitting smoke or catch fire. The idea is to avoid delays.

However, despite announcements, passengers ignore this instruction and keep power banks or portable electronic devices in bags placed in overhead bins.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

The biggest concern remains airlines taking cabin bags from passengers at boarding gates to be kept in the aircraft's baggage hold.





These bags may contain PEDs and power banks, and a fire in the belly baggage hold may go undetected.

The civil aviation ministry is aware of the issue and is working to resolve it.

"Another aircraft has been arranged to continue the journey to Chennai. We regret inconvenience caused to our customers due to this unforeseen situation and are making all efforts to minimise it, including offering refreshments and sharing updates. At IndiGo, safety of our customers and crew remains our top priority," the spokesperson added.

World.title: El Nino sets temperature record in key Pacific zone: EU monitor
World.content:
An intensifying El Nino broke a temperature record in a key zone of the Pacific in September, the EU’s climate monitor said on Monday (October 12, 2026), in another sign the weather pattern is gaining exceptional strength.

Global forecasters have been warning for months that this El Nino would likely become the strongest ever observed and the latest record has tumbled even before the episode’s expected peak later this year.

The warming phase of a natural climate cycle, El Nino raises sea temperatures in the tropical Pacific, triggering changes in weather that can increase the risk of drought and flooding, and exacerbate man-made global warming.

The Copernicus Climate Change Service said sea surface temperatures in a tell-tale El Nino monitoring region of the Pacific, known as Nino3.4, had reached an “all-time high” of 29.70C last month.

This exceeded the peak temperatures of previously strong El Nino events of 1982/1983, 1997/1998 and 2015/2016, “underscoring the exceptional intensity of the current El Nino”, the EU monitor said.

But in a statement to AFP, Copernicus said it “cannot yet say that the current El Nino is the strongest ever recorded”.

As climate change raises ocean temperatures, it can make recent El Nino events appear stronger than past ones, complicating historical comparisons.

Copernicus said it had adopted a new index, which accounts for the warming of tropical oceans, that suggested the current event is not yet stronger than past ones.

But the values observed in September “point to an already exceptionally strong El Nino, especially given that the event has not yet reached its peak”, Copernicus told AFP.

Not all forecasters use the same scale to interpret El Nino.

On Friday, Japan’s weather agency said that El Nino conditions had reached their “strongest intensity on record”, with temperatures in the phenomenon’s monitoring area 4C above normal.

Record ocean temperatures

As El Nino gathers strength, global average sea surface temperatures hit a record 21.05C for September, topping the previous high of 20.92C for the same month in 2023, according to Copernicus.

Overall, the world experienced its second hottest September on record, with surface air temperatures averaging 16.27C, the EU service said.

September was 1.63C hotter than the pre-industrial average, a period defined as 1850-1900.

Nations agreed at the 2015 UN climate talks in Paris to keep global warming “well below” 2C above pre-industrial levels, while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5C, in order to limit the effects of climate change.

But the United Nations declared in September that the long-term 1.5C target would be missed in a matter of years.

“We are in a new run of months above 1.5C, and with a strong El Nino still intensifying it is likely to last into 2027,” Copernicus director Carlo Buontempo said in a statement.

“Crossing the Paris Agreement’s long-term limit is only a matter of time. How far we overshoot, and for how long, is still up to us,” he said.

Scientists say it is crucial to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels to limit the period of “overshoot” above 1.5C and bring temperatures back down as quickly as possible.

Experts have warned that this El Nino would likely push global temperatures to a new record in 2027.

El Nino warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns.

It typically takes place every two to seven years and lasts around nine to 12 months.
