World.title: Iran says US response to its proposal to reopen Hormuz ‘insufficient’
World.content:
Iran is 'no longer in the process of responding to the Americans,' says Iran's security chief

DUBAI, UAE – The United States’ response to Iran’s seven conditions in a proposal to reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz was “insufficient,” Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, was quoted by state media on Sunday, October 11, as saying.

Iran presented a proposal during the UN General Assembly under which the Strait of Hormuz waterway could be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days if the conditions were met, to which the US later replied via Qatari intermediaries.

Washington needs to clarify the issues that remain unclear to Tehran, Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, said, adding “we presented seven conditions to the Americans and clearly stated that the Strait of Hormuz would not be opened to them, and no negotiations would take place, until these conditions are met.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Rezaei said Iran is “no longer in the process of responding to the Americans.”

“In their response, they have accepted some of our conditions, while others remain unclear,” he added.

Tehran said late in September that it had received a US response to its latest proposal to resurrect the collapsed ceasefire in the Gulf, days after US President Donald Trump said he had rejected it.

Qatar and other mediators have transmitted messages between Washington and Tehran in an effort to end the conflict and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the conduit for a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas before the war that began at the end of February with US and Israeli attacks on Iran. – Rappler.com

World.title: Saudi Arabia reports injuries in new attack at Riyadh airport, day after strike kills 13
World.content:
FOOTAGE. Surveillance footage shows people reacting amid smoke at the moment of an attack at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, October 10, 2026, in this frame from a handout video.

The situation results in travel warnings from the UK and US, while Saudi Arabia continues military operations in Yemen, with the Houthis threatening further escalation

Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis claimed responsibility for a Saturday strike on Riyadh’s international airport that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, while Saudi authorities reported that people were injured in a new attack on the airport on Sunday, October 11.

Saudi-led coalition forces in Yemen said an unidentified projectile had targeted Riyadh’s international airport Terminal 4 on Sunday, causing a fire. An unspecified number of people were injured, the Saudi civil aviation authority said, adding it was still assessing the damage.

The coalition forces also said Saudi air defenses had intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of King Khalid International Airport. They later added that a drone had been intercepted and destroyed in the country’s Eastern Province.

The strikes have exposed vulnerabilities in Saudi defense capabilities as the kingdom wages an air campaign against the Houthis, who are fighting a ground war in Yemen against the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.

Footage released by Saudi state television of the Saturday attack on the Riyadh airport showed scores of religious pilgrims lined up at a gate as they prepared to travel to Islam’s two holiest sites. A bright orange flash sent people running in panic, while parts of the roof appeared to cave in.

The airport was closed after the attack.

Houthis claim responsibility

In a televised speech on Sunday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed responsibility for Saturday’s attack and said the group had struck the airport in Dammam in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province and two facilities of Saudi oil giant Saudi Aramco.

The Saudi government’s media office and Aramco did not respond to requests for comment.

The Saudi civil aviation authority confirmed the strike on Dammam’s King Fahd International Airport late on Sunday, adding that “damage assessments and safety inspections of airport facilities are under way.”

An eyewitness aboard a taxiing aircraft at Dammam told Reuters that around 8:30 pm (1730 GMT) on Sunday, they saw a projectile strike the tarmac beside several parked aircraft, causing a fire. The witness said the aircraft returned to the gate. Passengers disembarked and were told to leave.

Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 showed several delays and cancellations on Sunday for arrivals and departures at Dammam airport, the kingdom’s third-largest.

The Houthis earlier on Sunday had renewed their warning against using Saudi airports. “We urge everyone to take our warnings seriously, and Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions,” the group said.

Britain’s embassy in Saudi Arabia in a post on X advised British citizens against all but essential travel to Jeddah, Dammam and all airports in the kingdom except the airport in Medina.

US aviation authorities issued a notice to US airlines to use caution while flying to or over the kingdom.

‘Worse is yet to come’

Saudi Arabia has recently stepped up its military involvement in Yemen, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a government counteroffensive after the Houthis seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month.

The Houthis said on Sunday that Saudi Arabia carried out 124 air strikes in Yemen in the past 24 hours. “Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing,” Yemen’s Houthi-run foreign ministry said in statements carried by Al Masirah television.

US President Donald Trump said on Saturday the United States was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the wider war with Iran that the US and Israel launched in February.

In a post on Telegram, Iran’s foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said he told his Saudi counterpart that Tehran was ready to help facilitate dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

Energy conference still going ahead

A five-day conference of international energy organization WPC Energy opened as planned on Sunday at a convention center about 10 km from the Riyadh airport, the Saudi energy ministry said.

A ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum also went ahead, according to a media advisory from the ministry. It was not clear which ministers attended.

Italy’s energy minister, Gilberto Pichetto Fratin, whose country was co-hosting, had said on Friday he would participate remotely via video link.

German officials were trying to organize a return flight for economy minister Katherina Reiche. She was supposed to return to Berlin from Riyadh on Monday but the ministry said it appeared likely her flight would be unable to take off.

Separately, Saudi authorities announced that in-person classes at schools in Riyadh would be shifted to remote learning from Sunday until Thursday.

In Saturday’s attack, the third on Riyadh’s airport in a week, the dead included four Saudis while the remainder were foreign nationals, Saudi authorities said. India’s embassy in Riyadh said on Sunday one of its citizens injured in the attack had died, adding to the initial death toll of 12.

Four people were killed in the two previous attacks on the airport earlier in the week. One attack also caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane parked on the tarmac. – Rappler.com

World.title: Lino Cayetano is Marcos’ 6th communications chief
World.content:
LINO CAYETANO. TV director and producer Lino Cayetano during the the 2025 election campaign. He ran for Taguig 1st District congressman.

The Presidential Communications Office has undergone several leadership changes throughout the Marcos administration

MANILA, Philippines – People’s Television Network (PTV) General Manager Lino Cayetano is the next secretary of the Presidential Communications Office (PCO), President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. confirmed on Sunday, October 11.

Cayetano will replace Dave Gomez who was bypassed by the Commission on Appointments.

“Na-bypass si Dave (Dave was bypassed) so I guess immediately, at least, who will take his place will be Lino,” Marcos said in an interview with Philippine media at the end of his Singapore trip.

Cayetano will be the sixth PCO chief under the Marcos administration, which has seen frequent changes in leadership of the government’s communications arm.

The PCO is responsible for coordinating the messaging of the executive branch and the Office of the President, including communicating government policies, programs, and official activities to the public and maintaining relations with the media.

Cayetano, a former television director and politician, was appointed general manager of the state-run network in June 2026.

He is the younger brother of senators Alan Peter and Pia Cayetano, both of whom have criticized the Marcos administration.

His relationship with Alan has also been marked by political differences. In the 2025 elections, Cayetano ran for representative of Taguig’s First District but lost to Ading Cruz, who was backed by his sister-in-law, Taguig Mayor Lani Cayetano.

Before joining PTV, Cayetano served as Taguig City mayor from 2019 to 2022 and represented the city’s Second District in the House of Representatives from 2013 to 2016.

He earned a degree in Mass Communication from the University of the Philippines and a diploma in film from the New York Film Academy. He is also a co-founder, producer, and director at Rein Entertainment.

The PCO has undergone several leadership changes since Marcos took office in 2022. Its previous chiefs included Trixie Cruz-Angeles, Cheloy Garafil, Cesar Chavez, and Jay Ruiz before Gomez assumed the post in July 2025. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Inside the Newsroom] How Rappler uncovered Sara Duterte’s company contracts with Davao City Hall
World.content:
Rappler has exposed government officials' conflicts of interest involving infrastructure projects. The story of Sara Duterte and Gencorp revealed that this kind of scheme can also happen in food contracts. And perhaps there are similar stories hiding in procurement records across the country.

Hello, I’m Patrick Cruz, Rappler’s public finance reporter.

My job is to follow the money — the people’s money — and track how it is allocated, spent, and misused.

My coverage, however, somehow shifted when I was tapped as one of three Rappler reporters assigned to cover the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte. I was assigned to cover the senator-judges, which meant reporting on the proceedings, the atmosphere inside the courtroom, and the decisions of the senator-judges.

One of the stories I wrote on July 20, 2026, involved the impeachment court’s issuance of subpoenas for the bank and tax records of companies linked to Duterte and her husband, Mans Carpio.

REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK. Rappler multimedia reporter James Patrick Cruz takes notes on the third day of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on July 8, 2026.

That got me thinking: Are these companies also doing business with the government?

(After all, our country is run by politicians whose companies or their relatives’ companies earn billions of pesos out of infrastructure projects funded by hard earned money of Filipinos. We mapped them out here.)

I checked the companies linked to the Vice President one by one against government procurement records.

There, I found that Gencorp had won millions of pesos worth of food contracts from Davao City Hall and the PhilHealth Davao Regional Office.

That was the beginning of my two-month investigation.

Following the paper trail

I compiled the contracts into a Google Sheet and verified them one by one. I reviewed Duterte’s Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) across several years and went through bidding documents, purchase orders, notices of award, and other procurement records.

We also bought Gencorp’s General Information Sheet filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). (Yes, we have to pay for these types of documents for our stories.)

But, instead of giving me more clarity, it brought me to another question: Why doesn’t Duterte’s name appear in the SEC records?

And then I also found something interesting: that businessman Jaime Tan Cruz is a shareholder of Gencorp.

Cruz is no stranger to former president Rodrigo Duterte, Sara’s father. The Duterte patriarch appointed him as Special Envoy to the People’s Republic of China for Trade and Investment. He was also considered for the post of PhilHealth president and CEO.

INVESTIGATIVE BOARD. The chart shows the connections between the shareholders of Gencorp Industries Inc. and the Dutertes.

It later turned out that Cruz is a business partner of the Duterte siblings: Vice President Sara Duterte, Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte, and Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo “Pulong” Duterte.

The headline of our report, however, was criticized as “misleading” by Duterte’s spokesperson, Paolo Panelo. He argued that Gencorp was not the Vice President’s company.

So why did Duterte declare Gencorp as among her businesses in her SALN? Well, the Vice President has yet to answer this question. The fact remains that Gencorp is in the sworn SALN of the Vice President.

After our investigative report was published, the issue was tackled in the impeachment court in relation to Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth.

Davao City Mayor Baste Duterte, who was initially not listed as a witness in the trial, was compelled to appear before the court and answer questions about government contracts won by a company linked to his sister.

Before the court, Mayor Duterte said he did not know that his sister had an interest in Gencorp or that the company had won millions of pesos worth of contracts from the city government he is running.

In fact, he said the company had received even more contracts than those identified in our initial report.

Curiosity moves the story forward

At Rappler, our managers and editors often remind us to “move the story forward.”

For me, that starts with curiosity.

I could have stopped after reporting on the impeachment court’s subpoena for the records of Duterte-linked companies and called it a day. Instead, I dug into government procurement records to see what else the paper trail might reveal.

That, to me, is what it means to move a story forward. It means not stopping at the obvious news peg or covering a press conference, but digging through documents, checking records, following names, and pursuing the next lead.

Sometimes, that trail leads somewhere you did not expect.

That discipline has helped Rappler reporters produce investigative stories exposing conflicts of interest involving infrastructure projects in the wake of the flood control corruption scandal.

The story of Sara Duterte and Gencorp revealed that this kind of scheme can also happen in food contracts.

And perhaps there are similar stories hiding in procurement records across the country.

Maybe your local officials or their relatives have business interests that intersect with government contracts. Maybe they own a Jollibee or McDonald’s in your city and their business also supplies food for government events. Maybe they are suppliers of sound systems, laptops, or security services. Maybe they own a gas station where government vehicles buy their fuel.

If you know of a similar scheme, please report it to us at investigative@rappler.com.

You can also support more in-depth stories by donating to our investigative fund or joining the Rappler+ membership program. – Rappler.com

World.title: Between adolescence and parenthood: Photo stories of Filipino teen parents
World.content:
YOUNG MOM. “Joyce” holds her child in a photograph titled, “Hindi hadlang ang pagiging ina sa pag-aaral” (Motherhood is not an obstacle to studying), reflecting her experiences of pursuing her education while raising a child.

“I’m a student, a worker, and a mother. Sometimes, I feel like I have three bodies.”

For this senior high school student, motherhood meant learning to carry several parts of herself all at once. Her days meant moving between school, work, and caring for her child — growing into adulthood, even while already being responsible for someone else.

This ongoing negotiation of identity, in which teens experience the push and pull of being adolescents and parents, is vividly illustrated in a new study from Ateneo de Manila University that explores through photographs — a research technique called “photovoice” — what it means to grow up while becoming a parent.

Teenage parenthood remains a pressing concern in the Philippines, with an estimated 150,000 teenage pregnancies recorded in 2022 and a 35% rise in births among girls younger than 15. Behind these statistics, studies point to gaps between existing laws and programs and teenage parents’ lived experiences, including stigma and inaccessible or irrelevant services.

Positioning teenage mothers and fathers at the center of the research process, this Ateneo study was conducted as a needs assessment to inform the development of a parenting program for teenage parents. It was designed and implemented by researchers Dr. Liane Alampay, Dr. Bernice Landoy Mamauag, and Jennel Reyes, in partnership with Masayang Pamilya Organization, Inc.

The researchers invited nine Filipino teenage parents, aged 15 to 20, from low-income communities in two provinces in Central Luzon, areas identified by the researchers’ partner organization as priorities because of their high rates of teenage pregnancy.

Researcher Nina Capulong with study participants during the data collection process, where teenage parents were invited to represent and share their experiences through photographs and stories. Photo courtesy of Masayang Pamilya Organization, Inc.

Through the photovoice approach, participants documented their lives by capturing or choosing images that represented their experiences and sharing the stories behind them, allowing their perspectives to inform the support and programs being developed for them.

There were no photography lessons, no tips on lighting or framing. Instead, participants were simply asked to make sure that their photographs represented something meaningful to them.

That distinction mattered. Because taking photographs was already part of the participants’ everyday lives, the method provided a familiar way to express their experiences. Some participants even used photographs symbolically rather than literally: crayons became a representation of family, while a permanent marker represented the lasting effects of sexual interactions.

What those images revealed was a life that could not be reduced to the label ‘teenage parent.’

Through their photographs, the young parents offered glimpses into lives shaped by responsibilities that arrived alongside adolescence. They spoke about uncertainty and conflict in their relationships, changes in friendships and family dynamics, and the demands of caring for a child while pursuing education or employment.

For one participant, motherhood existed alongside being a first year college student and a food server. For another, friends became family, highlighting the role of peers as a source of support and a safe space to speak openly.

Across their photographs and discussions, the researchers identified eight core themes: managing stresses and conflicts in partner relationships; peers as a source of emotional support; support and strain in family relationships; shifts in normative adolescent experiences and priorities; strain and agency in balancing roles; desire to enhance parenting knowledge and skills; environmental drivers of early sexual exposure; and sexual knowledge from social media.

Viewed through the lens of Life Course Theory, these challenges are shaped by relationship dynamics and structural norms in low-resource contexts, influencing the transition to parenthood.

The researchers found that teenage parents navigated these circumstances in different ways. Some continued their education or pursued employment, while others expressed a desire to improve how they cared for and related to their children. The researchers saw these choices as forms of agency amid the constraints they faced.



Fathers and partners emerged in the narratives in contradictory ways: as sources of both stress and support.

Several mothers described conflict-laden relationships marked by imbalanced household responsibilities, financial control, and verbal and physical conflicts, tensions compounded by the adolescents’ still-developing emotional regulation capacities. Yet when fathers shared caregiving, this enabled mothers to continue their education, illustrating how paternal involvement functions as a critical resource.

The paper calls for gender-responsive strategies to bring young fathers meaningfully into support programs to strengthen family functioning, and to shift the traditional gender norms that leave adolescent mothers disproportionately bearing the burdens of early parenthood.

The Ateneo study underscored the need for accessible counseling, healthier communication and conflict resolution, and stronger support systems for young parents, alongside comprehensive sexual and reproductive health education.

At the heart of the study is the recognition that teenage parenthood is shaped by more than its challenges. It is also shaped by the relationships, circumstances, and choices through which young people find their way.

The photographs did not offer a single story of teenage parenthood — one where becoming a parent becomes the whole story of a young person’s life.

Instead, they opened a window into lives shaped by relationships, responsibilities, uncertainty, support, and choices. They revealed young people who are still growing and still finding their way while learning to care for someone else. What emerged were stories still unfolding, of young people still becoming. – Rappler.com

Nina Linly Capulong, Liane Peña Alampay, Bernice Landoy Mamauag, and Jennel Drezza Fe C. Reyes published their research, “Using Photovoice and Life Course Theory to Understand the Lived Experiences of Filipino Teenage Parents,’ in the August 2026 issue of the Journal of Research on Adolescence.

World.title: Trump calls for replacing Ukraine’s Zelenskyy in tussle over diesel deal with Russia
World.content:
TRUMP. US President Donald Trump speaks to members of the media after disembarking Air Force One, after attending a campaign rally in Clarksville, Tennessee, at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, US, on October 10, 2026. Eric Lee/Reuters

'I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president,' US President Donald Trump says

US President Donald Trump on Saturday, October 11, called for Ukraine to replace its leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy and railed against Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil infrastructure, a day after announcing a diesel supply deal with Russia that had drawn a sharp rebuke from Zelenskyy.

In some of his harshest criticism yet of the White House, Zelenskyy linked the US lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel with a Russian attack on Saturday, October 10, that killed 20 people, including 3 children, in the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia.

A steep rise in global diesel prices, which followed the outbreak of the Iran war in February, has become a political liability for Trump’s Republican Party ahead of next month’s midterm elections, when opposition Democrats could gain control of one or both houses of Congress.

“I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” Trump told reporters at the White House, saying Zelenskyy had hurt global diesel supplies with strikes on Russian refineries.

“He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world.”

Zelenskyy says diesel deal emboldens Russia

Earlier in the day, ZelZelenskyyensky said Trump’s announcement on Friday of the diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin had emboldened Moscow. Kyiv has instead urged Washington to pressure Moscow for serious negotiations to end the 4-1/2-year-old war.

The Russian government said on Saturday it had partially lifted a ban on diesel exports.

“Today, Russia said thank you for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said.

“Last night provided yet more confirmation that Russia perceives any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly keep fighting, that it can supposedly keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed.”

The southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia has been a regular target of Russian bombardment with strikes intensifying in the past few months.

On Saturday, a 6-year-old girl was among those killed in Zaporizhzhia when one strike reduced part of an apartment block to rubble. Her grandfather, Anatoliy Chumniy, stood sobbing over her body, laid on the ground in a white bag, after rescuers pulled it from the wreckage.

“Her birthday would have been at the end of the month,” he said through tears.

It was the third mass-casualty attack on Ukraine this week.

Nearly 80 civilians were killed in Russian strikes on Wednesday and Thursday, including at least 30 killed by a bomb in the eastern garrison city of Kramatorsk and 22 others by a missile in the town of Pryluky, about 130 km (80 miles) east of Kyiv.

The diesel deal was also criticized by US lawmakers, including one of Trump’s fellow Republicans, Representative Don Bacon, who said it was time to apply more sanctions that Congress had recently passed, not lift them.

Analysts said the agreement was unlikely to lead to sustained lower fuel prices, with the volumes still much lower than what Russia usually exports when its refineries are not under attack.

Britain vows to strengthen Russia sanctions

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham spoke with Zelenskyy on Saturday and said Britain would strengthen its sanctions on Russia, according to a Downing Street spokesperson, who added that the two leaders would meet in person in the coming days.

The latest strikes followed talks between Ukrainian and European officials with US negotiators in Miami on Friday, which were aimed at developing a common proposal for ending the war, according to a person familiar with the discussions.

Trump announced the diesel deal while the negotiations were under way, a move Zelenskyy said had caught Kyiv by surprise.

The Ukrainian delegation was headed home on Saturday, presidential aide Dmytro Lytvyn was cited by the Interfax Ukraine news agency as saying.

Putin said after a call with Trump on Friday that an immediate resumption of ‌peace ⁠talks was unlikely, citing Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow.

US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner may visit Moscow within the next two weeks, Russian state news agency TASS reported on Saturday, citing a source.

In his remarks at the White House, Trump criticized Zelenskyy over the lack of a peace deal, while demanding an end to Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities.

“I said to him, ‘Do what you want. Don’t hit refineries. There’s plenty of targets. Don’t hit refineries.’ And he went out and he hit,” Trump said. “He better damn well stop.”

“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals, but for some reason he never does,” he added. – Rappler.com

World.title: The Regime Is Laying a Trap for the US. Will Washington Fall for It?
World.content:
Myanmar has become increasingly salient in Washington’s economic and national security calculus.

However, the country is far from simple. Its military and political power is dispersed across multiple centers, demanding deft handling and nuanced thinking.

In the absence of a single like-minded counterpart, Washington may be tempted to look for a shortcut and treat the military regime as the easiest channel through which to advance U.S. interests. Doing so would risk falling into the trap laid by Naypyitaw: mistaking access to the military regime for access to Myanmar itself.

Will Washington take the bait? Or will Washington resist this temptation and build a strategy around navigating Myanmar’s intricate and decentralized landscape?

Washington’s calculus

For Washington, the central question will be how to address two particular interests that converge in Myanmar as cost-effectively and reliably as possible. Washington is seeking to reduce dependence on China-dominated rare earth supply chains while confronting a rapidly expanding form of transnational organized crime that directly harms Americans. The country borders India and China, links mainland Southeast Asia to the Indian Ocean and is the world’s fourth-largest producer of rare earths. Myanmar also serves as one of the primary hubs for scam compounds that directly defraud Americans of billions of dollars.

Under the Trump administration, Washington’s foreign policy has fundamentally changed. Longstanding traditions of promoting human rights and democracy have now been deprioritized in favor of an “America First” approach interpreted narrowly as protecting core national interests. The 2025 National Security Strategy (NSS) signed by Trump last November identifies “flexible realism” as one of its guiding principles. Under this approach, Washington seeks good relations and peaceful commercial ties with countries without requiring them to adopt democratic principles.

This change may have significant ramifications for Myanmar, where the U.S.’ concerns over democracy and human rights have historically been prioritized, constraining diplomatic engagement with the country’s military rulers and business deals that could benefit them.

Equally important, the NSS also recognized the Indo-Pacific as “among the next century’s key economic and geopolitical battlegrounds” and emphasized that successful competition in the region is essential to American prosperity. As Washington seeks to rebalance its economic relationship with China and reduce its dependence on China-dominated supply chains, Myanmar’s strategic importance could grow.

Washington’s calculus is also shaped by regional governments, including U.S. partners, and by its own private sector. Global volatility and geopolitical shocks have exposed vulnerabilities in regional supply chains and energy security. The added threat of economic coercion has placed greater pressure on governments, including the U.S., to seek stability and secure critical supply chains. To this end, regional governments have started high-level engagements with the regime to explore possibilities. These engagements may increase the appeal of normalizing relations with the military regime in Naypyitaw for Washington.

American businesses, whose voices carry weight, are watching these shifts as well. As regional governments signal openness to normalization with the regime, Myanmar may appear to become a viable market for foreign investment. These businesses may perceive that U.S. sanctions and other regulations could leave them at a competitive disadvantage to regional competitors. The first entrants into uncertain and unstable markets often absorb the greatest risks, but the willingness of American businesses to pursue investment despite uncertainty may make the prospect of securing an early foothold difficult to dismiss.

Washington’s blind spot

For Washington, this renewed attention on Myanmar has revived an older policy problem that it had tried to work around, as it struggled to develop a coherent approach to the country. For much of the 1990s and 2000s, Washington tended to work through a small number of central political actors, even though political authority and armed power were far more dispersed. Myanmar’s ethnic armed organizations, despite being political and military stakeholders, did not fit neatly into the U.S.’ engagement model. In practice, Washington’s political focus remained on Aung San Suu Kyi and the military regime, and its engagement with ethnic armed organizations was largely reduced to a national reconciliation framework, excluding powerful groups that did not participate in the ceasefire process.

Today, Myanmar’s political landscape has changed. For decades, Aung San Suu Kyi served as Washington’s principal democratic interlocutor in Myanmar, but she remains under detention today. The opposition is dispersed among the National Unity Government, ethnic armed organizations and other resistance actors. Intensified war since the 2021 coup has further shifted political and military power toward ethnic armed organizations. No single actor represents the opposition as a whole. Engaging Myanmar today therefore requires moving beyond an approach built around a select few central political actors, and Washington has yet to adapt to a decentralized political landscape, as Beijing has.

Understanding this blind spot, the military regime in Naypyitaw has positioned itself to exploit an intensifying geopolitical competition and unresolved gap in Washington’s approach to Myanmar. The military regime has paid millions of dollars to influential lobbying firms to help tailor its message to current U.S. priorities, pitching itself as a partner capable of advancing them. What remains uncertain this time, however, is whether Washington will take the bait.

A familiar bargain

Under sanctions and growing isolation, the regime has repeatedly staged political openings with pitches for engagement to the U.S. throughout its history. This history, however, offers a clear lesson: the military will act in bad faith and abandon its agreements whenever it sees fit.

In May 2002, the military released Aung San Suu Kyi from house arrest. One week later, it registered a firm in Washington to lobby for normalizing relations with the U.S. The regime pitched cooperation on issues prioritized by the Bush administration, including counternarcotics, terrorism, trade and public health. The opening did not last. In May 2003, regime-paid attackers assaulted Aung San Suu Kyi’s convoy near Depayin, and the military detained her again.

Another opening came under President Thein Sein in March 2011. That August, he met with Aung San Suu Kyi in Naypyitaw. Subsequently, his government released political prisoners, relaxed censorship, allowed the National League for Democracy to reenter electoral politics and pursued ceasefires with ethnic armed groups. Washington responded by sending Secretary of State Hillary Clinton to Burma in December 2011, restoring ambassador-level diplomatic relations and easing restrictions on investment and financial services. The political opening lasted nearly a decade before the military, under Senior General Min Aung Hlaing, seized power in February 2021 and detained Aung San Suu Kyi again.

The 2011 opening, notably, was different. Thein Sein and other reform-minded officials made significant concessions and pursued genuine, if imperfect, political reforms. The changes allowed political freedoms and economic opportunities that had been unimaginable under previous military governments. Myanmar experts and analysts will continue to debate what could have been done differently to preserve that opening, but for Washington, dwelling on the past or trying to recreate it would only distract from addressing Myanmar’s present realities and building a better future.

The 2011 opening, and any hope of returning to it, was shattered by the 2021 coup and the military’s subsequent campaign of violence against its own people. The present reality is that the military leadership now ruling in Naypyitaw is not the one that pursued those reforms, but the one that overturned them.

The price of a shortcut

Normalizing relations with the regime is highly unlikely to secure access to rare earths or curb the scam compounds it supports. Instead, normalization would exacerbate these issues by giving a lifeline to the Min Aung Hlaing regime as it faces growing internal tensions, a new round of military defeats and economic pressures.

The military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party recently postponed its congress, reportedly due to leadership disputes. At the same time, the elevation of Min Aung Hlaing’s loyalists over more senior generals has raised questions about tensions within the armed forces. While exaggerating its success on the battlefield, the military now relies heavily on conscripts. Reportedly, more than 70 percent of its frontline troops are conscripts. While these developments do not necessarily indicate an imminent collapse, they contextualize the growing strains within the regime at a time when it is seeking international engagement.

The regime is also struggling militarily. In Kachin State, the military has failed to break the Kachin Independence Army’s resistance around Bhamo, while losing additional positions to resistance forces. In Rakhine State, a major offensive launched in September to retake territory from the Arakan Army has failed to achieve significant gains despite the deployment of thousands of troops backed by air and naval support. In Karen State, the Karen National Liberation Army and allied forces have continued to contest the military’s attempts to regain lost positions around Kawkareik.

Economic pressures are also adding to the regime’s mounting difficulties. Even Min Aung Hlaing, who has long presented an optimistic picture of Myanmar’s economy, recently acknowledged the regime’s failure to make meaningful progress. The regime’s pursuit of a loan arrangement with Belarus with high interest rates further suggests growing financial pressures and a need to secure alternative sources of financing. The regime’s efforts to circumvent international jet fuel sanctions also suggest that these measures are imposing constraints. With technical and material support from Chinese companies, the regime is developing its own aviation fuel production capacity at the Thanlyin refinery near Yangon to reduce its dependence on imported jet fuel. The project underscores the lengths to which the regime is going to secure a reliable fuel supply for its air force.

Will Washington take the bait?

The trap is laid. Washington’s recent actions indicate a trajectory towards normalization, but these three key drivers will shape what happens next in U.S. policy toward Myanmar.

Will Congress take a strong bipartisan stand? Although members of Congress have expressed concerns about engagement with the military regime, statements alone may do little to influence the administration’s calculations. The more consequential test will be whether Congress will press the Trump administration to implement the BURMA Act and pass the BRAVE Burma Act, which would “ turn the screws

World.title: Over Two-Thirds of Myanmar’s Population Poor or at Risk of Poverty: UN
World.content:
More than 37 million people—over two-thirds of Myanmar’s population of more than 54 million—are experiencing or at risk of “multidimensional poverty,” according to the latest report from the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) released on Thursday.

Drawing data from a nationwide household survey of nearly 7,500 people in 2025, the UNDP’s latest analysis examines what it calls multidimensional poverty, which looks beyond income and also covers non-financial deprivation, including access to education and healthcare, and other basic needs, amid economic and political crisis and natural hazards.

It said nearly 18 million people (32.6 percent) in Myanmar are multidimensionally poor, while more than 19 million (35.5 percent) others are vulnerable. That brings the total figure to more than 37 million people (68 percent) who either face poverty or are at risk of falling into it.

“Myanmar may no longer dominate international headlines, but the hardships facing millions of people continue to deepen,” said Kanni Wignaraja, UN assistant secretary-general and UNDP regional director for Asia and the Pacific. “We are seeing a depth of poverty in Myanmar that is eroding human development itself. This is a no-win war. Everyone is losing. The core muscle of the country is being systematically eroded.”

The survey found that people in rural areas are poorer than those in urban areas.

In terms of both severity and scale, the UNDP report highlights Rakhine State as the worst-affected area, with approximately 1.66 million residents enduring the most intense multidimensional poverty. Sagaing Region followed with a larger total of approximately 2.38 million people experiencing less severe poverty. Ayeyarwady Region ranked third.

The UNDP’s analysis indicated that poverty is driven by a combination of long-standing household vulnerabilities, including low education levels, insecure jobs and limited income, and wider pressures such as rising prices, natural hazards and armed conflict.

In war-torn Rakhine and Karenni (Kayah) states, poverty has been compounded by conflict, displacement and restrictions on movement.

To address poverty effectively, the report concluded that aid must provide intensive support to hard-hit conflict zones while reaching larger numbers of poor residents elsewhere, with assistance tailored to local needs.

World.title: Regime Shuts Down Myanmar’s Surging Online Gold Market
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime has moved to ban online sales of gold and jewelry, citing the risk of flawed products and market destabilization.

On Wednesday, the Commerce Ministry announced it has suspended issuance of licenses for selling gold, raw gold, jewelry, art objects, and household items via online platforms. It threatened unlicensed traders with prosecution under the 2013 Essential Commodities and Services Law, which carries six months to three years in prison and fines up to 500,000 kyats (roughly US$ 240).

Under existing rules, online sellers must obtain a Commerce Ministry license, while those dealing in gold and gemstones must also secure a permit from the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environmental Conservation.

Industry insiders told The Irrawaddy that more than 700 businesses have applied for licenses to sell gold and jewelry online in recent years. However, the ministry has now refused to extend expired permits, with inspections and enforcement expected to begin at the end of this month.

Online gold and jewelry shopping has become popular in Myanmar over the past few years, with internet outlets hiring actors and celebrities to promote their livestream sales.

Traders say the clampdown follows growing complaints from buyers that jewelry purchased via livestream “flash sales” was later rejected by pawnshops or gold shops.

“Online customers have no way of verifying the weight, quality, or reference price of their purchases. That leads to disputes and losses,” one Yangon jeweler explained.

Last month, Mandalay police announced the arrest of 11 foreign nationals and 17 Myanmar citizens accused of running online gemstone scams. Authorities said the suspects were using fake jade to defraud buyers in livestream sales.

Online gemstone sales remain permitted provided merchants hold a license from the Myanma Gems Enterprise and refrain from selling gold.

While the Yangon Region Gold Entrepreneurs Association has set the domestic reference price for 24K gold at 7.1 million kyats per tical, the market price exceeds 10 million kyats — a gap of 3 million kyats. Before the 2021 coup, a tical sold for under 1.4 million kyats.

Business owners warn that banning online sales will hurt digital commerce and marketing, which had surged during the pandemic. “Shops that relied on livestream promotions will struggle. Now we can only depend on walk-in customers,” one trader said.

World.title: China Takes Top Investor Crown in Myanmar, and More
World.content:
China now Myanmar’s top investor, trade partner

China is now officially the top foreign investor and trading partner in Myanmar, consolidating its economic grip as others retreat, according to a report by Japan External Trade Organization.

In fiscal year 2025 ending this March, Myanmar approved US$472.6 million in foreign direct investment, down another one-third or 31.5 percent from a year earlier. But inflow from China rose 2.1‑fold to $201.1 million, meaning it now accounts for 42.6 percent of the total.

The previous leader due to long-standing commitments, Singapore, dropped to second place with $155 million, while Hong Kong contributed $54.9 million, the report said citing data from Directorate of Investment and Company Administration.

Much of the Chinese and Hong Kong capital is in light industry, particularly garment and shoe factories.

Myanmar’s exports to China also climbed 24.7 percent to $4.312 billion over the period, while imports surged 42.6 percent to $5.952 billion. That means China now accounts for over one-third of of Myanmar’s total trade or 35 percent, up from 27.8 percent the previous year.

With the border disruptions, trade has shifted to alternative routes, says the report. The figures did not count China’s trade with territories controlled by the Brotherhood Alliance in northern Shan State bordering Yunnan.

Chinese documentary maps scam empires in lesser-known Shan hubs

A docuseries aired this week by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV has shed light on scam syndicates that thrived in four areas along Myanmar’s northern border. While Kokang’s scam empires have long made international headlines, the documentary focuses on three lesser‑known hubs—Wa, Mongla and Muse—as it boasts of Beijing’s “achievements” in cracking down on them.

The show identifies quasi-autonomous Wa territory as the incubator of regional scam economy. At the height of the boom, Mong Pawk alone hosted 265 scam centers involving nearly 60,000 people. But unlike the Kokang clans, who resisted Beijing’s demand to halt operations, the long- ruling United Wa State Army (UWSA) cooperated after one leader was arrested in Kunming and warrants were issued for others.

In October 2023, Wa authorities launched large‑scale sweeps of scam compounds, the documentary reveals. Since then, the UWSA has reported regular transfers of Chinese suspects and illegal immigrants, introducing procedures for voluntary return. More than 1,400 Chinese nationals have been reportedly handed back this year.

But it was in Mongla, controlled by the National Democratic Alliance Army (NDAA), where Beijing started its crackdown in September 2023, and the group cooperated with Chinese authorities. A second strike in July 2024 led to a border law enforcement cooperation agreement between Yunnan police and Mongla authorities, establishing monitoring and repatriation mechanisms.

The crackdown proved most difficult in Muse, where Beijing identified 33 distinct local armed groups and militias, each with over 100 members, alongside Myanmar military‑aligned forces. Unlike the fortified scam parks in Kokang, Muse syndicates operated out of ordinary hotels, apartments, and villas. Despite joint raids in April 2024, scam sites keep popping up like a game of Whac-a-Mole, with arrests continuing this year.

Scam arrests in junta-aligned territory

This week Naypyitaw reported the arrest of 87 scammers—75 Chinese nationals and 12 Myanmar—in the remote valley of Hopong in the Pa-O Self-Administered Zone in southern Shan. They were reportedly operating in makeshift huts, with dozens of computers, more than 500 phones and Star Link satellite dishes.

The self-administered zone, which also includes Hsihseng and Pinlaung townships, is controlled by the Pa-O National Army that is allied to the Myanmar military. Its leaders including Aung Kham Hti have close ties to regime chief Min Aung Hlaing.

The Chinese docuseries admitted that scam centers once entrenched in northern Shan State near the China–Myanmar border have relocated to Karen State’s Myawaddy on Thai border since the crackdown in late 2023 but did not say where else they have scattered. The Institute for Strategy and Policy-Myanmar has been identified scam operations in at least 17 townships in Shan including Tangyan, Laihka, Tachileik and Muse.

Taiwan warns against travel to Myanmar

Taiwan issued a fresh warning against travel to Myanmar this week, citing risks related to online scam centers, escalating conflict, and limited options for citizens’ rescue. The Taiwanese Foreign Ministry singled out the regime’s aerial massacre in Kyauktaw, Rakhine State in late September which killed at least 50 and injured 58, as evidence of insecurity.

At a press conference in Taipei, Michael Lin of the ministry’s Department of East Asian and Pacific Affairs said fighting between ethnic groups and the military regime make emergency rescues “extremely difficult.” He also warned of risks from scam centers, which are known to abduct unwary travelers, noting that its overseas missions have “almost no options” to assist citizens who get into trouble.

“If you know relatives or friends who insist on visiting these areas, make every effort to dissuade them, to avoid unnecessary trouble for themselves and their families,” Lin added.

The warning comes as the military regime intensifies its efforts to woo Chinese tourists from mainland China. Myanmar drew barely over 250,000 Chinese visitors in 2025, a sharp decline from the pre-coup boom.

Chinese explosives depot in KIA territory blows up

A blast at a Chinese road-building firm’s explosives warehouse in the village of Lagwi in Kachin State’s Chipwi Township killed seven and injured 11 on Oct. 2. The area is under the control of the Kachin Independence Army (KIA), which seized it in 2024 to secure its major export to China—rare earths.

The blast was so powerful it destroyed nearby homes and school buildings and was the third deadly incident at explosives depots in ethnic armed group territories this year. On May 31, a warehouse controlled by the Ta’ang National Liberation Army in Namhkam Township blew up, killing more than 50 and injuring over 70. And on Sept. 8, a site under the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) in Hseni exploded, leaving at least 15 dead. Chinese companies are involved in mining in both areas.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: Myanmar Regime Leader Says Will Take Back Migrants From Malaysia ‘as Soon as Possible’
World.content:
PUTRAJAYA, Malaysia—Myanmar will accept more returning migrants currently held in Malaysia “as soon as possible,” the war-torn nation’s leader said Thursday despite human rights concerns over the opaque repatriation scheme.

Min Aung Hlaing made the pledge on a visit to his counterpart in Malaysia, as he works to bring his country back into the international fold after staging a 2021 coup.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim invited Min Aung Hlaing, now installed as civilian president, for a two-day visit to discuss the return of thousands of migrants to his country.

Malaysia has historically offered safe haven to those exiled from Myanmar, hosting 190,000 refugees or asylum seekers from the nation—mostly Rohingya—according to the UN.

But Anwar is making a repatriation push amidst an uptick of anti-migrant sentiment in Malaysia, defying concerns from the UN that his scheme cannot guarantee their safe return.

The country has been wracked by war since Min Aung Hlaing’s putsch, and there are fears the persecuted Rohingya may return to a country where they suffer violent persecution many deem genocide.

“We will take those verified nationals back as soon as possible,” Min Aung Hlaing said at a joint news conference with Anwar, in Putrajaya, the administrative capital.

‘Enhance collaboration’

Min Aung Hlaing has been a pariah in many capitals abroad since his putsch unleashed a civil war, but Anwar invited him for talks about returning Myanmar migrants.

Nearly 1,500 migrants arrived in back in Myanmar on Sunday after a five-day navy vessel voyage from Malaysia, where they were being held in detention centers before being shipped out.

Anwar in July announced that Myanmar agreed to take back 5,000 Rohingya members, but the Malaysian government later said those sent back would be of “various ethnicities,” not only Rohingya.

Myanmar last month pledged “safe and dignified” returns for its citizens displaced abroad, after criticism from the UN and rights groups.

Min Aung Hlaing’s two-day trip also comes as he makes a push for diplomatic recognition after being installed in April as civilian president, following elections branded a charade by democracy watchdogs.

Leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) said in July they were seeking “gradual” engagement with Myanmar.

The 11-nation organization has frozen Myanmar out of high-level summits since the coup, presenting a united front to pressure its leaders into engaging in its conflict resolution plan.

But analysts say the consensus is now fraying.

Malaysia is the fifth ASEAN nation to host Min Aung Hlaing since he transitioned to ruling the country as nominally civilian president.

A five-point peace plan adopted by ASEAN’s leaders in April 2021, which among other things call for an immediate cessation of violence in Myanmar, has shown very little signs of progress.

This was highlighted by a Myanmar military airstrike late last month on a market in western Myanmar killing some 50 people—one of the deadliest recent bombings of the civil war.

Said Anwar on Thursday: “Malaysia will do whatever is possible to make sure that we enhance this collaboration.”

The aim ultimately was to “take Myanmar as part of our community of nations without prejudice, and particularly in the context of ASEAN.”

World.title: From Refuge to Repatriations: Malaysia’s Myanmar U-Turn
World.content:
KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia—Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim once urged his Muslim-majority nation to show solidarity with the persecuted Rohingya who fled Myanmar en masse, but this week rolled out the red carpet for the man accused of orchestrating their genocide.

Min Aung Hlaing touched down on Wednesday, invited for a two-day visit to discuss thousands of Myanmar migrants being sent back under a repatriation scheme touted by Anwar.

Malaysia has historically offered safe haven to those exiled from Myanmar by persecution or conflict.

The nation hosts 190,000 Myanmar refugees or asylum seekers, according to the UN, two-thirds of them from the Muslim Rohingya ethnic group.

But experts say fears that they burden Malaysia have been amplified by a cocktail of misinformation and an embattled Anwar, who hopes to capitalize on anti-Rohingya sentiment ahead of upcoming elections.

To carry out the repatriation plan, he has welcomed Min Aung Hlaing—previously shunned and credited with ordering the 2017 crackdown that sent legions of Rohingya fleeing to Malaysia in the first place.

Domestic hostility

Myanmar says it has repatriated around 8,000 citizens by air and 1,500 by sea so far this year, while Malaysia announced it is preparing 3,500 more to go back.

Kuala Lumpur has declined to say what proportion of returnees are Rohingya.

But experts say Malaysian attitudes towards migrants, particularly the Rohingya, soured during the COVID-19 pandemic when they became targets of misinformation about the disease.

“That hostility did not simply disappear afterwards,” Khoo Ying Hooi, an associate professor at Universiti Malaya, told AFP.

“This year there was another very visible surge in anti-Rohingya rhetoric online, alongside harassment.”

Newer resentments include claims that Malaysians are losing jobs to migrants, as well as the narrative that they are straining public resources or involved in crime.

“The early sympathy was very strong because Malaysians largely encountered the Rohingya through the language of persecution,” said Khoo.

“They were Muslims fleeing horrific violence in Myanmar, so religious solidarity and humanitarian sympathy came together quite naturally.”

But James Chin, a Malaysia expert at the University of Tasmania in Australia, said the nation was now dealing with a popular backlash against “allowing too many Rohingya to come”.

“This is ironic, because the only reason they were allowed to come in the first place is due to Islamic solidarity,” he told AFP.

“It has now changed completely the other way around.”

‘Election ploy’

In the past, Anwar appealed to Malaysians for solidarity towards migrants who fled upheaval in Myanmar credited to Min Aung Hlaing.

Min Aung Hlaing was the leader of the military when it began a 2017 crackdown evicting Rohingya in droves from their homes in western Myanmar.

The campaign is currently being weighed as a potential genocide by the International Court of Justice, but many rights monitors and some nations already deem it one.

Anwar’s about-face, which has seen him welcome Min Aung Hlaing and send back migrants, is partially due to a shift in domestic politics, experts say.

His Pakatan Harapan coalition has suffered setbacks in recent state elections in the runup to regional and national polls, which must be held by February 2028.

Among their defeats were losses to a coalition fronted by the United Malays National Organization, a formerly dominant party that draws much support from the Malay majority.

Yap Lay Sheng, a senior human rights specialist with NGO Fortify Rights, said Anwar’s repatriation push was an “election ploy” to court the vote of ethnic Malays.

“Anwar is being outflanked from the right in Malaysia. The conservatives and the nationalists have fashioned themselves as champions of the Malay majority interests.”

Targeting immigrants allows him “to be seen as a defender of the collective interest against outsiders,” said Yap, a powerful message for political campaigning.

‘Greater scrutiny’

Malaysia says all returned migrants have been sent from detention centers where they made voluntary decisions to go home.

But the UN has panned the scheme for being opaque and failing to provide guarantees of safety on return, as required by international law.

Min Aung Hlaing staged a 2021 coup that plunged the country into a grinding civil war, causing a fresh wave of upheaval sending yet more citizens fleeing abroad.

He is now making a push to normalize diplomatic ties after being installed as civilian president in April, following elections staged by his military junta and derided by democracy watchdogs.

Deals to return migrants may improve Anwar’s electoral prospects at home, but experts say it could tank Malaysia’s credibility abroad.

The repatriation came days after Malaysia’s foreign minister spoke at the UN General Assembly, advocating for international law to come to the aid of Palestinians.

“Malaysia speaks so strongly about the protection of civilians, humanitarian principles and the consistent application of international law in Palestine,” said Khoo of Universiti Malaya.

“There will inevitably be greater scrutiny of how those same principles are applied closer to home.”

World.title: Malaysian Firms Linked to Myanmar Military Aviation Supply Chain: JFM
World.content:
Several Malaysian companies, including some with direct financial ties to the state, are actively supplying or seeking to supply aircraft parts and maintenance services to the Myanmar military, which has been widely condemned for bombing its own civilian population, an investigation by Justice For Myanmar (JFM) revealed Wednesday.

JFM’s findings, based on leaked documents and commercial trade records, were announced during Myanmar coup president Min Aung Hlaing’s controversial official visit to Malaysia on October 7-8 at the invitation of Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.

The rights group said three Malaysia-based aerospace procurement and services companies—FJ Global Aeroparts (M) Sdn Bhd, Asia AeroTechnic Sdn Bhd (AAT), and Skyways Technics Asia Sdn Bhd—supplied or sought to supply parts to the regime military and its brokers, or in one case was approached to perform repairs, between 2023 and this year.

FJ Global sought to supply the regime with spare parts and critical components including weapons system parts for Russian- and Chinese-made aircraft used by the regime in its aerial campaigns, JFM said, adding that the company has sent multiple requests for quotations to international suppliers for spare parts for the regime’s warplanes and drones.

In February, FJ Global secured financing from state-backed Perbadanan Usahawan Nasional Berhad (PUNB), a company under the Prime Minister’s Department that is wholly owned by Yayasan Pelaburan Bumiputra, which is chaired by Anwar.

AAT is wholly owned by MARA Corporation, which is owned by MARA, an agency of Malaysia’s Ministry of Rural and Regional Development. According to JFM’s sources, regime military engineers visited the company in February 2026 regarding repairs to an Airbus A-319 owned by the Myanmar military.

JFM also claimed that Skyways Technics Asia, the Malaysian subsidiary of Denmark-based Skyways Technics A/S, has made numerous shipments of aircraft parts to arms brokers Light Head Group of Companies, KLS Aviation, United Five and Lucky High, which are registered suppliers to the Myanmar army’s Directorate of Procurement. JFM assessed that the Air Force was the likely end user.

Regime-controlled Myanmar National Airlines and Mingalar Aviation Airline (formerly Air KBZ), owned by the 24Hour Group founded by tycoon Aung Zaw Zaw, a crony with close ties to the junta boss, have also sought export approval to send aircraft parts to Skyways Technics in Malaysia for repair or exchange, the rights group said.

It noted that by knowingly providing support to the Myanmar military, which is widely accused of committing war crimes and crimes against humanity, Malaysian businesses could be aiding and abetting the regime’s crimes.

JFM also highlighted Malaysia’s ongoing facilitation of the regime’s participation in regional defense and security programs. Kuala Lumpur has invited a police official of the regime’s notorious Special Branch to attend the 29th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Intelligence Community Conference (AICC) in Kuala Lumpur in November.

Regime military officials were also allowed to participate in the 14th ASEAN Defense Minister’s Meeting (ADMM)-plus Experts Working Group on Counter-terrorism, which was jointly chaired by Malaysia and India in 2025.

The rights group said Malaysia’s support for the regime exposes the hypocrisy of its stated commitment to ending violence in Myanmar.

“It is deplorable that Malaysia is awarding false legitimacy to the war criminal Min Aung Hlaing and handing people back to his criminal junta while doing nothing to stop its companies from supplying a military that is committing mass atrocities,” said JFM spokesperson Yadanar Maung.

The rights group added that “Instead of taking steps to cut off the resources needed for the junta to continue its violence, Malaysia has turned a blind eye to business complicity, while providing false legitimacy to the junta and handing Myanmar people to a murderous military that threatens their lives.”

“Malaysia’s stance on the Five-Point Consensus [ASEAN’s peace plan for Myanmar] and its calls for peace in Myanmar ring hollow while it fails to stop its companies from providing the military equipment and services that support its campaign of terror against the people,” Yadanar Maung said.

On September 28, regime airstrikes on a busy market and surrounding areas in Arakan Army-administered Kyauktaw town, Rakhine State, killed 50 civilians and injured nearly 60. The deadliest-ever aerial attack on civilians in the state drew global condemnation. However, the regime has continued its deadly aerial campaign of bombing civilian targets in resistance-controlled areas across the country.

Malaysia has faced widespread criticism from international rights groups and politicians for rolling out the red carpet for Min Aung Hlaing, who faces an arrest warrant issued by an Argentine court over the military’s persecution of the Rohingya. The International Criminal Court’s prosecutor has also sought a warrant for his arrest over alleged crimes against humanity.

Malaysia recently defended its invitation as a necessary gesture to the coup leader for agreeing to receive deported Myanmar nationals.

World.title: Chinese Docuseries Hails Scam Victory as Myanmar Fraud Empire Rebuilds
World.content:
A Beijing-sanctioned docuseries on Myanmar’s scam industry has hailed the extradition of fugitive tycoon She Zhijiang as the crowning achievement of China’s crackdown. Yet the telecom fraud empire he built in the border town of Myawaddy continues to thrive despite international pressure.

Once a bustling trade hub, Myawaddy is now among the most complicated combat landscapes in Myanmar, fought over by resistance forces, splinter factions, and regime‑aligned militias each tied to cross‑border commerce and illicit economies.

The fraud industry’s origins trace back to 2016–2017, when She Zhijiang’s Yatai International Holdings struck a deal with warlord Saw Chit Thu, commander of the military-aligned Karen Border Guard Force (BGF). Marketed as a U$ 15‑billion “New City” project, Shwe Kokko was pitched as a blockchain hub but quickly morphed into casinos, call centers, and cyber‑fraud parks.

Belt and Road Beginnings

Yatai stated the project was part of the Belt and Road Initiative, Beijing’s flagship international infrastructure development scheme. Thousands of Chinese nationals poured in. But by 2020, civil society groups were sounding alarms about criminal activities under militia protection, prompting the Chinese Embassy in Yangon to declare that the project had nothing to do with the BRI.

Aung San Suu Kyi’s NLD government ordered a suspension, but admitted it was difficult to enforce given the involvement of armed groups. After the 2021 coup, civil war engulfed the country and the scam industry boomed.

Today, Myawaddy’s scam compounds are hosted by the BGF (now rebranded as the Karen National Army—KNA) and the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army (DKBA), both allied with the regime. The documentary aired this week by China’s state-run CCTV made no mention of either militia.

At its peak, more than 40 heavily guarded scam compounds operated in Myawaddy, according to a Chinese police source quoted in the docuseries.

She Zhijiang was arrested in Bangkok in August 2022 and later extradited to China, but his legacy lives on in Myanmar’s borderlands.

Crackdown ‘Backfired’

The arrest of She Zhijiang had limited impact on the Myawaddy scam economy because he was just one of many investors, said one local China analyst.

“There are other criminal syndicates with longer tentacles than She Zhijiang. Since his arrest, nearly five dozen scam sites have sprung up across Karen and Shan states,” he said, adding that Beijing’s crackdown may have worsened the problem by forcing the syndicates to relocate deeper into Myanmar.

Beijing itself admits that syndicates uprooted from northern Shan State in late 2023 regrouped in Myawaddy, swelling the scam economy there.

China finally intervened in early 2025, forced into action by public anger over the trafficking of Shanghai soap actor Wang Xing into a scam compound. Wang was lured by a fake casting offer in Bangkok, whisked across the Moei River, and resold three times in four days by Myawaddy scam compounds before being rescued.

In March 2025, Beijing established a trilateral ministerial mechanism with Bangkok and Naypyitaw to combat scam syndicates operating along the Thai-Myanmar border, pinpointing Myawaddy as a key target.

Later that year, under mounting international pressure, Myanmar’s military demolished scam compounds in Shwe Kokko and KK Park during high-profile raids. However, locals reported that syndicates simply relocated to less conspicuous sites in Myawaddy and neighboring townships, under DKBA and KNA protection.

Regime-Aligned Scam Militias Untouched

“We have a zero‑tolerance policy for crimes like online fraud and gambling,” regime boss Min Aung Hlaing declared on Police Force Day earlier this month. Yet his BGF/KNA allies—Saw Chit Thu, Saw Mote Thone, Tin Win and others—remain untouched along with scam compounds they protect that have defrauded billions of dollars from American citizens, according to US authorities.

The CCTV documentary also celebrates the extradition of Chen Zhi, accused of running a multibillion‑dollar cyberscam network from Cambodia.

Meanwhile, China’s Public Security Ministry claims telecom fraud cases have declined since October 2025, following the crackdown in northern Myanmar. Not so, states the International Organization for Migration (IOM), which reports a sharp rise in trafficking to scam centers across Asia, with victims from more than 80 countries coerced into the trade. The UN estimates compounds in Myanmar, Cambodia, and Laos still employ around 300,000 people.

Last month, Beijing unveiled the International Alliance Combating Telecom and Cyber Fraud with much fanfare, listing 46 founding countries including Myanmar. Officials hailed it as a landmark in global cooperation. Yet on the ground in Myawaddy, the scam industry remains a lucrative lifeline for militias and regime allies—a shadow economy still flourishing despite raids, indictments, and international pressure.

World.title: Kazakhstan Builds 312 Cultural Facilities in Push to Expand Arts Access, Global Reach
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan has built 312 new cultural facilities over the past seven years as part of efforts to preserve its national heritage, support domestic artists and modernize cultural infrastructure, according to the Ministry of Culture and Information’s press service.

The measures have covered theaters, museums, libraries and cultural centers, alongside the renovation of existing institutions, upgrades to equipment and efforts to expand access to cultural services across the regions.

The government has also focused on creative education and library modernization. A roadmap for upgrading libraries through 2027 is underway, while regional cultural centers are receiving infrastructure improvements. A branch of the Kazakh National University of Arts has opened in Petropavl, and work is underway to establish a University of Culture and Arts in Shymkent.

Theater network and national repertoire expand

Theater development has been one of the main priorities. Five new state theaters have been established in Astana, Atyrau, Kyzylorda and Shymkent over the past seven years. New buildings have also been provided for the Kalibek Kuanyshbayev Theater in Astana, the Sabit Mukanov Theater in Petropavl and the Turkistan Musical Drama Theater.

Construction of theaters is continuing in Aktobe and Konaev, while projects are being considered in Shymkent, Kyzylorda and Semei. Reconstruction is also underway at the Mukhtar Auezov Theater and the Natalia Sats Theater.

The status of leading cultural institutions has been strengthened. Over the past six years, 10 institutions received national status, while 10 national and regional organizations were designated academic institutions. The honorary title of People’s Artist of Kazakhstan was also reinstated after a pause of nearly three decades.

Domestic theaters have expanded their national repertoire with productions including the ballets “Kozy Korpesh – Bayan Sulu,” “Altyn Gul,” and the historical drama “Jochi Khan.”

Museums modernize as heritage preservation advances

Kazakhstan’s museum network has expanded, with the number of museums increasing from 250 to 286 over the past seven years. Museum collections grew by 68,669 items.

Five visitor centers have been completed and opened at the Tanbaly site in the Almaty Region, Otyrar and Ordabasy in the Turkistan Region, Ulytau in the Ulytau Region, and Sarayshyk in the Atyrau Region. New visitor centers are also being developed at Sauran and Gaukhar-Ana in the Turkistan Region and at Esik in the Almaty Region.

Other initiatives include the opening of Golden Horde exhibition halls in two museums, a paleontology hall and a crafts center. One of the major projects is the Bozok open-air archaeological park. The Abilkhan Kasteev National Museum of Arts has also undergone a major renovation.

Digitalization has become another focus. In 2025, Kazakhstan introduced the E-museum platform, bringing together information on 284 museums. More than 66,000 museum objects have been entered into its digital catalog, alongside 750 three-dimensional models and 15 virtual tours.

International cooperation has also expanded. Kazakh collections have been exhibited in Russia, Italy, France, China and Azerbaijan. In 2025, works from the Kasteev National Museum of Arts were displayed at the State Tretyakov Gallery, while Kazakh national projects were presented at the Venice Biennale and the Guimet Museum of Asian Arts in Paris.

In 2026, Kazakhstan hosted the International Museum Congress and the Kazakhstan-France Museology Forum.

Authorities have also strengthened legal protections for historical and cultural heritage, improved regulation of archaeological activities and established a special legal status for Turkistan as a spiritual, historical, cultural and tourism center.

Domestic cinema gains audiences and international recognition

Kazakhstan’s film industry has also expanded. From 2019 to 2025, 150 film projects received state support, of which 124 have been completed. The law on cinematography, adopted in 2019, established a legal framework for the sector’s development.

Domestic cinema has recorded growth in both releases and box office revenue. The number of Kazakh films released in theaters increased from 94 in 2024 to 103 in 2025.

Kazakh films have also gained international recognition. “Akyn,” “Scheme” and “Ademoka’s Education” received awards at film festivals in Tokyo, Berlin and Warsaw. In 2024 alone, seven Kazakh films won a combined 34 international awards, while “Bauyryna Salu” was selected as Kazakhstan’s submission for the Academy Awards.

According to the World Intellectual Property Organization’s Global Innovation Index 2024, Kazakhstan rose from 61st to 31st place in the indicator for national feature films, placing among Asia’s top three.

Kazakh cinema has also broadened its international reach, with national film days held in more than 30 countries. Cooperation with foreign film producers continues, alongside efforts to develop domestic animation and expand Kazakh-language content.

Cultural diplomacy expands Kazakhstan’s international presence

Over the past seven years, Kazakhstan has expanded its cultural presence abroad through international festivals, exhibitions, competitions and cultural exchange programs. Kazakhstan Culture Days have been held in 15 countries.

In 2023, cultural events took place in Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan. Cairo hosted events marking the 800th anniversary of Sultan Baybars, including the opening of the Sultan al-Zahir Baybars Mosque. Cultural exchanges continued in subsequent years, including with Turkmenistan.

In 2025, Kazakhstan opened a cultural center in Beijing to promote its national arts and traditions. That year, Aktau was named the Cultural Capital of the Turkic World.

Cooperation with UNESCO has also remained a priority. Kazakhstan’s World Heritage properties include the Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi and the Tamgaly petroglyphs. The source materials also identify the rock-cut mosques of the Mangystau Peninsula as an addition in 2026.

Fourteen elements of Kazakh culture are included in UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. They include the art of performing kuis on the dombra, traditional yurt-making, aitys and the betashar wedding ritual. In 2026, Kazakhstan approved a comprehensive plan to promote UNESCO cultural heritage for 2026–2028.

World.title: Rollan Seisenbayev At 80: Writer Who Carried Kazakhstan’s Voice Abroad
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan marks the 80th birthday of prominent Kazakh writer, playwright, translator, publisher and public figure Rollan Seisenbayev on Oct. 11, marking eight decades of a life closely intertwined with Kazakhstan’s literary and cultural history.

Born in Semei on Oct. 11, 1946, Seisenbayev graduated from the Semei Engineering and Technology Institute in 1970 before moving to Moscow in 1975 at the invitation of writer Georgy Markov. There, he completed the Higher Literary Courses and began a period of literary work that would bring him recognition across the Soviet Union and beyond.

His works include plays such as “Finding Yourself,” “At A Crossroads and Night Dialogue,” as well as collections of stories and novellas, including “The Day The World Collapsed.”

Seisenbayev is a winner of several international literary awards, including the Antoine de Saint-Exupéry International Prize, the Jack London International Literary Prize and an award from Columbia University. For his contribution to world culture, he was awarded the Gold Officer’s Cross of Poland, the Grand Gold Knight’s Cross of Hungary and the Order of Friendship of Cuba, all in 2006.

He is also a member of the Kazakh Writers’ Union and an academician of the World Academy of Art and Culture. Over the years, he has been named an honorary professor of several universities in Kazakhstan.

A writer shaped by life and travel

Between 1976 and 1991, Seisenbayev served as the representative of the Writers’ Union of Kazakhstan in Moscow. During those years, several of his best-known works were published, including “The Last Snow,” “The Road That Meets At The Mountain Top,” and “The Dead Wander In The Sands.”

The books established him as one of the widely read Kazakh authors of his generation and brought the realities of Kazakhstan to a broad Soviet readership. “The Throne Of Satan,” in particular, was translated into several foreign languages and received international literary recognition in Europe.

His friend, Abai scholar and candidate of technical and philosophical sciences Asan Omarov, remembers Seisenbayev as a writer who regarded life experience as an essential part of his craft.

During one journey together, Seisenbayev told Omarov that great literature could not emerge from an uneventful life. He spoke of spending decades traveling across Russia, Siberia and Kazakhstan, later extending his journeys to Europe and the United States.

“How many people I met, how many I became acquainted with — I even met unfortunate people who were in prison,” Seisenbayev recalled, according to Omarov.

Those journeys became part of the writer’s literary world. His works are marked by close attention to people, their choices and inner conflicts, alongside a deep attachment to Kazakhstan and its landscape.

“The Kazakh steppe, fragrant with wormwood, is silent. (…) You want to walk freely and peacefully across this boundless steppe. The dormant honour of the Kazakh people and their spirit, unable to flare up to their full strength, live in this vast steppe. Undoubtedly, the golden cradle of Kazakh happiness is here, in this boundless steppe,” Seisenbayev wrote in one of his works.

Omarov sees this combination of intellectual reflection, human experience and national consciousness as one of the defining features of Seisenbayev’s writing.

Preserving the memory of the Semipalatinsk tragedy

Perhaps one of the most powerful examples of Seisenbayev’s literary engagement with Kazakhstan’s history is “The Day The World Collapsed,” written in 1988 about the Semipalatinsk nuclear testing site.
