The work recalls the first hydrogen bomb test in the region through the eyes and memories of those who witnessed it.

In one passage, Seisenbayev describes the confusion in a village near the Shyngystau mountains:

“The residents of the Shyngystau area encountered this disaster in the summer of 1953. It came suddenly, unexpectedly. (…) We, the children, could not understand what God had disturbed the peace of our quiet village. We stood bewildered, unable to understand anything. Has the war begun?”

The account then moves from confusion to the terrifying moment of the explosion. For Omarov, the importance of the book extends beyond its literary value. It preserves the testimony of a generation that experienced the consequences of nuclear testing first-hand.

“Almost all the witnesses of this terrible tragedy, of these scenes as if the end of the world had come, have passed away,” Omarov writes. “Therefore, we should be immensely grateful to Rollan-aga [a respectful Kazakh form of address] for preserving this tragedy in a book and leaving it for future generations.”

The work was translated into numerous languages and brought Seisenbayev international recognition.

A lifelong commitment to Abai

Seisenbayev’s connection to Abai is another important thread running through his literary and cultural work. During his years in Moscow, he contributed to promoting Abai’s legacy internationally. His wife Klara Seisenbayeva translated Abai’s “Qara Sozder” (Words of Wisdom) into Russian.

His commitment to the great Kazakh thinker later took a more institutional form. In 1995, Seisenbayev helped open the Abai House in London. In 2001, he established the International Abai Club and the Amanat literary magazine. Through the club and the magazine, some 200 volumes of works by classics of world literature were published, creating a platform for cultural exchange between Kazakhstan and the wider literary world.

These efforts reflected Seisenbayev’s understanding of literature not simply as a profession, but as a way of preserving cultural memory and connecting societies.

More than a writer

Seisenbayev’s life has also included a less familiar chapter: sport. Omarov recalls watching the young Seisenbayev compete in a wrestling tournament in Semei in 1968, when he was still a student at the Technological Institute.

“We were a group of schoolchildren watching the final,” Omarov recalls. “Suddenly the hall erupted. One of the young wrestlers lifted his opponent, threw him over his shoulder and, after turning several times, slammed him onto the mat.”

A spectator sitting nearby identified the athlete as Seisenbayev, describing him as a student of the Technological Institute who repeatedly won using the same technique.

Seisenbayev later received the title of master of sport of the Soviet Union in wrestling. For Omarov, however, one of his friend’s most important qualities was not his literary fame or sporting achievements, but his willingness to support the work of others.

Supporting the next generation of scholars

Omarov recalls this personally. In 2008, he completed a research book on the life of Shakarim Kudaiberdiuly ahead of the poet and philosopher’s 150th anniversary. After completing the manuscript, Omarov struggled to find a way to publish it. He eventually learned that Seisenbayev was preparing Shakarim’s collected works in Almaty and sent him the manuscript.

“Two or three days passed, and Rollan-aga called me himself: ‘I read your book and could not put it down until dawn. Even tears came to my eyes. My dear Asan, your work is wonderful. I will immediately include it in the third volume, so don’t worry!’” Omarov recalls.

The study was subsequently published in the third volume of Shakarim’s collected works. Later that year, in an interview with Egemen Kazakhstan, Seisenbayev spoke warmly of Omarov’s research.

“There is a talented young man named Asan Omarov in Semei. He is thoroughly and carefully studying the biography of Kudaiberdiuly, pursuing deep analysis and discoveries that encourage new thinking. His pen is swift, his heart is pure, and he possesses many qualities of a true researcher. I was impressed by him,” Seisenbayev said.

For Omarov, the episode remains an example of his friend’s broader contribution to Kazakhstan’s cultural life, supporting not only his own literary work but also those engaged in preserving the country’s intellectual heritage.

A legacy beyond literature

Looking back at Seisenbayev’s career, Omarov sees a writer whose work has been closely connected with the major questions of his time: the human cost of nuclear testing, national identity, the legacy of Abai, the relationship between generations and the place of Kazakh culture in the wider world.

His literary career has also been accompanied by extensive public and publishing work, from promoting Kazakh literature abroad to bringing works of world literature to Kazakh readers. Now living in Almaty, Seisenbayev continues to share his experience with younger generations through lectures and meetings with students, keeping his connection with readers and aspiring writers alive.

World.title: Yuezhi Mystery: Archaeologists Search Kazakhstan for Lost Traces
World.content:
ASTANA – Chinese and Kazakh archaeologists have launched a joint study of archaeological sites in Kazakhstan that may link to the ancient Yuezhi people, Wang Jianxin, chief professor at Northwest University’s Research Center for Archaeological Cooperation on the Silk Road in Xi’an, said on the sidelines of an international archaeological symposium in Astana.

The Yuezhi were an ancient people known primarily through Chinese historical records. According to Wang, the Greater Yuezhi are recorded in Chinese literature, while the location of archaeological remains associated with them remained largely unknown.

In 2000, Chinese archaeologists began excavations in northwestern China and identified what they believe was a major Greater Yuezhi settlement on the eastern edge of the Tianshan Mountains. Following conflicts with the Xiongnu, part of the Yuezhi population moved westward from China to Central Asia, passing through Zhetysu toward the Amu Darya basin.

“Western sources contain very little information about Yuezhi. That is why I began researching the subject 26 years ago. I initially searched for traces of the Yuezhi in China and later continued my research in Kazakhstan and other parts of Central Asia,” Wang told Kazinform news agency. .

Wang said sites associated with the Yuezhi may have existed in what is now Kazakhstan as early as the Early Iron Age.

The joint research by Chinese and Kazakh scholars is currently focused on two areas, such as the Altai Region in the East Kazakhstan Region and the Kazakh part of Zhetysu.

The first stage will involve archaeological surveys. Researchers will look for similarities between sites in Kazakhstan and previously studied sites in China that have been associated with the Yuezhi.

“First, we will clarify the findings. Then, we may conduct small-scale excavations,” Wang said.

Wang has conducted archaeological research along the Silk Road since 1999, focusing in part on locating traces of the ancient Yuezhi in Central Asia. In 2009, he led a Chinese archaeological team to Uzbekistan to conduct field surveys. The team identified the Sazagan site, associated with Kangju-era noble tombs, and the Rabat site, where researchers found remains believed to be linked to the Yuezhi.

According to Wang, some Yuezhi sites in Kazakhstan may have been discovered and even studied by archaeologists, but their connection to the ancient people has not yet been established.

Archaeologists may have already discovered and studied some Yuezhi sites in Kazakhstan, but their connection to the ancient people has yet to be established.

“These sites may have been excavated, but their identity was not recognized,” Wang said.

He plans to publish annual reports on the joint research results and eventually prepare a monograph.

World.title: Why Belgium’s Royal Visit to Kazakhstan Matters Beyond Diplomacy
World.content:
ASTANA – Belgium’s King Philippe and Queen Mathilde will make their first state visit to Kazakhstan on Oct. 11-14, bringing a high-level government, business and academic delegation to talks on critical minerals, transport routes, health care and artificial intelligence as the two countries seek to expand economic ties.

The visit, the first Belgian state visit to Central Asia, comes as Europe looks to diversify critical raw material supplies and strengthen transport links with the region. For Kazakhstan, closer ties with Belgium offer access to European technology, investment and logistics expertise as Astana works to broaden its economic partnerships and reduce its dependence on traditional export routes.

The royal couple will visit Astana, where they are scheduled to meet President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, before travelling to Almaty. They will be accompanied by a 110-member delegation, including senior Belgian government officials, 25 business executives and academic representatives.

The foreign ministries are also expected to sign a 2026-2029 roadmap, according to an official government release, and the fourth meeting of the Kazakh-Belgian Business Council is also scheduled.

“It will provide an opportunity to highlight success stories and explore new forms of cooperation in logistics and agriculture, two areas in which Belgium and Kazakhstan already enjoy close collaboration,” reads Belgium’s official government release.

Philippe previously visited Kazakhstan three times as crown prince, in 2002, 2009 and 2010. This will be his first visit as king. As a crown prince, he travelled to Baikonur cosmodrome in 2002 and 2009 for the launches of Belgian astronaut Frank De Winne’s missions to the International Space Station. He returned in 2010 to lead an economic mission to the country.

The royal visit also reflects a broader effort by Kazakhstan to strengthen European partnerships as geopolitical tensions reshape trade routes, investment decisions and access to strategic resources.

President Tokayev paid an official visit to Brussels in November 2021, which was his first official visit to Europe since the pandemic and his first to Belgium as the country’s president. He also traveled to Brussels in June and Berlin and Munich in September this year, underscoring Astana’s efforts to translate closer political relations into investment, trade and industrial cooperation.

“In the face of current geopolitical challenges, Belgium intends to diversify its partnerships and strengthen its presence in a region that offers significant strategic opportunities. It wishes to deepen its cooperation with Kazakhstan, in order to build a more sustainable, resilient and prosperous future together,” reads an official Belgium government release.

What do the two countries trade

Belgium’s trade with Kazakhstan has also grown over the past several years, although the latest figures show uneven momentum. Bilateral trade reached $582.4 million in 2025, up nearly 28% from the previous year, according to the Kazakh government. Kazakhstan exported $311.5 million in goods to Belgium and imported $270.9 million.

Kazakhstan is also an important Central Asian market for Belgian exporters. Figures from the Belgian Foreign Trade Agency show that Belgian goods exports to Kazakhstan in 2025 were nearly five times those to either Uzbekistan or the Kyrgyz Republic.

Within the European Union, Belgium ranked seventh among exporters of goods to Kazakhstan in 2025, accounting for 5.7% of the bloc’s 10.6 billion euros (US$11.9 billion) in exports. It ranked 14th among EU importers of Kazakh goods, with a 0.5% share of the EU’s approximately 30.9 billion euros (US$34.6 billion) in imports.

The two countries trade largely different products. Pharmaceuticals lead Belgium’s exports to Kazakhstan. Chemical and pharmaceutical products, primarily medicines, immunological products and vaccines, accounted for 48.4% of Belgian goods exports in 2025, worth 292.5 million euros (US$327.8 million). Machinery and equipment, along with transport equipment, were also among the leading export categories.

Kazakhstan’s exports to Belgium remain concentrated in a handful of commodities. Vegetable products, primarily linseed, accounted for 46.2% of Belgian goods imports from Kazakhstan, worth 74.6 million euros (US$83.6 million). Mineral products, largely molybdenum ores and concentrates, followed at 61.1 million euros (US$64.5 million), or 37.9%. Base metals, including ferroalloys and refined copper, made up another 8.8%.

Belgium has also been a substantial source of foreign investment in Kazakhstan, with gross foreign direct investment inflows exceeding $14 billion between 2005 and 2025, including $1.045 billion last year. To facilitate trade cooperation, Belgium established a Trade Office AWEX in Almaty in 2007. In 2021, a Chamber of Commerce for the countries of Benelux, Belgium, the Netherlands, and Luxemburg, was launched.

“Kazakhstan and Belgium have significant potential to expand cooperation, particularly in investment, transport and logistics, industry and technology. For Kazakhstan, Belgium is not only an economic partner in its own right but also a major industrial, financial and logistics hub within the European Union,” Alisher Abdreshev, a lead expert in the Department for European and American Studies at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies, told The Astana Times.

He sees Kazakhstan’s appeal extending beyond its domestic market. “Kazakhstan can offer Belgian businesses an integrated platform for industrial production, logistics and access to the wider Eurasian market,” he said.

“Kazakhstan can offer opportunities in specific export sectors. In 2025, Kazakh exports to Belgium rose 48% to $311.5 million, with linseed accounting for a significant share. Kazakhstan is already a leading supplier of linseed to the European Union, while Belgium is the largest European market for Kazakh linseed,” said the expert.

Agricultural processing offers one potential avenue for moving beyond commodity trade. In August, Kazakhstan’s Foreign Ministry reported talks with Belgian companies Maselis Group and Borlix NV on food ingredients, processing and possible investment projects.

Critical minerals: moving beyond raw material exports

Critical minerals are also expected to feature prominently in the discussions, reflecting Europe’s efforts to diversify its supplies of materials essential for clean energy technologies, electronics and advanced manufacturing. Kazakhstan says it has 21 of the 34 raw materials identified as critical by the European Union.

“Belgium, meanwhile, has a well-developed chemical industry, advanced metallurgical technologies and expertise in materials processing. This creates opportunities to move beyond trade in raw materials toward joint manufacturing projects that generate greater added value,” said Abdreshev.

“Potential areas of cooperation include metals processing, industrial component manufacturing and the development of resilient supply chains serving European markets. Such partnerships would support Kazakhstan’s efforts to diversify its economy while aligning with the European Union’s goal of diversifying its sources of strategic raw materials,” he explained.

The two countries have explored cooperation in sustainable metallurgy and critical raw materials through Belgian research institutions, including KU Leuven. The cooperation also aligns with the strategic partnership on sustainable raw materials, batteries and renewable hydrogen that Kazakhstan and the EU established in 2022.

Transport connectivity

Transport and logistics are another priority as Kazakhstan seeks to strengthen its position along trade routes connecting Asia and Europe.

Kazakhstan’s Caspian ports of Aktau and Kuryk, which form part of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, could open opportunities for Belgian logistics companies seeking access to Central Asian and Chinese markets, Abdreshev said. One of the companies with ongoing projects is Jan De Nul, a major Belgian family-owned engineering and construction company specializing in dredging, marine and port infrastructure, offshore energy and complex engineering projects.

The expert also pointed to Kazakhstan’s existing investment infrastructure and experience working with European companies.

“Kazakhstan is seeking Belgian technology and management expertise to develop the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, also known as the Middle Corridor. The Port of Antwerp-Bruges, one of Europe’s largest logistics hubs, could play a key role in these efforts. Its expertise in digitalizing port operations, multimodal transport and cargo management could help modernize Kazakhstan’s ports of Aktau and Kuryk,” said Abdreshev.

Technology, health care and academic cooperation

The royal visit is also expected to advance cooperation in artificial intelligence and health care.

During Tokayev’s June visit to Brussels, Kazakhstan signed cooperation agreements with Ghent University and KU Leuven covering joint research, academic exchanges and technological development. One of them brought together the Serikbayev East Kazakhstan technical University, KU Leuven and the SIM2 KU Leuven Institute for Sustainable Metals and Minerals, along with Astana Hub.

The Ghent University partnership focused on establishing a mirror research laboratory in Kazakhstan focused on mathematical modeling, scientific computing, digital twins and AI. The agreements provide a foundation for further collaboration between Kazakh and Belgian universities, including research projects linked to European scientific programs.

Health care is another established area of economic cooperation, given Belgium’s strong pharmaceutical exports to Kazakhstan. The visit could provide opportunities to explore further cooperation in medical technologies, pharmaceutical production and research.

“The greatest potential for Kazakhstan-Belgium cooperation therefore lies in moving beyond traditional trade toward deeper investment and technological partnerships. Belgium could become an important partner in Kazakhstan’s efforts to modernize its industries and expand access to European markets. For Belgian businesses, Kazakhstan offers opportunities as Central Asia’s largest economy and a gateway to broader regional markets,” said Abdreshev.

“The upcoming visit of the King of Belgium to Kazakhstan could provide an opportunity to translate this potential into concrete results, including a portfolio of joint investment and infrastructure projects aimed at strengthening long-term economic ties,” he added.

Broader European push

“Amid continued tensions between Russia and the West, the restructuring of global supply chains and growing competition for strategic resources, Europe is showing increasing interest in Central Asia,” said Abdreshev. “Kazakhstan holds particular significance for the European Union as an energy supplier, a country with substantial mineral reserves and a key transit link between Europe and Asia. Astana, in turn, is seeking to attract European investment and technology while diversifying its export routes.”

“What is particularly important is that Kazakhstan is increasingly approaching its relations with Europe through the lens of its own economic interests,” he added.

For Kazakhstan, closer engagement with Belgium fits into a broader effort to diversify its economic partnerships while maintaining relations with other major powers. The European dimension offers opportunities to attract technology and investment, develop alternative trade routes and build industries that extend beyond raw-material exports.

World.title: Türkiye Opens EU-Backed Railway Link to Boost Europe-Central Asia Connectivity
World.content:
ASTANA — Türkiye inaugurated a new railway section near its border with Bulgaria on Oct. 9, marking a step in the European Union’s efforts to strengthen transport links with Central Asia and reduce shipping times along the Middle Corridor.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos attended the opening of the 153-kilometer Cerkezkoy-Kapikule section, part of the larger Halkali-Kapikule railway connecting Istanbul to the Bulgarian border.

The project received 275 million euros ($308 million) in EU grant funding through the Instrument for Pre-Accession Assistance (IPA II), according to an Oct. 8 statement from the European Commission.

The commission described the railway as the largest infrastructure project undertaken so far in EU-Türkiye cooperation and the first concrete result of its cross-regional Connectivity Agenda, which seeks to strengthen transport, energy and digital connections between Europe and Central Asia through the South Caucasus and the Black Sea region.

The new railway section is expected to ease congestion and improve freight capacity along the western end of the Middle Corridor that links China and Europe through Kazakhstan, the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkey.

According to the commission, the new high-speed connection will help reduce transit times along the corridor, which has gained strategic importance as countries seek alternative trade routes between Europe and Asia.

The newly opened section is the longest stretch of the 229-kilometer Halkali-Kapikule railway project. The new section begins in Cerkezkoy in the northwestern province of Tekirdağ and extends to Kapikule, a major road and rail border crossing near Edirne in northwestern Türkiye.

Erdogan said the broader project is expected to reduce freight transport times between Halkali and Kapikule from 8.5 hours to 3.5 hours, while cutting passenger journeys from four hours to 1.5 hours.

Rail capacity is also expected to increase approximately fourfold, with annual freight capacity projected to rise from 1.5 million tons to 9.5 million tons, according to the Turkish officials.

The inauguration follows the EU’s launch of its Connectivity Agenda Platform in June, when it announced agreements with international financial institutions expected to mobilize up to two billion euros for strategic transport and infrastructure investments in the Black Sea region and the South Caucasus.

A day before the railway inauguration, Kos attended an international conference on Corridor VIII in Sofia, Bulgaria, where officials discussed efforts to complete missing transport connections through Bulgaria, North Macedonia and Albania.

“Europe has learnt the hard way that excessive dependencies make us vulnerable. We have seen that energy blackmail, critical raw material shortages, or overreliance on a small number of key trading routes can all limit our freedom to act. We need to diversify our options,” she said at the conference.

The opening of the section also comes less than two weeks after a World Bank report highlighted the economic potential of improved transport connections along the corridor. The Sept. 28 report estimated that targeted investments and reforms could more than triple trade volumes, halve transit times and create two million additional jobs across the region by 2040.

World.title: Can Kazakhstan Turn North-South Transit Into Economic Gains?
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan’s development of the North-South transport corridor could open new export markets, diversify trade routes and strengthen the country’s position as a regional transit hub, according to Kazakh experts. They say realizing these opportunities will depend on infrastructure improvements, competitive tariffs and closer coordination among participating countries.

The corridor gained fresh attention on Oct. 8, when President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev addressed the eighth Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan in Turkmenistan’s Avaza National Tourist Zone. Tokayev highlighted growing demand for the Middle Corridor while reaffirming the strategic importance of the North-South route.

The two corridors serve different geographical directions. The Middle Corridor connects China and Central Asia with Azerbaijan and European markets through the Caspian Sea, while the North-South network provides access to Iran, the Persian Gulf and South Asian markets.

According to Arman Yeshmuratov, a political scientist and expert at the Kazakhstan Institute for Public Development (KIPD), Tokayev’s remarks reflect Kazakhstan’s strategy of diversifying transport routes and expanding economic partnerships.

“Developing the North-South route could expand Kazakh enterprises’ access to new markets and boost freight transportation. Achieving this requires infrastructure modernization, coordinated logistics solutions and simplified customs procedures,” said Yeshmuratov.

The geographical advantages of the route are particularly relevant for Kazakhstan’s landlocked economy, where access to distant markets depends on reliable and commercially competitive transit connections.

KIPD expert Almat Nukenov said the corridor’s economic benefits should ultimately be measured through the opportunities available to Kazakh businesses.

“For Kazakhstan, its value should be reflected in orders for domestic carriers, revenue from logistics services and opportunities for exporters. The outcome depends on tariffs, delivery reliability and how the benefits are distributed among participants,” said Nukenov.

“The wider the choice available to our enterprises, the less dependent they are on individual routes and the stronger the country’s negotiating position. The North-South route should be assessed precisely by how much it expands that choice,” he added.

The approach is consistent with Kazakhstan’s broader transport policy. In his September 2025 state-of-the-nation address, Tokayev identified the North-South, East-West and Trans-Caspian corridors as interconnected components of the country’s transit system, calling for infrastructure investment, digitalization and greater economic returns from freight transportation.

Growing freight demand and access to markets

Recent government figures indicate increasing demand for the southern transport direction, creating opportunities for Kazakhstan to expand its participation in regional and international trade.

According to Kazakhstan’s Ministry of National Economy, freight transportation along the North-South corridor increased 12% in 2025, reaching 3.5 million tons. Trade turnover between Kazakhstan and Iran grew 26.4% to $430.2 million over the same period.

The ministry reported these figures during bilateral discussions on transport corridors, port infrastructure and investment cooperation. Kazakhstan also proposed developing a joint infrastructure modernization road map with Iran, aimed at increasing the corridor’s capacity to 20 million tons annually.

Didar Tebayev, a KIPD expert, pointed to Kazakhstan’s railway connections with Turkmenistan, which form part of the eastern branch of the North-South corridor.

According to the Ministry of Transport, railway freight transportation between Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan increased 46% in the first five months of 2026, reaching 1 million tons, while cargo volumes along the China-Kazakhstan-Turkmenistan-Iran route grew 2.5 times.

Tebayev also highlighted the potential for expanding business activity along the corridor, particularly in logistics, manufacturing and higher-value exports.

“These measures will help establish transport, logistics and manufacturing enterprises along the route and facilitate the supply of higher-value goods. The combined effect of joint projects will create new jobs, support small and medium-sized businesses and help build a sustainable, self-sufficient trade and production system,” he said.

Tebayev emphasized that businesses also need predictable transportation costs and delivery conditions to take advantage of these trade opportunities.

“Businesses need clear conditions for accessing infrastructure, predictable transportation costs and accountability for delays or cargo safety. Mutual recognition of electronic transport documents and advance data exchanges between customs authorities should also be expanded,” he said.

Infrastructure and the cost of coordination

The growing demand for freight services places attention on how efficiently participating countries can manage cargo across their respective transport networks.

At a forum in Ashgabat on Dec. 12, 2025, Tokayev emphasized the modernization of railway, port and road infrastructure to create a seamless transport system, Tebayev recalled. He noted that the practical challenge is ensuring that border crossings and changes between transport operators do not result in additional delays and unpredictable expenses for businesses.

The Ministry of National Economy has also highlighted efforts to improve coordination among countries along the route. During talks with Iran, officials discussed a forthcoming four-party tariff agreement involving Kazakhstan, Russia, Turkmenistan and Iran, alongside an existing five-party railway agreement involving China, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran and Türkiye.

These arrangements address different aspects of corridor development, from freight tariffs to railway cooperation, with their commercial value depending on how effectively participating countries implement them.

Kamila Amurtayeva, an expert consultant at KIPD, emphasized that major transport projects require long-term investment and dependable agreements among the countries involved.

“Transport projects are always designed to last for years. They involve significant investment, infrastructure and commitments from several states. Before investing, partners need to understand how reliable the agreements will be and whether their shared interest will remain in the future,” said Amurtayeva.

She noted that maintaining established partnerships while developing new transport opportunities can strengthen the predictability of Kazakhstan’s economic relationships.

“The ability to expand the range of opportunities while maintaining consistency in partnerships gives foreign policy strategic stability. For Kazakhstan, the more reliable its agreements with partners are, the greater its opportunities to turn its geographical position into a lasting economic advantage,” she said.

World.title: Art of Betashar: Issatay Issabayev’s Lifelong Dialogue with Kazakh Tradition
World.content:
ASTANA – The centuries-old Kazakh tradition of betashar, the ceremonial unveiling of a bride’s face, takes center stage in an exhibition of works by renowned Kazakh artist Issatay Issabayev, which opened in Astana on Oct. 8. The exhibition continues a nationwide series of events marking the 90th anniversary of Issabayev’s birth.

According to Saltanat Sabyr, the exhibition’s curator, the event offers a variety of perspectives on the artist, who is best known as a graphic artist and illustrator.

“This exhibition is radically different from all the previous ones. Its uniqueness lies in the fact that it is based on a single work and theme – betashar,” Sabyr told The Astana Times.

Literature was one of the main sources of inspiration for Issabayev, particularly Kazakh folklore and epic works. For this exhibition, however, he is presented not simply as an illustrator but as an independent researcher of Kazakh traditions.

“He is not illustrating someone else’s work or folklore. Instead, he presents his own analysis and perspective on the culture and traditions of the Kazakh nomads,” Sabyr said.

According to the artist’s daughter, Aliya Tulenova, the works on display are part of a series exploring a theme her father worked on throughout much of his life.

“In 1967, my father created a work dedicated to Mukhtar Auezov, which includes a small episode of Abai’s wedding to his wife. In 1968, he worked on a piece dedicated to Kambar Batyr, which also features a wedding theme. In 1973, he traveled to Semey and designed a cinema, where he made sketches, including a scene with a bride,” Tulenova said.

She noted that Issabayev later developed the theme through a series of graphic works inspired by Kazakh heroic epics.

“In 2002, he created a 2-by-3-meter canvas painting devoted specifically to the theme of betashar. From 1965 until the end of his life, he continued to explore this subject,” Tulenova said.

Explaining her father’s longstanding interest in the tradition, Tulenova said wedding scenes were a natural part of his work because of his focus on Kazakh epic literature.

“Epics contain several important moments. There is the birth of a batyr, his heroic deeds and, when he grows older, his marriage. A wedding is one of the stages in many epics. I think that is why the theme of weddings was also present in my father’s work,” she said.

The meaning behind betashar

Betashar is a traditional Kazakh wedding ritual in which the bride’s face is initially covered and then unveiled as she is formally introduced to her husband’s relatives. In Kazakh tradition, covering a person’s face carries a strong symbolic meaning and is traditionally associated with death. Against this cultural background, the unveiling of the bride’s face during betashar can be understood as a symbolic end of her previous life and the beginning of a new one as a member of her husband’s family. The bride is thus symbolically “reborn” into a new stage of life, receiving blessings as she enters her new family.

Another important element of the ceremony is the bride’s introduction to her new relatives. A traditional singer or dombyra player names the members of the groom’s family, helping the bride recognize her new relatives and her place within the family.

In 2024, betashar was inscribed on the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization’s (UNESCO) Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

World.title: Nation Commemorates Kassym Amanzholov’s 115th Anniversary: Voice That Shaped Kazakh Poetry
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan marks the 115th anniversary of the birth of Kassym Amanzholov, one of the most influential Kazakh poets and translators of the 20th century, on Oct. 10. He is remembered for his distinctive poetic voice, powerful wartime poetry and contribution to the development of modern Kazakh literature.

Amanzholov was also among the poets who expanded the expressive possibilities of Kazakh verse, including through the use of a 10-syllable line that allowed poetry to more naturally convey conversational intonation.

He was born in 1911 in what is now the Karkaraly district of the Karaganda Region. He lost his parents at an early age and was raised by his older brother for several years. Amanzholov received his first education at a newly established rural school. In 1924, his brother enrolled him in a boarding school in Semipalatinsk, where he studied until 1927. He then spent three years at the Semipalatinsk Veterinary College, where he wrote his first poems.

In 1930, Amanzholov moved to Almaty and worked for the “Leninshil Zhas” newspaper. A year later, he entered the Forestry Institute in Leningrad, now St. Petersburg. However, health problems and a lack of interest in the field led him to return to Kazakhstan several years later.

He joined the “Ekpindi Kurylys” newspaper in Uralsk, now Oral, where the city played an important role in his development as a poet and public figure.

Finding his voice

Amanzholov’s early poems appeared in newspapers including “Leninshil Zhas,” “Kyzyl Asker,” and “Pioner”. In Uralsk, he wrote some of his first poems about love and youth.

In 1935, after completing his military service, Amanzholov organized a theater troupe and became its artistic director. The troupe soon developed into a full-fledged theater, while Amanzholov’s talents as a poet, singer and performer attracted wider public attention.

He was a gifted musician who played the dombyra, accordion, violin, and piano. He also composed music for his own poems, including “Dariga” and “Tugan El,” which remain among his best-known songs.

From 1936 to 1941, Amanzholov lived in Almaty and worked for “Socialist Kazakhstan” and the Union of Writers of Kazakhstan. Alongside poetry, he wrote articles, essays and satirical pieces. He published his first collection, “Omir Syry” (the Secret of Life), in 1938.

The following years marked a period of major creative growth. Poems such as “Nar Tauekel,” “Dauyl,” “Kokshetau,” “Oramal,” “Zaula, Zaula Turksib” and “Sultanmakhmut Turaly Ballada” reflected the breadth of his ideas, emotional depth and expressive language.

His work as a translator further expanded his literary horizons. He translated poetry by Alexander Pushkin, Mikhail Lermontov, Taras Shevchenko, Lord Byron and Vladimir Mayakovsky into Kazakh.

In 1940, he translated nearly a dozen of Mayakovsky’s poems. The translations were published in 1941 as a collection titled “Bar Dauyspen” (In Full Voice).

Poetry shaped by war

When the Second World War began, Amanzholov was called up for military service. Although he was eligible for an exemption, he refused it and volunteered for the front.

On his way to the front, his train passed through Uralsk. The journey inspired his famous poems about the Ural River, in which he addressed the river as a symbol of his homeland while preparing to leave for war.

Between 1941 and 1943, Amanzholov served in the Far East before being transferred to the western front. He remained there until the end of the war.

The experience profoundly influenced his poetry. Works such as “Oral,” “Saryarka,” “Baikal” and “Otip Baryp Zhatyrmyn” captured his feelings about his homeland and the long journey across Kazakhstan. Other poems, including “Ustimde Sur Shinelim,” “Martbek” and “Zhenis Dauysy” reflected the realities of military life. Meanwhile, “Elge Khat,” “Dostar Qaida Zhursinder?” and “Agaiyga’ focused on the inner world of a soldier separated from his homeland, family and friends.

One of Amanzholov’s most significant works emerged in 1943. He dedicated his poem “Akyn Olіmi Turaly Anyz” (The Legend of the Poet’s Death) to his friend, young poet Abdulla Zhumagaliyev, who was surrounded by enemy forces and died in battle. The poem brought Amanzholov widespread recognition and became one of the landmark works of Kazakh wartime poetry.

A literary bridge between generations

After the war, Amanzholov continued publishing his wartime poetry while producing new works. His poem “Bizdin Dastan” and the collection “Dauyl” appeared during the postwar years. Other collections, including “Balbobek,” “Nurly Dunie” and “Tandamaly Shygarmalar” (Selected Works), followed between 1949 and 1952.

Kazakh writer and Honored Figure of Kazakhstan Sabit Dosanov, who studied Amanzholov’s work and wrote about his life, described him as a “golden bridge” between two generations of Kazakh poets.

According to Dosanov, Amanzholov emerged between the generation of poets who were repressed during the Soviet period and the literary generation that followed. After the deaths and persecution of major figures such as Magzhan Zhumabayev, Shakarim Kudaiberdiuly, Saken Seifullin and Ilyas Zhansugurov, Amanzholov helped fill a major gap in Kazakhstan’s literary development.

“Amanzholov was a poet-innovator who moved away from the didactic traditions of earlier poetry. His war poems were distinguished by their realism and emotional depth, portraying not only heroism and patriotism but also the pain of war and the longing of young soldiers for their homeland and peaceful life,” Dosanov said.

Amanzholov’s health began to deteriorate in 1947, and he was periodically confined to bed. Yet illness did not stop him from writing. His poem “Ozim Turaly” (About Myself) reflects on his life and his calling as a poet.

He took part in the opening of the Third Congress of Writers of Kazakhstan in September-October 1954. His health worsened later that year, and he died on Jan. 18, 1955, at the age of 43.

Despite his relatively short life, Amanzholov left a substantial literary legacy. Some of his poems and songs have been lost, but his surviving works were collected in a four-volume edition published between 1977 and 1980.

World.title: Saturday march in Tbilisi highlights systemic problems in prisons. “Protests in Georgia” video podcast
World.content:
The “Saturday marches” are part of an ongoing protest movement that has continued in Georgia for 682 days.

Protesters are demanding that Georgia return to the path of European integration and that all political prisoners be released. They are also calling for the repeal of all anti-democratic laws passed by the ruling Georgian Dream party over the past two years.

Protesters and opposition parties point out that part of Georgian society still does not recognise the results of the parliamentary election held in autumn 2024. They are calling for early parliamentary elections.

Over the course of nearly two years of protests, dozens of people have been arrested. Many have been charged with criminal offences and sentenced to prison.

For the first time in independent Georgia’s history, the country has around 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the independent media outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. She was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer.

The protests continue despite an intensifying crackdown on civil society and the media.

World.title: Georgia’s Prosecutor’s Office launches investigation into National Bank Council member
World.content:
Georgia national bank member in corruption probe

Georgia’s Prosecutor’s Office has launched an investigation into the possible unlawful involvement of Nana Keinishvili, a member of the National Bank of Georgia’s Council, in business activities.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office, its investigative department launched a probe under Article 337 of the Criminal Code, which criminalises the unlawful involvement of a public official or an equivalent person in business activities. The investigation follows complaints by the management of Bitexchange LLC, which were forwarded by the National Bank.

According to an investigation by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, the National Bank fined cryptocurrency company Bitexchange, in which Keinishvili had unsuccessfully sought a stake, in what could be seen as an act of retaliation.

The National Bank said that, in order to protect the institution’s reputation, its Council would consider at its next meeting temporarily suspending Keinishvili’s participation in Council meetings while the investigation is under way, until the circumstances of the case are fully clarified.

Nana Keinishvili was elected to the National Bank’s Council in September 2023. From 2012 to 2016, she served as a member of parliament representing the ruling Georgian Dream party and as deputy chair of the parliamentary Finance and Budget Committee.

Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili said former president Salome Zourabichvili should be asked how she selected Nana Keinishvili as a candidate for the National Bank of Georgia’s Council.

“This once again shows how important it is for parliament to also familiarise itself with these matters and, in this case, examine in detail the issues surrounding the election of Council members. Salome Zourabichvili herself should answer the remaining questions. What matters is that the state is responding to this issue,” Papuashvili said.

He added, however, that he could not go into the details of the investigation.

It has emerged, however, that the parliament speaker, like current Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, voted in parliament in favour of appointing Nana Keinishvili to the National Bank of Georgia’s Council.

Details of the case

According to the National Bank, it reviewed submissions from the management of Bitexchange LLC and conducted a preliminary internal investigation within the scope of its authority.

The materials were forwarded to the relevant authorities for legal assessment, as the matter falls outside the mandate established for the National Bank by law. The bank expressed hope that the facts of the case would be established objectively as soon as possible.

The bank also explained that Bitexchange, a virtual asset service provider, had been fined following a routine inspection for violating anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing regulations.

Nana Keinishvili

According to the Prosecutor’s Office, the management of Bitexchange claims that Keinishvili is involved in business activities and directly controls a network of companies subject to regulation by the National Bank.

They allege that shares in these companies are registered in the names of her family members and affiliated individuals. The company’s management also claims that Keinishvili attempted to acquire a stake in their business.

The Prosecutor’s Office notes that Georgia’s Law on the Fight Against Corruption prohibits public officials from engaging in business activities. Furthermore, under the Organic Law on the National Bank of Georgia, members of the National Bank’s Council and their family members are prohibited from being partners in a Georgian financial sector entity or a legal entity affiliated with one.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office, the investigation will examine the circumstances surrounding Nana Keinishvili’s possible unlawful involvement in business activities. The public will be informed of the results of the investigation in due course.

Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty investigation

The National Bank has not disclosed the amount of the fine. However, according to the investigation by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, Nana Keinishvili demanded a stake in a cryptocurrency company regulated by the National Bank. The company’s owner refused to give up a share, after which the National Bank fined the company 572 million lari (approximately $211.85 million).

The investigation also found that Keinishvili and her family members own and manage profitable businesses regulated by the National Bank.

Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty obtained documents indicating that the National Bank and the State Security Service had been aware of information about Keinishvili’s alleged violations for at least several months. Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty sent inquiries to both agencies on 6 October.

News in Georgia

World.title: Georgia’s Communications Commission bans two TV channels from using 93 words and phrases
World.content:
Georgia’s National Communications Commission has banned the critical TV channels Formula and TV Pirveli from using 93 words and phrases.

The list includes “regime”, “political prisoners”, “prisoners of conscience”, “oligarch”, “repressive laws” and “judicial clan”.

Transparency International Georgia (TI) believes the Commission is using content regulation mechanisms to punish critical media outlets and undermine their financial position.

According to information published by TI, the Communications Commission has issued seven official reports over the past six months. Four concerned Formula TV and three concerned TV Pirveli. The Commission initially gave the broadcasters verbal warnings, then fined each of them 2,500 lari ($926) for the first offence and 5,000 lari ($1,852) for the next. On 1 October, it imposed an additional fine of 10,000 lari ($3,704) on Formula TV.

TI warns that TV Pirveli could face a similar fine if the Commission continues along the same lines. The organisation notes that the Commission fines the broadcasters in turn, while the financial penalties place an additional burden on TV channels already operating under difficult economic conditions.

TI is particularly concerned that the Commission also has the power to suspend broadcasting licences. The organisation believes that the use of these powers could pose a serious threat to the operations of critical TV channels.

Where is the line between impartiality and censorship?

The Communications Commission mainly accuses the TV channels of violating the principle of impartiality by covering current affairs through the lens of journalists’ personal attitudes and opinions. It uses these allegations to justify its demand that broadcasters refrain from using certain words and expressions.

Transparency International Georgia examined all seven reports prepared by the Commission. It found that the Commission had deemed 33 words and phrases unacceptable for TV Pirveli and 68 for Formula. Some expressions appear on both lists, bringing the total number of banned words and phrases to 93.

However, the organisation says the Commission’s demands go beyond the use of individual words. According to the reports, broadcasters must also present news in a form stripped of as much evaluation and analysis as possible.

In one example, a journalist discusses the creation of an informal movement backed by the authorities and calls it a “morality police”. In another report, a journalist claims that the Georgian authorities have copied the Chechen model, under which officials give athletes an official mandate and allow them to use violence.

The expressions deemed unacceptable by the Commission also include phrases about the detention of activists, a visit by ruling party representatives to Washington and Georgia’s EU accession process. In one of the reports that prompted sanctions, a journalist accuses the authorities of spreading disinformation. The journalist also says the government blames Europe’s policies for the suspension of Georgia’s European integration instead of taking responsibility for its own decisions.

The Commission argues that such wording reflects the broadcaster’s personal attitude and opinion. It says this violates the requirement for impartiality when covering public policy issues, as set out in Article 54(5) of Georgia’s Law on Broadcasting.

Monitoring pro-government channels and the political context

Transparency International says the Commission threatened critical broadcasters with monitoring after the UK imposed sanctions on the pro-government TV channels Imedi and POSTV on 24 February 2026.

The UK cited the deliberate spread of false information about Russia’s war against Ukraine and support for Russian disinformation as grounds for the sanctions.

The Communications Commission also placed the pro-government channels Imedi, POSTV and Rustavi 2 under monitoring. However, Transparency International argues that this process is largely a formality designed to make the Commission appear impartial, while the authorities direct actual pressure at independent media.

The organisation also raises concerns about the Commission’s membership and independence. According to TI, the fact that some commissioners are loyal to or have ties to the ruling Georgian Dream party raises further doubts about the impartiality of the decisions they make.

Media financial sustainability under threat

Fines against critical TV channels are increasing even as the broadcasters struggle with difficult financial conditions. Repeated penalties and the possibility of licence suspension make their ability to continue operating an even more pressing concern.

Transparency International argues that the Communications Commission should not act as a censor or use its powers to punish media outlets for criticising the authorities. In TI’s view, media self-regulation should take precedence when the Commission considers disputed journalistic content. The Commission’s main role should be to support self-regulation, rather than punish broadcasters for criticising the government and exposing its representatives.

World.title: Armenian AI factory rejects Russian allegations of intelligence gathering
World.content:
Firebird AI rejects Russian espionage allegations

“Claims circulating about Firebird AI’s activities are untrue and have no factual basis,” the Armenia-based company Firebird AI said in response to remarks by Alexei Shevtsov, deputy secretary of Russia’s Security Council.

On 8 August 2026, Firebird AI opened the first AI factory in the city of Hrazdan. It is the largest data centre in the region and plans to expand its operations further. The facility already uses more than 6,000 NVIDIA Blackwell B200/B300 graphics processing units (GPUs). By the end of 2027, the company plans to deploy more than 70,000 NVIDIA Blackwell and Vera Rubin chips. The project has received around $500 million in initial investment. Total investment could reach $4 billion or more.

The Russian official claimed that this powerful data centre could be used for espionage: “Such centres could support analytical and intelligence operations on behalf of Western intelligence agencies, including against Iran, Russia and countries in the South Caucasus and Central Asia.”

This is not the first time Alexei Shevtsov has criticised projects under way in Armenia. Around the same time, he also expressed concern about the Armenian-American TRIPP initiative, known as the “Trump Route”, which aims to unblock regional transport links. According to Shevtsov, the project could lead to the deployment of US private military companies and intelligence infrastructure in Armenia.

“The computing capacity is used exclusively for civilian purposes”

Firebird AI said its AI factory is a technology company that develops and operates high-performance computing infrastructure.

“The US export licence issued to the company restricts the use of the relevant computing capacity exclusively to civilian purposes.”

Firebird AI’s management said the Russian Security Council deputy secretary’s claims showed a lack of understanding of how AI computing infrastructure operates.

“The geographical location of these services does not, in itself, determine the nature or purpose of their use.”

What concerns Russia

Alexei Shevtsov said that Firebird AI’s US jurisdiction could allow US intelligence agencies to access all the data stored on its servers.

“This means that data belonging to Armenian government agencies, companies and citizens could become accessible to the United States without the consent of the Armenian authorities.”

However, the main concern centres on the possibility that the data centre could gather intelligence. This could allegedly affect not only Russia’s interests but also those of Iran, for example.

The Russian Security Council representative then turned to Armenia’s energy capacity.

“According to announced plans, Firebird intends to increase the capacity of its Hrazdan complex to 300 MW by the end of 2027. This represents almost a quarter of Armenia’s winter peak electricity demand of 1.3 GW. The announced plans will require additional generating capacity to keep the centre running.”

This issue concerns Russia because Armenia plans to build a new nuclear power plant, and Russia hopes to secure the contract. Russia built the existing Metsamor nuclear power plant. Against this backdrop, Shevtsov questioned the need to diversify Armenia’s partnerships in the nuclear energy sector.

Armenia may instead opt for the small modular reactors that the United States has offered, as previously discussed. In that case, Shevtsov said:

“I would like to emphasise that the United States has not built and is not building any small modular reactors abroad. Meanwhile, Rosatom is currently building 30 power units abroad, including small modular reactors. The choice, as they say, is obvious.”

Firebird AI rejects Russian espionage allegations

World.title: ‘Civil society has the right to participate safely’: OSCE chair responds to Georgian authorities
World.content:
At the OSCE Human Dimension Conference in Warsaw, a representative of Switzerland, the organisation’s chair for 2026, said that the Chairpersonship was concerned about remarks made by the authorities in Georgia regarding the participation of Georgian civil society representatives in the conference, as well as information received from human rights defenders.

The Swiss representative’s statement followed comments by Georgian Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili about NGO representatives attending the conference in Warsaw. On 7 October, Papuashvili said he did not understand how they had paid for the trip or who was funding them:

“How do they pay for these trips, and who funds them? These organisations are not registered in the transparency register. If they do not disclose [the source of their income] to the state, it means they are funded by ‘black money’. This is further evidence that organisations in Georgia receive ‘black money’, including from various European institutions,” the speaker said.

What did the Swiss representative say?

“Providing a platform where civil society representatives can participate and engage with OSCE participating States and executive structures is one of the OSCE’s core values. They must be able to do so without facing any negative consequences.

This is essential for the OSCE’s mechanisms to function. We are concerned about comments made in connection with the participation of Georgian civil society representatives in this conference, as well as reports received from various human rights defenders attending the OSCE Human Dimension Conference in Warsaw. We reiterate the importance of ensuring safe participation in OSCE events, without any reprisals.”

Incident at the conference

The conference in Warsaw is attended by Baia Pataraia, head of the Georgian NGO Sapari, and Tamar Oniani, head of the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association.

On 5 October, during a speech by a representative of the Georgian delegation, Pataraia held up a banner reading: “Free all Georgian political prisoners.”

Pataraia says her protest was peaceful and silent, and that she had arranged it in advance in accordance with OSCE rules.

“Wherever I find myself alongside the [Georgian] government, I will remind them that prisons are full of political prisoners and that the Georgian people will never accept this,” she says.

Pataraia adds that Germany, Slovenia and other countries have urged Georgia to implement the recommendations of the Moscow Mechanism and stop persecuting media representatives, politicians and civil society members.

In this context, she also criticised the Georgian authorities’ bid to make Georgia the OSCE chair in 2027.

“They want benefits, money, prestige and power from everyone, but they themselves fulfil none of their obligations,” Pataraia said indignantly.

The ruling Georgian Dream party is seeking to secure the OSCE chairpersonship for 2027. Georgian Foreign Minister Maka Bochorishvili says the country has already submitted its application to the OSCE and hopes to win the support of participating States. However, according to the publication Rapporteur, EU member states do not support Georgia’s bid.



OSCE conference in Warsaw

World.title: Abkhazia plans pension reform, new law to take work history into account
World.content:
The government of Abkhazia has drafted a pension reform bill aimed at streamlining pension legislation, taking employment history into account when calculating pension payments and introducing specific support measures for socially vulnerable groups.

The draft pension law was prepared by the Ministry of Social Welfare and Demographic Policy. According to Minister Kama Adzynba, the bill aims to streamline regulations governing employment-related, insurance-based and funded pensions, as well as payments for special services to the country.

One of the key principles of the proposed reform is to take individuals’ employment history into account when determining pension payments. Currently, pensions in Abkhazia stand at 6,000 roubles [approximately $70], a standard amount paid to everyone, regardless of whether they have worked for many years or have never been formally employed.

Pensioners who hold dual Abkhaz-Russian citizenship and also receive a Russian pension have their Abkhaz pension reduced to a largely symbolic 500 roubles [around $6].

The new system is intended to address this “injustice”. It also provides for survivor’s pensions and other social benefits, which are expected to exceed the basic social pension.

The bill also introduces special pensions for distinguished service to the country. Recipients of state orders and veterans of the 1992-93 Georgian-Abkhaz war are among those proposed for inclusion in this category.

The draft law will be submitted to parliament for consideration.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s $90bn reserves draw criticism from former opposition leader
World.content:
Azerbaijan’s foreign currency reserves

Ilgar Mammadov, former chairman of Azerbaijan’s Republican Alternative (ReAl) party, has criticised the country’s accumulation of $90bn in foreign currency reserves. In a Facebook post, he argued that there was little reason to take pride in such substantial reserves when some elderly citizens were forced to survive on modest social benefits.

Mammadov proposed using part of the reserves to improve living standards while expanding economic freedoms.

“There are no reasonable grounds for a country like Azerbaijan to hold $90bn in foreign currency reserves,” the politician wrote.

What makes up Azerbaijan’s $90bn in foreign currency reserves?

Azerbaijan’s strategic foreign currency reserves comprise the Central Bank’s foreign exchange reserves and the assets of the State Oil Fund (SOFAZ). According to figures published by the State Statistical Committee, their combined value stood at $90.77bn as of 1 September 2026. This represents the total value of funds held in various financial assets.

The two institutions’ reserves serve different purposes. The Central Bank’s reserves are used to maintain stability in the foreign exchange market and mitigate risks associated with external payments.

The State Oil Fund accumulates revenues from oil and gas production, invests them, makes transfers to the state budget and builds up savings for future generations. Its assets are invested in bonds, equities, gold and property.

The authorities regard the substantial reserves as an indicator of the country’s financial resilience. Speaking at the Azerbaijan International Investment Forum in September, President Ilham Aliyev stressed that the reserves were approximately 20 times greater than the country’s external public debt.

According to Aliyev, this demonstrates the strength of Azerbaijan’s financial system and the stability of its national currency.

‘These $90bn have become a symbol of shame and disgrace’

Mammadov also approaches the issue from the perspective of public welfare. He argues that elderly citizens have contributed to the creation of national wealth not only through formal employment but also through domestic and agricultural work.

“Only the government of the New Azerbaijan Party (YAP) can proudly boast of having $90bn in foreign currency reserves in a country where 180,000 elderly citizens receive no retirement pension and are forced to make do with an old-age allowance of $130. This is simply shameful.

“People over the age of 65 have contributed to society throughout their lives through their labour and their role as consumers in the economy, helping to create the conditions for accumulating $90bn in foreign currency reserves.

“Whether it was a housewife who spent years supporting her husband as he worked as a labourer or engineer, or a man who worked in the fields for a pittance, supplying city residents with fresh fruit and vegetables, they all contributed to building up these reserves.

“This is a hardworking generation that the YAP authorities have left with virtually no means of subsistence in old age, while continuing to boast about the country’s foreign currency reserves.”

Mammadov argues that taking pride in growing reserves while this generation faces financial hardship is also morally unacceptable.

“Viewed from this perspective, even the question of economic efficiency becomes secondary. These $90bn have become a symbol of shame and disgrace.”

Assets held abroad and dependence on oil

Mammadov also argues that holding substantial foreign currency reserves abroad carries political risks. He cites Iraq and Libya as examples, pointing to the depletion of their financial resources during wars and the freezing of their assets. He links these events to the interests of external powers and suggests that Azerbaijan could face similar risks.

“By maintaining foreign currency reserves on this scale, Azerbaijan is merely provoking major players in the current world order, who are accustomed to playing by their own rules. It is like putting on our most expensive jacket, stuffing its pockets with bundles of cash and going for a walk at night down the most crime-ridden street in the city.

“There are plenty of historical examples. In 1980, Iraq’s foreign currency reserves stood at 36bn–40bn. In today’s money, that is just over $90bn. And what happened? A war with Iran was soon orchestrated, partly for the sake of that money, though not exclusively. As a result, all the money was spent on purchasing weapons from abroad, and the reserves were exhausted. Who benefited? The arms dealers.

“In 2011, Libya’s foreign currency reserves had barely reached $150bn when the country was plunged into turmoil. Some of the money was spent on arming the sides in the civil war, while around a third of the assets were frozen in foreign financial institutions (and someone is still profiting from them). The rest has never been traced.

“In today’s world, where the law of the jungle prevails, there is no point in keeping such substantial foreign currency reserves abroad. One day, a provocation could be staged against us too, and the money could be seized,” he wrote.

Mammadov also sees a potential collapse in financial markets as a serious threat. He believes securities are significantly overvalued and that a sharp fall in their prices could result in substantial losses for Azerbaijan.

Another of his arguments concerns the economy’s dependence on oil. Recalling the currency devaluations of 2015, he notes that the country’s foreign currency reserves failed to prevent the sharp depreciation of the manat.

“The reason reserves are rapidly depleted during a crisis and cannot serve as a financial safety net lies in the unhealthy state of our economy and its dependence on oil.”

According to Mammadov, if oil prices remain low for a prolonged period, substantial foreign currency reserves alone cannot guarantee economic security.

What does Mammadov propose?

Mammadov is not calling for Azerbaijan to spend all its foreign currency reserves. He believes some funds should be retained to deal with economic crises and natural disasters, although he does not specify how much should be set aside.

“There is an urgent need to improve people’s living standards, particularly those of the elderly. At the same time, economic freedoms must be expanded without delay so that citizens can realise their creative and entrepreneurial potential and generate new wealth,” the politician wrote.

Mammadov sees the rule of law as a fundamental prerequisite for these reforms. He concluded his post by urging voters to support the Republican Alternative (ReAl) party.

World.title: Pashinyan on extradition of Azerbaijani soldier, meeting Aliyev and Medvedev’s statement
World.content:
Pashinyan on Azerbaijani serviceman’s extradition and other issues

The extradition of Azerbaijani serviceman Nasimi Musayev is not under discussion, and Baku has not made such a request. Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan told journalists this during his traditional hour-long briefing.

“What extradition are you talking about? There is no such issue, and we are not discussing it. Azerbaijan has made no request,” he said.

At the same time, he stressed that Armenia would have returned Musayev on the same day if he had not committed a crime.

Pashinyan described the Azerbaijani serviceman, who illegally crossed into Armenia and shot a resident of the village of Shaki, as having committed an “ordinary crime”. The prime minister drew parallels with other forms of cross-border crime:

“We also have other cases of cross-border crime. Drugs are constantly exported to Armenia and transported through Armenia in transit. There is no need to turn this into an apocalypse.”

The prime minister does not believe the incident in Shaki could threaten the peace process between Armenia and Azerbaijan.

He considers the peace that Armenia and Azerbaijan have established an achievement that requires protection. He warns that they could destroy it in a day, while reaching the current state of relations could take another 30 years. For this reason, he does not consider it appropriate to make statements that could threaten the peace process.

On 1 October 2026, Nasimi Musayev illegally entered the village of Shaki in Armenia’s Syunik Province. Local residents found him inside a house, where he opened fire with an assault rifle and wounded a 39-year-old woman. Her three children witnessed the incident. Her two sons also suffered injuries, while her daughter has yet to recover psychologically.

Musayev fled after the shooting, but authorities detained him shortly afterwards in another house. The Armenian Prosecutor’s Office brought criminal charges under five articles of the Criminal Code. The charges include illegally crossing the border, causing serious bodily harm to a local resident and violating the inviolability of a home. A court ordered his detention for two months.

During the briefing, the prime minister also addressed Dmitry Medvedev’s controversial statement about turning Armenia into a “new Ukraine”, a possible meeting with Aliyev at the CIS summit and the issue of missing persons.

“No official meetings are planned”: on contacts with Putin and Aliyev

On 8-9 October, Pashinyan will attend the CIS summit in Turkmenistan. Asked about possible meetings with the presidents of Russia and Azerbaijan, he recalled that his latest meetings with Putin and Aliyev took place in Bishkek last month. He also spoke to the Russian president by phone the day before.

“The format is such that contacts with the president of Russia and the president of Azerbaijan will certainly take place. We will be in the same place today and tomorrow. No official meeting is planned. If it turns out that such a meeting is necessary, it may take place,” he said.

“Armenia has already faced such a threat”: response to Medvedev

People in Armenia continue to discuss Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev’s statement. He said that Armenia’s leadership had decided to change the country’s course and that this would not lead to anything good.

“The worst thing that could happen to Armenia is for it to turn into a new Ukraine,” Medvedev said.

Journalists asked Pashinyan whether Armenia could face such a threat. He replied:

“Armenia has already faced a similar danger and situation. In September 2022, [during the Azerbaijani armed forces’ invasion of Armenia’s sovereign territory], the CSTO failed to fulfil its obligations.”

The Collective Security Treaty Organisation is a military alliance led by Russia. Armenia is a member of the CSTO. Under the organisation’s charter, its allies had to provide military assistance to a member state, but that did not happen.

The Armenian prime minister could not explain why Medvedev was making such statements and threats:

“Following the same logic, someone else could say: ‘We do not want Armenia to turn into a “new Russia”, given that explosions can be heard in various parts of Russia.’ This is an unfortunate genre.”

He assured that Armenia would not turn into anything else and would instead become an even more independent state.

“Some circles in Azerbaijan use this issue for political purposes”: on missing persons

Azerbaijan periodically demands that Armenia provide information about the fate of missing Azerbaijanis and the locations of their graves. President Ilham Aliyev repeated the demand at an international conference on missing persons in Baku.

According to Armenia’s prime minister, both sides should make joint efforts to establish the fate of missing people:

“We have stated that we are ready to cooperate. The problem is that some circles in Azerbaijan use this issue for political purposes, including to generate hostile rhetoric and pursue other aims.”

According to figures Pashinyan presented, the whereabouts of around 1,000 people who went missing during wars since the 1990s remain unknown in Armenia.

He says the wording itself — “their whereabouts are unknown” — shows how little information the authorities have about these people:

“Some circles in Azerbaijan sometimes try to create the impression that we know where these people are and refuse to share the information. But that is not the case.”

Pashinyan believes the two sides should resolve the issue through cooperation and close this chapter. He said that in Bishkek, he and the Azerbaijani president also discussed stepping up joint efforts by the relevant commissions of the two countries.

Pashinyan on Azerbaijani serviceman’s extradition and other issues

World.title: Uzbekistan ranks fifth in cotton fiber production with 1.4M tons
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 12. Uzbekistan ranked fifth among six major cotton-producing countries, with an estimated 1.4 million tons of cotton fiber derived from its 2025 raw cotton harvest.

The figures were reported by Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Agriculture.

The ministry compared Uzbekistan’s 2025 production results with international figures for the 2025/26 cotton season, expressing output in terms of cotton fiber to facilitate comparison.

China ranked first, with 7.79 million tons of cotton fiber, followed by India with 5.18 million tons and Brazil with 4.08 million tons. The United States ranked fourth, with 3.03 million tons, while Uzbekistan placed fifth, ahead of Pakistan, which recorded 1.15 million tons.

According to the ministry, Uzbekistan harvested 3.986 million tons of raw cotton in 2025 from 875,600 hectares. Applying a fiber yield rate of 35% to the harvest gives an estimated 1.395 million tons of cotton fiber, rounded to 1.4 million tons.

According to Trend’s calculations, Uzbekistan’s average raw cotton yield reached approximately 4.55 tons per hectare in 2025, while its estimated cotton fiber yield stood at around 1.59 tons per hectare.

Uzbekistan’s estimated cotton fiber output exceeded Pakistan’s reported volume by approximately 245,000 tons, or 21.3%, but remained about 54% below the US figure.

The comparison should be interpreted with regard to the different reporting periods: Uzbekistan’s figures cover the 2025 calendar year, while the international figures refer to the 2025/26 cotton season.

The ministry attributed Uzbekistan’s progress in cotton production to the adoption of high-yielding varieties, modern agricultural technologies, improved farming practices and efforts by farmers to increase productivity.

The country’s priorities extend beyond increasing raw cotton output. According to the ministry, key objectives include raising yields per hectare, improving fiber quality, increasing processing efficiency and strengthening the value chain from cotton cultivation to finished products.

Expanding value-added processing is particularly important because cotton fiber serves as a raw material for yarn, fabrics, garments and other textile products. Developing these production stages can increase the domestic value generated from each ton of harvested cotton.

The ministry’s comparison therefore highlights Uzbekistan’s position among the leading cotton fiber producers included in the ranking, as well as its focus on improving agricultural productivity and developing a more integrated cotton and textile industry.

World.title: Google Chrome retains lead in Azerbaijan's browser market
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 12. Google Chrome retained its leading position in Azerbaijan’s browser market in September, with a 78.33% share.

According to Trend’s analysis of data from StatCounter Global Stats, Chrome’s market share decreased by 2.15 percentage points compared with the previous month. StatCounter’s September data puts Chrome’s share at 78.33%, followed by Safari at 8.49% and Firefox at 5.47%.

Safari’s market share in Azerbaijan increased by 1.04 percentage points during the month, reaching 8.49%.

Firefox ranked third, with its market share increasing by 0.65 percentage points to 5.47%.

Samsung Internet’s share increased by 0.25 percentage points to 3.92%, while Edge’s share rose by 0.18 percentage points to 2.09%.

Opera’s market share increased by 0.03 percentage points to 1.07%. Yandex Browser’s share increased by 0.02 percentage points to 0.39% in September.

Meanwhile, Google released Chrome 155 for Android on Oct. 6, with version 155.0.8059.39. The update is being gradually rolled out through Google Play and includes stability and performance improvements, according to Google.

The stable desktop version was also updated on Oct. 6 to version 155.0.8059.39/.40 for Windows and Mac and 155.0.8059.39 for Linux.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s imports rise 5.5% as purchases of consumer goods decline
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 12. Kazakhstan’s imports of goods increased by 5.5% year-on-year to $31.5 billion in the first half of 2026, driven by higher purchases of intermediate and investment goods, while consumer goods imports declined.

This was reflected in a press release published by Kazakhstan’s Ministry of National Economy, citing Kazakhstan’s Bureau of National Statistics.

According to the publication, intermediate goods accounted for 47.6% of total imports, reaching $15 billion after a 14% increase. Investment goods imports rose by 10.6% to $8.1 billion.

Trend’s calculations show that intermediate and investment goods together accounted for approximately 73.3% of Kazakhstan’s total imports, or $23.1 billion, in January-June 2026.

The increase in these two categories added approximately $2.6 billion to imports compared with the first half of 2025. Meanwhile, consumer goods imports declined by around $1 billion, partly offsetting the increase in production-related purchases. These estimates are based on reported growth rates and rounded values.

Consumer goods imports fell by 10.5% to $8.3 billion. Non-food consumer goods imports declined by 15.4% to $5.6 billion, according to the ministry, citing the Bureau of National Statistics.

Under the National Bank’s balance of payments methodology, imports increased by 6.2% to $32.3 billion. Intermediate goods imports rose by 13.8%, while non-food consumer goods imports decreased by 11.2%. Exports grew by 27.1%, more than four times faster than imports.

The increase in investment goods imports coincided with stronger capital investment in Kazakhstan’s manufacturing industry. According to the ministry, citing the Bureau of National Statistics, investment in fixed capital rose by 9.6% in real terms to 9.5 trillion tenge in January-June 2026. Investment in manufacturing increased by 33.3% to 1.43 trillion tenge, accounting for approximately 15% of total investment.

Manufacturing output grew by 9.8% during the period, while machinery production increased by 23.1% and chemical industry output by 20.7%.
