Imports of several categories of industrial equipment also recorded significant increases. Purchases of electric generating sets rose by 83%, machinery for lifting, handling, loading and unloading by 70.1%, and equipment for sorting and grinding earth by 2.1 times.

Intermediate goods imports were supported by higher purchases of natural gas, up 96.3%; turbojet engines and gas turbines, up 2.7 times; petroleum products, up 41.6%; uranium, up 2.6 times; and gold, up six times.

Meanwhile, imports of passenger cars declined by 21.9%, pharmaceutical products by 18.7%, suitcases and bags by 49.4%, women’s textile clothing by 38.9%, and air conditioners by 34.3%.

According to the ministry, citing the National Bank, imports of non-food consumer goods have declined for 11 consecutive quarters since the fourth quarter of 2023.

The decrease in passenger car imports coincided with an expansion in domestic production. Kazakhstan produced 88,886 passenger cars in January-June 2026, up 37.2% year-on-year, while sales in the official dealership segment remained stable. This trend points to a potential partial substitution of imports by domestic assembly.

World.title: Iran's Hormozgan ports handle 3.84M tons of cargo in six months
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 12. A total of 3.84 million metric tons of oil and non-oil products were shipped through the ports in the western part of Hormozgan Province, located in southern Iran, during the first six months of the current Iranian year (March 21 through September 22, 2026).

According to the Iranian Ports and Maritime Organization, this was announced by Amin Sadeghi, director of the Ports Authority in the western part of Iran’s Hormozgan Province.

"Of the cargo loaded and unloaded at ports in the western part of Hormozgan Province, 2.49 million metric tons were non-oil products and 1.34 million metric tons were petroleum products," he noted.

Sadeghi also stated that during the first six months, 1.27 million metric tons of petroleum and non-oil products were exported through the ports in the western part of the province. During that period, 1.04 million metric tons of non-oil products and 230,000 metric tons of petroleum products were exported.

Moreover, the official stated that 1.75 million metric tons of oil and non-oil products were transported via coastal shipping over the six months.

"Over the past six months, 62,900 TEU containers with a total weight of approximately 644,000 metric tons were loaded and unloaded at ports in the western part of Hormozgan Province. During this period, approximately 31,500 TEU containers with a total weight of 322,000 metric tons were exported through these ports," he noted.

According to him, over the past six months, 89,900 metric tons of oil and non-oil products, as well as 46,100 passenger cars, passed through the ports in the western part of Hormozgan Province. The passenger cars were shipped to Iraq and Central Asian countries.

Sadeghi noted that over the past six months, 11,800 cargo ships called at ports in the western part of Hormozgan Province. Of these, 1,410 had a capacity of more than 1,000 metric tons, while more than 10,000 had a capacity of less than 1,000 metric tons.

According to Trend's calculation, based on information from the Iranian Ports and Maritime Organization, during the first six months of the previous Iranian year (March 21 through September 22, 2025), a total of 3.68 million metric tons of oil and non-oil products were exported from ports located in the western part of Hormozgan Province. The volume of non-oil products exported amounted to 2.06 million metric tons, while the volume of oil products was 1.62 million metric tons.

Meanwhile, 10 ports are operating in the western part of Iran’s Hormozgan Province. Among them, the busiest are the ports of Lengeh, Charak, Siri, and Lavan.

World.title: Iran's Sistan and Baluchestan customs record $110M exports
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 12. Product exports through the Chabahar, Pishin, and Rimdan customs offices in Iran's southeastern Sistan and Baluchestan Province totaled 809,000 tons, valued at $110 million, during the first six months of the current Iranian year (March 21 through September 22, 2026).

The Iran Customs Administration reported this, citing Reza Ghorbani, director general of Chabahar Customs.

Exports through the Chabahar, Pishin, and Rimdan customs offices increased by 59% in value but decreased by 9% in volume during the six months compared with the same period last year (March 21 through September 22, 2025), Ghorbani said.

"Additionally, goods from other parts of the country totaling 624,000 tons and worth $355 million were exported via the Chabahar, Pishin, and Rimdan customs offices," he said.

Ghorbani added that the main products exported through the three customs offices during the six-month period included liquefied gas, bitumen, cement, ceramics, food products, and vegetables.

He also said that 1.6 million tons of goods worth $1.23 billion were imported into the country through the three customs offices during the same period. Imports increased by 28% in value and 57% in volume compared with the same period last year.

According to Trend's analysis based on data from the Iran Customs Administration, 2.37 million tons of goods worth $352 million were exported through the customs offices of Sistan and Baluchestan Province during the first 10 months of the previous Iranian year (March 21, 2025 through January 20, 2026).

Exports increased by 39% in value and 14% in volume compared with the same period of the preceding Iranian year (March 20, 2024 through January 19, 2025).

During the first four months of the current Iranian year (March 21 through July 22, 2026), 713,000 tons of goods worth $108 million were exported through the customs offices of Sistan and Baluchestan Province. Exports increased by 61% in value and 3% in volume compared with the same period last year.

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 12, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 12. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The erupted 44-day Second Karabakh War ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation.

Trend presents the chronicle of the 16th day of the Second Karabakh war:

- President Ilham Aliyev gave an interview to the Turkish Haber Global TV channel.

- The territory of Aghdam district came under fire from the Armenian Armed Forces. The commander and large manpower of the forces were killed.

- As a result of an exploded shell in the village of Kangarli, Tartar district, Firudin Baylarov (born 1970) was seriously injured and hospitalized.

- The Azerbaijani Defense Ministry shared a video of the destruction of three Armenian UAVs.

- Mobile support points for the Azerbaijani troops participating in the hostilities were created.

- The Azerbaijani Defense Ministry shared a video from the liberated village of Suleymanly, Jabrayil district.

- The death toll as a result of missile attacks on Ganja city by Armenia reached 10 people.

World.title: Azerbaijani boxer becomes European champion
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 11. Another Azerbaijani boxer has won gold at the European U-17 Championships in Budva.

Mahammadali Istamov (57 kg) claimed the title after defeating England’s John Elam 4:1 on points in the final (29:28, 30:27, 28:29, 29:28, 29:28).

With this result, the Azerbaijani team concluded the U-17 European Championships with eight medals: two gold, three silver, and three bronze.

Before Istamov, Jamila Muradli (57 kg) won gold, Hasrat Mammadov (46 kg), Ismayil Nasirzade (52 kg), and Sama Abbasova (66 kg) claimed silver, while Gardash Rahimov (54 kg), Hidayat Mammadov (70 kg), and Khumar Jafarli (+80 kg) earned bronze medals.

A total of 473 athletes, including 314 boys and 159 girls, from 40 countries competed in the championship.

World.title: Azerbaijan boosts oil exports to Greece by 22%
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 11. Azerbaijan exported 284,400 tons of oil and oil products obtained from bituminous minerals to Greece worth $182.8 million in January–August 2026.

According to foreign trade customs statistics published by the State Customs Committee, the figure increased by $53.8 million, or 41.7%, in value terms and by 52,000 tons, or 22.4%, in volume terms compared with the same period of 2025, according to Trend’s calculations based on the data.

During the reporting period, Greece ranked tenth among countries importing Azerbaijani oil.

In January–August 2025, Azerbaijan exported 232,400 tons of oil and oil products obtained from bituminous minerals to Greece worth $129 million.

According to the State Customs Committee, Azerbaijan exported 368,700 tons of oil and oil products obtained from bituminous minerals to Greece worth $224.3 million in 2024, while exports amounted to 702,400 tons worth $367.7 million in 2025.

Exports in 2024–2025 showed significant growth in both physical volume and value. Supply volumes increased 1.9 times, while export value rose 1.6 times.

Specifically, export volumes increased from 368,700 tons to 702,400 tons, or 1.9 times, while export value rose from $224.3 million to $367.7 million, or 1.6 times.

World.title: Adidas alleges White Fox Boutique infringed its three-stripe trademark
World.content:
When is a stripe not a stripe? According to sportswear brand Adidas, when it's part of its trademark.

The global sportswear giant is suing Australian online fashion retailer White Fox Boutique for selling items allegedly "deceptively similar" to its iconic three-stripe logo, in a case experts say could test the trademark's registration.

The German-based brand has filed a trademark infringement claim against the Sydney-based company, popular with teenagers, in the Federal Court of Australia.

According to court documents, Adidas accuse White Fox of replicating its trademark across multiple items of clothing and advertising content that feature four parallel stripes of equal width in a colour contrasting with the colour of the clothing.

Adidas claim this design is "deceptively similar" to its three-stripe trademark which it has used in Australia for more than 65 years and globally for more than 75 years.

White Fox is defending the case, which will play out in court hearings next year.

A White Fox Boutique  seen on the back of a bus. (Supplied)

According to the documents, White Fox Boutique has promoted and supplied articles of clothing with four parallel stripes on them since March this year, including s on buses, bus stops and on social media.

Adidas said it asked White Fox to remove the garments from sale in March, and to stop using the four-stripe design, which White Fox declined to do.

Adidas further claimed White Fox had used genuine Adidas shoes, in the same colours as its clothing, in some promotional material, which it said took advantage of the brand's reputation and may lead consumers to draw an association between the two companies.

An Instagram post advertising a White Fox Boutique outfit paired with genuine Adidas shoes. (Supplied)

It alleges the actions of White Fox are likely to cause damage to its reputation.

In court on Friday, White Fox's barrister Ed Heerey KC said the online fashion retailer would argue the four stripes emblazoned on the label's clothing were simply decorative rather than a trademark.

He highlighted similar items bearing the four stripes from other brands including fast-fashion labels Princess Polly, Glassons, and Shein.

Intellectual property law expert Muhammad Abbas said this case was not just about a fourth stripe.

"Adding a stripe is neither a complete answer to a trademark claim nor automatically an infringement," Dr Abbas, a lecturer at the Queensland University of Technology, said.

He explained a 2023 High court decision considered the impression a notional buyer, "allowing for imperfect recollection", would have of the registered trade mark, compared to the impression created by the sign used.

"Counting stripes is only the start," he said.

Adidas trademark at risk

The three-stripe design dates back to the brand's foundation in 1949 but wasn't trademarked until 1952 after Adidas discovered a Finnish brand Karhu had come up with the same logo and trademarked it.

Founder Adolf Dassler struck a deal, and traded two bottles of whiskey and the equivalent of 1600 euros for the logo, which it has been extensively protective of ever since.

In 2013, it successfully sued Pacific Brands over its use of a four-stripe design on some of its Dunlop and Grosby shoe designs, with the court ruling that three of the 12 designs in question were "deceptively similar".

However, senior lecturer at the University of Technology Sydney School of Law, Sarah Hook, said challenges overseas had led to Adidas losing its trademark registration in some jurisdictions.

In the US, Adidas unsuccessfully took high-end designer Thom Browne to court over a four-stripe design.

Designer Thom Browne wore socks with the four-stripe design to court in New York. (Reuters: Eduardo Munoz)

Thom Browne then challenged the trademark registration in the UK which ultimately saw the High Court rule the trademark was invalid.

"That's because the court said that the trademark itself wasn't very clear and distinct about what it would cover and which variations it would cover," Dr Hook said.

Adidas loses court battle Fashion designer Thom Browne emerges from a New York courthouse victorious over sportswear giant Adidas.

Director of Intellectual Property Law studies at the University of Melbourne, Benjamin Hopper, said distinctiveness was a core doctrine of trademark law, meaning it has to be distinguishable from other goods or services from other traders in the same marketplace.

"For example, if I owned a company that sold chairs, armchairs, lounge chairs, dining room chairs, office chairs, theatre chairs, it was just chairs and I called it the chair company or I called it chairs and I said, 'I want to get a trademark for chairs,' it would just completely not be distinctive because the word chair has zero capacity to distinguish my chair in the marketplace from the chairs of other traders," he said.

"The argument here is that, three-stripe, the clothing is just so simple and just not unique that if other traders wanted to adopt that to brand or distinguish their own clothes, they should be able to because it's just so simple, like a circle or a triangle."

Was it a deliberate act?

The court case could test the limits of Adidas's trademark. (Supplied)

Dr Hook noted in Australia, Adidas's trademark stated a single or two stripe design would not infringe.

"The fact that [White Fox have] done four stripes seems deliberate because it seems like they've looked at what [Adidas] are covering in the monopoly in the trademark, which is the three stripes, and thinking, 'well, let's have a look at four stripes'," she said.

"So maybe this is testing the limits of that."

What does Katy Perry's loss in the High Court mean for her business? Australian fashion designer Katie Perry has won her long-running trademark battle against pop star Katy Perry, but questions about whether the singer will be able to sell her clothing merchandise as part of any future tours remain.

Dr Hopper speculated White Fox may have used the four-stripe design for several reasons.

"One, it was a deliberate act to garner sort of PR.

"Two, they had advice that this is fine; it's not going to be trademark infringement or passing off or breach of the Australian Consumer Law, or they think that there's a pretty good case to be made.

"Thirdly, they had advice that maybe they could revoke the trademarks on which Adidas has sued them."

The case has been set down for a hearing in early 2027.

Adidas and White Fox Boutique have been contacted for comment.

ABC/AAP

World.title: One Nation Vic deputy denies AI-generated campaign video was racist
World.content:
One Nation's Victorian deputy leader has defended an AI-generated campaign video featuring a suicide bomber and a home invader, denying it was racist.

The video, shown at the party's campaign launch in Melbourne earlier this month, features a young man of African appearance wielding a machete and a suicide bomber who appeared to be of Middle Eastern descent.

"I don't accept the premise that it is racist," Colleen Harkin told 774 ABC Melbourne on Monday morning.

"It is big issues that need to be addressed."

In a wide-ranging interview with host Raf Epstein, Ms Harkin also claimed that climate change was irrelevant to the Australian economy and said One Nation was serious about rescinding Victoria's landmark Treaty.

Colleen Harkin says she has been concerned about the Liberal Party's direction for years. (Facebook)

As for the AI-generated video, she said it tackled the "general view about all the things that are going wrong in Australia" and what was needed to fix them.

"I think most people are looking at some of those things and they're saying, you know, we do have problems with crime in the state, we do have problems with social cohesion and where it's coming from."

The campaign video earlier sparked a row between a Tasmanian cafe owner who was offended by the clip and Pauline Hanson's daughter, who is a customer at the business.

When Epstein pressed Ms Harkin on whether the video was judging people not as individuals but as part of the group they might be part of, Ms Harkin denied there was any prejudice involved.

"Would you complain if it was a white-skinned person or a female with blonde hair?" she said.

When asked about the campaign video over the weekend, federal One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce indicated that he had not seen it, but said crime was a significant issue in Victoria.

Barnaby Joyce was asked about the campaign video over the weekend. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"Machete crime has been an incredibly scary thing," he told the ABC.

"People are terrified of the law-and-order issues in Victoria and it should be dealt with."

One Nation Victoria 'not interested' in coalition with Liberals

Ms Harkin also said One Nation's Victorian branch was not interested in a coalition with the Liberals but would urge voters to preference that party over Labor.

"Labor is our political enemy and the Liberal Party is our political competition," she said.

"We will work with anybody to remove Labor, anybody."

Ms Harkin, who was a long-standing Liberal member before she moved to run for the upper house with One Nation, said her values and principles "hadn't changed one iota over the years".

But she said she remained in touch with many of her Liberal friends and was privy to "interesting intel" that she may not have otherwise had access to.

Ms Harkin is also the director of education at the conservative think tank, the Institute of Public Affairs.

Climate change 'irrelevant' to economy

In June, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson labelled climate change and global warming a "hoax".

Asked if she held the same belief, Ms Harkin said: "I think climate changes all the time".

"The issue for Australia is what are we doing about energy security and what is it costing us?"

Epstein posited that climate science had shown that humans were the problem when it came to climate change.

Victoria is about to have the most unpredictable election in living memory Much has been written about the rise of Pauline Hanson's One Nation in the past 12 months. The Victorian election will give us our best look yet at the decline of the two-party system.

"I think it's irrelevant to our economy. So what we do is we dig up minerals, we send it off overseas and we buy it back," Ms Harkin responded.

"If the world is serious about climate, it's not Australia that's causing the problem."

There is strong evidence linking rising temperatures to mounting costs to the economy, for example through growing insurance and clean-up bills from natural disasters.

In Monday's ABC interview, Ms Harkin also echoed a previous statement from Ms Hanson that she had "no time for radical Islam".

"Radical Islam is a problem for Australia and I don't think many people would disagree with that," she said.

Ms Harkin said Muslims should stand up to other Muslims radicalising young people and "do it louder".

"I have access to Muslim people but in terms of how those kids are being engaged with and who's radicalising them, I don't," she said.

World.title: World's timekeepers will vote to ditch the 'leap second' this week
World.content:
On 27 days in the past century, time has gone backwards for a second.

Or, at least, our clocks have.

These extra "leap seconds" were added to keep our ultra-precise atomic clocks aligned with the Earth's slightly less reliable rotation.

But we have probably already leapt our last second.

Later this week, delegates will meet near a French palace in Versailles to decide whether to abandon the leap second for good.

In its place, if the vote succeeds, it will ask people centuries in the future to observe a "leap hour".

How Earth's spin affects clocks

By traditional definition, a second is an 86,400th of a day.

But Earth's rotation is not perfectly uniform. Our 24-hour days can vary in length by a thousandth of a second (a millisecond).

There are a number of reasons for this inconsistency.

Earth's rotation is generally slowing down, thanks mostly to the pull of the Moon. Astronomers see this in historical records of solar eclipses from more than 3,000 years ago.

Astronomers found that written records of solar eclipses in ancient China and the Middle East did not match astronomical models – until the Earth’s slowing rotation was factored in. (Wikimedia Commons: Kalan, CC BY 3.0)

But over shorter time periods, our planet occasionally spins faster.

Since about 2020, Earth has sped up.

Lucia McCallum, a geodesist at the University of Tasmania, said a number of things can affect the Earth's spin.

"Atmosphere, wind, big ocean currents, glaciers melting, big volcanoes, redistribution of mass in the inner Earth," Dr McCallum said.

This slight variation means the traditional definition of a second isn't precise enough for technologies like GPS, which needs to measure fractions of milliseconds to work.

Atomic time more precise

In the late 1960s, the governing body of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM), which standardises the world's measurements, adopted a more precise definition of a second based on measurements of caesium atoms.

This is what underpins coordinated universal time (UTC).

UTC is tracked by atomic clocks, currently the most accurate measures of time, although newer "nuclear clocks" may soon surpass them.

The National Measurement Institute maintains atomic clocks, which are the most accurate methods of keeping time. (Supplied: National Measurement Institute)

Michael Wouters, leader of time standards at Australia's National Measurement Institute (NMI), said the atomic second was as close to the traditional second as possible.

" There was no exact value to begin with, because it was changing all the time. "

Dr McCallum helps measure the speed of Earth's rotation, using telescopes pointed at extremely distant black holes.

"We use those black holes as anchor points," Dr McCallum said.

Radio telescopes, like this one at Hobart's Mt Pleasant Observatory, can observe an ultra-distant black hole and compare their signals to establish how quickly the Earth is spinning. (Supplied: Jim Lovell)

These observations are vital for satellite navigation, and they are also used to tell when Earth's rotation falls out of sync with UTC, prompting a leap second.

Since their introduction in 1972, leap seconds have been added to our clocks 27 times, most recently at the end of 2016.

How leap seconds mess with modern life

Leap seconds have become increasingly difficult to deal with in the computer age.

Darryl Veitch, a researcher in computer networking at the University of Technology Sydney, said leap seconds break some of software's assumptions about time, such as that it only moves forwards and there are 60 seconds in a minute.

But Dr Wouters said people "forgot about this problem, and they wrote software that then crashed when time went backwards".

Several things slow down the Earth's rotation, but the influence of the Moon and tides is a major factor. (Supplied: NASA)

Unlike time zones or daylight saving, leap seconds are irregular, scheduled only six months in advance.

Previously, they have caused platforms like internet technology provider Cloudflare and social media site Reddit to crash.

In 2022, the BIPM's governing body decided to abandon the leap second by 2035 and start discussing a different method of keeping Earth's days in sync with UTC.

But the decision needed to be fast-tracked when Earth started speeding up, because it meant the next leap second may need to be "negative".

Increasingly interconnected systems mean that a timekeeping error in one place can snowball. (Unsplash: Lukas Blazek)

Dr Wouters said a negative leap second was less likely to cause problems because it involves time jumping forwards rather than backwards, but Professor Veitch was not so sure.

"It's never happened before, and therefore the software for that has never been tested," Professor Veitch said.

Since leap seconds will soon be retired, introducing a negative one seems an unnecessary risk.

"It's being cautious about an unusual event that's prompting the accelerated timetable," Dr Wouters said.

Nor are there any clear economic or practical arguments for preserving leap seconds, beyond keeping software engineers busy.

"Some people have a philosophical objection to [losing leap seconds], and that's because we're disconnecting the way we count time from our actual experience of it," Dr Wouters said.

" But clocks themselves are a very artificial thing. "

Vote may create 'leap hour'

The governing body of the BIPM will vote on leap seconds at its meeting on 12 –15 October.

The leading proposal is to let UTC drift from Earth's rotation until it is an hour out of sync, and then observe a "leap hour" to bring it back.

Ceasing leap seconds means that Earth's day and night will slowly fall out of sync with official time, but it will take more than a century for a minute of difference to build up. (ESO: Anton Yankovyi, CC BY 4.40)

Earth's rotation currently loses less than a second per year, so it could take more than a millennium for this leap hour to become necessary.

Our current timekeeping systems are less than a century old, and it is likely they will look very different by then.

"I would imagine in 100 years, software would be completely automated, and we just won't have the kinds of problems we have now," Professor Veitch said.

New ultra-precise nuclear clocks developed The clocks are so accurate they could run for 30 million years and only lose a second of time.

Dr McCallum said it does not matter whether UTC is seconds behind Earth's days.

" What we still have to maintain is measuring Earth's rotation. "

If the vote succeeds, Dr Wouters said there would be one difference to his work.

In the past, leap seconds were often added on December 31, so some staff at the NMI had to work on New Year's Day to check there were no time measurement problems.

"I'm not too unhappy that that won't be necessary anymore."

World.title: Almost 80,000 older Australians expected to ditch private health over changes
World.content:
Nearly 80,000 older Australians are expected to dump their private health cover by the end of the decade as a result of the federal government's controversial proposed changes.

The latest estimate is nearly double the 44,000 figure repeatedly cited by the federal government in defence of the policy.

The proposal would wind back the rebate Australians aged 65 and over receive on their private health cover, banking about $3 billion to spend elsewhere in the aged care system.

However, health department analysis released under Freedom of Information (FOI) laws reveals that while 44,000 Australians are expected to drop their cover in 2028-29, that is forecast to rise to 78,000 just one year later.

The Coalition said Health Minister Mark Butler had consistently used the smaller figure to defend the policy.

Anne Ruston says older Australians cannot afford to live without private health insurance. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

"Either he didn't read his own briefs, or he's been deliberately misleading older Australians," Shadow Health Minister Anne Ruston said.

The health department said the estimate of 44,000 represented the "initial effect of the policy at a point in time" and noted the estimates were subject to uncertainty, as they were based on historical data and responses that might not reflect future behaviour under new policy settings.

Calls for Greens to block legislation

The proposal has come under increasing scrutiny, with the states and territories, aged care advocates and the private health insurance industry all raising concerns about whether the move would heap pressure on the public health system and affect vulnerable older Australians.

The federal government is counting on the $3 billion in expected savings from the changes, having already promised to funnel the money into other major aged care commitments.

Private health changes appear doomed The Greens signal they will not back the government's controversial private health insurance changes as they stand.

However, with the Coalition already vowing to block the legislation in the Senate, the federal government must get the Greens on board for the bill to pass.

The minor party has been playing hardball, declaring last week it would not support the legislation in its current form.

Last month, the ABC revealed about $1.6 billion of the forecast savings would be clawed back from pensioners, according to Parliamentary Budget Office analysis.

Health department figures also revealed that of the more than 3.2 million older Australians affected by the changes, about 2 million live on less than $37,000 a year.

The Greens are now canvassing different options to amend the legislation, such as exempting pensioners from the changes.

Independent MP Monique Ryan called on the Greens to thwart the bill.

"This is a measure which affects pensioners more than any other group, and particularly affects low-income pensioners, so the Greens should come to the table and they should block this measure," Dr Ryan said.

"This is a government which is refusing to be transparent about a really important measure and Australians need to hold them to account."

Outside parliament, health economists including former health department boss Stephen Duckett backed the policy, saying the impact on the public health system would be trivial.

Public policy think tank The Australia Institute also argued the money could be better spent on services that improve health and reduce hospital demand.

Mark Butler announced the changes to private health for older Australians in a pre-budget speech earlier this year. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

A federal government spokesperson said the changes were about "making the private health insurance rebates fairer" and the overall number of people with private health insurance would continue to increase.

"The current additional rebate is simply not the best way to spend precious taxpayers' dollars on behalf of older Australians when we need to do so much heavy lifting in aged care," they said.

"Every dollar will be reinvested to deliver more aged care beds, more packages and better care for older Australians."

World.title: Man pushes cousin 42km in Melbourne Marathon, carries him over line
World.content:
For Nick Morrison, the 42.2 kilometres of the Melbourne Marathon were more gruelling than for most of his 20,000 fellow competitors: He was pushing his 21-year-old cousin, Toby Holt.

"It's so big for my family and I to be able to do this," Mr Morison said.

" The more I think about the last 100 metres of the race, I get goosebumps every time. "

Toby Holt is a Wagga Wagga local and lives with Juvenile Huntington's Disease (JHD). (Supplied)

Mr Holt, from Wagga Wagga in New South Wales, was diagnosed four years ago with juvenile Huntington's disease (JHD), a rare hereditary neurodegenerative disorder with no cure.

He uses a wheelchair as the disease affects his speech and movement.

Mr Holt told the ABC he was excited about being part of the marathon and was surprised when Mr Morrison, from Brisbane, offered.

"That's crazy," Mr Holt said.

Making every moment count

Mr Holt's mother, Louise Holt, said she became emotional when her nephew, Mr Morrison, called to ask whether she thought it would be a good idea to take her son on the trek.

"I had no words at the time, marathons aren't easy things to do, let alone pushing Toby," Mrs Holt said.

" I'm so proud of the man he is and the love that he has for Toby. "

Since Mr Holt's diagnosis, his family and community have been rallying around him to bring him once-in-a-lifetime experiences including a trip to the United states, one to New Zealand for extreme sports, skydiving, and now a marathon.

When asked whether he had any more adventures in the near future, Mr Holt said: "No, because I have done all the crazy things I could do."

More than 20,000 runners took part in the Melbourne Marathon over the weekend. (Supplied)

"He's a thrillseeker, he'll get in and do anything," Mrs Holt said.

"It's just amazing … the man he is, he's accepted this in his everyday life and never complained."

Mrs Holt said watching how her son has navigated his diagnosis has been moving, because her husband also has Huntington's disease.

"The hard thing is for my husband because he's diagnosed as well," she said.

" Stephen can see what's happening to Toby, it's happening to him as well but in a different way. "

Crossing the finish line

Mr Morrison said he decided to take Toby out of his wheelchair just before the finish line.

"We stopped just shy of the line, and I've helped Toby out of the chair and carried him over the finish line.

"So we could cross it together and he could walk over the finish line himself."

Mr Morrison saw his desire to do a marathon as a great opportunity to not only share the moment with his cousin, but to give better public exposure for the disease and raise funds for research.

They have raised more than $4,000 for Huntington's Australia, the peak national body providing support and services to people and their families living with Huntington's disease.

"And do something that my family and Tobes will never forget," he said.

Before he flew from Brisbane to Melbourne to run his cousin around the track, Mr Morrison said he found good support in addition to a running coach.

The family of Nick Morrison and Toby Holt were cheering the pair on during the race. (Supplied)

"One of my close mates has a disabled brother and their family friend ended up doing a marathon with him," he said.

"I've been using their pram and pushing her brother for a few runs."

Mr Morrison said while he was responsible for the physical exertion required to get the boys over the line and into some "cheeky beers", his cousin was the inspiration in his life.

"To be able to do this with him and make the most of his life and mine — I'm extremely grateful," he said.

World.title: Melbourne imam named by Emirati officials in flydubai terror probe breaks silence
World.content:
The imam of a Melbourne mosque allegedly linked to the suspect in the attempted hijacking of a flydubai plane has taken to social media to claim "the righteous will always be attacked" and referred to "false allegations", while not directly addressing the allegations.

In a statement released via state media last week, the United Arab Emirates attorney-general said the 29-year-old terror suspect, widely reported as Omani national Hammam Al-Hammami, started to "drift towards extremism and terrorism" while studying in Melbourne.

Mr Al-Hammami is accused of attacking his co-pilot with an axe in the skies over Saudi Arabia as they were flying a flydubai plane carrying more than 170 passengers.

Emirati authorities allege he was trying to take control of the plane to crash it into Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv, Israel, in a "suicide attack".

How the flydubai incident unfolded Passengers and crew members survived terrifying mid-air moments to save flight FZ1073 from disaster.

Emirati Attorney-General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said during Mr Al-Hammami's time in Melbourne, the suspect began "reading extremist literature and following online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks".

According to the statement, the man met individuals associated with the My Centre mosque in Broadmeadows in 2017 while studying at RMIT and that "the centre was managed by a Lebanese man known as Abu Hamza".

Samir Mohtadi, known as Abu Hamza, says: "The best thing sometimes is not to say anything." (Facebook)

The mosque's leader, Samir Mohtadi, known as Abu Hamza, invoked Jesus and Mary in a social media video in which he concluded: "The best thing sometimes is not to say anything."

"Right through the ages … those who're righteous, they've always been attacked, abused, accused, killed, imprisoned — and this is the way it is," Mr Mohtadi said.

He recounted a story of Mary, known in Islam as Maryam, being accused of wrongdoing, to which he said she responded: "I swear by Allah, I'm not going to speak to anyone."

"There are circumstances, my beloved brothers and respected sisters, regardless how much you explain yourself to people, they're fixated with their ideas and that's it; you can't change them," Mr Mohtadi said.

"So the best thing sometimes is not to say anything.

" They're going to continue accusing you … making false accusations. "

He also said worshipping God, rather than defending oneself, was a better use of one's time.

The ABC does not suggest that Mr Mohtadi or My Centre radicalised Mr Al-Hammami or were otherwise connected to the flydubai incident; simply that the authorities in the UAE have raised the connection.

Mr Mohtadi and My Centre, which is run by the Islamic Information & Services Network of Australasia (IISNA), were contacted for comment.

Hammam Al-Hammami was allegedly associated with people linked to the My Centre mosque in the Melbourne suburb of Broadmeadows. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

RMIT University has confirmed Mr Al-Hammami studied engineering there but did not successfully complete his degree.

Mr Al Shamsi, the Emirati attorney-general, said during the interrogation of Mr Al-Hammami it emerged he had been inspired by the September 11 terror attacks.

"[He] also said that he had prepared himself both psychologically and physically to carry out the plot by intensifying his exposure to material promoting terrorism and training in boxing under a private coach," the news agency reported.

Last week, the Australian Federal Police confirmed it had launched an investigation into Mr Al-Hammami's time in Australia.

Islamic Council of Victoria president Mohamed Mohideen told the ABC he condemned "all forms of extremism".

"The [Muslim] community should not be demonised for the actions of the two Bondi shooters," he said.

"We also want the public to note that the Muslim community does not hold other Australians responsible for the Christchurch massacre of 52 individuals."

World.title: Customer 'lucky to be alive' after 4WD smashes cafe frontage
World.content:
Two people remain in hospital with serious injuries after a car smashed into a shopfront in northern Tasmania yesterday evening.

Two people sitting outside and a staff member inside the Shearwater Food Company, at Shearwater near Devonport, were all injured.

The crash caused extensive damage to the building. (ABC News: Sandy Powell)

Tasmania Police Inspector Michelle Elmer said a 26-year-old woman was taken to the Launceston General Hospital (LGH).

"She remains in the LGH with serious injuries," Inspector Elmer said.

"A 60-year-old man was taken to the North West [Regional] Hospital with injuries and was later released, and the staff member was transported to the North West Regional Hospital and is still in hospital with serious but stable injuries."

The crash, involving a four-wheel drive vehicle, took out the front of the building and caused extensive damage inside.

The circumstances of the crash are still under investigation. (ABC News: Sandy Powell)

Inspector Elmer said there were two people in the vehicle, and the male driver was treated at the scene by paramedics but did not need to go to hospital.

The male passenger also received minor injuries.

Police earlier described the driver as "elderly", and that he had been "attempting to park outside" the cafe.

"It's believed that it [the vehicle] was in a parking manoeuvre prior to it going over the footpath," Inspector Elmer said.

"It wasn't at road speed; however, it was still significant enough to cause injuries and hit the building."

Inspector Elmer said no charges had been laid.

"Initial investigations indicate that this was not a deliberate action on behalf of the driver, but as to what caused the crash is still under investigation," she said.

A woman who was sitting outside the cafe at the time of the crash says she feels "lucky" to have escaped serious injury. (ABC News: Sandy Powell)

'Lucky to be alive'

A woman who narrowly escaped being struck said she felt "lucky to be alive".

The woman, who did not wish to be named, said she was sitting at a table near the door of the cafe on Club Drive when she heard tyres screeching about 6:45pm.

"I swung around, and I saw the car coming through the glass window and it missed me by inches," she said.

" Everything just happened so quickly. "

The woman said that, while she was not hit, if the crash had happened even a few minutes earlier, that may not have been the case — due to where she had previously been standing.

" It's still a huge shock, I'm still in shock now and I think I'm going to be for a little while. "

Inspector Elmer said police wanted to talk to anyone else who was at the cafe at the time, any other witnesses or anyone with information that may help the investigation.

World.title: Woman dies after alleged assault in trouble-stricken NT community
World.content:
Northern Territory Police say a woman in the remote community of Alpurrurulam, west of Mount Isa on the Queensland border, has died after she was allegedly physically assaulted in the early hours of this morning.

Police have said they are treating the death as suspicious, with specialist police units currently travelling to the location, about 1,500 kilometres from Darwin, and less than 20km from the Queensland border.

Superintendent Mark Bland has confirmed a male is in custody and "assisting with police inquiries" over the incident.

Alpurrurulam is about 360 kilometres from the nearest city, Mount Isa. (ABC News: Victoria Pengilley)

"Around 5:30am this morning, police received a report from the local clinic that a woman had died after allegedly being physically assaulted," police said in a statement.

"Local police, with assistance from Avon Downs police, are currently responding to the incident with detectives from the Crime Command and Forensics travelling to the community."

Police have not yet released the victim's or the alleged offender's ages or any further details of the incident.

Alpurrurulam, also known as Lake Nash, has been struggling with internal community unrest, which caused the recent evacuation of its clinic staff from the community.

It is also currently unclear what level of staffing was at the clinic at the time of the woman's assault and death.

NT Health has been contacted for comment.

No permanent police presence

There has not been a permanent police station in Alpurrurulam since 2018, with the closest officers stationed 170 kilometres away at remote Avon Downs.

Alpurrurulam is a dry community, but the Barkly Regional Council has reported large quantities of black market supply are being transported over the border from Queensland.

The electorate's NT MP, Chansey Paech, said in a statement this morning he was "deeply saddened to hear reports this morning of a tragic loss of life in Alpurrurulam".

Chansey Paech has questioned why additional police resources have not been directed to Alpurrurulam. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"[This is] a community that has been desperately calling out for more help, resources and support in recent months," he said.

"My thoughts are with the family, loved ones and the entire community at this difficult time.

" But serious questions need to be asked about what is being done to support this community and respond to the concerns residents have been raising. "

Mr Paech accused the NT government of "ignoring the bush" and urged it to take action on extra police resourcing for the community and efforts to better combat illegal alcohol supply.

The NT government has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Senior police officer facing sack over claims of rough, non-consensual sex
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland Police Senior police officer facing sack over claims of rough, non-consensual sex Julius Dennis October 12, 2026 — 1:34pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A senior Queensland police officer could be sacked over claims he had non-consensual rough sex with two women, but will not be prosecuted over the allegations. It was alleged the detective senior sergeant spiked the women’s drinks before engaging in extreme sex, though a criminal investigation found there was not enough evidence for him to be charged. The details of the incidents came to light during a Queensland Civil and Administrative Tribunal hearing over the Queensland Police Service sanction against the officer. The officer does not dispute he had sex with the women. Queensland Police Service The women, who met the officer at a gym where he was an instructor, had reported the incidents to the Crime and Corruption Commission, and then the police in 2020, after they realised they had had similar experiences in 2016 and 2018.



The first woman told police the officer had watched her in a public bathroom and attempted to have sex with her at her home, and then slapped her while they were drunk. Another time, he had rough sex with her in a public shower at a camping ground. On another occasion, he used zip ties and rope to restrain her during sex, and poured a red substance over her while restrained. The second woman said she was plied with alcohol, slapped in the face multiple times, engaged in rough and demeaning sex, and was restrained with bondage materials during sex. The officer did not deny the events happened, but believed the sex was consensual, and the intoxication was “mid-range”, QCAT Member Richard Oliver said. “On the females’ recollection, it was forced upon them and there is even an inference that they were drugged,” he said.



Following an investigation by the QPS Ethical Standards Command, Assistant Commissioner Maurice Carless decided the officer should be dismissed for misconduct in February 2022. Related Article Public service Former LNP MPs tapped for roles on legal sector disciplinary tribunal The officer called for a review of the misconduct finding, which relied heavily on the fact the investigation had not found the sex was non-consensual. Oliver said it was not disputed the alleged misconduct occurred during the officer’s private time, and it was not alleged that he used police resources to commit any alleged crimes. “The only relevant feature of the factual circumstances, in relation to each of the females involved, is that they knew the applicant was a police officer,” he said.



Under this reading, the only important matters were whether his actions were disgraceful, improper or unbecoming of an officer, showed unfitness to be an officer, or did not meet the standards expected of an officer, Oliver said. Oliver said while there was little evidence the officer used his position to groom the women or build trust, he still acted in a way that was “disgraceful and improper and crossed the line to render it misconduct”. The matter will return to the tribunal to hear material on the severity of the sanction after the appeals process runs out on November 1. World.title: Giant Kiwis hunting Kangaroos in World Cup opener
World.content:
SportNRLRugby League World Cup Giant Kiwis hunting Kangaroos in World Cup opener Christy Doran Updated October 12, 2026 — 1:31pm ,first published 1:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Did somebody say roadkill? The Kangaroos have been warned about a Kiwi steamroller heading their way on Thursday night in Sydney. In props Naufahu Whyte, captain James Fisher-Harris, Moses Leota and Joseph Tapine, the Kiwis might have the best collection of props in the country’s history. Naufahu Whyte and James Fisher-Harris are two members of New Zealand’s big World Cup forward pack. George Chan That’s certainly the belief of NRL premiership-winning coach Shane Flanagan “There’s no stronger forward pack,” Flanagan said last week on The Bye Round podcast.



Former England enforcer James Graham agreed: “Have they got the best four props? Not just as a group, but if you’re ranking the best props in the world … I think Naufahu Whyte has been the best prop this year, and you could make a strong case that positions two, three and four would be filled by Tapine, Leota and Fisher-Harris.” And after Lindsay Collins was ruled out through injury, the Kangaroos pack looks a bit light on in the middle, despite still having Tino Fa’asuamaleaui, Keaon Koloamatangi and Patrick Carrigan in their ranks. Fisher-Harris, however, does not want to get caught up in the off-field chat. “I don’t really care what everyone is saying,” the humble Warriors captain said. “I know what we’ve got, but we need to get to work, bro. “If anything, we know everyone can play big minutes. We’re chasing quality – quality and work ethic. This is not our first rodeo, so we’re looking forward to it.”



Raiders hardman Tapine is another who doesn’t want to get swept up in the headlines. “You can’t just rely on a paper team,” he said. “We’ve got to go out and deliver, so we’ve been talking about that.” Just don’t ask Leota about Kayln Ponga’s hit that floored the Panthers prop during the preliminary final. “Ronaldo’s given me shit, but he’s [Ponga] a humble dude, and I’m excited to see him play for us,” Leota said.



It is difficult not to get excited about the collision coming on Thursday night in the World Cup opener. While State of Origin has long been seen as the pinnacle of rugby league, the relaxation of international eligibility laws to equalise the talent across the game has been a boost for Test football in recent years. Naufahu Whyte was outstanding for the Roosters as they claimed the 2026 NRL title. Getty Images The Kiwis’ big four are sure to figure in Australia’s planning for Thursday night, with the need to negate the strength in the middle of the field crucial to victory. Whyte, who was named in the Dally M team of the year alongside Fisher-Harris, is even happy to come off the bench. It’s a scary prospect given the destruction he caused this year, including in the Roosters’ 19-18 grand final win over the Knights.



“Honestly … we come in with no thought of being the big dog,” Whyte said. “We may be that at our individual clubs, but once we put this black jersey on, there’s no ego, there’s no one who’s meant to be the top dog in our forward pack. Everyone just goes out there doing their job. “If that’s starting or coming off the bench, I’ll still put my best foot forward and do whatever it takes.” James Fisher-Harris will lead a powerful Kiwi side in the 2026 Rugby League World Cup. Getty Images Whyte is already licking his lips at the chance to play against a couple of his Roosters teammates. Fullback James Tedesco and halfback Sam Walker aren’t yet assured of playing, but Whyte won’t spare anyone punishment.



“Anyone that’s wearing green and gold, I’m eyeing anyone now,” he said. Despite the Kiwis’ big men wanting to let their actions do the talking, there’s an inner confidence and excitement brewing. Jahrome Hughes is set to play for the Kiwis for the first time since 2023. Getty Images Fisher-Harris presented Whyte with his debut jersey a few years ago, hoping that he would one day take over the mantle as the side’s enforcer. Now, he’s reached the summit. “In 2023, he was our 18th man in all three games in the Pacific Championship,” Fisher-Harris said. “It’s just cool to see him get better and better each year at the Roosters and obviously in the international land.



“Right now, he’s probably the hardest to handle forward. It’s pretty cool to have him on our team.” Tapine is another blown away by Whyte’s rapid rise. Tino Fa’asuamaleaui (centre) will likely have a big role to play against New Zealand. Getty Images “We were in camp last year together, and I said, ‘Man, he’ll be the best front row in the next three to four years’. He’s done it this year; he’s been the best in the comp,” the Raiders forward said. While the Kiwis’ big four are looking forward to locking horns, they’re not the only ones.



Fit-again halfback Jahrome Hughes is another rubbing his hands together. “I’ve been lucky enough to play with some pretty good forward packs, but I think the calibre of players that we have [in our] forward pack are right up there with the best,” said the Kiwi halfback. “I’m really excited. I’m going to let them do their thing. I can just do mine by talking and helping the team around the park.” Related Article Rugby League World Cup ‘Misunderstood’ Luai leads Samoan infusion at Parramatta With rugby league growing in popularity in New Zealand with the rise of the Warriors, the Kiwi big men want to continue to win the hearts and minds of the country’s youngsters.



“I remember the time when the boys won the 2008 World Cup; that still sits in my mind,” Fisher-Harris said. “It’s pretty cool. I was a kid then. I just hope little kids will be watching us soon.” Tapine, too, wants to inspire the next generation. “That’s always the goal for us,” he said. “I remember watching [Jared] Waerea-Hargreaves, Jesse Bromwich, and I want to do the same, and that’s our job to try and get that next generation through as well.”

World.title: Fight erupts between union and ABC’s head of news
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMedia & marketing Fight erupts between union and ABC’s head of news Calum Jaspan October 12, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The ABC’s new head of news Simon Robinson is staring down the barrel of a staff revolt just four weeks into joining the public broadcaster, with its union committee labelling a threat of disciplinary action against a senior journalist an attack on press freedom. The ABC’s Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance house committee called an urgent meeting for its members on Monday after Michael Slezak, who is also the federal president of the union, was threatened with disciplinary action over a piece he wrote in The Australian Financial Review. The ABC’s new head of news has threatened a senior journalist and union representative with disciplinary action. Paul Jeffers Robinson, who joined the ABC as director of news last month, called Slezak into a meeting last week to raise concerns over his conduct, an email from the union to its members alleges. Robinson and national and digital news boss Lee Glendinning said he may have breached the ABC’s external work policy and code of conduct over the article, which advocated against plans to limit publicly available information about company directors in Australia.



In the piece, Slezak said that ASIC and its chief executive Mark Rigotti was using the Bondi terror attack as a “shield” to help push forward changes to an issue it has long pushed for, access to personal information of prominent company directors. The pair refused to rule out the possibility of disciplinary action or dismissal, the email sent out to about 1000 union members on Monday said. The union has called a meeting of members for Tuesday and called on ABC management to rule out action on Slezak and ensure union representatives can undertake legitimate advocacy in future “without intimidation or reprisal”. Any attempts to intimidate elected staff representatives “must be met with a collective response from the members they represent”, the email said. The ABC’s new news boss Simon Robinson joined last month from Reuters. The ABC has strict rules that demand its staff follow an external work request process.



However, the union says that Slezak had a pre-existing written agreement with the broadcaster that predated Robinson’s arrival, which permitted him to engage in public comment on behalf of journalists, as part of his senior and public role with the MEAA. Related Article On Background ABC hopes embarrassing radio U-turn will deliver ratings dividend Robinson joined the ABC last month following the exit of Justin Stevens in May. Robinson joined from news agency Reuters where he was the outlet’s second most senior editor globally. Robinson and the ABC were approached for comment. Slezak and the union were also approached for comment. The article in question was published by the AFR last Monday. In it, Slezak argued against proposed changes to the corporate regulator, ASIC, which would limit the amount of public information made available about company directors.



“The ABC cannot publicly champion press freedom while privately targeting a national union representative for doing the same thing,” the union’s ABC house committee said. “What message does targeting the highest profile ABC union member, by the biggest media organisation in the country, send to union members, delegates and journalists across newsrooms across the country? “Our union representatives are elected to advocate for us. They cannot do their jobs if they are only permitted to say things with which their employers agree. The ABC’s targeting of Michael is an attack on press freedom and an attack on our freedom of association.” The ABC has had a tense relationship with its unionised staff over the past 12 months as a drawn-out enterprise agreement bargaining process led to its first strike in two decades. Union representatives and management clashed at several points throughout the process, before an agreement was finally struck in March shortly after a staff walk-out. World.title: Australian engineer Robert Pether released from Iraqi prison
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalIraq Australian engineer Robert Pether released from Iraqi prison Andrew Probyn October 12, 2026 — 1:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australian engineer Robert Pether has left Iraq after more than five years in detention, following a protracted campaign to secure his release. Pether, 51, and his Egyptian colleague Khalid Zaghloul were arrested in April 2021 in Baghdad while working on a $1 billion project to build the new headquarters of the Central Bank of Iraq. Australian Robert Pether has left Iraq after more than five years in detention. DFAT Australian officials on Monday escorted Pether to the airport, where he planned to fly to Ireland to reunite with his wife and children. An Iraqi judge found Pether guilty of deception in August 2021, although his lawyers said he should not be held responsible for the actions of the engineering company, CME Consulting.



Related Article Iraq ‘This is a life sentence’: Sydney businessman jailed in Iraq and fined $12 million His wife Desree has demanded his release ever since, asserting it was a travesty of justice and that his imprisonment amounted to arbitrary detention. Pether’s health deteriorated during his imprisonment as he lost a lot of weight and battled cancer. Foreign Minister Penny Wong said she was relieved that he had been freed. “The Australian government welcomes the decision by the Iraqi government to allow Mr Pether to leave,” Wong said.



“I spoke with Robert Pether this morning. I expressed to him our relief that he had been released and my hope that he recovers, but most importantly, I wished him well for his reunion with the family and for his recovery in the future.” Wong said the government had made 280 separate representations “at all levels” since his detention. The Iraqi government had insisted that Pether or the company must pay a $US12 million fine. “I’ve made it clear that the Australian government doesn’t make monetary contributions in relation to alleged offences, but what we do do is make sustained advocacy a part of how we engage on these issues, and that’s what we’ve done,” Wong said. World.title: Critica lands inaugural 160Mt WA rare earths resource
World.content:

Critica Limited has hit a significant de-risking milestone at its mammoth Jupiter rare earths project in Western Australia, delivering a maiden indicated resource of 160 million tonnes grading 1700 parts per million (ppm) total rare earth oxides (TREO). The update, prepared by independent consultant SRK Consulting, follows a targeted infill drilling campaign that successfully converted 10 per cent of what Critica describes as the largest clay-hosted rare earths resource into a higher-confidence category. Rare earth-bearing mineral samples from Critica Limited’s Jupiter project, the nation’s largest clay-hosted rare earths resource near Mount Magnet in Western Australia. Infill drilling on a 125m by 125m grid across 3.3 square kilometres of the project’s 42-square-kilometre resource footprint delivered the upgrade. The tighter spacing gave Critica sufficient confidence in the geology and grade continuity to support the move from inferred to indicated status, while the balance remains inferred on broader drilling. Jupiter’s total inventory stands at a colossal 1.7 billion tonnes grading 1700ppm TREO, comprising 160 million tonnes in the indicated category and 1.5 billion tonnes in the inferred category.



‘The delivery of Jupiter’s first Indicated Mineral Resource is an important milestone and demonstrates the effectiveness of the targeted infill drilling completed over the past year.’ Critica Limited chief executive officer Jacob Deysel For reporting purposes, the updated estimate used a 1000ppm TREO lower cut-off, excluding any material grading below that level. Critica says the cut-off grade is more conservative than many peer projects and was selected due to Jupiter’s shallow, consistent mineralisation and preliminary metallurgical results. Notably, valuable magnet rare earth oxides (MREO) make up a solid 25 per cent of the total rare earths within the new indicated resource, hitting a grade of 420ppm. These elements - neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium and terbium - are essential for the high-performance permanent magnets used in electric vehicles, wind turbines and defence applications, making them a key driver of project value. Critica Limited chief executive officer Jacob Deysel said: “The results provide increased confidence in the geological and grade continuity of the infill-drilled area, while the vast majority of the Jupiter resource remains classified as Inferred.” With the resource upgrade now in the bag, the company says the all-important Jupiter scoping study is progressing and will be released shortly, offering the first detailed look at the giant deposit’s potential economics. Sedgman has been engaged to do the initial study, with prefeasibility work planned afterwards, including flora and fauna, cultural heritage, groundwater, water bores and resource-definition drilling.



This is the first time part of Jupiter’s enormous tonnage has entered the indicated category, a crucial step in Critica’s transition from explorer to developer. The result strengthens confidence in the drilled area and demonstrates the potential for further infill drilling to upgrade more of the inferred resource, paving the way for the company to systematically de-risk the deposit. Jupiter forms part of Critica’s flagship and wholly owned Brothers project, a semi-contiguous 1700-square-kilometre landholding 550km north-east of Perth and 60km west of Mount Magnet in Western Australia’s Mid West. The deposit is less than 10km from the sealed Geraldton–Mount Magnet Road and 250km from Geraldton’s port. The Mid-West gas pipeline runs alongside the road and electricity infrastructure runs 40km to the southwest. Its shallow, flat-lying clay-hosted profile may support simpler mining than a deep hard-rock operation. The rare earths sit in fine phosphate minerals and are highlighted by low uranium and thorium levels, which could offer processing, handling and permitting advantages. As part of the developing flowsheet, metallurgical studies have pinpointed a process of magnetic separation and flotation before acid baking, water leaching, impurity removal and rare earth precipitation. Pilot optimisation, by-product recovery and product qualification continue.



Critica says its beneficiation testwork has delivered an impressive 81 per cent recovery of magnet rare earths, upgrading the concentrate grade 14-fold to about three per cent TREO while rejecting a whopping 95 per cent of the unwanted material. The result could slash the volume of material requiring costly downstream processing, potentially delivering a significant boost to the project’s economics. Critica is also advancing Mt Lindsay in north-west Tasmania, one of the world’s largest undeveloped tungsten-tin systems. The new scoping study has thrown up some eye-watering numbers, boasting $1.42 billion pre-tax net present value (NPV), a stellar 64.9 per cent internal rate of return and a lightning-fast 1.9-year payback, all for a comparatively modest upfront capital outlay of $244.5 million. Together, both Jupiter and Mt Lindsay give the company exposure to a broader suite of critical minerals as Western governments seek more secure and diversified supply chains outside China. With a maiden indicated resource now defined, Critica has taken a major step in turning Jupiter’s jaw-dropping scale into a credible development proposition. All eyes will now be on that upcoming scoping study to see just what kind of economic heft this massive critical minerals deposit might carry. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Rain is on the cards for Brisbane with an outside chance of thunderstorms following a stretch of warmer weather.

World.title: Moonee Ponds vendors reduce price hopes to sell $2,817,500 renovated home
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Moonee Ponds vendors reduce price hopes to sell $2,817,500 renovated home Elizabeth Redman Updated October 12, 2026 — 12:29pm ,first published 11:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 Gift this free article Share full article with anyone — no subscription needed to read it. A Victorian home in Moonee Ponds with an elegant renovation passed in at auction on Saturday and later sold for $2,817,500 after the vendors cut their price hopes. The five-bedroom house at 58 Vine Street has arched windows and hallway arches, a marble kitchen, a reading nook and an entertaining deck with a barbecue. The property was one of 710 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne last week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 58 per cent from 508 reported results throughout the week, while 78 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. It was the final weekend before new auction rules, starting on October 16, will make it compulsory to publish the vendor’s reserve price a week before auction.



Related Article Auctions Unrenovated Carlton North terrace with listed reserve sells for $1,152,000 The Moonee Ponds house was listed with a price guide of $2.7 million to $2.9 million. Proceedings began with a vendor bid of $2.6 million, followed by a genuine bid of $2.62 million. Two bidders pushed the price in mostly $20,000 increments until it reached $2.78 million. But after a rise of $10,000, the price stalled at $2.79 million and the home passed in.



The reserve was $2.85 million but the vendors, who are moving to Queensland, were willing to meet the market. The buyer is a local upsizer and the underbidder was a family. McDonald Upton selling agent Georgie Maggs said the home was renovated in the past 12 months, as the vendors had intended to stay. “The opportunity to get a turnkey home under $3 million in Moonee Ponds is becoming pretty rare these days,” she said. “This home would have sold for more in a better market. There is definitely value there. The buyer bought well but the vendor had an opportunity there, so it was a commercial decision for them.”



Maggs said the market was in a transition phase before the new auction rules. She said interest rate rises and the rising cost of living were putting a ceiling on buyer budgets, and she noted the state election due next month. “I would describe the market as patchy. I think these turnkey family properties are still performing quite well,” she said. In Yarraville, a converted shopfront home drew three bidders and surpassed its reserve to sell for $1,265,000 at auction. The three-bedroom home at 55 Ballarat Street has an open-plan living and dining area that leads to a timber deck and lush courtyard. Its price guide was $1.1 million to $1.2 million.



Bidding began at the bottom of the price range and rose at pace to the top of the range, which was also the reserve price, but then it slowed. Related Article Auctions Upsizer gets a $45,000 discount on Essendon home with stylish reno An owner-occupier moving from regional Victoria who has family in the inner west landed the keys. The underbidder was a family looking to downsize and move to the area, while the third bidder was a first home buyer. The vendors are downsizing. Jas Stephens Real Estate selling agent Elise Nemer said the shopfront-style home was “very unique, they don’t come up that often”. “The market is really good. Properties are still selling. We are still having buyers coming through,” she said.



In neighbouring Kingsville, a renovated three-bedroom cottage passed in at auction and sold after for $1.34 million. The three-bedroom house at 124 Chirnside Street had a price guide of $1,275,000 to $1,375,000. A downsizer made a bid of $1.3 million. It was countered with a vendor bid of $1.32 million. But the reserve was $1.34 million and with no more bids forthcoming, the home passed in.



It sold in post-auction negotiations at the reserve price. The vendors had previously lived in the property but had leased it out in recent years. Related Article Property market How much Australian property is overvalued by now Village Real Estate selling agent Raymond Abilameh had expected a one-buyer auction, although a mix of downsizers, young professionals and families were interested during the sales campaign. He said homes like this were transacting well, albeit without as many bidders as in the past. “Renovated properties in good locations, they still seem to be transacting well,” he said.



“The unrenovated stock, that seems to be the stuff that is struggling more.” AMP chief economist Shane Oliver said Melbourne’s clearance rate of 58 per cent is still soft and likely to be revised a few percentage points lower. “We’ve got rising interest rates, the tax [changes] on investors and poor levels of confidence partly associated with high petrol prices,” he said. But he thought Melbourne’s auction market may be past the worst, although it was unlikely there would be a big recovery any time soon. “It’s not getting hit anywhere near as badly as some of the other cities.”

Assistant Minister for Citizenship Julian Hill says he needs more information in relation to grants given to a mosque that has reported links to alleged flydubai hijacker and pilot Hamam al-Hammami.

Al-Hammami began his descent into extremism while living in Melbourne, according to UAE authorities, this masthead has reported. He was pursuing a mechanical engineering degree at Melbourne’s RMIT University, and reportedly admitted he regularly attended a mosque affiliated with the university. He reportedly became acquainted with individuals associated with MyCentre, an Islamic organisation based in Broadmeadows.

On September 30, the 29-year-old Omani co-pilot allegedly attacked the captain of flydubai Flight FZ1073, which was travelling from Dubai, with the intent of crashing the plane into Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv.

Today, the Herald Sun reported that the Australian Federal Police and the federal government gave grants of more than $70,000 to the mosque.

World.title: Senior police officer facing sack over claims of rough, non-consensual sex
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland Police Senior police officer facing sack over claims of rough, non-consensual sex Julius Dennis October 12, 2026 — 1:34pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A senior Queensland police officer could be sacked over claims he had non-consensual rough sex with two women, but will not be prosecuted over the allegations. It was alleged the detective senior sergeant spiked the women’s drinks before engaging in extreme sex, though a criminal investigation found there was not enough evidence for him to be charged. The details of the incidents came to light during a Queensland Civil and Administrative Tribunal hearing over the Queensland Police Service sanction against the officer. The officer does not dispute he had sex with the women. Queensland Police Service The women, who met the officer at a gym where he was an instructor, had reported the incidents to the Crime and Corruption Commission, and then the police in 2020, after they realised they had had similar experiences in 2016 and 2018.



The first woman told police the officer had watched her in a public bathroom and attempted to have sex with her at her home, and then slapped her while they were drunk. Another time, he had rough sex with her in a public shower at a camping ground. On another occasion, he used zip ties and rope to restrain her during sex, and poured a red substance over her while restrained. The second woman said she was plied with alcohol, slapped in the face multiple times, engaged in rough and demeaning sex, and was restrained with bondage materials during sex. The officer did not deny the events happened, but believed the sex was consensual, and the intoxication was “mid-range”, QCAT Member Richard Oliver said. “On the females’ recollection, it was forced upon them and there is even an inference that they were drugged,” he said.



Following an investigation by the QPS Ethical Standards Command, Assistant Commissioner Maurice Carless decided the officer should be dismissed for misconduct in February 2022. Related Article Public service Former LNP MPs tapped for roles on legal sector disciplinary tribunal The officer called for a review of the misconduct finding, which relied heavily on the fact the investigation had not found the sex was non-consensual. Oliver said it was not disputed the alleged misconduct occurred during the officer’s private time, and it was not alleged that he used police resources to commit any alleged crimes. “The only relevant feature of the factual circumstances, in relation to each of the females involved, is that they knew the applicant was a police officer,” he said.



Under this reading, the only important matters were whether his actions were disgraceful, improper or unbecoming of an officer, showed unfitness to be an officer, or did not meet the standards expected of an officer, Oliver said. Oliver said while there was little evidence the officer used his position to groom the women or build trust, he still acted in a way that was “disgraceful and improper and crossed the line to render it misconduct”. The matter will return to the tribunal to hear material on the severity of the sanction after the appeals process runs out on November 1.
