World.title: Giant Kiwis hunting Kangaroos in World Cup opener
World.content:
SportNRLRugby League World Cup Giant Kiwis hunting Kangaroos in World Cup opener Christy Doran Updated October 12, 2026 — 1:31pm ,first published 1:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Did somebody say roadkill? The Kangaroos have been warned about a Kiwi steamroller heading their way on Thursday night in Sydney. In props Naufahu Whyte, captain James Fisher-Harris, Moses Leota and Joseph Tapine, the Kiwis might have the best collection of props in the country’s history. Naufahu Whyte and James Fisher-Harris are two members of New Zealand’s big World Cup forward pack. George Chan That’s certainly the belief of NRL premiership-winning coach Shane Flanagan “There’s no stronger forward pack,” Flanagan said last week on The Bye Round podcast.



Former England enforcer James Graham agreed: “Have they got the best four props? Not just as a group, but if you’re ranking the best props in the world … I think Naufahu Whyte has been the best prop this year, and you could make a strong case that positions two, three and four would be filled by Tapine, Leota and Fisher-Harris.” And after Lindsay Collins was ruled out through injury, the Kangaroos pack looks a bit light on in the middle, despite still having Tino Fa’asuamaleaui, Keaon Koloamatangi and Patrick Carrigan in their ranks. Fisher-Harris, however, does not want to get caught up in the off-field chat. “I don’t really care what everyone is saying,” the humble Warriors captain said. “I know what we’ve got, but we need to get to work, bro. “If anything, we know everyone can play big minutes. We’re chasing quality – quality and work ethic. This is not our first rodeo, so we’re looking forward to it.”



Raiders hardman Tapine is another who doesn’t want to get swept up in the headlines. “You can’t just rely on a paper team,” he said. “We’ve got to go out and deliver, so we’ve been talking about that.” Just don’t ask Leota about Kayln Ponga’s hit that floored the Panthers prop during the preliminary final. “Ronaldo’s given me shit, but he’s [Ponga] a humble dude, and I’m excited to see him play for us,” Leota said.



It is difficult not to get excited about the collision coming on Thursday night in the World Cup opener. While State of Origin has long been seen as the pinnacle of rugby league, the relaxation of international eligibility laws to equalise the talent across the game has been a boost for Test football in recent years. Naufahu Whyte was outstanding for the Roosters as they claimed the 2026 NRL title. Getty Images The Kiwis’ big four are sure to figure in Australia’s planning for Thursday night, with the need to negate the strength in the middle of the field crucial to victory. Whyte, who was named in the Dally M team of the year alongside Fisher-Harris, is even happy to come off the bench. It’s a scary prospect given the destruction he caused this year, including in the Roosters’ 19-18 grand final win over the Knights.



“Honestly … we come in with no thought of being the big dog,” Whyte said. “We may be that at our individual clubs, but once we put this black jersey on, there’s no ego, there’s no one who’s meant to be the top dog in our forward pack. Everyone just goes out there doing their job. “If that’s starting or coming off the bench, I’ll still put my best foot forward and do whatever it takes.” James Fisher-Harris will lead a powerful Kiwi side in the 2026 Rugby League World Cup. Getty Images Whyte is already licking his lips at the chance to play against a couple of his Roosters teammates. Fullback James Tedesco and halfback Sam Walker aren’t yet assured of playing, but Whyte won’t spare anyone punishment.



“Anyone that’s wearing green and gold, I’m eyeing anyone now,” he said. Despite the Kiwis’ big men wanting to let their actions do the talking, there’s an inner confidence and excitement brewing. Jahrome Hughes is set to play for the Kiwis for the first time since 2023. Getty Images Fisher-Harris presented Whyte with his debut jersey a few years ago, hoping that he would one day take over the mantle as the side’s enforcer. Now, he’s reached the summit. “In 2023, he was our 18th man in all three games in the Pacific Championship,” Fisher-Harris said. “It’s just cool to see him get better and better each year at the Roosters and obviously in the international land.



“Right now, he’s probably the hardest to handle forward. It’s pretty cool to have him on our team.” Tapine is another blown away by Whyte’s rapid rise. Tino Fa’asuamaleaui (centre) will likely have a big role to play against New Zealand. Getty Images “We were in camp last year together, and I said, ‘Man, he’ll be the best front row in the next three to four years’. He’s done it this year; he’s been the best in the comp,” the Raiders forward said. While the Kiwis’ big four are looking forward to locking horns, they’re not the only ones.



Fit-again halfback Jahrome Hughes is another rubbing his hands together. “I’ve been lucky enough to play with some pretty good forward packs, but I think the calibre of players that we have [in our] forward pack are right up there with the best,” said the Kiwi halfback. “I’m really excited. I’m going to let them do their thing. I can just do mine by talking and helping the team around the park.” Related Article Rugby League World Cup ‘Misunderstood’ Luai leads Samoan infusion at Parramatta With rugby league growing in popularity in New Zealand with the rise of the Warriors, the Kiwi big men want to continue to win the hearts and minds of the country’s youngsters.



“I remember the time when the boys won the 2008 World Cup; that still sits in my mind,” Fisher-Harris said. “It’s pretty cool. I was a kid then. I just hope little kids will be watching us soon.” Tapine, too, wants to inspire the next generation. “That’s always the goal for us,” he said. “I remember watching [Jared] Waerea-Hargreaves, Jesse Bromwich, and I want to do the same, and that’s our job to try and get that next generation through as well.”

World.title: Fight erupts between union and ABC’s head of news
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMedia & marketing Fight erupts between union and ABC’s head of news Calum Jaspan October 12, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The ABC’s new head of news Simon Robinson is staring down the barrel of a staff revolt just four weeks into joining the public broadcaster, with its union committee labelling a threat of disciplinary action against a senior journalist an attack on press freedom. The ABC’s Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance house committee called an urgent meeting for its members on Monday after Michael Slezak, who is also the federal president of the union, was threatened with disciplinary action over a piece he wrote in The Australian Financial Review. The ABC’s new head of news has threatened a senior journalist and union representative with disciplinary action. Paul Jeffers Robinson, who joined the ABC as director of news last month, called Slezak into a meeting last week to raise concerns over his conduct, an email from the union to its members alleges. Robinson and national and digital news boss Lee Glendinning said he may have breached the ABC’s external work policy and code of conduct over the article, which advocated against plans to limit publicly available information about company directors in Australia.



In the piece, Slezak said that ASIC and its chief executive Mark Rigotti was using the Bondi terror attack as a “shield” to help push forward changes to an issue it has long pushed for, access to personal information of prominent company directors. The pair refused to rule out the possibility of disciplinary action or dismissal, the email sent out to about 1000 union members on Monday said. The union has called a meeting of members for Tuesday and called on ABC management to rule out action on Slezak and ensure union representatives can undertake legitimate advocacy in future “without intimidation or reprisal”. Any attempts to intimidate elected staff representatives “must be met with a collective response from the members they represent”, the email said. The ABC’s new news boss Simon Robinson joined last month from Reuters. The ABC has strict rules that demand its staff follow an external work request process.



However, the union says that Slezak had a pre-existing written agreement with the broadcaster that predated Robinson’s arrival, which permitted him to engage in public comment on behalf of journalists, as part of his senior and public role with the MEAA. Related Article On Background ABC hopes embarrassing radio U-turn will deliver ratings dividend Robinson joined the ABC last month following the exit of Justin Stevens in May. Robinson joined from news agency Reuters where he was the outlet’s second most senior editor globally. Robinson and the ABC were approached for comment. Slezak and the union were also approached for comment. The article in question was published by the AFR last Monday. In it, Slezak argued against proposed changes to the corporate regulator, ASIC, which would limit the amount of public information made available about company directors.



“The ABC cannot publicly champion press freedom while privately targeting a national union representative for doing the same thing,” the union’s ABC house committee said. “What message does targeting the highest profile ABC union member, by the biggest media organisation in the country, send to union members, delegates and journalists across newsrooms across the country? “Our union representatives are elected to advocate for us. They cannot do their jobs if they are only permitted to say things with which their employers agree. The ABC’s targeting of Michael is an attack on press freedom and an attack on our freedom of association.” The ABC has had a tense relationship with its unionised staff over the past 12 months as a drawn-out enterprise agreement bargaining process led to its first strike in two decades. Union representatives and management clashed at several points throughout the process, before an agreement was finally struck in March shortly after a staff walk-out. World.title: Australian engineer Robert Pether released from Iraqi prison
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalIraq Australian engineer Robert Pether released from Iraqi prison Andrew Probyn October 12, 2026 — 1:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australian engineer Robert Pether has left Iraq after more than five years in detention, following a protracted campaign to secure his release. Pether, 51, and his Egyptian colleague Khalid Zaghloul were arrested in April 2021 in Baghdad while working on a $1 billion project to build the new headquarters of the Central Bank of Iraq. Australian Robert Pether has left Iraq after more than five years in detention. DFAT Australian officials on Monday escorted Pether to the airport, where he planned to fly to Ireland to reunite with his wife and children. An Iraqi judge found Pether guilty of deception in August 2021, although his lawyers said he should not be held responsible for the actions of the engineering company, CME Consulting.



Related Article Iraq ‘This is a life sentence’: Sydney businessman jailed in Iraq and fined $12 million His wife Desree has demanded his release ever since, asserting it was a travesty of justice and that his imprisonment amounted to arbitrary detention. Pether’s health deteriorated during his imprisonment as he lost a lot of weight and battled cancer. Foreign Minister Penny Wong said she was relieved that he had been freed. “The Australian government welcomes the decision by the Iraqi government to allow Mr Pether to leave,” Wong said.



“I spoke with Robert Pether this morning. I expressed to him our relief that he had been released and my hope that he recovers, but most importantly, I wished him well for his reunion with the family and for his recovery in the future.” Wong said the government had made 280 separate representations “at all levels” since his detention. The Iraqi government had insisted that Pether or the company must pay a $US12 million fine. “I’ve made it clear that the Australian government doesn’t make monetary contributions in relation to alleged offences, but what we do do is make sustained advocacy a part of how we engage on these issues, and that’s what we’ve done,” Wong said. Jupiter forms part of Critica’s flagship and wholly owned Brothers project, a semi-contiguous 1700-square-kilometre landholding 550km north-east of Perth and 60km west of Mount Magnet in Western Australia’s Mid West. The deposit is less than 10km from the sealed Geraldton–Mount Magnet Road and 250km from Geraldton’s port. The Mid-West gas pipeline runs alongside the road and electricity infrastructure runs 40km to the southwest. Its shallow, flat-lying clay-hosted profile may support simpler mining than a deep hard-rock operation. The rare earths sit in fine phosphate minerals and are highlighted by low uranium and thorium levels, which could offer processing, handling and permitting advantages. As part of the developing flowsheet, metallurgical studies have pinpointed a process of magnetic separation and flotation before acid baking, water leaching, impurity removal and rare earth precipitation. Pilot optimisation, by-product recovery and product qualification continue.



Critica says its beneficiation testwork has delivered an impressive 81 per cent recovery of magnet rare earths, upgrading the concentrate grade 14-fold to about three per cent TREO while rejecting a whopping 95 per cent of the unwanted material. The result could slash the volume of material requiring costly downstream processing, potentially delivering a significant boost to the project’s economics. Critica is also advancing Mt Lindsay in north-west Tasmania, one of the world’s largest undeveloped tungsten-tin systems. The new scoping study has thrown up some eye-watering numbers, boasting $1.42 billion pre-tax net present value (NPV), a stellar 64.9 per cent internal rate of return and a lightning-fast 1.9-year payback, all for a comparatively modest upfront capital outlay of $244.5 million. Together, both Jupiter and Mt Lindsay give the company exposure to a broader suite of critical minerals as Western governments seek more secure and diversified supply chains outside China. With a maiden indicated resource now defined, Critica has taken a major step in turning Jupiter’s jaw-dropping scale into a credible development proposition. All eyes will now be on that upcoming scoping study to see just what kind of economic heft this massive critical minerals deposit might carry. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? World.title: Moonee Ponds vendors reduce price hopes to sell $2,817,500 renovated home
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Moonee Ponds vendors reduce price hopes to sell $2,817,500 renovated home Elizabeth Redman Updated October 12, 2026 — 12:29pm ,first published 11:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 Gift this free article Share full article with anyone — no subscription needed to read it. It won't deduct your gift credits. Learn more Share article as gift Share A A A

A Victorian home in Moonee Ponds with an elegant renovation passed in at auction on Saturday and later sold for $2,817,500 after the vendors cut their price hopes. The five-bedroom house at 58 Vine Street has arched windows and hallway arches, a marble kitchen, a reading nook and an entertaining deck with a barbecue. The property was one of 710 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne last week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 58 per cent from 508 reported results throughout the week, while 78 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. It was the final weekend before new auction rules, starting on October 16, will make it compulsory to publish the vendor’s reserve price a week before auction.



Related Article Auctions Unrenovated Carlton North terrace with listed reserve sells for $1,152,000 The Moonee Ponds house was listed with a price guide of $2.7 million to $2.9 million. Proceedings began with a vendor bid of $2.6 million, followed by a genuine bid of $2.62 million. Two bidders pushed the price in mostly $20,000 increments until it reached $2.78 million. But after a rise of $10,000, the price stalled at $2.79 million and the home passed in.



The reserve was $2.85 million but the vendors, who are moving to Queensland, were willing to meet the market. The buyer is a local upsizer and the underbidder was a family. McDonald Upton selling agent Georgie Maggs said the home was renovated in the past 12 months, as the vendors had intended to stay. “The opportunity to get a turnkey home under $3 million in Moonee Ponds is becoming pretty rare these days,” she said. “This home would have sold for more in a better market. There is definitely value there. The buyer bought well but the vendor had an opportunity there, so it was a commercial decision for them.”



Maggs said the market was in a transition phase before the new auction rules. She said interest rate rises and the rising cost of living were putting a ceiling on buyer budgets, and she noted the state election due next month. “I would describe the market as patchy. I think these turnkey family properties are still performing quite well,” she said. In Yarraville, a converted shopfront home drew three bidders and surpassed its reserve to sell for $1,265,000 at auction. The three-bedroom home at 55 Ballarat Street has an open-plan living and dining area that leads to a timber deck and lush courtyard. Its price guide was $1.1 million to $1.2 million.



Bidding began at the bottom of the price range and rose at pace to the top of the range, which was also the reserve price, but then it slowed. Related Article Auctions Upsizer gets a $45,000 discount on Essendon home with stylish reno An owner-occupier moving from regional Victoria who has family in the inner west landed the keys. The underbidder was a family looking to downsize and move to the area, while the third bidder was a first home buyer. The vendors are downsizing. Jas Stephens Real Estate selling agent Elise Nemer said the shopfront-style home was “very unique, they don’t come up that often”. “The market is really good. Properties are still selling. We are still having buyers coming through,” she said.



In neighbouring Kingsville, a renovated three-bedroom cottage passed in at auction and sold after for $1.34 million. The three-bedroom house at 124 Chirnside Street had a price guide of $1,275,000 to $1,375,000. A downsizer made a bid of $1.3 million. It was countered with a vendor bid of $1.32 million. But the reserve was $1.34 million and with no more bids forthcoming, the home passed in.



It sold in post-auction negotiations at the reserve price. The vendors had previously lived in the property but had leased it out in recent years. Related Article Property market How much Australian property is overvalued by now Village Real Estate selling agent Raymond Abilameh had expected a one-buyer auction, although a mix of downsizers, young professionals and families were interested during the sales campaign. He said homes like this were transacting well, albeit without as many bidders as in the past. “Renovated properties in good locations, they still seem to be transacting well,” he said.



“The unrenovated stock, that seems to be the stuff that is struggling more.” AMP chief economist Shane Oliver said Melbourne’s clearance rate of 58 per cent is still soft and likely to be revised a few percentage points lower. “We’ve got rising interest rates, the tax [changes] on investors and poor levels of confidence partly associated with high petrol prices,” he said. But he thought Melbourne’s auction market may be past the worst, although it was unlikely there would be a big recovery any time soon. “It’s not getting hit anywhere near as badly as some of the other cities.”

World.title: Eden Park wants platform upgrades, pedestrian bridge to stop rail delays for fans
World.content:
Rail platform upgrades and a pedestrian footbridge across Sandringham Road needed are urgently needed to prevent delays for Eden Park fans, the chief executive says.

Rugby fans using the train after the All Blacks' Bledisloe Cup clash against the Wallabies on Saturday were left waiting as long as 40 minutes, frustrating both fans and event management.

Auckland Transport said about 15,000 people used rail to get to and from the game, but a delay to a level crossing closure stopped trains on the east-west line, leaving hundreds of people waiting at Kingsland Station.

Eden Park chief executive Nick Sautner told Morning Report the connectivity between Eden Park and the rail network hadn't improved for a decade despite investment in the City Rail Link.

"We've invested in a $6 billion CRL but the adjacent infrastructure, whether it be the level crossings or platform upgrade and a footbridge into Kingsland, needs urgent attention.

"We were monitoring the area and we could see the frustration of our patrons. And with 40 percent of our match-day costs being integrated ticketing and traffic management, it's an area that hasn't improved over the last 10 years and it needs to improve.

Eden Park chief executive Nick Sautner at the stadium. Sharon Brettkelly

He said that equated to as much as $300,000 when major events take place at Eden Park.

"Almost 50,000 fans had a wonderful experience. We had 3000 staff employed. But their last experience, many of them, was waiting at a train station," Sautner said.

"We know that with the additional throughput of the CRL train through Morningside the level crossing will need to be either above or below ground.

"We want to see more patrons using the CRL."

He said patrons needed to have confidence they would be able to use the infrastructure to get to and from events safely.

"Auckland Transport's indicated only 15,000 people use public transport. We'll be having events like State of Origin with 50,000 plus and Bruno Mars with 65,000 plus. Every patron that attends a game has an integrated ticketing levy that pays for public transport."

Sautner said a major sports ground so close to the city should be used to full advantage.

"I've experienced being at Wembley Stadium for Taylor Swift with young children and it took three hours to get back.

"We are blessed and fortunate to have a venue only seven minutes from the CBD. But we always want to be better. We want to be world class. The experience delivered on field was world class, but that's only part of the experience. We want to see the entire experience to be world class."

World.title: Youth advocates urge rangatahi to vote as homelessness concerns grow
World.content:
Youth and housing advocates are urging whānau to haere ki te pōti, saying political decisions can have a real impact on youth homelessness.

Only 62 percent of 18 to 24-year-olds are currently enrolled to vote for this year's general election, and the figure is even lower for rangatahi Māori, with only 50 percent enrolled.

Twenty-year-old youth advocate, Platinum, said young people need to pay attention to party policies, particularly those affecting housing and vulnerable youth.

"I think it's so important that rangatahi get out there and enrol to vote especially if you're 18, even if you're younger than 18, just doing your research on what policies are being pushed through," she told RNZ.

"It is important that we're seeing the right people come into power through the next election who are actually going to fix these problems [homelessness] because at the end of the day I wouldn't want my cousin or my whānau who's as young as 14 on the road."

Platinum said all political parties could do more to address homelessness in Aotearoa, but particularly youth homelessness.

"There are not enough houses for our whānau right now and that is so sad."

She disagreed with the saying that being homeless "is a choice."

"I think some people would rather do the rough sleeping than be in an unsafe environment and that's sad, that's why we're here, we need to get our whānau out of those environments but not into a situation where they don't have a home, don't have a place."

Research shows that more than half of people experiencing homelessness in New Zealand are under the age of 24.

Māori are disproportionately impacted by homelessness, with over 28.8 percent of people experiencing homelessness having Māori whakapapa, despite accounting for 17.1 percent of the population.

Research by the Coalition to End Women's Homelessness found Wāhine Māori make up over 50 percent of the total homeless population and account for at least a third to a majority of those experiencing severe housing deprivation. In OECD countries, women "typically account for 22 percent of people experiencing homelessness, on average," the coalition said.

World Homeless Day 2026 activation in West Auckland. RNZ / Coco Lance

Platinum was a part of the World Homeless Day activation on Saturday organised by Youth Homelessness Collective Manaaki Rangatahi.

It brought together many different housing and youth services based in Tāmaki Makaurau, offering many different services for free, including hair cuts, kai packs, clothing and health checks. The Electoral Commission were also in attendance, checking enrolments and helping whānau to enrol to vote.

A key kōrero throughout the day from all whānau from was to make your voices heard and "haere ki te pōti."

Platinum said the government were focussing on the "wrong things," pointing to the Summary Offences (Move-on Orders) Amendment Bill which passed its third reading, under urgency, and became law on 24 September.

The legislation, brought forward by Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith and the coalition government, gives police the power to issue move on orders to people if they are being disorderly, begging or rough sleeping. Anyone disobeying the order will face a fine or possible jail sentence.

"I think they are not looking at the bigger problem which is the unsafetiness of actually being homeless," Platinum said.

"It's important that we see that homelessness isn't just about the home itself it's about the environment, it's about the people it's about the community everything plays a part into homelessness, housing insecurities, overcrowding housing, moving from places to places that's all considered homelessness.

"So it's important that we get that out there and actually show everybody the reality of what some of our youth are living, the situations that they're in. A home is supposed to be a whare haumaru, it's supposed to be a safe space and a place where we feel protected and feel heard and seen and everything."

At the World Homeless Day activation, RNZ spoke to many rangatahi and frontline workers who have seen first hand the reality of youth homelessness in New Zealand. One teenager RNZ spoke to was homeless from the age of 12 to 16. She was sleeping in stolen cars and abandoned houses.

One frontline worker said he had recently helped a 12-year-old the night before the event, and said the homeless youth they help everyday are in his words, "getting younger."

World.title: Ex-police officer Matthew Rogers seeks no conviction for possessing objectionable publications
World.content:
A police officer of nearly four decades, who pleaded guilty to possessing objectionable publications, is seeking to be discharged without conviction.

Auckland-based officer Matthew Rogers was one of three police staff to be charged following the rapid review carried out by police in October 2025.

The review was sparked by the resignation of former Deputy Police Commissioner Jevon McSkimming, after child sexual exploitation and bestiality material were found on his work devices.

Court documents revealed that between August 2023 and October 2025, Rogers used a police-issued device to conduct searches for pornographic and sexualised material.

Searches included "nude teen", and there were nine images he'd viewed that matched what was previously categorised as Category 2B Child Sexual Abuse Material.

At a sentencing hearing on Monday at the Manukau District Court, Rogers' lawyer Todd Simmonds KC prefaced his arguments for discounts and a discharge without conviction, emphasising that nothing put forward is an attempt to minimise what's occurred.

He asked Judge Clare Bennett to consider the context of "relatively modest" number of images involved in Rogers' case, the fact that images weren't downloaded, and that the scale of offending is "not an apple with an apple" compared to the McSkimming case which involved thousands of objectionable images.

"This could be far, far worse is the short point I make" he said. Simmonds said what mattered most for Rogers is that the presence of a conviction would make a "material difference" to his future employment, and is seeking discharge without conviction.

He said Rogers resigned a couple of months ago after nearly 40 years of service to the community.

Simmonds said many job applications require applicants to disclose previous convictions, and that this is not a case of the horse having bolted with previous reporting on Rogers' offending, but that a conviction would still make a material difference to Rogers' job prospects.

When Judge Bennett asked what kind of work Rogers would be seeking, Simmonds replied that Rogers doesn't have an answer to that yet and is looking to explore what opportunities come his way.

Police prosecutor Kristy Li said they need to see evidence of Rogers not being able to secure employment and how the consequences of a conviction will make a difference to Rogers' future work.

She asked for the sentencing to be adjourned to wait for that material.

Simmonds said he will clarify that with Rogers, and Judge Bennett has adjourned the sentencing to November.

Rogers has been remanded at large.

Meanwhile, Simmonds also made a series of arguments for mitigating factors for a reduction to the potential sentence of 12 to 18 months as a starting point sought by the prosecution.

He proposed a 25 percent reduction for Rogers' early guilty plea.

Simmonds said Rogers' nearly four decades of service to the community also speaks to his previous good character; adding that Rogers is genuinely remorseful in his own way, and asked for a discreet reduction for those factors.

In total, Simmonds is seeking a total discount of 40 percent for his client.

World.title: Man charged with murder after Te Puke crash
World.content:
A man has been charged with murder after a single car crash in Te Puke on Saturday.

One person was killed in the crash at the intersection of Te Puke Highway and Rangiruru Road on 10 October.

Another person was taken to hospital in a critical condition.

The Serious Crash Unit conducted a scene examination following the incident.

Detective Senior Sergeant Natalie Flowerdew-Brown said a homicide investigation has been launched and a 25-year-old man charged.

He is due to appear in the Tauranga District Court on Monday.

"As part of our investigation, Police ask anyone with information, CCTV, or dashcam footage of a white 2005 Toyota Caldina travelling in the Brown Road area to come forward," Flowerdew-Brown said.

World.title: State school becomes first to convert to charter school
World.content:
The associate education minister estimates about 6000 students will be enrolled in charter schools next year.

David Seymour announced that Pakaraka School in Northland has become the first state school to convert to a charter school today.

Pakaraka School is now run by the Society of Holistic Learners - a charitable trust led by the school parents.

"These guys have always wanted to do things their way...That whole community has got behind converting to a charter. They are effectively taking back control of education in their community the way that Tomorrow Schools promised," said Seymour.

Pakaraka School in Northland is now run by the Society of Holistic Learners. Google Maps

He said charter schools afforded more freedom to schools to tailor their education to students' needs.

He said the local community had driven the changes - in a survey conducted by the trust, 95 percent of respondents were in favour of the conversion and none supported remaining a state school.

The school would have to prove its students were achieving as well as comparable state schools, using the same testing as them, Seymour said.

He said the conversion had opened the floodgates for more charter schools - 2000 students were enrolled in charter schools in the 18 months since they began operating, and he expected 21 charter schools to open by next year.

He said they were cheaper to set up and run per student than state schools, with no extra money budgeted for them.

Uniforms

Seymour also said he welcomed Labour "copying" ACT's policy on cutting costs for school uniforms.

Labour announced its policy to make school uniforms cheaper and allow for "affordable, generic" alternatives to be used as well.

ACT had announced a policy to cut uniform costs which included a cap of three branded items in school uniforms and allowing generic items from retailers like The Warehouse and Kmart, back in June.

"There's no limit to what you can achieve if you don't care who takes the credit. If Labour copying the Act Party's school uniform policy saves parents money in a cost-of-living crisis, I think we should welcome that."

World.title: NRL claims it was blindsided by NZ Rugby injunction bid
World.content:
The NRL says it has been "blindsided" by New Zealand Rugby's urgent bid to stop Papua New Guinea's incoming NRL franchise from using the Chiefs name, while NZR claims it has been left "shadow-boxing" in unsuccessful attempts to engage with rugby league officials over the trademark dispute.

The opening salvos in the escalating legal battle were heard before Justice Karen Grau in the High Court in Wellington on Monday, as the NZR seeks an interim injunction to prevent the use of "PNG Chiefs", "Chiefs" or similar names in New Zealand.

The NRL has accused New Zealand Rugby of waiting up to 10 months to act on its concerns over Papua New Guinea's incoming NRL franchise using the Chiefs name, arguing the delay makes its urgent High Court injunction application unfair.

But NZR said it has repeatedly tried to engage with NRL and PNG Chiefs officials to resolve the dispute, only to be met with a lack of meaningful response. It argues the urgency has increased as the PNG club's official launch approaches.

Justice Grau is expected to rule later on Monday whether NZR's application should proceed urgently, with a two-hour hearing scheduled for later this week, or whether the matter should be heard in full early next year.

Counsel for the Australian Rugby League Commission (ARLC), which is representing the interests of the NRL and the PNG team, Joe Edwards, said the escalation to formal legal proceedings had come as a surprise.

Edwards told the court the ARLC was notified of NZ Rugby's concerns about PNG adopting the Chiefs name four days after the initial team launch in October last year. He added ARLC outlined its position in December last year, but heard nothing further from NZ Rugby until last month.

"This has come out of the blue and blindsided people," he said, arguing that if the matter was genuinely urgent, it should have been raised months earlier.

He asked the court to instead set the matter down for a substantive hearing, questioning why NZ Rugby was seeking urgent relief after such a lengthy period.

"We're querying why there is urgency now when they've had so long to file."

The new PNG club will join the NRL in 2028 as the competition's 19th franchise. Facebook / PNG Chiefs

NZ Rugby counsel Earl Gray rejected the suggestion the application was a "blindside move", saying a draft statement of claim had been provided to the defendants on 28 September.

"This was a last ditch effort to get resolution or at least engagement ... there was no response to that," Gray told the court.

"At the moment we've just been shadow-boxing because we've had no engagement."

Gray also argued NZR only recently became aware of the PNG club's plans for an official brand launch on 21 October, which prompted the need for urgent action.

"The date of the announcement ... has been the trigger, because we all know the launch of a brand and logo is the start of a real ramping up," Gray said.

Chiefs v Chiefs

At the centre of the legal battle is NZ Rugby's claim that allowing the PNG team to use the Chiefs name risks confusion and damage to a brand the Waikato-based Super Rugby club has built over more than 30 years.

The legal battle threatens to disrupt the PNG club's plans to formally unveil their inaugural jersey and branding in Port Moresby next week. The PNG team, which is set to join the NRL in 2028 as the competition's 19th franchise, is backed by a $600 million Australian government funding package.

NZR have argued that allowing another professional sporting franchise to use the same name in the same trans-Tasman market risks undermining a brand it has spent three decades building.

NZR chief executive officer Steve Lancaster said for 30 years the Chiefs and their players have built an "incredibly strong identity that is widely recognised and loved by fans".

"We want to be absolutely clear, this is not about rugby league's growth in the Pacific. We welcome the development of the Pacific region through sport and the passion that the people of Papua New Guinea have for both rugby and rugby league."

"For 30 years the Chiefs and their players have built an incredibly strong identity that is widely recognised and loved by fans. We have raised our concerns with the ARLC directly and consistently over the last year in attempting to find a resolution. We now have a responsibility to protect the Chiefs brand," he said.

Peter V'landys. NRL Photos 2020

The Waikato side has used the Chiefs name since 1996 and holds registered trademarks covering its logo in New Zealand and internationally, including Australia.

The Super Rugby club's position appears to be backed by IP Australia, which has reportedly raised repeated concerns about the PNG's club's attempts to secure trademark protection for its name.

The ABC reported earlier this month the NRL has received three adverse reports in response to the PNG club's trademark applications, with IP Australia declaring there is a "real and tangible danger" of brand confusion.

However, ARLC executive chair Peter V'landys has criticised NZR's position as "mind-blowing hypocrisy", pointing to the use of the Blues name by both rugby league and rugby union teams.

"The NSW Blues have been around since the 1900s," V'landys told The Australian.

"They've been using the Auckland Blues since the 1990s and never consulted us. They took our name, the Blues, and we were never concerned then they go ahead and do this.

World.title: Politicians can't 'dance alone' on superannuation - Nicola Willis
World.content:
National's Nicola Willis says politicians need to put aside the "pettiness" and come to the table on superannuation, while leader Christopher Luxon says its a "Kiwi issue", not an ideological one.

National has confirmed the fiscal plan announced on Monday was the party's superannuation policy - maintaining its plans to raise the retirement age, but not stating when exactly that would happen.

National has released its fiscal plan, dangling tax cuts for voters, but not until the books are back in surplus - which isn't forecast until at least 2029.

It has proposed raising the age gradually, and that remains its policy - supported by ACT, but opposed by Labour, Greens and New Zealand First.

It comes at a time when the polls are tight, and raising the age is an unpopular move. An RNZ Reid Research poll from July showed a clear majority of respondents - 58 percent - wanted the age of eligibility to remain at 65.

It also comes after Labour's Barbara Edmonds and National's Nicola Willis agreed on Sunday to a cross party discussion on the wider issue of retirement and aged care.

Luxon was pleased with this, but said on Monday it was "unhelpful for parties to come with pre-ordained or predetermined outcomes on that".

Willis said on Monday she'd been open and up front about gradually increasing the age, but that she doesn't get to "dance alone" on the issue.

She said she'd invited other parties to the dancefloor, but other politicians were quick to play politics on the issue, referring to this years Budget where warned that any party that ignores the size of the problem is doing so for its own benefit.

She said she was open to discussions about what a sustainable future for superannuation looked like.

"If other parties wish to bring specific ideas to the table, then of course, as finance minister, I would consider those in good faith.

"What is needed is for political parties to be honest and upfront about what their proposals are for ensuring that this entitlement can remain consistent into the future."

Willis said she did think super should be a universal entitlement.

"Every New Zealander at retirement should get New Zealand superannuation. I think together we can work out settings that achieve that. But I'm inviting other political parties to come to the table."

She committed to discussions within the first 100 days of office.

"We will have to consult on a terms of reference and parties will each have to come to the table in the spirit of finding an enduring solution so that New Zealanders can plan with confidence."

World.title: Izzi Batt-Doyle smashes Australian marathon record with run in Chicago
World.content:
Adelaide's Izzi Batt-Doyle is Australia's new marathon queen after breaking the national record with a stunning run at the year's penultimate major, the Chicago Marathon.

Batt-Doyle ran a time of 2:20:38 to take 46 seconds off the mark set by fellow South Australian Jess Stenson in Valencia in December.

It also lowered the 31-year-old's own personal best by two minutes and 21 seconds.

"I'm very, very happy. I feel a sense of relief, because it's something I really felt I could achieve and it's been on my mind the past couple of years," Batt-Doyle said.

"I'm really proud I could achieve it today and I'm so happy."

Assefa's Achilles rupture Tigst Assefa ran the final two kilometres of the Berlin Marathon with a badly damaged Achilles tendon, which required immediate surgery to repair. She still ran the third-fastest women's marathon in history.

Batt-Doyle was sixth overall in the women's race, which was won by defending champion Hawi Feysa of Ethiopia in 2:13:33.

"The field here is so great, but smaller on the professional side," Batt-Doyle said.

"You don't have masses of people in groups."

Batt-Doyle was paced by her fiancé Riley Cocks.

"[We were] isolated the whole race," she said.

"The gun went off and second kilometre it was just the two of us, because we were running between groups.

"I spent most of the race trusting our plan and the pacing strategy we had hoped to run the first half in, and hope that I would feel strong in the second half."

Batt-Doyle's race was a model of control, with her splits barely moving. Every 5km block landed between 16:36 and 16:47, holding her at about 3:19 to 3:21 per kilometre from the opening kilometres to the final stretch.

Eliud Kipchoge wins Melbourne Marathon Marathon legend Eliud Kipchoge has time to slow down and wave at the crowds at the MCG and still break the race record at the Melbourne Marathon.

She went through halfway in 1:10:29 and then ran the second half in about 1:10:09, giving her a 20-second negative split.

"We went through halfway in under the time needed to run 2:21, but I wasn't sure because I felt like I was slowing in the second half as it was warmer, and just the general fatigue of the marathon," Batt-Doyle said.

"It was quite warm and we knew going into this week that it was going to be a bit warmer than ideal marathon conditions, but we did what we could do to prepare for that.

"That's hydrating a lot beforehand, and every opportunity that there were water cups I was splashing three or four water cups to keep cool."

But Batt-Doyle didn't fade in the conditions, with her quickest 5km split of 16:36 coming between 35km and 40km. She covered the last 2.2km at about 3:14 per kilometre, when she started to sense the record was hers.

"There is a small hill about 400 to go, and then you turn into the last 150 metres, and I saw the clock and that's when I really started celebrating," she said.

"It was quite emotional. You can think you can do it and hope you can do it, and be on pace to do it, but there is so much that can happen in the last 5 kilometres, or last 1 kilometre or even the last 400 metres.

" People can cramp and have all sorts of things happen. I feel you can't really celebrate or have that sense of finish line relief until you actually get there. "

Batt-Doyle said she was proud to join the list of previous Australian record-holders that included Stenson, Sinead Diver and Benita Willis.

"I think it's really validating for the hard work I've put in and it feels really special to be part of history, because there have been some fantastic runners before me, and fantastic runners to come," she said.

"I really feel honoured, that sums it up. To be in that class of athletes. I'm really proud of that."

Kenya's Amos Kipruto won the men's race in 2:01:09.

World.title: Time the enemy for Aussies in first Test after Smith's day in Durban
World.content:
What is it that separates the best cricket teams from the merely good ones? There were hints sprinkled throughout an absorbing day three of the Durban Test, in which Australia's most formidable obstacle on the path to victory is now time.

All the fundamentals Australia had to get right with the ball today, it did: tight lines, safe hands, bowling in partnerships to coherent plans. In the face of this, South Africa simply lost its head.

The Proteas scraped together a first innings total of 284 — a 106-run deficit that Nic Maddinson and Travis Head extended to 139 by the time bad light prematurely stopped play for the third day running.

Renshaw resurrects Aussies, Test career in Durban With his epic 190 in Durban, Matt Renshaw not only changes the game, but shows he is capable of the real Test batting the Australian cricketing public is longing for.

But the moment of brilliance that highlighted Australia's edge in this context came not from a bowler or batter, but in the field: Steve Smith leapt like a salmon for four highlight-reel catches that moved him to the top of the all-time list for Test catches, and one in particular will linger in the memory long after this game is done and dusted.

It was Smith's third catch of the day, aptly reviewed by his most vocal teammate: "Oh my God, Smudge," bellowed a disbelieving Marnus Labuschagne. For that one, Smith seemed to have a better idea of the flight path of Kyle Verreynne's reverse sweep of Nathan Lyon than the batsman did.

Darting to his right from the standard slip position while the batsman was still constructing his shot, Smith then dived at full stretch to reel in the catch, like a security guard nabbing a shoplifter before he'd even fully grasped his loot.

The English cricket writer John Arlott once settled on a similar scenario as an exemplar of what makes Australian cricketers a different breed. It was a catch taken by Sid Barnes in a tour match during the 1948 Invincibles summer.

Like Smith, Barnes was something of an eccentric. On this particular day, he was going to field a bat-length away from Essex batsman Ray Smith at silly mid-on. "You can't drive me away," Barnes warned the batsman, but Smith gave it a go, thumping a drive so crisply it ricocheted off Barnes's boot and out to the boundary.

When a silent Barnes refused to budge, Smith tried it again, crunching an even lustier blow directly into the Australian's chest, whereupon an unflinching Barnes stuck out his hand, caught the deflection and repeated himself to the dismissed batsman: "You can't drive me away."

Arlott dubbed this attitude "Australianism". Steve Smith has it in spades. It was not just the sheer absurdity of the Verreynne catch, nor the skill it required, but the domineering attitude Smith was projecting: you shall not pass.

Otherwise, it was Australia's bowlers and their captain's efficient organisation of them that told the story of the day.

Where Temba Bavuma had let things slide for the home team on day two, Pat Cummins was a model of enterprise, rotating his attack as the circumstances demanded while bowling with tremendous vigour and skill himself to take three wickets.

The disappointment, as far as the hope of a more even contest goes, rests on the shoulders of South Africa's top order, which had teased early in the day. An 84-run second-wicket partnership between World Test Championship final hero Aiden Markram and the stylish number three David Bedingham was hurtling along at four an over and at that point, the game looked like a genuine contest.

Aiden Markram looked set for an important innings for South Africa before Mitchell Starc sent him back to the pavilion on day three. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Gerhard Duraan)

As is so often the case, up stepped Mitchell Starc to take the initiative. The left-armer came around the wicket, pulled back his length and roughed up the batsmen with a nasty blow to the hands for both. Soon after, Markram was gone. Later, like clockwork, Starc returned to nip another 50-run partnership in the bud.

And as has usually been the case in Australia's recent run of 13 wins in 16 Tests, each of the frontline bowlers posed his own unique problems for the Proteas. Cummins attacked the off-stump relentlessly. Josh Hazlewood sat in cruise control, slightly back of a length, impossible to get hold of for long.

Unlike the local spinners, who'd been paddled and swept into submission by Matt Renshaw, Nathan Lyon was at his jagged, probing best and deserved more than his two wickets.

"Bavuma — caught Smith bowled Lyon 3 (26)" doesn't read too dramatically, but the Proteas skipper was subjected to a genuine ordeal before finally losing the plot and departing the same way as Verreynne.

There lay another telling difference between these two sides so far: whereas Australia's imposing total was, in the end, built on discipline and patient accumulation, the South Africans constantly lost the micro-battles.

Bedingham, who made a sparkling 49, was denied scoring shots for a frustrating 20-minute period before finally losing his patience. Trying to move things along when there was no need, Travis Stubbs and Wiaan Mulder squandered starts with similarly impetuous shots.

From South Africa's perspective, what was so deflating about the general approach of the top six was that bad light had already truncated this game significantly and was likely to continue to do so. The tail battled gamely, but it's unlikely it'll be enough this time around.

The remaining questions are how quickly Australia can get to a defendable total and how many overs it reasonably expects to be played. Advantage Australia, in other words.

World.title: Key moments that won Bathurst for DJR and left another team in tears
World.content:
The faces of Brodie Kostecki and Todd Hazelwood as they stood atop their Ford Mustang at Mount Panorama said it all — stunned.

The Dick Johnson Racing (DJR) duo had the 2026 Bathurst 1000 at their mercy, then one bad pit stop seemingly ended all hope.

However, Kostecki proved why he is one of the great Supercar drivers, not just of his generation, but ever, and the motorsport gods smiled down on DJR in a wild and chaotic finish.

Here are the major moments from a drama-filled final 36 laps that decided the Bathurst 1000.

Lap 125: Slow pit stop sinks Kostecki from first to fifth

Through 125 laps of the Great Race, the number 17 was outstanding.

Starting second on the grid, Kostecki and Hazelwood drove a near-flawless race to establish a healthy lead with 36 laps to go.

That is when the DJR team called in Kostecki for what would be his second-to-last stop for the race — and disaster struck.

The team elected to change brakes, which had been an issue across many teams due to the warm temperatures and relentless pace of the race at Mount Panorama.

But there was an issue changing the brakes on the front-right of the car.

The number 17 car should have come out of the pits and retained the lead of the race.

However, Kostecki drove his Mustang back onto the mountain in fifth position, with the leads out of sight, out of reach, and the win seemingly out of the question.

Lap 139–140: Team 18 plays its ace as De Pasquale pits

As lap after lap of green flag racing passed, the race appeared to be a battle between Zach Bates (Matt Stone Racing, number 10) and Anton De Pasquale (Team 18, number 18).

Bates, the 22-year-old Supercars rookie who claimed pole with a stunning lap in Saturday's Top 10 Shootout, had his lead slashed by a charging De Pasquale as they approached the final pit stop phase.

Bates had tyres that were 10 laps older, and he was also much lower on fuel than De Pasquale. Despite this, Team 18 pulled De Pasquale into the pits just as he caught the back of Bates's Chevrolet.

It looked to be a masterstroke.

Rather than waiting for its fuel load to run out, Team 18 was going to perform the undercut and not give Bates the chance to pit first and drive on fresh rubber while De Pasquale was racing on older tyres.

Matt Stone Racing had no choice but to pit on the next lap. Knowing they were going to be stationary for longer than De Pasquale because they needed more fuel, the team could not afford to let Bates run any longer on old tyres.

In all, Bates was stationary for 15 seconds longer than De Pasquale for their final pit stop.

De Pasquale was clear, and Bates would need to make up that time in 21 laps to complete the most unlikely of comebacks.

Lap 155: Leader De Pasquale told to 'maximum fuel save'

Anton De Pasquale was told he needed to save fuel in the final laps. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

The crew at Team 18 was glued to the monitors. Anton De Pasquale had a big lead in the Bathurst 1000, and the chequered flag was getting closer.

But Bates was eating into the gap.

What was a 15-second advantage was reduced to 12, then 10, then eight, then seven seconds.

Was Bates finding extra pace in his car? Was De Pasquale just taking it easy and not taking unnecessary risk?

But then there was a far more critical question that needed to be asked: Does De Pasquale have enough fuel in the car?

We got our answer when De Pasquale started to ease off the throttle at the end of the long straights.

Then car 18's race engineer, Andrew Donnelly, came on the radio and told De Pasquale he needed to "maximum fuel save".

Bates and the number 10 car were back in the race.

Lap 156: The first and only safety car comes on track

It looked certain that the 2026 edition of the Bathurst 1000 was going to go without a safety car, until Chaz Mostert slammed into the wall at Forrest's Elbow.

The reigning Supercar champion was out of the race, and the safety car was called — setting a new record for the longest time ever taken for the first safety car in the Bathurst 1000.

De Pasquale was leading, but now he had Bates on his rear wing, and the charging Kostecki in third place.

De Pasquale also had a major issue: he didn't have enough fuel in his car.

There was hope for the Team 18 crew that the two laps behind the safety car might be enough to help them save enough fuel.

Lap 159: Kostecki passes Bates, De Pasquale puts the foot down

When the safety car rolled back into the pits, there would be a three-lap sprint for Bathurst glory.

De Pasquale set off and got a brilliant getaway. He put a nice gap between himself and Bates, with the latter under threat from a flying Kostecki.

As they approached the final corner of lap 159, Kostecki struck.

He dived up the inside of Bates, forced the 22-year-old wide, and took second place.

Now Kostecki was the man who was going to chase a fuel-saving De Pasquale.

Meanwhile, Bates's woes continued as he was out of position following Kostecki's overtake, and vulnerable to Brown making a move of his own.

In the blink of an eye, Bates went from second to fourth, and his chances of winning were over.

Lap 161: Team 18 left in tears as De Pasquale's car runs out of fuel

One lap to go. That is all the number 18 car had to do.

De Pasquale, co-driver Lee Holdsworth and the entire Team 18 crew were praying there was enough fuel in the tank.

Glory was there — and then it wasn't.

De Pasquale's Chevrolet ran out of fuel, and Team 18 was left devastated.

Crew members could be seen in tears. Holdsworth was shell-shocked as he bravely stood for an interview just moments after his dream turned into a nightmare.

In the neighbouring garage, the roars could be heard by the fans at the top of the mountain.

After throwing away the win with a poor pit stop on lap 125, Brodie Kostecki charged his way back through the field, took advantage of others' misfortune, and took the lead of the Bathurst 1000 with 22 corners remaining.

"Like I've always said, the mountain chooses the winner," Kostecki said after winning.

Mount Panorama chose Kostecki and Hazelwood on Sunday, but made sure they worked very hard for it.

World.title: Piastri suffers tyre puncture, Verstappen roars to Singapore F1 win
World.content:
Oscar Piastri has battled to a hard-fought fifth place at the Singapore Grand Prix, helping his McLaren team salvage some pride and useful championship points from an otherwise frustrating weekend at the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

Australian star Piastri finished one place behind teammate Lando Norris, just outside the podium spots.

But the result can be judged a positive outcome, a day after both McLaren drivers received a public dressing down from team chiefs for a collision between them on the final lap of Saturday's sprint race.

Meanwhile, once Norris knew he had lost out for the final podium slot, McLaren's reigning world champion offered to ease up and help teammate Piastri as he tried to pass Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton in the final laps.

But 25-year-old Melburnian Piastri, despite suffering bad luck when forced to pit a second time thanks to a slow puncture, still had the composure to do it his own way, overtaking seven-time champion Hamilton on the final lap.

"The puncture was a shame, but I think fifth place was the maximum we could have done today," Piastri said.

"We didn't quite have the pace to challenge the Red Bull and the Ferraris, although being able to get that final position from Lewis made it worthwhile. It was a reasonable chunk of points for the team."

The weekend, however, belonged to Red Bull flyer Max Verstappen, who roared home to victory on his 250th grand prix start, capping a remarkable 24 hours in which the four-time world champ also banked two pole positions and a classy victory in the sprint race.

Starting from his 50th career pole place, it was the Dutchman's second straight victory after winning the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia last weekend, and leaves him fourth in the championship standings.

Verstappen's triumph means Red Bull is now seven points behind constructors' champion McLaren in the battle for third place.

"It's taken a while but I think this race was very good. We had pace when we needed to have it on the soft tyre, even though I think the medium tyre for everyone was more of ⁠a struggle," Verstappen said.

"But it worked ‌out, ​so of course very happy to win here … The last two races have ​been really positive ‌for us and it's just great to see."

Ferrari's Charles ‌Leclerc finished second and Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli ​was ​third, extending his ‌championship lead over teammate George Russell to 102 points and knowing he can mathematically win his maiden title in the next round in Austin, Texas from October 23-25.

"Can ‌I? Really?" the 20-year-old Italian said when he was ⁠told the news after his 14th podium of the season.

"Well, let's not worry about that. Let's try to do the best ​weekend as possible and finish the job."

AAP

World.title: Quick hits: Smith snatches record with miracle grabs and Marnus fumes
World.content:
Steve Smith takes a hat-trick of spectacular slip catches, while Marnus Labuschagne is livid to see his effort chalked off.

Here are the quick hits from day three of the first Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. Smith's stunners snatch Root's record

We are lucky enough to bear witness to two of the greatest Test batters at the same time, but in Joe Root and Steve Smith we also have the two most prolific fielders of all time, with Smith pulling ahead on day three in Durban with three brilliant slip catches.

The first was a lovely piece of anticipation when Temba Bavuma reverse swept off spinner Nathan Lyon, and Smith saw it coming early, moved rapidly at first slip and snaffled a sharp chance right in front of his face.

That tied Root with 220 Test snares, but he surpassed England's captain with perhaps a better catch three overs later, when he held a diving chance above his head and in front of Matt Renshaw at first slip.

Remarkably, he improved on both of them with his third, once again moving early when he saw Kyle Verreynne shaping to reverse sweep and this time forced to stick just one hand out to take a brilliant reflex catch.

Smith has taken his 222 grabs in just 126 matches compared to Root's 220 in 169, and the Aussie has a chance to pull away further with 12 more Tests between Durban and the start of next year's Ashes, while England has just five on the horizon.

2. Marnus livid with the third umpire

It was certainly a morning for slip catching in Durban.

In the final over before the lunch break, Marnus Labuschagne did his best Smith impression in taking a fine low grab to dismiss Wiaan Mulder off the bowling of Lyon.

Mulder's thick edge dropped sharply and Labuschagne did exceptionally well to get both hands between ball and turf.

It appeared he had, anyway.

With Mulder already halfway to the sheds, the third umpire was asked to check if it was a fair grab.

After a significant delay and a plethora of freeze frames, it was concluded there was ball touching grass as Labuschagne took the catch.

The technology showed the ball had made contact with grass as Labuschagne stooped to take the catch. (Fox Cricket)

Judging by the look on his face, it's safe to say the Queenslander wasn't in agreement.

Labuschagne was clearly uninpressed with the third umpire's decision. (Fox Cricket)

3. Starc finds his feet after pitch maintenance

Starc called for some assistance from the Kingsmead ground staff early on day three. (Fox Cricket)

More than perhaps any Test bowler in the world, Mitch Starc likes to feel level ground under his feet.

Given the explosiveness and athleticism of his bowling action, that's understandable — even a little divot at the bowling crease could spell disaster for the 36-year-old.

And it wasn't long before Starc called for the mallet on day three, with a member of the Kingsmead ground staff frantically hammering the Australian's area of concern at the top of the wicket.

At first, it looked like the adjustments had done absolutely nothing for the left-hander, with the fluent David Bedingham peeling off three consecutive boundaries straight away.

But Starc had well and truly found his feet in his very next over, nicking off the dangerous Aiden Markram to claim a vital early scalp for the Aussies.

4. Stubbs falls into the trap

With South Africa's top order all back in the shed, the Proteas were in need of a player to stand tall in the same way Matt Renshaw had done for the Australians.

Could the precociously talented Tristan Stubbs, having made his way into the 30s, be that man?

No.

With Cummins having already sent two men out behind square on the leg-side boundary for an obvious short-ball barrage, the Australian captain proceeded to put a fielder deep on the other side of the wicket as well.

Cummins drew attention to the off-side red herring with a length ball outside off, before firing down a bouncer that Stubbs couldn't help but take on.

Sure enough, Stubbs's top edge was gobbled up by Josh Hazlewood at deep-backward square leg.

South Africa was 6-162 and quickly running out of candidates to play the Renshaw role.

5. Maddinson's six ends the day

With South Africa eventually bowled out for 284 late in the day, the Australian openers faced a tricky little period as the Durban skies began to darken.

But after a historic 33-ball duck in the first innings, Nic Maddinson had just one thing on his mind: to get off the mark, and to get off the mark quickly.

He did so straight away, standing up to Marco Jansen's opening ball and hooking it to the boundary.

Having finally scored his first Test runs in a decade, you could almost feel the weight lifting from his shoulders.

Maddinson continued the over in similarly adventurous fashion, finishing the set with another commanding boundary, this time through backward point.

And the Aussie wasn't done there, proceeding to flick Wiaan Mulder for six on his way to reaching stumps on 17 from 19 deliveries.

That final boundary signalled another premature stumps due to bad light, with boundary fielder Ryan Rickelton completely losing the ball against the gloomy Durban skies.

World.title: Georgia Voll smashes quickfire ton as Aussies wrap up Bangladesh series
World.content:
Opener Georgia Voll has smashed her third ODI century in just her 15th match to secure Australia a comfortable nine-wicket win over Bangladesh and a series victory.

Earlier, Bangladesh centurion Sobhana Mostary played one of the great ODI knocks to lift the visitors to 6-220 as records tumbled at Brisbane's Allan Border Field.

Mostary, 24, made a magnificent 118 off 134 deliveries and with her captain Nigar Sultana (74no off 114) added 195 for the fourth wicket — the highest partnership against Australia in women's ODI history.

But making a mockery of the run chase, Voll and Phoebe Litchfield added 162 off just 119 deliveries in an opening stand that combined brute strength and creativity to the maximum, setting Australia up for an unassailable 2-0 lead in the series.

Litchfield (70 off 51) played strokes all around the ground in her entertaining knock while Voll's power game came to the fore as she bludgeoned anything loose.

Voll's unbeaten 131 off 97 deliveries became the highest individual women's ODI score at the venue, breaking a record Mostary had equalled only hours earlier.

The player of the match's strong bottom hand came to the fore and she was also dominant through cover when given width as Australia coasted to victory in 28.1 overs.

Voll, 23, became the first woman to score two ODI centuries at AB Field after making 101 against India at the venue in 2024.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

Mostary and Sultana's stand was the largest for any Bangladesh wicket in women's ODIs and was the foundation of the team's highest total against Australia.

It was not enough to challenge Australia but it was achieved with immaculate stroke play, tactical nous and plenty of courage.

The two Bangladesh heroes came together with their side desperate at 3-8 in the eighth over and embarked on their rescue mission with class.

Mostary brought up her fifty with a cut shot off leg spinner Alana King after driving her through cover with panache to the fence.

She earlier struck three exquisite boundaries through the offside in leggie Georgia Wareham's first over.

Litchfield fireworks help Australia to ODI victory over Bangladesh A quickfire half-century to Phoebe Litchfield has helped Australia to a commanding seven-wicket victory over Bangladesh in their first ODI in Brisbane.

Mostary now holds the record for the highest all-time score by a No.5 against Australia in women's ODI history, and the best by a Bangladesh batter.

Sultana was strong off her legs, with two immaculate flicks to the fence with perfect balance a highlight. She played the perfect foil to Mostary.

Australia quick Megan Schutt (4-36) was the pick of the bowlers, including ending Mostary's epic knock when she struck her leg stump.

Veteran Bangladesh opener Fargana Hoque (0) has faced two deliveries from Schutt in this series and lost her wicket both times.

Fellow opener Sarmin Sultana (five) was trapped in front after quick-thinking wicketkeeper Beth Mooney called for DRS when bowler Kim Garth was unsure.

An inswinging yorker by Schutt accounted for Sharmin Akhter (0) and the visitors were in all sorts in the eighth over.

Australia sent Bangladesh in for the second time in the ODI series as they believed rain may have impacted the run chase.

Both sides were unchanged from Friday's opening match of the three-match series, which Australia won by seven wickets.

AAP

World.title: Roos get past Dockers as Blues and Hawks taste victory
World.content:
Ash Riddell and Jasmine Garner have delivered a devastating one-two punch as North Melbourne recovered from an early scare to post a 28-point win over Fremantle at Arden Street.

In this afternoon's other AFLW matches, Nell Morris-Dalton kicked a career-high four goals to lift Carlton to a 27-point win over Sydney, while Hawthorn defeated Brisbane by 25 points.

Against the Kangaroos, the Dockers looked set to cause an almighty upset after kicking three straight goals to take a one-point lead during the second quarter.

But with Riddell and Garner in top form, the Kangaroos turned on the afterburners to kick six goals to one, sealing a 9.4 (58) to 4.6 (30) win.

Riddell finished with 38 disposals, four clearances and a goal.

Suns continue to shine in AFLW Gold Coast Suns continue their run as the surprise packets of the AFLW season, consolidating their top-four spot with a victory over Melbourne.

Garner was also destructive with 33 disposals, four clearances and a goal.

Kiara Bowers battled hard for Fremantle on the way to 31 disposals and eight clearances, with Aisling McCarthy (26 disposals) providing support.

The result ensures the Kangaroos finish the round on top of the ladder, while Fremantle slipped out of the top eight.

Fifth-placed Carlton is just 1.7 per cent adrift of fourth-placed Gold Coast after defeating Sydney 8.11 (59) to 4.8 (32) at Henson Park.

Morris-Dalton was the star of the show with 4.1, while Darcy Vescio kicked two goals.

The Blues will sweat on the availability of skipper Abbie McKay, who limped off with an ankle injury in the second half.

Brisbane's Jade Ellenger (left) attempts to get a disposal away while being tackled by Mackenzie Eardley. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

In Melbourne, out-of-form Brisbane threatened to pull off an upset against Hawthorn after taking a two-goal lead into quarter-time.

But the Hawks turned the match with a five-goals-to-nil second term to set up the 9.11 (65) to 6.4 (40) win.

Aine McDonagh kicked three goals from 20 disposals for Hawthorn in a powerful display.

Former Lion Kaitlyn Ashmore celebrated her 100th AFLW match with a stunning set-shot from the boundary-line pocket in the second quarter.

The victory moved Hawthorn into eighth spot, while the Lions are out of the finals equation.

AAP
